The first stop, at 15 Blair Avenue, offered a glimpse of a home just coming to market. Built in 1911 and lovingly held by the same family for 60 years, the four-bedroom home had been carefully refreshed. The Map of last week’s walk walkers were welcomed inside, where cool water and donut holes proved as popular as the updated interiors. From there, the group climbed and wandered through a series of homes that showcased the range of Piedmont architecture and pricing. A Craftsman on Bonita Avenue, built in 1896, had already attracted 15 offers in just two weeks and was heading pending, likely well above its list price. On Waldo Avenue, a recently sold home illustrated the competitive nature of the market, closing significantly over asking. Each stop brought its own story, historic details, thoughtful renovations, and the occasional reminder that location, such as proximity to a busy street, still matters. The tour’s grand finale came on Monte Avenue, where three homes in close proximity offered a kind of real estate trifecta, from classic brown shingle to stately Italianate. One home had yet to officially hit the market, but word had already spread among those in the know, including the walkers. After about 90 minutes and eight homes, the group made its way back toward the Exedra, a bit warmer, a bit wiser, and perhaps quietly calculating what their own homes might fetch. It was a hot morning, but as more than one walker observed, not nearly as hot as the Piedmont real estate market. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. articles.text: Last month Duckhorn Vineyards celebrated their 50th anniversary by hosting a vertical tasting of their wines at the Paraduxx facility in Napa Valley. The tasting began with five vintages of the three Palms Merlot spanning from 1986 to 2014. All wines were alive and in great shape. The older vintages had taken on earthy, leathery Bordeaux-like complexity. My favorite was the 2014 that had beautiful cherry, raspberry fruit, opulent mouthfeel and soft supple tannins on the finish. It has at least 20 years to go. The tasting also included two Merlots and three Cabernet Sauvignons from the 2014 vintage. All were outstanding but the standout was the 2014 Rector Creek Merlot. Enormously complex with eucalyptus and menthol notes, medium body and a lush fruit-filled finish. Few wineries have had as profound an impact on modern Napa Valley as Duckhorn Vineyards, a producer whose history mirrors the rise of California wine itself. Founded in 1976 by Dan and Margaret Duckhorn, the winery began with a clear and unconventional vision: to champion Merlot at a time when Cabernet Sauvignon dominated Napa Valley. From its earliest vintages, Duckhorn demonstrated that Merlot could achieve the same depth, structure, and age-worthiness as Napa’s more established varietals. The winery’s first releases in 1980, sourced from top sites such as Three Palms Vineyard, quickly gained attention and helped redefine Merlot’s reputation in the United States. Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, Duckhorn expanded its vineyard holdings and influence, becoming a cornerstone of Napa Valley’s collaborative wine culture. The founders played active roles in organizations such as Napa Valley Vintners and the Wine Institute, helping to shape standards of quality and stewardship that continue to guide the industry today. The winery’s evolution accelerated in the 21st century. Investment partnerships beginning in 2007 enabled Duckhorn to grow into a broader portfolio of luxury wine brands, including Goldeneye, Paraduxx, and Decoy. GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2026 GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2026 Twenty wine writers and industry professionals attended the Duckhorn Vertical tasting. The Duckhorn Three Palms Merlot vertical tasting included their wines from 1986 to 2014. a family startup into a major force in American wine. More recently, in 2024, the Duckhorn Portfolio was acquired by private equity firm Butterfly Equity, marking a new chapter of ownership while maintaining its Napa Valley roots. In 2026, Duckhorn Vineyards celebrates its 50th anniversary, a milestone that highlights not only longevity but continued relevance in a rapidly changing wine landscape. The winery has marked the occasion with a yearlong celebration, including a “50 Stories” initiative that documents the people, vineyards, and philosophies that have defined its legacy. The anniversary serves as both reflection and renewal, underscoring Duckhorn’s role in shaping modern Napa Valley and elevating Merlot to global prominence. Today, Duckhorn remains synonymous with elegance, balance, and varietal expression. Its flagship wines, particularly the famed Three Palms Vineyard Merlot, continue to earn critical acclaim, while its broader portfolio reflects a commitment to innovation and terroir. After five decades, Duckhorn Vineyards stands as both a pioneer and a standard-bearer— proof that vision, persistence, and a willingness to challenge convention can transform not only a winery, but an entire category of wine. Dan Duckhorn who was alive on the day of the 50th Anniversary celebration died a few weeks later at his home in Napa. He was 87 years old. We lift a glass in grateful thanks to him. Following the vertical tasting, lunch was served outdoors on the patio on a glorious sunny Napa Valley day. The following wines were the current releases that were poured. • 2023 Duckhorn Huichica Hills Chardonnay, $64 The wine offers and intense and elegant bouquet of ripe fruits and lemon rind intertwined with fine oak aromas. This full-bodied wine is round and rich but elegant on the palate, driven by mineral freshness and balanced with texture. This well-made Chardonnay should have wide appeal and go with a wide variety of foods. • 2023 Duckhorn Oakville Cabernet Sauvignon, $80 Dark ruby red in color the wine shows mixed currants and cherries on the nose, joined by hints of dark chocolate, while the palate is medium to full-bodied, rich, expansive and velvety with a lingering mouthwatering finish. • 2023 Duckhorn Rutherford Cabernet Sauvignon, $80 The Rutherford Cab reveals vibrant cassis, plum and raspberries notes with hints of soil and cedar. Medium-bodied, with plenty of lively black and red fruits, it has a firm frame of ripe, tannins and a long, youthful finish. • 2019 Duckhorn “The Discussion” Red Blend, $200 Their flagship wine is made from 67% Cabernet Sauvignon, 31% Merlot and a splash of Malbec and Cab Franc. An enchanting nose of blackberry fruit and vanilla oak jumps from the glass. In the mouth it is full and round with gigantic body. It shows layers of complex berry fruit and earth with leather and spice. Drinking beautifully now this wine is built to last another two decades. articles.text: Attendance more than doubled, from 70 people last year to 150 this year, giving families a clearer look at how decisions are made. Manalo-LeClair brings a personalized approach to counseling from MHS to the larger PHS community. “I really enjoyed having oneon-one time with students. It made me feel grounded in the work that I do, to actually connect. I feel like that’s really what my job was and has been; it is about making connections and building relationships,” she said. When questions about college and careers begin to pile up, Ms. M.L. often brings students back to the present. “What can we do now, and how can we build on that later?” she asks her students. Manalo-LeClair emphasizes fit over rankings when guiding students through college choices. “Students say ‘I want to go a good school,’ and I tell them, it’s a good school if it has what you’re looking for, that’s a good school. It’s not because of the way it’s ranked. It’s because of what you’re going to get out of it, what you’re going to do,” she said. She is also helping students navigate a rapidly changing admissions landscape. While SAT scores faded in importance during the pandemic, she says some schools, particularly on the East Coast, are bringing them back into consideration. Most California liberal arts colleges still do not factor SAT scores into admissions, except in some STEM cases or for course placement. “Even a student who might be on the fence about applying to schools that require [the SAT] I say, if you can prepare for it, take it. That way you don’t close any doors.” The month wraps with the March 31 “Future-Ready” panel, where four local experts, including Marco Casalaina from Microsoft and Abby Scott from UC Berkeley Haas, will discuss how AI is influencing college majors and career paths. “[We] are hearing concerns about the future of work, especially with increased use of AI, geopolitical issues in the news, and an overall uncertainty of what the future may hold. Students don’t know what to expect with so many changes in the world, so we wanted to invite some experts in a range of fields to share their insights on how to view these changes and how they might prepare,” said event moderator and PPN Co-President Ironside. As acceptance letters arrive throughout March, Piedmont students have a steady guide in Manalo-LeClair, ready to help them navigate the decisions ahead. pages.text: Wednesday, March 25, 2026 29 Manalo-LeClair Continued from page 1 Attendance more than doubled, from 70 people last year to 150 this year, giving families a clearer look at how decisions are made. Manalo-LeClair brings a personalized approach to counseling from MHS to the larger PHS community. “I really enjoyed having oneon-one time with students. It made me feel grounded in the work that I do, to actually connect. I feel like that’s really what my job was and has been; it is about making connections and building relationships,” she said. When questions about college and careers begin to pile up, Ms. M.L. often brings students back to the present. “What can we do now, and how can we build on that later?” she asks her students. Manalo-LeClair emphasizes fit over rankings when guiding students through college choices. “Students say ‘I want to go a good school,’ and I tell them, it’s a good school if it has what you’re looking for, that’s a good school. It’s not because of the way it’s ranked. It’s because of what you’re going to get out of it, what you’re going to do,” she said. She is also helping students navigate a rapidly changing admissions landscape. While SAT scores faded in importance during the pandemic, she says some schools, particularly on the East Coast, are bringing them back into consideration. Most California liberal arts colleges still do not factor SAT scores into admissions, except in some STEM cases or for course placement. “Even a student who might be on the fence about applying to schools that require [the SAT] I say, if you can prepare for it, take it. That way you don’t close any doors.” The month wraps with the March 31 “Future-Ready” panel, where four local experts, including Marco Casalaina from Microsoft and Abby Scott from UC Berkeley Haas, will discuss how AI is influencing college majors and career paths. “[We] are hearing concerns about the future of work, especially with increased use of AI, geopolitical issues in the news, and an overall uncertainty of what the future may hold. Students don’t know what to expect with so many changes in the world, so we wanted to invite some experts in a range of fields to share their insights on how to view these changes and how they might prepare,” said event moderator and PPN Co-President Ironside. As acceptance letters arrive throughout March, Piedmont students have a steady guide in Manalo-LeClair, ready to help them navigate the decisions ahead. purpose, and support adjustments as needs and opportunities change. Unlike most services at Piedmont Church, Maundy Thursday worship takes place at 6pm in Guild Hall during a family-friendly dinner called an Agape Meal (pronounced uh-gah-pay). Agape is a Greek word which means unconditional, sacrificial and selfless love. The meal will conclude with Communion. The cost is $20 for adults, $10 for children. Scan the QR code in the photo to register no later than Wednesday, April 1, 5pm. Good Friday, April 3, is observed with a traditional service of Tenebrae, the Latin word for “darkness”. The service begins at 7:30pm in the sanctuary. This is a dramatic and moving ritual. As the story of Jesus’ path to death on a cross is read out loud, candles and lights are gradually extinguished, until the entire Sanctuary is in darkness, except for one candle. At the conclusion of the service, everyone departs in silence. Easter Sunday services, celebrating the joyous resurrection of Jesus three days after his crucifixion, will be held Sunday, April 5 at 8:30 and 10am. There will be a beautiful display of Easter lilies in the Sanctuary. The services are identical and include liturgy, a sermon by Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted and special music provided by Dr. Stephen Main and the Chancel Choir. The 10am service will also be live streamed on our website at PiedmontChurch.org. You are most welcome to participate in any or all of these events. Maundy Thursday worship takes place at 6pm in Guild Hall during a family-friendly dinner called an Agape Meal. Holy Week is the most important week in Christianity. It begins on Palm Sunday, March 29 this year, and concludes on Easter Sunday, April 5. Observances in preparation for Easter include Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday and Good Friday. Palm Sunday, March 29, commemorates the triumphant entry of Jesus into Jerusalem, riding on a donkey and fulfilling an Old Testament prophecy about the Messiah. People spread palm branches on the ground to welcome him. At the 10am service, our young children will process around the Sanctuary holding palm branches. A group of our middle school students will be confirmed into membership in the church concluding several weeks of learning, discussion, writing, reflection and prayer. Maundy Thursday worship takes place at 6pm in Guild Hall during a family-friendly dinner called an Agape Meal. Holy Week is the most important week in Christianity. It begins on Palm Sunday, March 29 this year, and concludes on Easter Sunday, April 5. Observances in preparation for Easter include Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday and Good Friday. Palm Sunday, March 29, commemorates the triumphant entry of Jesus into Jerusalem, riding on a donkey and fulfilling an Old Testament prophecy about the Messiah. Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen speaking on behalf of the City Council and Community to thank Hendry for his service I will forever be grateful for the steady hand you’ve provided over the years.” “I speak for myself, and also on behalf of the Council, and the entire community, when I say thank you, Robb, truly. For 23 years, you have shown up for us on our worst days, in times of high stress and high stakes. And every time you have shown up ready to meet the challenge, not only with professional skills and training you possess, but with your thoughtful compassion and steadfast resolve,” said Mayor Andersen. Before his career as a firefighter, Hendry attended paramedic school and worked as a paramedic. Through his studies and work, he realized he was especially good under pressure. He had a unique ability to focus and stay calm under any condition. He believed the next logical step for him was to join the fire service. Hendry joined PFD in 2003 as part of a large class of seven recruits. He is known throughout the department for his calm, focused demeanor and his commitment to exceptional patient care in every situation. “I’d like people to remember that I was honest and genuine, and I just tried to be the best version of myself that I could be,” said Hendry. Hendry intends to live the next chapter of his life like his dog. “There’s a saying: ‘Be like your dog.’ Because all your dog is doing is living in the present. My whole life has been chasing. This career is a life of jumping through hoops, uncertainty, and being on all the time. Now, I feel like I can finally be like my dog,” said Hendry. articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery is inviting the community to attend the 18th Annual Tulip Exhibition at the cemetery’s Tower Chapel, this Friday through Sunday, March 20-22, from 10 a.m. - 4 p.m. This free event welcomes Spring with floral arrangements by Bay Area florists, garden clubs, and students from a college floral design class. Photographers, florists, flower enthusiasts, and nature and art lovers are welcome. Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s annual tulip exhibit has become a cherished community tradition. Under the guidance of Special Events Coordinator Kristie Ly, this year is the exhibit’s third year back after a hiatus due to COVID-19 restrictions. “A must-see free event for all nature, plant, and floral enthusiasts alike,” said Ly. Following the exhibition, guests may enjoy a Pop-up Arts Show at J. Miller Flowers to celebrate its 56th year. The pop-up show will take place from 11 a.m. - 3 p.m. Mountain View Cemetery (5000 Piedmont Avenue) is a historic garden cemetery in the foothills of Oakland and Piedmont. One of the oldest cemeteries in the Western U.S., it has served the community since 1863 and even includes a section for Civil War soldiers. For more information on the cemetery or its annual tulip exhibition, visit www.mountainviewcemetery.org. articles.text: To the Editor, As announced in the Piedmont Post last week, the League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring a No Kings 3 rally in Piedmont Park on March 28 from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. This will be one of hundreds of No Kings 3 rallies taking place across the country. Millions of people are expected to attend nationally. Why have a rally in Piedmont when nearby rallies are available to attend? March 28 No Kings rally in Piedmont Park To the Editor, As announced in the Piedmont Post last week, the League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring a No Kings 3 rally in Piedmont Park on March 28 from 10 a.m. to 12 p.m. This will be one of hundreds of No Kings 3 rallies taking place across the country. Millions of people are expected to attend nationally. Why have a rally in Piedmont when nearby rallies are available to attend? First, it enables older people and people with disabilities to attend who otherwise might not be able to. Second, it encourages community camaraderie since it is likely to be attended mostly by Piedmont residents. And finally, we are hoping for substantial participation by students in the Piedmont schools and other young people. We believe this will be best facilitated by conducting the rally in Piedmont. Whatever our age, we have never experienced a threat to the democratic form of government in this country during our lifetime. We believe there is power in gathering people of all ages in protest. We aspire to have an attendance of at least 400 people. Why 400? Political scientists Erica Chenoweth and Maria Stephan analyzed data from hundreds of resistance campaigns and showed that 3.5% of the population actively participating in sustained, nonviolent resistance is enough to make major political change highly likely. For Piedmont, 3.5% represents approximately 400 people. The need to resist is now, given the rapid rate at which our federal government is moving us away from a democracy in which the Constitution provides the foundation for our legal system, and towards an autocracy in which a dictator, king, or queen has absolute power and makes all laws according to his or her whims. We are currently planning brief speeches and a few songs. After these activities, we will walk along Highland Avenue, many with signs showing their support of democracy and opposition to autocracy: NO MORE KINGS! We hope to see you at the rally. – Steve Sidney, MD on behalf of the League of Women Voters of Piedmont JON ESSNER, Monticello Avenue I love the overall tone of the Piedmont Post. articles.text: The City Council will review a proposed framework for soliciting and evaluating developers interested in building housing in the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan area and provide direction to staff on ranking criteria, review process, and other priorities at their regular meeting on Monday, March 16. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, adopted in October 2025, provides a vision and framework for the construction of 132 new homes on City-owned land along Moraga Avenue, including road safety improvements, design and landscaping standards, and wildfire safety requirements. The next step to implementing the Specific Plan is for the City to identify a developer to partner with. City staff is proposing to issue a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) for potential developers this spring. This would solicit detailed information on the financial capability and experience of interested firms, as well as their general conceptual plans for development. This approach aims to generate a large pool of well-qualified developers while maintaining local control and ensuring quality future development. A review committee consisting of both senior City staff and subject matter experts in relevant fields, such as real estate finance, housing development, land use planning, or architecture, would evaluate responses and make a recommendation to City Council. The City would then enter into an exclusive negotiating agreement with the selected firm. At Monday’s meeting, Council will review the proposed framework for the RFQ and provide direction to staff on ranking criteria, review committee membership, preferred approach to the transfer of City-owned land, and any other Council priorities. Presentation materials will be available on the project website after the meeting. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is available for download at piedmont.ca.gov/ MCSP.
articles.title: City Council considers framework for soliciting Moraga Canyon developers

articles.text: One-year-old Minnie is a sweet tuxedo cat with a sensitive heart and a playful spark, waiting for someone patient enough to notice the wonderful cat she’s becoming, and who can see that her trust is definitely worth earning. Minnie can be hesitant when approached (and even a little flinchy at first). But a gentle, thoughtful guardian will observe her curiosity peeking through—and she’ll blossom with a bit of steady encouragement. When she feels safe, she relaxes into soft pets and begins to play, showing off the bright, energetic spirit hiding behind her cautious start. This affectionate young cat often rubs up against her feline neighbors at Cat Town, hoping for friendship and looking to her confident peers for reassurance. She’ll thrive in a home with a cat buddy who can help show her that the world is a Adopt Minnie through Cat Town friendly place. Minnie would do best in a calm, indoor-only home with an adopter who appreciates the rewards of growing close with a timid cat. For someone willing to go at her pace, Minnie can be the kind of companion who helps make life truly sweet. She’s spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www.cattownoakland. org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org! articles.text: From 2020-2023, catalytic converter theft was a huge driver of crime in Piedmont and the region. In recent years, the regional enforcement has helped reduce the numbers, but it’s still a threat that any resident could encounter. The catalytic converter, or “cat,” is an emissions component, usually located on the belly of the car; exhaust flows into it before going to the muffler. A cat uses rare earth metals in a chemical reaction to convert nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and hydrocarbons into less hazardous substances such as carbon dioxide, water vapor, and nitrogen gas. The catalyst in your converter is typically made of palladium (Pd), rhodium (Rh), and platinum (Pt). These rare earth metals are what thieves are targeting. Although there are only a few grams of palladium and platinum, they can still fetch hundreds of dollars. Platinum has reached an all-time high in 2026 and is currently valued at $2,141/ounce. Palladium, although its value isn’t close to its all-time high in 2020 at $2750, has significantly recovered in 2026, rising to $1,639/ ounce, after a fall in 2023. With prices rising again, thieves are on the lookout to try to reignite their business. Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies sat down with the Post to discuss what the officers in the region are doing to prevent this type of theft and what residents can do to help protect their vehicles. “There was a regional focus on enforcement around the chop shops and fences that were receiving catalytic converters for their precious metals. Because there was a regional effort to get those individuals in custody, we saw a huge reduction in thefts,” said Chief Shavies. Chop shops are illegal criminal enterprises where stolen vehicles and parts are dismantled and sold to other enterprises around the country. Fences are places where you can take stolen goods and sell those goods to another individual engaged in a larger criminal enterprise. Chief Shavies offered some recommendations for residents to help prevent this type of theft. “Once the sun goes down, try to park in a well-lighted area or in your garage. Scribe the license plate number onto the frame of the converter or install a locking device.” Chief Shavies wants residents to rely on Piedmont’s police department rather than confronting a thief themselves. “The biggest thing I want folks to take away from this is that we are here to serve. Call us. What I don’t want is anyone running out of their home to confront an individual who’s under their car. Call the police. We will be there,” said Shavies. Residents concerned with this theft should speak with their insurance company to ensure they are covered in case this happens to them. Police Chief Shavies and Commander Marin Morris at the reopened police department.

articles.text: Toto is a 2-year-old, 64-pound gentle pittie mix with an adventurous spirit and a deeply affectionate nature. He’s a go-with-the-flow kind of dog who loves being with his people and exploring his world. Toto is energetic and enjoys long walks and hikes, but he also knows how to settle and relax once the day winds down with a long nap. His foster believes he would be great with kids and that he is wonderful on the leash and responds to recall. Toto knows sit, takes treats gently, and is very responsive and eager to please, making him an excellent candidate for continued training. He’s potty trained, comfortable in a crate, and has done well left alone for short periods. With other dogs, Toto is a gentle player. He’ll do best with a well-matched dog in the home, or as a solo pup with appropriate canine pals. He has shown polite curiosity There’s No Place Like Home for Toto around cats while on leash. Toto truly wants to be someone’s loyal companion. He will thrive in an active home that can include him in any outdoor adventures and offer love. To meet Toto, submit your adoption questionnaire online at the shelter’s website and you will be contacted by his foster to arrange a meet-andgreet. articles.text: Ella Rey Nash is a local musician born and raised in Piedmont, who dreams of one day headlining her own tour. She has decided to pursue her passion and put her all into making a dream a reality. Nash, who describes her music as indie pop, is currently releasing one song a month, with the most recent single out titled “Simple Life.” Her next single will be released on Friday, March 27, titled “2 a.m. in Texas.” She records with a producer in Oakland and San Francisco. A PHS grad in 2020, Ella has been heavily involved in music her entire life. Throughout high school, she’d been in Piedmont choirs, the acapella program, and multiple musical and dance performances. “I was very drawn to anything music from pretty early on, and was kind of always writing,” said Nash. During the COVID-19 lockdown, Nash had a lot of time on her hands, so she began to write. She became addicted to telling stories through songs. “I think the songwriting part of my brain really clicked into place for the first time. Up until then, I was always writing, but I never really finished any of my songs and didn’t take any of them too seriously,” Nash continued. “But during COVID, I realized I could write a song and finish it and keep doing that over and over. I think that was when I realized. ‘Okay, I could do this.’” Nash’s song “Simple Life” is the first release of a six-song rollout and highlights her ambition. It’s inspired by her idea of how society teaches us to pursue certain goals in our lives, and how Nash’s ambitions may not fit. She wants more. As an independent artist, Nash has to work extra hard to get her songs noticed. “It’s very overwhelming,” she said. “There’s a never-ending list of things I could always be doing at any given minute. You’re kind of just always feeling it out and putting out new music and seeing what sticks with people, and learning as you go.” Thankfully for Nash, she’s found a strong community in the Bay Area and in Piedmont that has supported her creative endeavors. She works with a local producer and still writes songs Nash performing on stage with her friends as she did in high school. As an independent artist, your best friend is social media. The biggest for musical discovery is the social media platform TikTok. According to the platform’s Year-End Music Report in 2024, 84% of the songs that reached Billboard’s Global 200 last year went viral first on TikTok. Nash has embraced this idea and is on her “posting grind.” “My mindset is, every time I post, I’m trying to get the video or the photo or whatever, in front of new people each time,” she added. “I feel like social media is kind of today’s version of being on the radio. To be a big deal is [when] your song is going viral as a TikTok sound.” Ella’s goal for music is to one day go on tour either as an opener for another musician or on her own. She’s also passionate about the idea of writing music for television or movies. “I got a lot of my inspiration from movies and TV, and I think it would be kind of a cool challenge to have to write for something more specific,” she mentioned. In the pursuit of her creative dreams, she hopes others can be The cover photo for Nash’s single “Simple Life” inspired by her goals and pursue their own dreams as well. “I tried for a long time, tried to convince myself that I didn’t want to pursue this, because I don’t think I believed in myself enough,” Nash continued. “Once I released my first song, I realized that there is no world where I’m happy if I don’t try and do this. I think you just really have to listen to your gut. No one is going to walk into your life and tell you, ‘Okay, it’s time to pursue your dream now.’ If you want it bad enough, you can make it happen.” Those interested in finding Nash’s music can find her on platforms such as Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube. Local musician Ella Rey Nash Nash in the studio recording a song.
articles.title: COMMUNITY PROFILE Piedmont vocalist in pursuit of her dreams

Superintendent Dear PUSD Families & Staff: In my recent State of the District report, I raised several questions regarding our use of technology for learning at all grade levels. Over the last year, I have been considering the many promises made about EdTech, especially in light of recent research on cell phone and device use, including work by Jonathan Haidt and Jared Horvath. Both question the impact of technology on our children. While we have a strong record of students who achieve academically and socially, we must re-examine our use of technology and how constant connectivity, both inside and outside the classroom, impacts the experience of our students. To address emerging questions, I have recommended a comprehensive technology audit of our technology use. Through my meetings with our teachers, staff, and parents, I appreciate just how complex the uses of technology have become across our district. The audit will examine our backend infrastructure, staffing, data analysis, and student screen time and purpose. The timing is particularly appropriate as we are currently revising our District Technology Plan. We are still defining the final scope to determine which components require an outside consultant and which will be handled internally, as an external audit may not fully capture the nuances of individual classroom instruction. Given the decade-long development of our current systems, decoupling technology from our learning environment cannot happen overnight. Any changes must be the result of a thoughtful, evidence-based analysis involving our entire school community. As a first step, we are bringing a contract for a professional technology audit firm to the Board for approval at the March 18th meeting. We look forward to collaborating with our staff and families to ensure our technology use their digital training manuals with every team in the land, ensuring that as they grew, they pulled the whole community up with them. Like the old names carried by their machines, their story feels legendary. But their real magic is simple: they make more people believe they belong. The FIRST Impact Award goes to Team 8033! Congratulations Team 8033!
articles.title: Superintendent Jennifer Hawn’s Piedmont Pulse

The FIRST Impact Award is presented to the team judged to have the most significant measurable impact of its partnerships among its participants and community over a sustained period, not just a single build season. The winner is able to demonstrate progress towards FIRST’s mission of transforming our culture. The recipient team will be invited to the District Championship where it will compete for the FIRST Impact Award against winners from other qualifying events and compete with their robot. Superintendent By Jennifer Hawn Dear PUSD Families & Staff: In my recent State of the District report, I raised several questions regarding our use of technology for learning at all grade levels. Over the last year, I have been considering the many promises made about EdTech, especially in light of recent research on cell phone and device use, including work by Jonathan Haidt and Jared Horvath. Both question the impact of technology on our children. While we have a strong record of students who achieve academically and socially, we must re-examine our use of technology and how constant connectivity, both inside and outside the classroom, impacts the experience of our students. To address emerging questions, I have recommended a comprehensive technology audit of our technology use. Through my meetings with our teachers, staff, and parents, I appreciate just how complex the uses of technology have become across our district. The audit will examine our backend infrastructure, staffing, data analysis, and student screen time and purpose. The timing is particularly appropriate as we are currently revising our District Technology Plan. We are still defining the final scope to determine which components require an outside consultant and which will be handled internally, as an external audit may not fully capture the nuances of individual classroom instruction. Given the decade-long development of our current systems, decoupling technology from our learning environment cannot happen overnight. Any changes must be the result of a thoughtful, evidence-based analysis involving our entire school community. As a first step, we are bringing a contract for a professional technology audit firm to the Board for approval at the March 18th meeting. We look forward to collaborating with our staff and families to ensure our technology use their digital training manuals with every team in the land, ensuring that as they grew, they pulled the whole community up with them. Like the old names carried by their machines, their story feels legendary. But their real magic is simple: they make more people believe they belong. The FIRST Impact Award goes to Team 8033! Here’s what the competition had to say about our team and the award: The FIRST Impact Award is the most prestigious award at FIRST, it honors the team that best represents a model for other teams to emulate and best embodies the purpose and goals of FIRST. The FIRST Impact Award is presented to the team judged to have the most significant measurable impact of its partnerships among its participants and community over a sustained period, not just a single build season. The winner is able to demonstrate progress towards FIRST’s mission of transforming our culture. The recipient team will be invited to the District Championship where it will compete for the FIRST Impact Award against winners from other qualifying events and compete with their robot. articles.text: Over the years, humans have made incredible discoveries in space. A significant factor in our advancement has been the development of robotics. Robots have played a pivotal role in helping humans learn more about space. From using robotic spacecraft to study planets far from Earth to utilizing giant robotic arms on the International Space Station, robots are fundamental in the pursuit of space advancements. Robots help scientists explore planets and solar systems humans do not yet have the ability to In 1997, NASA launched the robotic Cassini spacecraft to study Saturn. The Cassini spacecraft is a complex autonomous robot, meaning it can work by itself! Using computers and powerful antennas, scientists sent commands from Earth for Cassini to complete. A great example of this is the launch of the Huygens probe in 2005. The Huygens probe, which was aboard the Cassini spacecraft when it launched, went to the surface of Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. The probe marked the first time a spacecraft landed on a moon in our outer solar system. For over a decade, the efforts of the Cassini spacecraft gave scientists unprecedented insight into Saturn and its many moons from the safety of Earth. Astrobees: Busy Workers Robots have been developed to help astronauts complete everyday tasks while on space missions. In 2018, NASA sent three colorful, cube-shaped robots named Bumble, Honey, and Queen to the International Space Station (ISS). Known collectively as Astrobees, these small, free-flying robots developed at NASA Ames were sent to help the crew aboard the ISS with routine tasks such as inventory, documenting experiments, and moving objects around the station. With the help of Astrobees, astronauts can turn their focus to other important areas of their work. Astrobees are helping to advance NASA’s goal of developing robots that will support exploration, maintenance, and monitoring in future space exploration. For NASA’s Artemis program, Astrobees are an essential factor to help deliver humans back to the Moon, to Mars, and beyond. In Chabot’s NASA Ames Visitor Center, one of only 11 in the country, you can see an Astrobee that has gone to space and learn more about the research happening at NASA Ames. articles.text: Lake Tahoe is one of my favorite places to be, especially in the winter. I love the smell of the trees, the stars in the sky, and most of all playing in the snow. That is why, for my Eagle Project, I wanted to introduce a group of kids to the Lake Tahoe area who had never experienced snow before. To do this, I partnered with the Boys and Girls Club of Oakland (BGCO), and on Saturday, February 28th, seven Scouts (Anna Benson, Holden Bloodworth, Elise High, Ryan McMurtry, Michael Sidbury, Cole Venner and Travers Kemp) guided 12 BGCO members through an amazing day at Lake Tahoe. The scouts and I started the day by meeting at Mulberry’s at 6:45 a.m. to pick up a delicious donation of sandwiches and freshly baked cookies for everyone to enjoy. Next, one car went to the West Oakland branch of BGCO so I could ride in the van with a dozen excited members. The ride to Tahoe seemed so much shorter than the three hours it took because we were talking and getting to know each other. In talking about the drive after the trip, Zemirah even said, “The laughter, the community, and all the fun on the way there were what really made the trip memorable.” Our first stop was at the Donner Lake lookout on highway 80, this is where the BGCO members were able to see Donner Lake for the first time. We told them a little bit about the Donner Party. From Travers Kemp standing in the “Magic Carpet”. BGCO girls sliding down the tubing path with Anna Benson.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 18, 2026 9 City to Snow Continued from page 8 there, we rushed over to SnoVentures, where Palisades Tahoe had generously donated tubing tickets to our group. After the kids were suited up in their snow gear donated by Sports Basement, we spent the next hour yelling, spinning, and laughing as the group slid down the tracks using big inflatable innertubes. When the tubing session was over, some kids made snow angels while others tried hiking or sledding in Olympic Valley. Two BGCO members did a fantastic job building their first snowman, which West Oakland Branch leader Rodney Cook proudly guarded to make sure it didn’t get accidentally damaged in the continued snowplay. After enjoying our delicious Mulberry’s lunch, we drove to Donner Memorial State Park which had donated parking passes for our vehicles. The kids marched to the monument, took pictures, and played a little more in the snow. Then we moved inside the Donner Memorial Museum to participate in a scavenger hunt which made it even more fun. Finally, after determining the winners, we all said our goodbyes, and the BGCO van headed back to Oakland with snacks and drinks donated by the Oakland Grocery Outlet. When I met with the BGCO members the following week to show them pictures from the trip, they all said the trip was “very fun,” they loved their scout helpers, and “definitely would do this trip again.” (Thanks to Nevaeh, Kei’lani, Love, and Ma’layah for their comments and feedback). Tiquan even called the trip “existentially great.” Everybody agreed that whether it is in the snow or in Oakland, we all wanted to see each other again. The group takes a “Thank You” photo with Dominic Antonucci from SnoVentures. Scouts and BGCO kids sledding down a big hill. Scouts and BGCO kids pose in front of the Donner Memorial. Scouts Cole Venner and Holden Bloodworth pose with their groups after getting 1st (Cole’s group) and 2nd (Holden’s group) in the scavenger hunt at the Donner Memorial State Park. Scouts and BGCO kids all line up one last time before heading back down to Oakland.

articles.text: Join Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund (DREDF) advocate Andrea Yu for a comprehensive look at the IEP process from start to finish. On Wednesday, March 25, from 7 - 8:30 p.m., Andrea will host a virtual walk-through on Zoom. The talk will teach parents how to navigate the IEP document, and practical steps families can take when the process isn’t working as it should. The session will also explore the foundational principles of the IDEA, covering key concepts such as free appropriate public education, the least restrictive environment, the right to an independent educational evaluation, and what meaningful parental participation truly looks like. Andrea Yu is an Education Advocate at DREDF, a leading national civil rights law and policy center founded in 1979 and directed by individuals with disabilities and parents of children with disabilities. Andrea brings seven years of hands-on school experience to her role, having worked as an afterschool program leader, preschool teacher assistant, and special education paraprofessional. Through that work, she discovered a deep passion for supporting students with disabilities and their families, a calling that led her to become a special education preschool teacher. She remains dedicated to the students and families she has worked with and looks forward to extending that impact to more communities through DREDF. To attend the meeting, scan the QR code in the poster or follow this link to join the meeting: https://bit.ly/4aVRnRX.

articles.text: New boys’ lacrosse coach Andy Kittler watches his team against Campolindo. Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team split its last two matches, beating Campolindo 12-6 on the road in Moraga on Thursday, March 12 but losing 12-8 at Acalanes in Lafayette two days earlier. “There are a lot of good individual efforts. We started to do some of the things we’re practicing on offense, but we’re still making mistakes and dropping the ball a lot. We’re starting to execute some of the concepts. Overall, it wasn’t the prettiest game, but we’ll take the win,” said first-year head coach Andy Kittler. With Kalamas, Ian Nguyen, and Connor Fredericks, the Highlanders are looking like they have their best three-headed monster in attack since 2023, when the school was headlined by Nate Fredericks, and the late Jack Nelson and Soren Dixon—who tragically passed away in 2024. Several players still have #1 and #16 decals on their helmets to honor the two. “We try to play for Jack and Soren every game. Most of us have their numbers on our helmet. We look at their numbers on the fence every day. We’re just trying to live up to their standard and carry on the tradition,” Kalamas said. Kalamas, mow in his fourth year on varsity, has had as many coaches during his time, which has made things difficult for him and the attack to settle in. “We have some new talent on the team, so we’re still developing chemistry but we’re working well together. I’ve had four different coaching staffs all four years, so it’s hard to keep that continuity game-to-game. But, we’re getting better every game,” Kalamas said. Piedmont was able to lean on its defense against Campo, limiting the Cougars to one goal in the first and fourth quarters. “We played solid today, but there’s always room for improvement. Things are starting to click. We want to get the little things right,” defensive captain P.J. Brayer said. 12-6 victory over Campolindo Ian Nguyen scored the first goal after two minutes, and Campolindo tied it at the 6:13 mark. Nearly a minute later, Kalamas assisted Connor Fredericks for a goal. With 49 seconds left in the first quarter for a 3-1 lead. After that, PHS went on a three-goal scoring run from #9 with 4:33 left, Nguyen with 2:12 left, and then #11 assisted Nguyen for a goal with 1:10 left—9-4. Campo got one back with 46 seconds left. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team capped off a strong week with three straight wins at the Corey Reich Tennis Center. They defeated Western Alameda County Conference rival Castro Valley 5-2 on Thursday, March 12, swept Marin Academy 7-0 the previous day on March 11, and also blanked Athenian 7-0 on Tuesday, March 10. The win over Castro Valley featured a rematch of last year’s WACC Individual Tournament semifinals between Lucas Smolko and CV’s Guhan Anandkumar, with Smolko winning 6-3, 6-4. In the 2025 Individual Tournament, Smolko defeated Anandkumar 6-3, 6-0, where the Trojans’ singles starter and coaching staff made some unusual chirping at Smolko. It was a similar intense atmosphere in Thursday’s meeting, with Castro Valley and Piedmont players both erupting in cheers after every point. “You never know what to expect. I was returning pretty well, but my serve wasn’t too consistent. In the beginning I was just trying to focus on my own game, but it got a little harder when I got tired. The crowd got into it more and everything escalated, especially when you have a history,” Smolko said. Locking down the No. 1 doubles spot is the sophomore duo of Joey Assalian and Ben Davis. Both played together in last year’s WACC Individual Tournament to win the consolation bracket. “Ben has a great forehand, and I have a good backhand. We fit together really well,” Assalian said. “It means a lot to be No. 1 doubles. It shows how much we progressed from last year. We’ve gotten better as a team and can build off each other,” Davis said. Freshman pair August Collins and Henry Van Den Bos have also made in impressive climb up the doubles order to the No. 2 spot despite being newcomers. “It’s really pushed us to be better as doubles partners and tennis players itself. articles.text: Piedmont High’s softball team pulled off a dominant 16-6 win over American on Friday, March 13 at the Witter Softball Field, improving its record to 3-2 overall. Things started slowly after trailing 2-0 deficit through the top of the second inning. But the Highlanders stormed back with three runs in the bottom of the second and exploded for nine runs in the bottom of the third. They closed the game by way of the 10-run rule by adding three runs in the bottom of the sixth. “It’s a young team. The first inning was rough but they settled down and started playing softball,” said coach Gene Denard. “We gained some momentum and scored 16 runs. American is young like us, so it was a good opportunity for us.” It marked the second win of the season for freshman pitcher Talia Perl, who threw 99 pitches in five innings of work. She struck out six batters and allowed three earned runs. As a freshman Perl is at the start of what could be a strong pitching career at Piedmont High. The last time PHS featured a freshman thrower was Izzy Epstein, who was a fouryear starter from 2019-2022. She was the Post’s 2022 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year and won the WACC Shoreline’s Pitcher of the Year award. “I’ve been playing softball for eight years,” said Perl. :It’s crazy to think that I started off so young and I always watched the big girls play. Now I’m one of the older girls. I think I’m definitely getting more consistent,” 16-6 over American Down 2-0 entering the bottom of the second, Piedmont went ahead 3-2 after Perl drew a oneout walk, while she came around to score on multiple passed balls. With two outs, Penelope Hopper hit a single, then Makenna Small drew a walk. Elly Mak then an RBI double to score pinch runner Hailey Navarro and Small, who came in on an error. Piedmont’s nine-run third inning started with Hannah Joeger, Rosemary Dickinson, and Perl drawing three straight walks, then Kajsa Benson drawing a walk with the bases loaded. Hopper then hit a two-RBI single to score Perl and Dickinson. Mak drew another walk to load the bases, leading to Edie Elmquist also walking on five pitches to score Benson to make it 7-2. articles.text: Distance runner Seb Swain returns from injury Staff Photos Claire Aubrecht snapped a school record in the 200 meters set by Lauren Remer in 2013. Piedmont High’s track and field team competed in two events over the past week, hosting a Western Alameda County Conference meet against Castro Valley at Witter Field on Wednesday, March 11 and participating in the San Leandro Invitational at Burrell Field on Saturday, March 14. At the San Leandro Invitational, junior Claire Aubrecht made school history by snapping Lauren Remer’s 13-year record in the 200 meters by just .01 of a second, recording a winning time of 26.15 seconds in a field of 26 sprinters. Remer was inducted into the Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame last April. “I’m really going for both the 100 and 200 records. Breah Bell set the 100 record a couple of years back, and I was just .08 off the 200 record. I’m just really, really trying to go for them,” Aubrecht said. It was a big week for Aubrecht who beat Castro Valley’s Idara Essien in both the 100 and 200 with times of 12.97 and 26.24 respectively. Essien notably won last year’s WACC title in the 200 and was No. 2 in the 100. “For four years, we’ve never had a girl beat Idara, and Claire went out and won both the 100 and 200 going toe to toe with her. The cherry on top of it all was that Claire came back on Saturday and broke the school record in the 200. All her work this offseason is already paying off,” said coach Pouyan Assadi. Wednesday’s meet also marked the long-awaited return of distance runner Sebastien Swain. He missed the entire cross country season last fall after undergoing knee surgery last summer. Swain won both the 800 and 1600 meters against Castro Valley, clocking respective times of 2:03.54 and 4:26.52 in fields of 12 runners. “It was a big confidence boost just to see where I’m comfortable and what my fitness level is. I’ve been putting in a lot of work. In rehab I did some strength work, but my motivation was low when I couldn’t go out and run. I didn’t do a lot for 12-16 weeks because I couldn’t do a lot of running. I’ve been slowly building since then,” Swain said. San Leandro Invitational For the boys’ team, senior Maddox Ma placed fourth of 36 sprinters in the 200 meters with a time of 23.10. Sophomore Aaron Bennett finished sixth of 48 in the 1600, clocking a 4:48.65. Raiden Holt was sixth of 10 in the 110 meter hurdles in 19.03. Aubrecht was the only member if the girls’ team to compete, winning the 200 with a school-record time of 26.15 seconds in a field of 26 sprinters. WACC meet vs. Castro Valley In the boys’ 100, Rehan Mumtaz won with a time of 11.39 in a field of 18. Derin Sabuncuoglu was second in 11.63. Mumtaz also was second of 15 in the 200 in 23.04, while Ma was third in 23.17. Ma also finished second of 17 in the 400 in 52.33. Next best for PHS was sophomore Noah Baldwin in fifth, 55.50. Sophomore Ben Gerber was second in the 800 meters in 2:11.54 and freshman Dylan Wallway was 2 seconds back, placing fourth in 2:13.40. After Swain in the 1600, Noah Sohn was third in 4:50.67, and Wallway was fourth in 4:51.51. Colby Hong won the discus with a distance of 117 feet, 3 inches in a field of 12 throwers. articles.text: Local pro soccer team off to a 2-0-0 start Don’t look now, but Oakland might have a successful professional sports franchise. The Oakland Roots professional soccer team in the USL Championship hosted a near soldout crowd of 14,419 for its home opener on Saturday, March 14, selling 96 percent of its 15,000 capacity at the Coliseum. Roots won the match 2-1 over New Mexico United, improving its record to 2-0-0 and currently in first place in the Western Conference. Sports in the City of Oakland is a sore subject after the Raiders left for Las Vegas, the A’s departed for Sacramento and soon Las Vegas, while the Warriors moved across the bridge to San Francisco. 2026 marks the second year that Roots are playing at the Coliseum. For players and coaches on Roots, seeing such a crowd is unusual in the USL Championship, which is the second division of American professional soccer. “That was special for the league as a whole. The fans really represented Oakland as a sports town. It helped give our guys a little extra juice to close out the game. I was in awe of what I saw. I’ve seen a lot of crowded stadiums, but not one with the collective energy and the collective belief in the city and the club,” said Roots head coach Ryan Martin. Before the match, the team’s diehard supporters in the Deep Roots section unveiled a “tifo,” which is a customary large-scale, choreographed visual display produced by devout soccer fans in leagues all over the world. This year Roots’ supporters creOakland Roots’ Peter Wilson (left) and Neveal Hackshaw celebrate a goal in their 2-1 win over New Mexico United. ated an image of Marvel Comics’ Guardians of the Galaxy character, Groot, with the caption: “We Are Roots.” “The atmosphere was incredible. I just spoke to my girlfriend and some friends; they were all blown away. We’ve been together for a variety of stops, and this was by far the best we’ve been to. The crowd was really special. We definitely feed off their energy,” said team captain Tommy McCabe. Roots begin the season with new energy and starting its campaign 2-0-0 for the first time in club history under Martin. Oakland missed the playoffs last year after finishing 10th of 12 teams. They are in first place for the only time in the team’s six years in the league. The club has a strong roster, boasting 2025’s Golden Boot winner, Peter Wilson, leading the attack. Coach Martin, meanwhile, came to Oakland as the longest tenured coach in the league after spending 2019-2025 at Loudoun United in Virginia. He is approaching his 220th game as a manager. Through its first five years in the USL Championship, Roots never hired a head coach with previous experience in the league, showing a sign of change for the young organization. The highest Roots finished in the Western Conference was seventh in 2024. Should Oakland achieve a top-four spot, they would host their first-ever playoff game in November. As things look right now, momentum and the financial backing is finally on their side. Piedmont Post sports editor Jonathan Comeaux is also a beat reporter and insider covering Oakland Roots SC. You can follow him on X @Jonathan_Como for consistent coverage. If you would like more Oakland Roots articles in The Post, please let us know at JonathanCX525@gmail.com or News@Piedmont-Post.com. articles.text: Play ends this Sunday American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) in San Francisco presents the North American premiere of Paranormal Activity, a new stage production based on the film franchise from Paramount Pictures, playing onstage now through Sunday, March 22. The new play presents an original story set in the world of the Paranormal Activity films created by filmmaker Oren Peli. The stage adaptation is written by Levi Holloway, whose credits include “Grey House,” and is conceived with director Felix Barrett. Illusions are designed by Tony Award winner Chris Fisher. The story follows James and Lou, who relocate from Chicago to London in an effort to leave their past behind. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet will present Don Quixote at the War Memorial Opera House from March 19 through 29. Based on the classic ballet by Marius Petipa and Alexander Gorsky, the production was reimagined in 2003 by San Francisco Ballet former artistic director Helgi Tomasson and choreographer Yuri Possokhov to mark the work’s 150th anniversary. Inspired by Miguel de Cervantes’ novel of the same name, the ballet is a rare comedic entry in the company’s classical repertoire and was last performed by the company in 2022. The production blends classical ballet with Spanish influences including flamenco-inspired choreography, guitar and castanets. The score, composed by Ludwig Minkus, underscores technically demanding moments, including the Act III pas de deux between Kitri and Basilio and the wellknown “Kitri jump.” Featuring 152 roles performed across four casts, the production showcases the full scale of the Opera House stage. Principal dancers alternating in the role of Kitri include Sasha De Sola, Nikisha Fogo, Wona Park, Madeline Woo and Katherine Barkman. Basilio will be performed by Cavan Conley, Gabriele Francesco Frola, Esteban Hernández, Wei Wang and Joshua Jack Price. Evening performances will include live flamenco in the lobby by Theatre Flamenco of San Francisco, featuring dancer Carola Zertuche, guitarist Jesse Torres and singer Clara Rodriguez. Opening night activations will take place after the performance, with subsequent events held before curtain. Select performances will also feature “Meet the Artist” talks. The production runs approximately 2 hours and 34 minutes, including intermissions. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ to purchase tickets online. articles.text: Opera San Jose closes its 2025/26 season with Verdi’s classic opera La Traviata, premiering Sunday, April 19. La Traviata is an opera in three acts by Giuseppe Verdi, based on the novel La Dame aux Camélias by Alexandre Dumas. Opera San Jose’s production includes Mikayla Sager, most recently seen as Mimì in La Bohème, as Violetta and former Opera San Jose Artist-in-Residence WooYoung Yoon as her young lover. Opera San Jose’s former Conductor in Residence Johannes Löhner returns to make his principal conducting debut with Director-in-Residence Tara Branham returning to direct La Traviata. Set in 19th-century Paris, it tells the tragic love story of the courtesan Violetta Valéry and the young nobleman Alfredo Germont. After meeting at a party, Alfredo confesses he has long loved Violetta. Though ill with tuberculosis and accustomed to a life of luxury and independence, she eventually falls in love with him. The two leave Paris to live together in the countryside. Their happiness is disrupted when Alfredo’s father, Giorgio Germont, asks Violetta to leave Alfredo. He argues that their scandalous relationship threatens his family’s reputation and his daughter’s marriage prospects. Mikayla Sager, most recently seen cast as the company’s Mimìs in La Bohème, is cast as Violetta in Opera San Jose’s production of La Traviata. Sacrificing her own happiness, Violetta secretly agrees and returns to her former life without explaining why. The opera will be performed onstage April 19 through May 3. Doors open 90 minutes before the performance, 12:30 p.m. for matinees and 6:00 p.m. for evening performances. May 1and 3 performances will be conducted by Conductor-in-Residence Noah Lindquist. A preshow discussion is held at 1:00 p.m. for matinees and 6:30 p.m. for evening performances. The organ player will be performing 30 minutes before curtain. Visit https://www.operasj.org/ productions/la-traviata to purchase tickets. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
articles.title: Opera San Jose closes season with La Traviata

articles.text: KAWS: FAMILY is on view at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) now through May 3. KAWS: FAMILY presents more than 100 works spanning three decades of the artist KAWS’ (born Brian Donnelly, 1974) career. Organized by the Art Gallery of Ontario, the exhibition explores KAWS’ evolution from his early graffiti practice in Jersey City and Manhattan to a multidisciplinary career encompassing sculpture, painting, drawing, product design and large-scale public art. KAWS: FAMILY is the artist’s first major West Coast museum exhibition. “KAWS has a distinct appeal to a vast array of audiences with his iconic characters and meticulous work in a stunning range of mediums,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “The playful and contemplative works, a dynamic blend of his street art practice and formal education, offer something for everyone. His large-scale public installations have wowed audiences worldwide, and his playful and poignant retrospective exhibition promises to connect museum visitors with art in entirely new ways.” KAWS’ work bridges consumer culture and fine art, working across multiple mediums, said Daryl McCurdy, curatorial associate of architecture and design and curator of KAWS: FAMILY at SFMOMA. “Though art history has tended to situate a critical divide between fine and commercial art, KAWS’s work across media and markets feels refreshingly indifferent to preconceived strata of aesthetic experience and art collecting,” McCurdy said. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art is located at 151 Third St. in downtown San Francisco. Visit www.sfmoma.org for more information. KAWS’ work bridges consumer culture and fine art.

pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, March 18, 2026 The Musical Gourmet On the road to adventure By Joseph Gold Friday the 13th is a star-crossed date. Maybe that is the reason Jonas Schunke (baritone) and Erdmute Kather (pianist) presented some songs from Die Winterreise (a Winter’s journey) by Schubert in their Friday the 13th concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. I don’t mean to be evasive, so please don’t get me wrong. The concert actually was a very festive one and featured a complete cross-section of vocal – piano music including the very sad songs by Schubert. We were treated to some very old songs by early English composers, art songs by two great German composers (Schubert and Schumann), and then more modern composers from England and America. The program was in chronological order… Well almost. From the beginning, it was The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet obvious that we were to be enticed by the singer’s intimate voice and the pianist’s fine and expressive tone. The entire program was well chosen. A musical program should be an adventure and that’s what this one was. Their background is interesting. The performers are from the north of Germany and have a friendly connection with Piedmont residents John and Sue Malick. Musicians have friends everywhere. The first half of the program was dedicated to composers of the past and the second half of the program was dedicated to more recent composers. The famous American composer Aaron Copland contributed three unusual compositions. We know him as one of the important American composers of the modern idiom. The three compositions which were featured in the concert were settings of old songs. They were not what you’d expect from Copeland. He was in a nostalgic and sentimental mood. However, as the concert progressed, it ended in a very upbeat tempo. The next day my adventure continued with a trip to Angel Island. My granddaughter was featured in a brief string Quartet which served as a prelude to some adventurous new music. The Angel Island immigration station has been featuring concerts by the del Sol Quartet. For those who like contemporary music, they should attend. I am more of a traditionalist. I listened to the music with an open mind and in many ways it was a mind blowing experience. articles.text: KPop Demon Hunters took the world by storm in 2025, becoming the most-watched movie in Netflix’s history at 236 million streams. At the 2026 Oscars, the movie was honored as the Best Animated Feature, and “Golden,” the headline song, won the Best Original Song. In the movie, we follow the KPop group, Huntrix, headlined by Rumi (Arden Cho), Zoey (Ji-young Yoo), and Mira (May Hong). These three are the new generation’s demon hunters trained by Celine (Yunjin Kim), a former demon hunter, who tasked them with protecting the Honmoon. A magical protective layer that prevents demon forces from entering the human world. For generations, demon hunters have been tasked with maintaining it through the power of their songs. With enough power, the Honmoon can become golden and, as a result, be strong enough to seal away the demon world permanently. Early into the film we learn that Rumi is secretly half-demon, a fact known only to her and Celine, who raised Rumi. Disquieted by the demonic patterns gradually spreading across her skin, Rumi pushes forward the release and live performance of Huntrix’s new single, “Golden”, hoping it will turn the Honmoon gold and thereby erase her patterns. However, as they prepare for the performance, Rumi begins to lose her voice. In the demon world, Gwi-Ma, The KPop group Huntrix Courtesy of Patrick T. Fallon / AFP via Getty Images Chris Appelhans, Maggie Kang, and Michelle Wong onstage accepting the Oscar for best animated film for KPop Demon Hunters. voiced by Lee Byung-Hun, is the main antagonist of the film as the supreme ruler. He draws his strength from consuming human souls and controls his demon subjects through psychological manipulation and cursed markings. Gwi-Ma tasks 5 humans turned demon to form a boy band called the Saja Boys to steal Huntrix’s fans and weaken the Honmoon. The group led by Jinu (Ahn HyoSeop) has a deal with Gwi-Ma. In exchange for destroying the Honmoon, he will erase Jinu’s painful human memories. As Huntrix watches the Saja boys’ debut, they realize that the group is composed of demons and later attack them. In the ensuing fight, Rumi’s patterns are discovered by Jinu, who surprisingly helps her cover them up from her bandmates. Privately, the two meet, and Jinu tells Rumi that Gwi-Ma uses feelings of shame to enslave the demons. 400 years prior, Jinu was granted fame and recognition that helped his family emerge from poverty, but then condemned him to the demon world; Jinu now lives with guilt over his family’s downfall. As the movie continues, the Saja Boys continue to grow in popularity, weakening the Honmoon, and Rumi’s demon markings start to spread. articles.text: Photo credit Peter Marcus Virginia Davis, owner of Yellow Door, is seen celebrating the April 2025 Taste of Montclair. The beloved Taste of Montclair Village returns on Tuesday, April 7, from 5–8 p.m. in Oakland’s vibrant Montclair Village district. This lively evening celebration invites guests to sample delicious bites and refreshing libations — including craft beer and artisan wines — at more than 30 local restaurants and businesses. Proceeds from the event benefit the Montclair Village Association, a nonprofit business improvement district that has proudly served the community for more than 75 years. Ticketed attendees will receive a tasting “Passport” granting access to culinary creations from Montclair’s talented chefs, along with beverage samples from local craft producers. Guests can enjoy their tastings at communal, table-style seating while taking in family-friendly entertainment from the Jazz Education Ensemble, returning this year to provide a festive soundtrack for the evening. Their performance brings together professional jazz musicians and school-age performers for a distinctive mentorship experience. The event offers fun for all ages. Kids can enjoy crafts, face painting, balloons, and more, while strolling guests will discover merchant-hosted activities throughout the district, including special promotions, giveaways, and opportunities to meet the business owners and staff who make Montclair unique. Local leaders and representatives from the Montclair Village Association will also be onsite to welcome attendees and celebrate the community. Join us for an unforgettable evening of food, drink, and community spirit in the heart of Montclair Village. For more information and for a growing list of participating restaurants and businesses, please visit MontclairVillage.com. Standard street parking will be available as well as ample paid parking in the Montclair Parking Garage (6235 La Salle Ave, Oakland). Ticket Information • Adult Passport ~ $50 ($53.24 w/ processing fee) • Under 15 Passport ~ $20 ($22.07 w/ processing fee) • Package of 4 Adult Passports ~ $200 (processing fees waived, savings of $12.96) About the Montclair Village Association: The MVA is a nonprofit 501(c)3 Business Improvement District (BID) with a mission to: increase the safety of Montclair, Oakland; support Montclair’s small businesses and merchants; expand opportunities for patronage and visitorship in Montclair; develop youth training programs for Oakland high school students and college interns seeking professional work experiences; expand artist representation in unused urban spaces; catalyze Montclair’s social capital and placemaking for business improvement; and ensure the enjoyment and livability of downtown Montclair for all Bay Area visitors and residents. For ongoing MVA news please consider signing up for our newsletter and following us on Instagram and Facebook.

articles.text: So you’ve decided that you’d like to give conformation dog showing a try. The Beginner Puppy (B-Pup) competition is a fun way to test the waters when your puppy is between four and six months old. Although many individuals do not purchase puppies from breeders specifically to show them, your puppy may surprise you at their first competition. When attending your first show, bathe your puppy and brush them beforehand. Different breeds have different grooming requirements. Avoid any fancy haircuts or trimming until you know exactly how your breed is typically groomed for the show ring. Trim their nails, brush their teeth, and clean out their ears. Now you’re ready to pack! Don’t forget to bring your grooming materials, a crate and x-pen, and a source of shade. Days at dog shows can be very long, so bring supplies to keep yourself comfy as well, such as lawn chairs and a cooler. Plan to arrive early so that you have plenty of time to set up. Could be you’ll meet someone with the same breed who is willing to give you a few tips! Check the judges program so you know what time your puppy must be in the ring. Complete any last-minute grooming, then head over to get your armband number from the ring steward table, which is next to the ring. Don’t forget to potty your puppy on the way! To show your puppy, you will need a specific show lead and either slip collar or show chain. Vendors at the show can advise you on what to buy. Additionally, keep plenty of treats (bait) in your pocket. Your puppy will have to stack, meaning stand in a particular fashion that demonstrates their structure. Dogs with good structure can typically stack on their own without much help. Use your treat to keep your puppy’s eyes forward while the judge examines them. The judge may give you instructions such as showing them the bite (teeth), trotting the puppy down and back, or trotting the puppy all the way around the show ring. Keep your pace slow and listen to the judge for instructions. It could be your puppy will win a blue ribbon! If your puppy wins first place for their breed, stick around as they may have a chance to compete for best in show! Have fun, and don’t stress; both you and your puppy are learning. This is a great chance to practice while your puppy is still under six months old. You can also use the knowledge of where your puppy places to decide whether your dog has a show career ahead of them. Most of all, it’s an exciting way to bond with your dog! Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com. Hopeful poses proudly after winning second place in the herding group at her first B-Pup competition.

Local leaders and representatives from the Montclair Village Association will also be onsite to welcome attendees and celebrate the community. Join us for an unforgettable evening of food, drink, and community spirit in the heart of Montclair Village. For more information and for a growing list of participating restaurants and businesses, please visit MontclairVillage.com. Standard street parking will be available as well as ample paid parking in the Montclair Parking Garage (6235 La Salle Ave, Oakland). articles.text: It was a sunny, summer-like morning last Wednesday when the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group gathered at the Exedra for their weekly walk. Along with the weather, the group marked Women’s History Month, which celebrates the contributions of women to American history and was officially recognized by Congress in 1987. This week’s walk focused on two influential figures in early Piedmont history, Sarah Requa and her daughter, Amy Requa Long. While past walks have highlighted Amy’s role in founding the Ransom and Bridges School, the group turned its attention to the family’s estate, “The Highlands,” and the legacy behind it. Isaac Requa, Sarah’s husband, arrived in San Francisco in 1850 after sailing around Cape Horn from New York. He built his fortune through Nevada silver mining, the Central Pacific Railroad, and the Oakland Bank of Savings. Sarah Mower Requa, born in Bangor, Maine in 1829, made her own journey west after her father’s death, traveling with her family to a San Francisco that was still a rough settlement of tents and ships. Sarah later lived in Nevada’s mining region, where her cooking became well known. She reportedly earned $14,000, a substantial sum at the time, serving meals to miners who paid as much as $50 per plate. There she met Isaac. The couple married in 1863 and eventually settled in the East Bay. In 1877, the Requas purchased about 80 acres of rolling land in the Oakland foothills and built a grand estate they called The Highlands. At the time, only a handful of homes stood in what is now Piedmont. Their mansion, perched on a prominent knoll near today’s Hazel Lane and Requa Road, became the largest and most notable residence in the area. The estate stretched across what are now Hazel Lane, Requa Road, Windsor Avenue, and Wildwood Avenue, with sweeping views of Lake Merritt, the Bay, and the San Francisco Peninsula. The site is also believed to be where Spanish explorer Gaspar de Portola camped during his 1772 expedition. The Highlands mansion was striking in both size and design. Painted yellow with brown trim, it stood out on the largely treeless hills and could be seen from San Francisco Bay. The home featured 22 bedrooms, a dining table that seated 24, and separate quarters for domestic staff. Eleven additional workers lived on the property. Because travel to Oakland was slow by horse-drawn carriage, the estate functioned largely as a self-sufficient compound. It included vegetable gardens, orchards, berry patches, a dairy herd, stables, its own gas plant, and a private water system. The grounds were landscaped with a wide variety of trees and included a fountain, croquet court, and formal entrance along what is now Highland Avenue, a street later renamed in honor of the estate. After Isaac’s death in 1905 and Sarah’s death in 1922 at age 93, the mansion was demolished the following year. Amy Requa Long later subdivided the property into a residential neighborhood of 42 homes. Education became a defining part of the family’s legacy. What began as a small school for Amy’s children and neighbors grew into the Ransom and Bridges School for Girls, Piedmont’s first school. In 1908, Amy commissioned architect Julia Morgan to design a new campus on five acres along Hazel Lane. The school opened in 1913 and expanded to include dormitories, classrooms, and a gymnasium, serving students from first grade through high school. The school thrived for years, attracting families from across California. By the late 1920s, it enrolled nearly 200 students. However, the economic strain of the Great Depression and the availability of the less expensive Piedmont High School led to declining enrollment. The school closed in 1932, and the site was later redeveloped into the Ransom Gardens neighborhood. Amy Requa Long, later known as Amy Requa Mitten after her remarriage, remained a prominent figure in Piedmont until her death in 1960 at age 83. During the walk, participants traced this history through the neighborhood. They followed Highland Avenue to Hazel Lane, where they discussed the early school, and continued through the surrounding streets that once formed the estate. Architect Jim Kellogg pointed out details of Albert Farr-designed homes in the area. The group paused at the former entrance to The Highlands, marked by brick pillars, and continued to Requa Place, where Amy spent her later years. From there, walkers could see Piedmont High School nearby, a reminder of how the area has evolved. The route continued past There was a large turnout of 51 walkers and four K-9 best friends on hand.
