articles.text: The Pardee Home Museum, a California Historical Landmark, an Oakland City Landmark, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, dates to 1868. The home recently underwent a renovation restoring its historic character. Visitors can view the results during a reserved tour on Sunday, March 22, 2026, at 2 p.m., featuring a special lecture and guided tour by Steve and Lisa Bauer of Bradbury & Bradbury. At 158 years old, the home has witnessed and contributed to both Oakland and California history. Over time, it has endured earthquakes, roof leaks and the natural settling that comes with age. While the first-floor interior was painted in recent years, the second-floor wall coverings had not been updated since the 1950s. The upstairs rooms required careful attention before any cosmetic work could begin. Preservation efforts focused on maintaining historical accuracy while addressing structural needs. To find an appropriate design, the museum partnered with the Bradbury & Bradbury Wallpaper Company, now based in Sacramento. The firm agreed to assist with the restoration, bringing expertise in historically accurate designs. Steve Bauer, owner of Bradbury & Bradbury, researched wallpaper styles from the late 1800s and created coordinated designs for the walls and ceilings of three bedrooms and the billiard room. One of the custom patterns developed for the project is now included in the company’s international catalog as “The Pardee.” Wallpaper installer Joel Lucas was hired to complete the work. The project required extensive wall repair and preparation before installation Master Bedroom - Before Photos courtesy of Pardee Home Museum Madeline’s Bedroom - Before Master Bedroom - After Madeline’s Bedroom - After could begin. Over four months, Lucas restored the surfaces and applied the custom designs. The result is a carefully executed restoration that reflects the home’s original elegance. With the project complete, the Pardee Home Museum continues to preserve its legacy while offering visitors a glimpse into its renewed historic interiors. The photos show much of the process, but a visit will truly show the magnificence of the finished project. Tickets for this event are available on Eventbrite at this link: https:// www.eventbrite.com/e/the-bigreveal-tickets-1983124824735. Twin Bedroom - Before Billard Room - Before Twin Bedroom - After Billard Room - After The Pardee Home Museum is lcocated at 672 11th Street, Oakland.

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors recently held their monthly meeting with four distinguished Piedmont City employees attending to address the group regarding the latest city improvements. They included Communications Program Manager Echa Schneider, Police Chief Frederick Shavies, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, and Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The core of the conversation revolved around the modernizing of Piedmont’s emergency response. The Police Department lobby re-opened recently following the completion of its new 9-1-1 dispatch center. It is Piedmont’s most significant public safety investment in decades. Previously, the nearly 80-year-old Police Department building was powered by a 200-amp electrical panel – a capacity more typical of a single family home than a 24/7 public safety facility – and lacked dedicated backup power. Now, this latest project has delivered a modern electrical core designed for today’s public safety operations, including secure, independent backup power, ensuring that the Police Department and dispatch center can remain operational during extended power outrages or major emergencies. While the 9-1-1 dispatch center replacement is one of an unprecedented number of capital projects completed, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales spoke about other significant infrastructure investments including Piedmont’s streets, storm drains, and a new sanitary sewer system. There will be an upgrade in street maintenance, sidewalks, street lighting, signage, and provisions to promote pedestrian and bicycle safety, as well as public landscaping and street tree maintenance. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan then spoke of helping the community prepare for emergencies as well as educating the community about fire prevention and disaster preparedness. With the recent upgrades to the system, the Piedmont Fire Department will now be better able to provide the community with comprehensive and superior emergency services to protect life, property, and the environment. It was a most educational day for all who attended. After the meeting a catered lunch was served to the delight of all. If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. Featured speakers at the recent Piedmont Seniors’ monthly meeting included: Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales (left), Police Chief Frederick Shavies, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, and Communications Program Director Echa Schneider.

articles.text: Allyson Huynh Weavers is a new community program designed to connect Piedmont seniors with local teens for companionship, support, and meaningful conversation. Founded by sophomores Luca LaForte and Allyson Huynh, Weavers pairs seniors with members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew to help reduce isolation and strengthen intergenerational ties. The spring pilot will match 15 seniors with 15 student volunteers. Pairs will meet once a week over a six-week period, with the option to continue together or be rematched at the end of the program. Visits may include conversation, light household assistance, or simply spending time together. The program is open to Piedmont seniors who would enjoy regular connection with younger generations. Families and caregivers are also encouraged to reach out on behalf of interested participants. To learn more or sign up, please contact the Weavers team. at http://beaweaver.com or contact piedmontweavers@gmail. com.

articles.text: We just saved one of our Honey Homes members $20,000. Not by being clever. By being honest. Her previous contractor said the drainage issue at her home would cost $20,000 to fix – dig up the pavement, replace the pipes, the works. She was stressed, overwhelmed, and ready to sign. Our handyman cleared the drain with a water jet during a regular visit. An hour and a half. Problem solved. No destruction. No bill shock. No regrets. We wish this story were rare. It isn’t – especially for seniors. Too many homeowners, particularly those who’ve lived in their homes for decades, get overcharged, misled, or pressured into repairs they simply don’t need. It happens because they don’t have someone trustworthy in their corner. My wife Avantika and I started Honey Homes right next door in Lafayette because we lived this ourselves. An irrigation specialist took a hefty deposit from us – and vanished. No work done. Didn’t even show up. That experience lit a fire in us, and Honey Homes was born. Piedmont’s homes are something special. Historic, full of character, full of stories. The Honey Homes Handy Man helping our member in their kitchen families who’ve cared for them deserve a home partner who shows up, tells the truth, and actually solves the problem - not someone looking to make a quick buck. Here’s what that looks like with Honey Homes: • One dedicated, fully background-checked handyman who gets to know your home • No upsells, no scare tactics - simplest fix first, every single time • A real partner, not a one-off transaction We’re proud to support over 400 Piedmont families and 3,000 families across 5 cities, and we’re just getting started. articles.text: I’m sorting this out in real time. This may not be the most uplifting column I’ve written, but it may be one of the most important. Not all of us have children nearby or family members able to step in as caregivers. Because of that reality, each of us must take responsibility for planning our future as we enter the golden years and beyond. Preparation deserves the same care we give to planning a vacation. You wouldn’t show up at the airport without a passport, a ticket, or a destination. Yet many people do exactly that when it comes to aging. Create a checklist. Identify the people who can support you. Think about where you might live in the future the same way you would research a hotel for a stay in a new city. When you plan ahead, you give yourself options and a softer landing. When you don’t, decisions are often made during a crisis. As I often say in Mindset in Motion, if you fail to plan, you are planning to fail. Jackie’s story Jackie’s story has brought that lesson into focus. Not long ago, Jackie fell. She lives in an independent living community, not assisted living. That distinction matters. Independent living offers housing and community, but not the medical or daily support someone may suddenly need after an accident. Even though it was “just a fall,” she was taken to the hospital by ambulance. Twice. If Jackie had close family nearby, someone might have driven her to urgent care or called her doctor. Instead, the system responded the way it is designed to. She was transported to the hospital. Because she could not get downstairs for meals she returned again. A hospital, however, is not long-term care. When someone has no strong support system, it can become a temporary place of refuge. Soon after, she was discharged to a rehabilitation facility. On the surface it looked like a quiet residential building, but inside it felt more like an extension of the hospital. Jackie spent long hours in bed. When I visited, her room was dark and she needed help simply getting to the bathroom. Her hip was sore from the fall, but days of inactivity caused new pain as well. Communication about her care was inconsistent. The evening nurse said physical therapy happened daily, Jackie begged to differ. Who was telling the truth? While I was away for two days, Jackie was discharged and sent home in a truck she barely remembers. She was so embarrassed she covered her head with a borrowed scarf. Moments like this highlight the limits of friendship in situations requiring professional care. I am not Jackie’s nurse or family member. I am a friend and neighbor doing my best to help. During this process I also learned that many of Jackie’s behaviors—frustration, forgetfulness, and sudden anger—may be signs of cognitive decline. Hearing that was difficult, but it explained much of the confusion. Months ago, Jackie gave me four phone numbers written on a small piece of paper for her fiduciary, attorney, a niece three states over whom I have never met, and the Neptune Society. I mentioned to Jackie that she should speak with her fiduciary, but she kept repeating that he is not needed until she passes. That isn’t accurate, yet she continues to resist the idea. He did explain that he could coordinate care and help manage important decisions if she asked him to step in. However, Jackie emphatically denies that this is part of his role. At the moment, we are at a standstill. He does have a copy of her trust and all the important paperwork in his possession for when the time comes. Just seven months ago we celebrated her move into independent living. Now we are preparing for the possibility of assisted living. Aging can change quickly. Jackie’s story is a reminder for all of us to ask ourselves a few important questions. Do you have a plan? Do you have trusted people who know your wishes? Have you prepared legally and financially for the years ahead? Planning for aging is not about fear. It is about dignity, choice, and control. The best time to create a plan is long before you need one. DiMaggio Betta Group, Corcoran Icon Properties, 510.414.6777, Debbi.DiMaggio@ corcoranicon.com

By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama, Even though my laptop is only two years old, I decided I am finding it just too hard to work and see the 13-inch screen. So, I want to get the larger one. I know Apple offers a trade in, but I wonder if there are better places to sell it. Apple only offers $650 dollars for my MacBook Air, and I paid over $2000 three years ago. Also, once I am ready, how do I remove all my information and get the computer ready for sale? James, Oakland Dear James, I’m going to answer your second question first; how to get your laptop ready for sale or to give away. Since your laptop is only two years old, even if you have not updated your operating system, you have the option to do an easy erase and reset with the “erase all content” option in System Settings. Any mac with at least Ventura (released in 2022) has this option. Here are the steps to do this: 1. Click on the Apple in the upper left of your screen and choose “System Settings”. 2. Click on “General” in the sidebar on the left. 3. Scroll down on the right until you see “Transfer or Reset”. 4. Click “Erase all content and settings”. 5. When the erase window comes up, you will be asked to sign in with your administrative credentials (NOT your Apple ID, your computer account, which is usually your name), and then put in your computer password. 6. You then might be asked if you want to back up your Mac with Time Machine, which you should have done before you started this process. 7. Then you will see a summary of all the things that will be erased, which will only affect the machine you are erasing. 8. You will also be asked to sign out of iCloud with your Apple ID and password, which should also disable Find My Mac (I disable Find My Mac and sign out of iCloud before I start the whole process). 9. Click the Erase All Content & Settings button. Your Mac will restart and be in “Recovery”mode, and you must activate it, which you do by clicking on the Wi-Fi signal in the upper right and joining your WIFI network. Once activated, it is in “out of the box” state, and ready for a new owner. Before you do all of this, as I said earlier, you should make sure you have a backup of your data, if you plan to use Time Machine to set up a new laptop. Other things you must do is sign out of any subscription software like Microsoft Office, Adobe products like Photoshop or Lightroom, or any software that uses licensing to control how many installations you can have. These licenses are often tied to your machine with a system ID, and if you forget to do this on certain software, it can be very difficult to get the license moved over. Also making sure that “find my Mac” is turned off, prevents the machine from being in your list of devices in your iCloud account even when it eventually belongs to somebody else. Let’s talk about some other places you can sell your machine. The best thing is a personal sale; someone you know who is looking for a used but current computer. Of course you must determine what your computer is worth. And for that, you could look at some of the online sales sites like, eBay or even Facebook marketplace. One of my favorite places to sell used devices is swappa.com, as they do not charge a commission, and the fee to sell is very low. To determine a price, look at the for-sale section and search for the specifics of your machine. You can also find prices on resale sites like mac2sell.net, itsworthmore. com, and sellyourmac.com. The downside of these online sites, as you have to arrange to ship your machine. That’s why I think that Facebook marketplace as I mentioned above is also a good place to sell locally. You would also be surprised, that if you start telling people that you have a two-yearold laptop for sale, you will often find someone interested. You can also use Craigslist, of course, but you have to be very careful about making sure potential buyers are legitimate. Craigslist is usually my last resort for electronics. Some people just do the apple trade-in because it’s convenient, but very likely your machine is worth a few hundred dollars more than Apple will offer you. Cookie Segelstein is the MacMama, an Apple Certified Service Professional that provides Apple computer consultation and trouble-shooting in your home and office. For more information, call 510-520-7760, email cookie@themacmama.com, or visit her website at www.themacmama.com Jackie’s story continues: Why planning is an act of self-care By Debbi DiMaggio I’m sorting this out in real time. This may not be the most uplifting column I’ve written, but it may be one of the most important. Not all of us have children nearby or family members able to step in as caregivers. Because of that reality, each of us must take responsibility for planning our future as we enter the golden years and beyond. Preparation deserves the same care we give to planning a vacation. You wouldn’t show up at the airport without a passport, a ticket, or a destination. Yet many people do exactly that when it comes to aging. Create a checklist. Identify the people who can support you. Think about where you might live in the future the same way you would research a hotel for a stay in a new city. When you plan ahead, you give yourself options and a softer landing. When you don’t, decisions are often made during a crisis. As I often say in Mindset in Motion, if you fail to plan, you are planning to fail. Jackie’s story Jackie’s story has brought that lesson into focus. Not long ago, Jackie fell. She lives in an independent living community, not assisted living. That distinction matters. Independent living offers housing and community, but not the medical or daily support someone may suddenly need after an accident. Even though it was “just a fall,” she was taken to the hospital by ambulance. Twice. If Jackie had close family nearby, someone might have driven her to urgent care or called her doctor. Instead, the system responded the way it is designed to. She was transported to the hospital. Because she could not get downstairs for meals she returned again. A hospital, however, is not long-term care. When someone has no strong support system, it can become a temporary place of refuge. Soon after, she was discharged to a rehabilitation facility. On the surface it looked like a quiet residential building, but inside it felt more like an extension of the hospital. Jackie spent long hours in bed. When I visited, her room was dark and she needed help simply getting to the bathroom. Her hip was sore from the fall, but days of inactivity caused new pain as well. Communication about her care was inconsistent. The evening nurse said physical therapy happened daily, Jackie begged to differ. Who was telling the truth? While I was away for two days, Jackie was discharged and sent home in a truck she barely remembers. She was so embarrassed she covered her head with a borrowed scarf. Moments like this highlight the limits of friendship in situations requiring professional care. I am not Jackie’s nurse or family member. I am a friend and neighbor doing my best to help. During this process I also learned that many of Jackie’s behaviors—frustration, forgetfulness, and sudden anger—may be signs of cognitive decline. Hearing that was difficult, but it explained much of the confusion. Months ago, Jackie gave me four phone numbers written on a small piece of paper for her fiduciary, attorney, a niece three states over whom I have never met, and the Neptune Society. I mentioned to Jackie that she should speak with her fiduciary, but she kept repeating that he is not needed until she passes. That isn’t accurate, yet she continues to resist the idea. He did explain that he could coordinate care and help manage important decisions if she asked him to step in. However, Jackie emphatically denies that this is part of his role. At the moment, we are at a standstill. He does have a copy of her trust and all the important paperwork in his possession for when the time comes. Just seven months ago we celebrated her move into independent living. Now we are preparing for the possibility of assisted living. Aging can change quickly. Jackie’s story is a reminder for all of us to ask ourselves a few important questions. Do you have a plan? Do you have trusted people who know your wishes? Have Advertise Here! you prepared legally and financially for the years ahead? Planning for aging is not about fear. It is about dignity, With the... Piedmont Post choice, and control. The best time to create a plan is long before you need one. Anian Pettit Tunney and her daughter Adrienne Tunney Krumins continue a family tradition that dates back to Piedmont’s earliest days. They are the 5th and 6th generation of a long line of accomplished women involved in Piedmont real estate and development beginning in 1877. Anian is the great-great granddaughter of Isaac and Sarah Requa, whose home, christened “The Highlands” in 1878, is variously credited with being the fourth or fifth house to be built in Piedmont. Real estate, in fact, brought Sarah Mower and Isaac Requa together. Sarah Mower was the first woman in the family to reach California and the first to live in Piedmont. In the early 1850s, at the age of 17, Sarah sailed on her own from Belfast, Maine, around Cape Horn to join her mother and sister in San Francisco. The three Mower women made a good living cooking and washing for the would-be miners who were on their way to the gold fields. In “The Highlands” c. 1880 as seen from present Highland Avenue. 1860 the ladies moved to Gold Hill, Nevada, where the miners cheerfully paid up to $50 for a hot meal. After only a few years, Sarah had made $14,000 – a small fortune at the time. It was in Gold Hill that Sarah met Isaac Requa. He arrived in California from Tarrytown, New York, in the early 1850’s, and achieved his first success when he devised a method to divert the course of the South Fork of the American River to open the streambed for the extraction of gold. A shy young mining engineer, he lived in the cabin next to the Mower women. Sarah initiated contact by leaning over the porch rail and observing that Mr. Requa had built his cabin a foot and a half off the property line. He protested, but when the line was measured, Sarah’s observation proved to be accurate. In 1863, Sarah and Isaac were married in San Francisco. Isaac would later say the he married Sarah for her good eyesight. They returned to Gold Hill where they lived for over a decade. Mrs. Requa later described their life in Gold Hill to a reporter. “[There were] many days of discouragement for the young pioneer couple, but they bided their time,” he wrote. Urged on by his young wife, Requa struck the first gold on the lower level of the Comstock Lode. He developed the famous Chollar Potosi mine, and before he was through with it, the mine had produced $13,985,000. Dreams had been fulfilled.” On their frequent visits to San Francisco, the Requas often looked out their Palace Hotel windows to the golden hills across the bay. While their Comstock friends, the Fairs, Floods and Huntingtons, were building huge homes on Nob Hill, the Requas were transfixed by the view across the bay. In 1877 the Requas acquired from Walter Blair 80 unimproved rolling acres awash with wildflowers, “in the foothills back of Oakland.” On a commanding knoll (near where Hazel Lane and Requa Road meet today), the Requas constructed a large wood frame house overlooking Lake Merritt and San Francisco Bay. It was Sarah who worked with architect H. W. Cleveland on the new house and the development of the estate while Isaac remained in the gold fields. Although the house was christened in 1878, it was not finished until 1880. That year the Requa family, including son Mark Lawrence and baby Amy, born in 1876 at the Palace Hotel, moved into their new home. Historian Edward T. Planer described “The Highlands” in The Knave: “The towered, gabled, high-windowed yellow house contained 22 rooms, all of ample dimensions, while an adjoining wing was solely for the domestic help. In addition, 11 hired hands had other quarters on the estate. Since it was a long trip to Oakland, the manor was, of necessity, all but self sufficient. ‘The Highlands’ had its own vegetable gardens, orchard, berry patches, dairy herd of 11 cows, stable with seven stalls and a grooming room, an illuminating gas manufactory and an independent water supply from wells on the property. The grounds were tastefully landscaped according to the style of the times [with] hundreds of trees and ornamentals of all types [which] enhanced the mansion as did a handsome Photos courtesy of City of Piedmont except where noted. Four generations of Requa women taken c. 1920 at “The Elms”: Sarah Mower Requa (left), Amy Requa Long, baby Cherie Sutton and Amy Long Sutton. “The Highlands,” date unknown, as seen from near the bottom of today’s Requa Place. Note snow on the roof and along the boardwalk. Two generations of Requa women, Anian Pettit Tunney (left) and daughter Adrienne Tunney Krumins. wooden fence and gateway along present Highland Avenue.” Highland Avenue was named for the Requa estate. Daughter Amy Requa wed General Oscar Long on October 7, 1896, an event so grand. Three hundred guests gathered for the wedding breakfast under a marquee set in the gardens of “The Highlands.” In 1909 the Longs built their own home (designed by Albert Farr between 1907-1909) on the Requa property, just down the hill from the big house. They named it “The Elms,” for the row of trees leading up the drive. In this grand Georgian Revival home, the Long’s raised their two daughters, Sally and Amy Long. After a long, full life, one in which she remained sharp to the end, Sarah Mower Requa died at “The Highlands” in 1922, a few months after celebrating her 91st birthday. She had lived in her home for almost 50 years. After her death, Sarah’s son and daughter decided that the house should be demolished. By the end of 1923 the house was gone. In 1926 The Oakland Tribune announced “Mrs. Oscar Long Enters Business.” Amy Requa Long expressed a desire to see her parents’ estate developed “as she herself would like it to be.” Mrs. Long was now a real estate developer. She closely supervised the subdivision of her parents’ estate. She personally saw to it that the streets were graded to follow the natural contours of the hills. At her direction, all power lines were placed underground from the start. The lots on both sides of Requa Road were positioned to take advantage of the wonderful Bay views. Each was large enough to accommodate a good-sized house, with room for an ambitious garden. Mrs. Long reviewed the plans for each house. Having set things in motion and seen to it that her new neighbors would live in an attractive environment, Amy Long engaged a team of sales representatives to sell the lots of “Requa Highlands.” In 1924, Mrs. Long’s daughter Amy, now Mrs. Charles Zook

articles.text: Early Bird Registration through March Piedmont Food Fest is turning five this year! The Bay Area’s most vibrant multicultural festival returns to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 25 from 11 a.m. - 4 p.m. Since launching in 2022, this volunteer-run event has become a community tradition of building shared experiences through food, drink, music, and arts. By connecting over 2000 attendees with 50 local businesses and community organizations, Piedmont Food Fest sets the stage for a day full of new experiences and memories for visitors of all ages. With its broad variety of sights, sounds, and tastes, Piedmont Food Fest has evolved into an event for the greater Bay Area, with many guests visiting from San Francisco, Marin, Fremont, and Danville. Piedmont residents often seize the opportunity to invite friends and family to spend the day together at the festival. articles.text: When I was asked: “did you like the music?” a famous story helped me. This is how I answered the question. When George Frederick Handel was a young composer living in Italy, he heard that one of his pieces was to be performed. He would attend the rehearsal and concert conducted by one of the greatest musicians of all time, Arcangelo Corelli. As Handel listened to the rehearsal, he became agitated by Corelli’s inability to play Handel’s music. He finally walked up to Corelli and took his violin and said: “THIS is how my music should be played. Do you understand?” Corelli was embarrassed to say the least. He responded very diplomatically by saying: “I’m sorry. I just don’t understand MODERN music.” It seems that differences of opinion make music as well as horse racing. We must keep an open mind. Music and adventure are virtually synonymous. And the adventure continues.

articles.text: It is intended to be a time of repentance, prayer, fasting, self-discipline, charity and giving. Many people give up something for Lent, like cookies or beer. There are charming stories of children - not quite clear on the concept - saying they will give up making their beds or eating Brussels sprouts. Lent begins on Ash Wednesday, which falls 40 days before Easter. This year Ash Wednesday was February 18. In many places, the day before Ash Wednesday is a day of feasting and partying before the more sober period of Lent begins. It is called Mardi Gras, Carnival or Fat Tuesday. On Ash Wednesday, Christians go to church and receive ashes on their foreheads in the shape of a cross, symbolizing mortality, repentance and a time of spiritual reflection. The last week of Lent is Holy Week, which begins with Palm Sunday. On this Sunday, Christians celebrate Jesus’ triumphal entrance into Jerusalem even as it foreshadowed the coming Last Supper, Crucifixion and Resurrection. These events are celebrated on Maundy Thursday, Good Friday and Easter Sunday, respectively. Christians receive ashes on their foreheads on Ash Wednesday to symbolize death, repentance and a desire to live in Christ’s image. Unlike Christmas, which is always on December 25, Easter - the most important celebration in Christianity - falls between March 22 and April 25.The actual date is determined by solar and lunar timing as it is the first Sunday after the first full moon that occurs on or after the March 21 Spring equinox. This formula was established by the Council of Nicea (AD 325) and ties loosely to Jewish Passover, since that is when scripture says the crucifixion and resurrection occurred. This year Easter falls on April 5. Lent is a 40-day period of preparation leading up to Easter. The 40 days reflects the 40 days that Jesus spent in the wilderness before beginning his ministry. 2026 LENTEN SERVICES Palm Sunday, March 29 at 10am Maundy Thursday, April 2 at 6pm Good Friday, April 3 at 7:30pm Easter Sunday, April 5 at 8:30 and 10am

articles.text: Reduction in property crime, rise in burglary Property crime declined in Piedmont in 2025, driven largely by a drop in larcenies, according to the Piedmont Police Department’s annual report presented to the City Council on Monday, March 2. Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies reviewed the report during the meeting. The report showed a significant reduction in property crime, driven largely by fewer larcenies. Burglary rose compared to Piedmont’s five-year average. Motor vehicle theft, assaults and robberies all declined in 2025. The addition of cameras in Piedmont and neighboring cities has helped officers respond more quickly and coordinate with other departments to address property crime. Police say many of these crimes are premeditated and often committed by repeat offenders. A regional effort to arrest major sellers of stolen goods has also contributed to the recent decline. Burglaries rose compared to Piedmont’s five-year average. Police plan to increase proactive patrols and deploy updated technology to improve response times. “We don’t want to be reactive to crime,” Chief Shavies said. “We want to be proactive, and we want to be out in our community. We want to make it uncomfortable for those who may think of coming into our community and committing crimes.” There was a sharp decline in motor vehicle theft in 2025. articles.text: Jerry Yu, a senior at Piedmont High School, represented the United States in Ljubljana, Slovenia from February 23–27 during the International Artificial Intelligence Olympiad (IAIO). The Olympiad brought together the top 95 high school students from around the world to solve advanced problems in machine learning, algorithms, and artificial intelligence theory. Yu was one of only four students selected nationwide to compete for Team USA at this prestigious global competition. The competition challenges participants through rigorous theoretical (scientific) and practical exams designed to test creativity, mathematical depth, and real-world A.I. application skills. The scientific round was structured like an exam with questions on different topics in machine learning theory, such as kernel methods and statistical learning theory. articles.text: Piedmont’s new Community Pool opens April 11. From April 11 through April 30, everyone can swim for $5 per visit. This limited-time preview pricing offers a low-cost way to see the new facility, get in the water, and try out the pools before deciding whether a pass is right for you. Starting May 1, visitors can choose between an annual pass, a summer pass, or a drop-in day pass. If you plan to swim more than occasionally, a pool pass is usually the best value. Annual passes are the best deal for regular swimmers and include the most perks for residents, including priority registration for summer swim lessons. Use the pool pass guide to find the option that best fits your household – or visit in-person assistance at the pool at upcoming front-desk help hours: Wednesday, March 11: 1-3 p.m., Thursday, March 12: 4-6 p.m., and Monday, March 16: 4-5 p.m. The Community Pool uses a flexible, “build-a-pass” model. Start with a base pass, Adult, Senior, or Family, then add household members if needed. Youth passes without add-on options are available for teens 14-18 who are the household’s only swimmer. Resident passholders receive additional benefits, including: priority registration for aquatics programs and swim lessons, and extra single-use guest passes. All Piedmont residents receive priority access to summer pass sales and early access to facility rentals. articles.text: Through February 24-26, the City of Piedmont removed a large redwood tree adjacent to the Tea House at the Community Hall. The city has been monitoring this particular tree for 10 years and removed it only after it was completely dead. The Park Commission plans to repurpose the tree in the Piedmont Park swing replacement project. pages.text: Volume 28, No. 21 Piedmont, California March 11, 2026 $1.81 Piedmont Post Piedmont Post A Community Newspaper Serving the Citizens of Piedmont Annual Police Report Reduction in property crime, rise in burglary By Jake Lannon Property crime declined in Piedmont in 2025, driven largely by a drop in larcenies, according to the Piedmont Police Department’s annual report presented to the City Council on Monday, March 2. Piedmont Police Chief Frederick Shavies reviewed the report during the meeting. The report showed a significant reduction in property crime, driven largely by fewer larcenies. Burglary rose compared to Piedmont’s five-year average. Motor vehicle theft, assaults and robberies all declined in 2025. The addition of cameras in Piedmont and neighboring cities has helped officers respond more quickly and coordinate with other departments to address property crime. Police say many of these crimes are premeditated and often committed by repeat offenders. A regional effort to arrest major sellers of stolen goods has also contributed to the recent decline. Burglaries rose compared to Piedmont’s five-year average. Police plan to increase proactive patrols and deploy updated technology to improve response times. “We don’t want to be reactive to crime,” Chief Shavies said. “We want to be proactive, and we want to be out in our community. We want to make it uncomfortable for those who may think of coming into our community and committing crimes.” There was a sharp decline in motor vehicle theft in 2025. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is sponsoring a No Kings 3 rally in Piedmont Park, 711 Highland Ave., Piedmont on Saturday, March 28 from 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. This will be one of many hundreds of rallies across the United States. These rallies are expected to draw millions of people who are concerned about the movement away from a society based on democratic principles, the Constitution, and toward an autocratic government headed by a “king” or “queen” who rules the country based on his or her whims. The rally will include brief speeches, songs, and a walk from the park along Highland Avenue. We encourage Piedmonters of all ages and others to come, experience the camaraderie, and, of course, bring your signs! The League of Women Voters of Piedmont is a nonpartisan, grassroots civic organization that encourages informed and active participation in government, works to increase understanding of major public policy issues, and influences public policy through education and advocacy. Membership in the League is open to people 16 years and older, of all gender identities. With over 100 years of experience, the League is one of America’s oldest and most trusted civic nonprofit organizations.

articles.text: The City is extending the deadline for Young Volunteer of the Year nominations to Wednesday, March 18. This year, the City is reviving the Volunteer of the Year award for the first time since 2019. The City is also introducing a new award: Young Volunteer of the Year (under age 25), intended to uplift the meaningful contributions young people make across Piedmont. Piedmont has long been known as the “City of Volunteers.” This award, first introduced in 2014, recognizes community members whose volunteer service helped strengthen Piedmont in 2025 – whether through neighborhood improvement, arts and culture, direct community support, or building a more welcoming and inclusive community. To nominate a volunteer, complete the online nomination form by Wednesday, March 18: https://form.jotform. com/260417487348162. Volunteer service can take many forms – from a long-running commitment to a concentrated effort that made a real difference in a single year. Nominations may recognize service that strengthened Piedmont through areas such as: • Community enrichment: improving neighborhoods and shared spaces, from beautification and clean-ups to public safety and neighborhood initiatives • Culture & Heritage: preserving local history, celebrating Piedmont’s diverse community, and supporting cultural events • Arts: strengthening the community through the visual and performing arts, arts educa- • • tion, events, and mentorship Social: direct community support and humanitarian service, including work with seniors, children, individuals with disabilities, families, and community health and safety Allyship: fostering belonging and solidarity, challenging bias, and helping make Piedmont a safe and welcoming community for everyone Nominations will be reviewed using a blind scoring process that considers measurable impact, service dedication, innovation and leadership, and character and values. Top-scoring nominees are then forwarded to a City Council subcommittee for final selection. Awardees will be recognized at the City’s annual Volunteer Appreciation Reception on April 20, 2026. articles.text: Create an account and view initial programs The Piedmont Community Pool’s new aquatics registration portal is now live. Visit rec.us/ piedmont to view initial program offerings and start setting up your household’s account. This site will contain information on pool passes, swim lessons, water fitness, and reservations for the new pool’s two rental facilities. The new system was selected for ease of use, works well on phones, and supports expanded payment options. Pass sales, rental bookings, and program registration will open on a staggered schedule. Before registration begins, community members should create their accounts and add household members who may participate in lessons or programs. Adding household members ahead of time helps ensure you are ready to register the correct participant when registration opens. The site also includes a “Fast Track” feature that works like a wish list. You can save programs you’re interested in and complete required forms in advance, making the checkout process faster when registration opens. Fast Track does not reserve space in a program. The rec department has provided a step-by-step guide on how to use the Fast Track feature at the following link: help.rec.us/ en/articles/9309226-how-to-usefast-track-your-ultimate-registration-hack The April 11 opening date marks the start of a ramp-up period. Hours and programming will be more limited at first, then expand over time as programs come online. Information about initial pool hours and other operating details will be shared closer to opening. Visit rec.us/piedmont to create your account, add household members, and explore offerings. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/pool for details on pool passes, pricing, and general information about Piedmont’s newest facility. The competition and activity pools at Piedmont Community Pool

articles.text: 18th annual event is March 20-22 Mountain View Cemetery invites the community to attend the 18th Annual Tulip Exhibition at the cemetery’s Tower Chapel, Friday through Sunday, March 20-22, from 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The free event welcomes Spring with striking f loral arrangements by Bay Area florists, garden clubs, and students from a college floral design class. Photographers, florists, flower enthusiasts, and nature and art lovers are welcome. Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s annual tulip exhibit has become a cherished community tradition. Under the guidance of Special Events Coordinator Kristie Ly, 2026 marks the exhibit’s third year back after a hiatus due to COVID-19 restrictions. “It is a must-see free event for all nature, plant, and floral enthusiasts alike,” said Ly. “Tulips on the Beach” by Patty Dunlap and Molly Ashford from the 2024 Tulip Exhibition Following the exhibition, guests may enjoy a Pop-up Arts Show at J. Miller Flowers, one block away, as it celebrates its 56th year in business. The pop-up show will take place from 11 a.m. - 3 p.m. Mountain View Cemetery (5000 Piedmont Avenue) is a historic garden cemetery in the foothills of Oakland and Piedmont. One of the oldest cemeteries in the Western U.S., it has served the community since 1863 and even includes a section for Civil War soldiers. For more information on the cemetery and its annual tulip exhibition, visit www.mountainviewcemetery.org.
articles.title: Tulip Exhibition at Mountain View Cemetery

Red-tailed and Cooper’s Hawks, Osprey and Barn Owls as well as a half dozen other raptors reside in the Bay Area. Enjoy a fascinating, engaging and feather-filled evening with Berkeley veteran raptor biologist Allen Fish, who has been studying birds of prey across California for more than 40 years.

articles.text: Staff The Bay Area Book Festival (BABF), will return to Berkeley for its 12th year on May 30–31, 2026, under the theme “Writing the Future.” Organizers say the festival will again transform Downtown Berkeley into a multiday celebration of literature, storytelling and cultural activism. This year’s event is expected to feature more than 300 authors and speakers across more than 120 programs on 21 stages, drawing more than 25,000 attendees from across the Bay Area. Festivalgoers will be able to attend 15 free writing workshops, book readings and author conversations, along with opportunities to connect with small presses, emerging writers, book artists and literary organizations. YouthLit, the festival’s youth and family programming track, will expand to two full days this year. Programming will be led by the Oakland-based Social Justice Children’s Book Fair and will include a special activation from ArtEsteem, a West Oakland nonprofit focused on healing arts. Inspired by the legacies of Octavia Butler and James Baldwin, this year’s theme encourages participants to move beyond reacting to crises and toward imaginative action aimed at building more just futures. articles.text: Ready for a new best friend? So is Koala! This 11-year-old tabby quickly overcomes her shyness to become a devoted companion—often curling up as the little spoon for movie night. Koala is wonderfully expressive. She’ll make soft eye contact and meow sweetly to invite you to follow her around the house, sometimes flopping down mid-walk for a surprise cuddle. When she’s at her happiest, she kneads enthusiastically, purrs loudly, and occasionally drools as she makes biscuits. This darling old lady knows what she likes, and that is to be the only cat in a calm, indooronly home, complete with her favorite litter box set-up (low sides, please!). Her daily medication and love of routine help her stay confident and comfortable. Although she’s not a kitAdopt Koala through Cat Town. ten anymore, Koala still has a playful side. She loves chasing her wand toy near you and goes wild for catnip. After a quick burst of play, she’s ready to settle in with an adoring gaze for close snuggles. Koala is ready to reward you with endless affection— and plenty of cuddles. Koala is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www. cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org.
articles.title: Adoptable Cat of the Week

articles.text: Arthur Spring is puppy season and Oakland Animal Services is looking for folks to help out by fostering a puppy or puppies. These two puppies, DW Read and Arthur Read, are available for adoption. Puppies are typically adopted very quickly and fostering one for even a weekend or a week is extremely helpful. Puppies can be fostered individually, in pairs or in larger numbers. Email dogfostering@oaklandsanimals.org with questions. Prospective fosters with a dog at home or child under 12 must bring them to meet the foster dog or puppy at Oakland Animal Services.

articles.text: Many parents today work hard to give their children every opportunity to succeed. Between school, homework, sports, and other activities, kids’ schedules can fill up fast. While structure is important, so is making room for unstructured fun. Unstructured fun is a time when children are free to play, explore, and interact without constant instruction or pressure. For kids in upper elementary and early middle school, this time is especially valuable. It helps them build confidence, independence, and social skills as they learn to solve problems, work through disagreements, and make decisions on their own. Parents also see the benefits emotionally. With increased academic demands and screen time, many kids experience higher levels of stress. Unstructured play offers a natural way to unwind, connect with peers, and enjoy being active without worrying about performance or results. These moments often lead to stronger friendships and improved well-being. Of course, unstructured does not mean unsupervised or unsafe. The best programs provide a balance: a safe, supportive environment with enough freedom for kids to take small risks, be creative, and grow. That balance is the foundation of Scherman Summer Camp, which has been running for six years and is led by the son of Piedmont Middle School teacher Ted Scherman. Campers spend mornings playing games and participating in group activities on Coaches Field, followed by lunch and free play at Piedmont Park. The Scherman Summer Camp runs from 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m.,

articles.text: Now celebrating its 57th year, Piedmont’s Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will take place on Friday, March 20, at 7 pm in the Alan Harvey Theater. The theme this year is ‘Free As A Bird’ and tickets may be purchased at https://piedmontbirdcalling.ludus.com/index.php The judges for this year’s contest are: • Jaime Chaves Jaime Chaves is a Professor in the Biology Department at San Francisco State University. He has been on the faculty since 2020. His projects are based on international multidisciplinary collaboration involving local students and communities. His specialties are Evolution, Phylogenetics, Phylogeography, Ornithology, Galapagos and Darwin’s finches. This is his first time serving as a judge for the Piedmont Bird Calling Contest. • Mercedes Foster Mercedes Foster has been a member of the Piedmont High School English Department since 2004. Though she didn’t attend PHS as a student, she played the part of a quail in a Bird Calling skit 20 years ago and is honored to participate as a judge this year. A life-long avian enthusiast, she has cared for parrots, parakeets, foundling doves, finches, parakeets, and, most recently, chickens. She is currently trying but failing to befriend the crows that hang out in her front yard. • Michael Poryes Michael Poryes is a Piedmont High alum of the Class of ‘73. As a PHS student, he always looked forward to attending the Bird Calling Contest. He has spent the past 45 years working in the entertainment industry in situation comedies. He was a writer and producer on many shows such as Who’s The Boss, The Facts of Life, Cybil, Veronica’s Closet and Saved By The Bell. He is most well-known for creating and Executive Producing the hit shows Hannah Montana and That’s So Raven. He’s very excited to once again be a judge at Piedmont’s Annual Bird Calling Contest.
articles.title: Judges for Bird Calling Contest announced

articles.text: Awe might seem like a luxury emotion. Something nice to experience on a vacation or in a dramatic moment, but not especially relevant to everyday life. In reality, awe plays a quiet but important role in creativity. When we experience awe, even briefly, our attention expands. We become more curious, more observant, and more open to possibilities we might otherwise overlook. Awe interrupts our routines and reminds us that the world is larger and more interesting than the narrow track our thoughts sometimes run on. When we talk about awe, though, we often imagine something huge. A sweeping landscape. A once in a lifetime trip. A moment so big it stops you in your tracks. Those moments are wonderful when they happen, but they are also rare. If awe depends on something spectacular, most of us will spend a lot of our time waiting for it. Lately I have been wondering if awe might be a little more available than that. Not the cinematic kind, but the quieter version that shows up in ordinary places if we slow down enough to notice it. A leaf that has turned exactly the color of copper. The geometry of frost on a window. The sound of a group of people laughing all at once. The way sunlight moves across a room over the course of an afternoon. The look in a child’s eye when they understand something new. None of these things are dramatic. In fact, most of them happen every day. But they are small reminders that the world is far more intricate and surprising than we usually give it credit for. The problem is not that awe is absent, it’s that we move through our days so quickly that we miss it. So here is a small experiment to try. For the next week, choose one ordinary moment each day and look at it a little longer than usual. Maybe it is something outside your window. Maybe it is a pattern, a sound, or a moment of interaction between people that grabs your attention. Stay with it for thirty seconds or a minute and see what you notice once your attention settles. You do not have to photograph it, analyze it, or turn it into anything. The key is just to notice it. Creativity often begins with this kind of attention. Before we make something new, we have to remember that the world itself is already full of interesting things. Awe does not always arrive as a thunderbolt. Sometimes it begins as a quiet realization that there is more here than we first saw. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Creativity experiment: Practicing awe at human scale

articles.text: In May 2025, the City Council approved a Civic Center Parking Plan to reduce congestion and improve pedestrian safety in the Civic Center. As a part of this plan, the City has installed a new pick-up and drop-off zone for Havens School on Highland Avenue across the street from the school. The City encourages families to use this area to drop off their students to reduce traffic. A crossing guard will assist students across Highland Avenue to the campus. The new zone will reduce turn movements and improve safety for students, families, and other road users during high-traffic school periods. Parking is only allowed in the white curb zone outside of school drop-off and pick-up hours. The new drop-off zone was one part of a series of changes in the Civic Center area, designed to improve safety and reduce congestion during Havens Elementary drop-off and pick-up. The area adds more visitor parking to support increased Civic Center activity when the new Community Pool opens and provides additional handicap parking. The next steps for civic center parking planned for next summer will include: • Converting Bonita Avenue between Vista Avenue and Oakland Avenue to one-way traffic (northbound toward Oakland Avenue) • Eliminating the school dropoff zone on Bonita • Adding additional ADA, time-limited, and employee parking spaces on Bonita The new pick-up and drop-off zone for Havens School on Highland Avenue across the street from the school
articles.title: New pick-up & drop-off zone for Havens families

pages.text: Wednesday, March 11, 2026 7 Tickets on sale for Spring Fling Gala By Heather Meil Piedmont Education Foundation has announced that its 2026 Spring Fling Gala will take place on Friday, May 1, from 6:00 to 11:00 p.m. at Bloc15 in Oakland. This year’s event will transform the venue into a glamorous, James Bond 007 inspired experience, bringing Beach, Havens, and Wildwood parents together for an evening of intrigue, celebration, and impact. Guests can expect an immersive atmosphere, lively entertainment, curated cuisine, and opportunities to invest directly in Piedmont’s public elementary schools. “This is one mission our entire community can rally behind,” said Gala Co-Chair Jenny Miller. “The Gala is not only a memorable night out, it’s one of the most important ways we fund the programs that make our schools exceptional.” Co-Chair Zeena Fakoury emphasized the role families play in the event’s success. “Every great operation depends on strong partners. Parent sponsorship is the most powerful way to maximize the impact of this evening and ensure our schools continue to thrive.” “We are thrilled to host this year’s Gala at Bloc15,” added Co-Chair Caroline Gershwin. “It’s a stunning space that perfectly captures the sophistication and energy of our Bond theme. We can’t wait to welcome the community for a night that’s both fun and deeply meaningful.” Early-bird tickets are now available. In addition to purchasing tickets, families and local businesses are encouraged to participate through sponsorship opportunities that directly amplify the event’s fundraising impact. For tickets and sponsorship information, please visit PiedmontSpringFling.org. The Education Foundation’s annual Spring Fling Gala will occur Friday, May 1. (510) 327-1325 | GRANDLAKEVET.COM 3331 GRAND AVE, OAKLAND, CA 94610 New pick-up & drop-off zone for Havens families By Jake Lannon In May 2025, the City Council approved a Civic Center Parking Plan to reduce congestion and improve pedestrian safety in the Civic Center. As a part of this plan, the City has installed a new pick-up and drop-off zone for Havens School on Highland Avenue across the street from the school. The City encourages families to use this area to drop off their students to reduce traffic. A crossing guard will assist students across Highland Avenue to the campus. The new zone will reduce turn movements and improve safety for students, families, and other road users during high-traffic school periods. Parking is only allowed in the white curb zone outside of school drop-off and pick-up hours. The new drop-off zone was one part of a series of changes in the Civic Center area, designed to improve safety and reduce congestion during Havens Elementary drop-off and pick-up. The area adds more visitor parking to support increased Civic Center activity when the new Community Pool opens and provides additional handicap parking. The next steps for civic center parking planned for next summer will include: • Converting Bonita Avenue between Vista Avenue and Oakland Avenue to one-way traffic (northbound toward Oakland Avenue) • Eliminating the school dropoff zone on Bonita • Adding additional ADA, time-limited, and employee parking spaces on Bonita The new pick-up and drop-off zone for Havens School on Highland Avenue across the street from the school The best quality in all departments Serving our community for 124 years CURRENT STORE HOURS Monday through Saturday – 9:00 am to 8:00 pm Sunday – 9:00 am to 7:00 pm Piedmont Avenue • Oakland, California 94611 • 510-653-8181 Open Seven Days • Free Parking

articles.text: Debate duo preps for NPDL National Parliamentary Debate League TOC in San Diego Piedmont High School’s Joey Assalian and Noah Sarlin turned in impressive performances in the 2026 Evergreen Invitational Parliamentary Debate Tournament last month finishing second. The team advanced through the competitive open division field in the online tournament before falling just short of the championship in a hard-fought final. Parliamentary debate is a fast-paced, two-on-two format modeled on the traditions of the British Parliament. Teams receive their motion, a resolution on a political, philosophical, or social issue, just minutes before the round begins, with no notes or prepared evidence allowed. The pair went 4-1 in preliminary rounds to earn a high seed heading into the elimination rounds, then rattled off three consecutive wins to punch their ticket to the championship round. There, they faced Nueva School’s Asudani & Bernhard, who ultimately claimed the title, in a finals that went Nueva’s way. Debaters must construct and deliver compelling arguments entirely on their feet, alternating speeches between the Government side, which defends the motion, and the Opposition side, which challenges it. Points of Information — brief interjections where opponents challenge a speaker mid-speech — add an extra layer of strategy to every exchange. A runner-up finish at the online invitational represents a significant milestone for the Piedmont duo, who have shown steady improvement throughout the season. Piedmont coach Holden Carrillo expressed pride in his debaters’ trajectory. “Joey and Noah have put in the work, and performances like this are a reflection of that,” Carrillo said. “Reaching the finals of a tournament this competitive tells you a lot about where they are as a team. The goal now is to take everything we learned here and be ready when it counts most.” “Getting to a final is great, but what excites me is how they’re thinking on their feet now — the speed of their analysis, the way they’re adapting mid-round,” said fellow Piedmont coach Will White. “That’s exactly the kind of debating that wins at a TOC.” Assalian and Sarlin will compete next at the NPDL Tournament of Champions, held April 10-12 at Canyon Crest Academy in San Diego. Described as the culminating celebration of high school parliamentary debate in the United States, the NPDLTOC draws qualifiers who have earned bids through sanctioned tournaments or at-large selection. Piedmont High School students Noah Sarlin (left) and Joey Assalian have found success as a Parliamentary Debate team.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 11, 2026 9 By Evolette Mak Before I went to Paris, I was convinced I wouldn’t like it as much as everyone else seemed to. I had seen the glossy photos and endless posts staged in front of the Eiffel Tower and assumed the city would feel overexposed, like it was performing for tourists. I also carried the usual stereotypes: Parisians are rude, impatient, dismissive if your French isn’t perfect. I expected to feel like an outsider. What surprised me while visiting during the school February break wasn’t that Paris was romantic but how the city felt grounded and deeply self-assured. My assumptions dissolved, not because the city dazzled me, but because it revealed how firmly it holds onto its identity. That realization began at the Salon International de l’Agriculture. In a global capital, I found massive halls dedicated to regional cheeses, livestock competitions, and farmers proudly representing their provinces. Families sampled products from across France, and conversations The Post’s intern explores Paris flowed easily between strangers. The festival was a celebration of national and regional identity. I saw the same authenticity in the weekend food markets that stretched for blocks. Streets were filled with produce, seafood, roasted meats, bread, and flowers. Parisians moved slowly from stall to stall, greeting vendors they clearly knew. The flea markets carried a sense of continuity: old postcards, vintage jackets, preserved butterflies, forgotten vinyl records. Every object felt like a fragment of someone else’s history. Nothing about it felt manufactured. Even at the Louvre Museum, I avoided the checklist approach. Instead of pushing toward the Mona Lisa, I found a quiet sketching room and sat drawing in stillness. That small, almost hidden space felt more reflective of Paris than the crowds did. Later, at 59 Rivoli, I encountered the opposite atmosphere: paint-splattered staircases, open studios, art that was playful, political, and unpolished. Together, those spaces showed me that Paris protects both its historical grandeur and The requisite photo of Paris’ iconic landmark, the Eiffel Tower A look down Rue Blanche in the 9th arrondissement of Paris, France its contemporary edge. The neighborhoods reinforced that impression. In Le Marais, I spent afternoons moving between secondhand shops and independent boutiques. Nothing felt standardized. Which led me to one of the biggest differences I noticed: the dominance of small businesses. Bakeries were single storefronts with regulars who were known by name. Cheese shops specialized. Butchers, florists, and designers operated on a human scale. Commerce felt personal. Coming from the United States, where convenience often means the same chains repeated city after city, the contrast was striking. Paris felt economically structured in a way that protects individuality. The prevalence of independent shops isn’t flashy, but it preserves character. Neighborhoods don’t blur together; they retain distinct identities shaped by the people who run them. By the end of the trip, Paris hadn’t dazzled me in the way I once imagined. What stayed with me were the ordinary experiences: the agricultural fair, the block-long markets, the flea stalls, the sketching room, the artist collective, the independent shops. I went expecting cliché and distance. I left recognizing Paris as a city that has preserved its identity in the face of globalization. articles.text: Former Piedmont Mayor Michael Bruck visited Columbia with 13 Oakland and Berkeley Rotary Club members plus seven guests in March of 2025. The group participated in hands-on service projects in and around Medellin, Colombia, learned about new projects that will assist other communities in need, and established friendships with members of Medellin, Colombia Rotary Clubs. Oakland Rotary Club is the third oldest Rotary Club in the world. There are now more than 45,000 clubs in the USA, but with more than 250 active members, Rotary Club of Oakland #3 remains one of the largest in size and impact. Grants for service projects go through local clubs, so the Oakland and Berkeley members sometimes travel to decide what projects to invest in while providing philanthropy on site. Members of the Oakland Rotary Club attended their first Rotary Project Fair in Cartagena, Colombia in 2016. The club met local Colombian Rotarians at this Project Fair and began building relationships ten years ago. Groups from Oakland Rotary Club traveled to Colombia in 2016, 2018, and 2019; in 2025 they returned for a 10-day visit with Berkeley members too. The representatives for Berkeley and Oakland Rotary conduct many layers of philanthropy including hands on work, meeting people in the community, and also researching for future projects for Rotary to fund. Adrián Gutiérrez (left), Mayor of Salgar, Colombia and former Piedmont Mayor Michael Bruck Oakland & Berkeley Rotary Club took part in the “Corre por Amor” or Run for Love, a 5K-12K race on March 16, 2025 to fundraise for individuals with spina bifida. Rotarians visited schools outside of Salgar that will be benefiting from the clean water and sanitation projects.

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District will continue to accept nominations for the 2026 Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award until March 13. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. Previous recipients include: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000); Lisa Lomenzo (2001); jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002); jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003); Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004); Cynthia Gorman (2005); Grier Graff (2006); Julia Burke (2007); Maude Pervere (2008); jointly to Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009); Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010); Andrea Swenson (2011), June Monach (2012), Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013), Ray Perman (2014), Jennifer Fox (2015), Katie Korotzer (2016), Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018), Cathy Glazier (2019), Sue Smegal (2020), Ken Li (2021), Eileen Ruby (2022), David Ragones (2023), Sarah Pearson (2024) and most recently, Cory Smegal in 2025. Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982. Art also was very active with the Piedmont Continuation High School (now called Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established in his memory by School Board member Dewey Watson. Nominations for this award are now being sought and will be kept strictly confidential. The deadline for nominations is March 13. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 6, Board of Education meeting, where the honoree’s good works will be acknowledged. Nomination forms are available on the bottom of the Superintendent’s webpage Piedmont. k12.ca.us/ref/superintendent, in the District Office (760 Magnolia Avenue), or by calling Rosalina Barrios, Executive Assistant to the Superintendent, at 594-2614. Rotarians also participated and assisted in the fundraising for the “Corre por Amor” or Run for Love, a 5K-12K race on March 16, 2025 that supported individuals with spina bifida and other disabilities. Rotarians and supporters of the race walked while many of the patients pushed their way in wheelchairs. The Rotary Group visited Fundacion Monica Uribe por Amor which also supports individuals with spina bifida, and spent time with patients to play ping pong, and have wheelchair races. “We had wheelchair races with the kids. I’ll give you one guess who won the races, and it wasn’t the rotarians,” Bruck said with a smile. Rotarians also visited the aquaponics project at Fundacion Hogar San Jose, where fish provide nutrients to grow vegetables. Rotarian funded projects brought clean water to rural schools by buying water filters, chlorination equipment, and renovating bathrooms for eights schools. Their efforts buoyed the support of both local Colombia and other international clubs to create water wells, tanks, and pumps for clean water, benefiting 7,500 indigenous residents in rural areas. “When you become a [Rotary] member, you get a little rotary pin with the rotary wheel. We tell [new members], ‘put on your pin, and you’ll be welcomed all over the world,’ and it’s really true,” said Bruck. articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team’s season came to an end on Thursday, March 5, in a 51-49 loss to No. 6 seed Central East of Fresno in the second round of the Division 1 CIF State tournament at Binks Rawlings Gym. Piedmont was the No. 3 seed. The team opened with a 63-57 win over No. 14 Antelope on Tuesday, March 3. “We knew Central East would be a tough team, obviously everyone at this stage is,” said PHS coach Bryan Gardere. “We had some costly turnovers, but collectively I thought we did a good job. We just ran out of time.” PHS opened strongly with a 19-4 lead by the end of the first period, but the Bengals stormed back to take a 28-22 by halftime. With an aggressive press, CEHS went on a 19-1 run to take a 23-22 lead with 1:17 left, and added five more points. “We got off to a good start, but the second quarter was obviously the difference in the game. I still think if you take a few mistakes away, we’re right there,” Gardere reflected. Trailing 51-41 with 2:11 left in the game, the Highlanders didn’t quit, going on an eight-point run to the final buzzer. It was a dramatic final seconds of the game, where Jenelle Solis stole a ball that led to a layup by Nia Jackson bouncing off the rim multiple times, leading to an offensive rebound by Andrea Martin. “Although it was a hard loss, we’re still staying together. We’re going to go into the offseason really working hard. When we get to this stage next year, we know what to do,” Martin said. Despite falling short, the Highlanders’ future is still bright. Martin, Solis, Savannah Dennig, and Jaden Jones will be juniors next season, Alexa Ba will be a sophomore, and Taylor White and Jackson are poised to be the only senior of the bunch. Saniyah Johnson is the only graduating senior on the team. “I’m really proud of our seniors. I’m just happy we got to play together. We’re losing one senior, but hey, it’s time for everyone to step up and get better,” Martin said. “We’re definitely going to use this as fuel. We only lose Saniyah, who is a big player to lose, but we still have a good core Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to an end against Central East in the second round of the D1 CIF State tournament. coming back. We’ll take this loss, learn from it, and take it into next season,” mentioned Ba. 51-49 loss to Central East Piedmont came out hot with a 19-4 lead in the first quarter, including 11 points from Martin and eight from Ba. But Central East was on fire in the second quarter, scoring 24 points, including four 3-pointers. In the third quarter, both teams traded baskets until the Bengals went on a 9-2 run to build a 10-point lead at 41-31 with two minutes remaining. After that Jaden Jones hit a 3-pointer, while Martin hit a pair of free throws and White converted a layup to end the quarter in a 43-38 deficit. Solis made a 3-pointer early in the second, but Central East followed with eight straight points to extend its lead to 51-41 with 2:11 left in the game. From there, PHS scored its eight remaining points to finish the game. Martin hit a layup, then Solis assisted Johnson, while Martin stole a ball, turning it to Solis for an assist to Ba with 1:06 left—51-47. After back and forth trades of possession, White stole a ball, leading to a bucket by Martin with 29 seconds left, putting PHS within one possession at 51-49. Central East gained possession, leading to a steal by Solis. Nia Jackson went up for a layup, and the ball dramatically bounced off the rim before falling away. Martin grabbed an offensive rebound with 14 seconds left, leading to a timeout. Then, on Piedmont’s ensuing inbounds play, Martin went up hoping for a pass on the mark, but it was slightly behind her, leading to a turnover with 10.5 seconds left. CEHS was able to kill the clock from there. Final stats: Martin finished with 22 points, Ba had 13 points, White and Johnson had four points, while Solis and Jones had three. 63-57 win over Antelope Antelope got out to a 19-14 lead in the first quarter, but Piedmont cut the deficit to 32-30 by halftime. PHS took a 47-46 lead in the third, while they outscored the Titans 16-11 in the final going. Martin had 32 points and eight rebounds. Ba had 11 points. White had six points, nine rebounds, and eight assists. Andrea Martin had 22 points on Central East and 32 points on Antelope. Nia Jackson goes up for a layup in the final seconds against Central East.

articles.text: Staff Photos Massimo Mittone hit a grand slam home run in Piedmont’s 4-2 win over Head-Royce. Piedmont High’s baseball team remains undefeated through its first three games of the season. They beat Head-Royce 4-2 at Humphries Diamond on Wednesday, March 4 and wound up tying Cal High 3-3 on Friday, March 6. The game was tied in the ninth inning after the sun set. The Highlanders came back from early deficits in both games. They trailed 2-0 to Cal High before scoring three runs in the bottom of the third, and trailed 2-0 to Head-Royce before Massimo Mittone smacked a grand slam in the same inning. “Mo is a big player for us on the mound and with the bat,” coach Eric Olson said. Piedmont was able to lean on its defense in both games. They had a double play against the Jayhawks and forced 13 ground outs against California. “I don’t know if there’s a better defensive infield in the East Bay. We really want our pitchers to pitch for contact and we’ll catch the ball for him,” Olson said. The pair of results brings Piedmont’s record to 2-0-1 (W-LT) to start its season. 3-3 tie with California Cal High led 2-0 after the top of the second inning, while Piedmont pulled one back in the bottom half. The Highlanders went ahead 3-2 in the bottom of the third, while California scored the tying run in top of the seventh. Neither team scored in the eighth inning, leading to a conclusion of play with a lack of sunlight. In the bottom second, Jack Meyjes led off with a walk, while freshman Ben Sorensen drew a one-out walk. Sophomore outfielder Aiden Bell then cracked a single to move Meyjes to load the bases. Enzo Ong grounded into a fielder’s choice to bring in Meyjes from third, but that was all the Highlanders could muster. Piedmont pulled ahead in the bottom of the third after Lucas Delventhal led off with a single, while Diego Delventhal drew a walk. Jonah Cha-Foster kept it going with a single to load the bases, once again. That’s when Jack Meyjes slugged a single to center field to tie up the game 2-2. Massimo Mittone hit a sacrifice fly to score Diego Delventhal, while Cal High was able to end the inning by throwing out Jonah Cha-Foster had two hits against Cal High, and one hit against Head-Royce to go along with a run and stolen base. Aiden Bell went 1-for-3 with a double against Head-Royce, and 1-for-2 against Cal High.

articles.text: Tennis is back at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, as the Piedmont High boys’ tennis team opened its season with a 4-2 record. The Highlanders lost 9-0 at Acalanes on Thursday, February 26, swept Arroyo 7-0 in San Lorenzo on Thursday, March 5, while they went 3-1 at the James Logan Tournament in Union City on Friday and Saturday, March 6-7. At the tournament, Piedmont claimed 4-3 wins over three schools, including Granada, Emerald, and Heritage. They closed with a 5-2 loss to Campolindo. “We’re off to a good start. We played Friday and Saturday, and did well even without our top player, Lucas Smolko. We took second and lost in the finals to Campolindo,” coach Jim Landes said. Smolko leads the singles lineup for the final year of his high school career. He’ll be the Western Alameda County Conference favorite to win his third consecutive league singles title, while he’s seeking his first North Coast Section title after reaching the finals in 2023 and 2025. Should he reach the NCS individual tournament singles’ title match, he’ll likely face HeadRoyce’s Dylan Donovan. Smolko lost to Donovan in three sets, 5-7, 6-1, 6-3, in last year’s final. “It’s possible for Lucas to take that next step, but he’s got Dylan to contend with again. I’m sure it’ll be another close battle between them,” Landes said. Behind Smolko is fellow fouryear starter, Nate Welch. Freshman Ari Moskovitz has emerged as Landes’ No. 3 singles starter, and sophomore Emilio Misra enters his second year on the squad at No. 4. “Nate is our No. 2, He’s starting to play pretty well. He’s got a huge serve; he just has to play more consistently. I want him to come to the net more. He’s got great reach and is about 6’3”. He’s a really offensive player and takes a lot of risks,” Landes said. “We have a freshman at No. 3. Ari plays at some of my clinics and he’s going to be really good. Playing No. 4 is Emilio who has improved from last year and is more of a defensive player. He has the ability to be an offensive player, but is hiding it sometimes,” Landes added. At doubles, sophomore duo Joey Assalian and Ben Davis are taking over the No. 1 spot. “Ben Davis and Joey Assalian are our top doubles team. Joey worked very hard in the offseason and is playing pretty darn well. Ben is just a natural. They went undefeated in the James Logan tournament,” Landes said. Behind them, Landes is keeping an eye on how things unfold. Freshmen August Collins and Henry Van Den Bos are competing with juniors Hunter Fasteau and Maximo Miller, in doubles. “It’s a toss-up. The freshmen are very even with Hunter and Maximo. They battled it out at the last challenge match. It’s hard to say who is #2 and two and who is #3,” Landes said. 5-2 loss to Campolindo At singles, Welch lost 6-1, 6-1 at No. 1. Moskovitz fell 6-1, 6-1 at No. 2, Collins lost 6-4, 6-2 at No. 3, and Van Den Bos lost 6-1, 6-0 at No. 4. At doubles, Davis and Assalian won 8-4 at the top spot. Misra and Fasteau won 8-4 at Staff Photos Lucas Smolko looks for his third WACC singles title, and reach his third NCS singles final. Nate Welch is the team’s No. 2 singles starter.
