articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team is 2-1 through its first three games, They opened the season with a 6-3 victory over Miramonte at Witter Field on March 3, an 18-6 win over Northgate in Walnut Creek on March 5, and a a14-8 loss to Clayton Valley in Walnut Creek on February 26. The Highlanders are embarking on their first season under Andy Kittler, the school’s fourth coach since 2023. Former coach Al Yu led PHS to the NCS Finals in 2023, Jeff Lamb had a one-year stint in 2024, and then former PHS graduate Paul Pappas took the reins in 2025. “We want to reestablish the traditions of Piedmont High School. When you lack continuity in a coaching staff, you lost some of it. First and foremost, we want to rebuild the pipeline from JV. It’s about inspiring a love of the game by seniors down to freshmen,” Kittler said. Kittler served as assistant coach under Lamb in 2024. He played collegiately for Princeton in 2008, and served as an assistant coach at Stanford for five years from 2010-2014. “You can never overemphasize fundamentals, and I think that goes all the way up to professional sports. Passing, catching, footwork, communications – we really want to emphasize things that are basic to every sport. We want to build a really positive culture,” Kittler said. Through three matches, Kittler is pleased with what he’s seeing. He’s focused on revitalizing the entire program. “It’s a small team, we have 21 on the varsity roster and 11 on the JV, which is quite a bit smaller than teams we play in terms of numbers. We have a really good core group of juniors and seniors. We have all the tools of a team that can make a good playoff run,” Kittler said. The squad has some key returners, like junior Connor Fredericks, a talented faceoff specialist. Senior Timmy Kalamas was the leading scorer on the squad last season, and senior Staff Photos New head coach Andy Kittler (right) pictured in 2024 alongside former coach Jeff Lamb. Ian Nguyen is another returning attacker. Junior Milo Stevenson is also expected to make an impact. “Those are the big contributors. Those guys are pivotal for us and Milo is on the verge of a breakout year, I think he’ll be a big player for us this and next year,” Kittler said. P.J. Brayer returns as the team’s top defender, while sophomore Jax Thayer also got time last season. Fischer Veltri is another key defender. “The defense has been strong. In high school lacrosse, it’s easier to be good at defense. Our defense is really solid; Jax, Fischer, and P.J. are a very athletic and talented group,” Kittler said. Piedmont faces the task of replacing four-year starting goalie Gus Von Metzsch. Senior Luke McAuliffe, who was a three-year starting goalie for the water polo team, has made the jump from the pool to the field. McAuliffe will split halves with junior Denis Radzik. 6-3 win over Miramonte Piedmont led 1-0 through the first quarter, while Miramonte Connor Fredericks (left) and Timmy Kalamas are two key returning players from last year.

The Highlanders lost 9-0 at Acalanes on Thursday, February 26, swept Arroyo 7-0 in San Lorenzo on Thursday, March 5, while they went 3-1 at the James Logan Tournament in Union City on Friday and Saturday, March 6-7. At the tournament, Piedmont claimed 4-3 wins over three schools, including Granada, Emerald, and Heritage. They closed with a 5-2 loss to Campolindo. “We’re off to a good start. We played Friday and Saturday, and did well even without our top player, Lucas Smolko. We took second and lost in the finals to Campolindo,” coach Jim Landes said. Smolko leads the singles lineup for the final year of his high school career. He’ll be the Western Alameda County Conference favorite to win his third consecutive league singles title, while he’s seeking his first North Coast Section title after reaching the finals in 2023 and 2025. Should he reach the NCS individual tournament singles’ title match, he’ll likely face HeadRoyce’s Dylan Donovan. Smolko lost to Donovan in three sets, 5-7, 6-1, 6-3, in last year’s final. “It’s possible for Lucas to take that next step, but he’s got Dylan to contend with again. I’m sure it’ll be another close battle between them,” Landes said. Behind Smolko is fellow fouryear starter, Nate Welch. Freshman Ari Moskovitz has emerged as Landes’ No. 3 singles starter, and sophomore Emilio Misra enters his second year on the squad at No. 4. “Nate is our No. 2, He’s starting to play pretty well. He’s got a huge serve; he just has to play more consistently. I want him to come to the net more. He’s got great reach and is about 6’3”. He’s a really offensive player and takes a lot of risks,” Landes said. “We have a freshman at No. 3. Ari plays at some of my clinics and he’s going to be really good. Playing No. 4 is Emilio who has improved from last year and is more of a defensive player. He has the ability to be an offensive player, but is hiding it sometimes,” Landes added. At doubles, sophomore duo Joey Assalian and Ben Davis are taking over the No. 1 spot. “Ben Davis and Joey Assalian are our top doubles team. Joey worked very hard in the offseason and is playing pretty darn well. Ben is just a natural. They went undefeated in the James Logan tournament,” Landes said. Behind them, Landes is keeping an eye on how things unfold. Freshmen August Collins and Henry Van Den Bos are competing with juniors Hunter Fasteau and Maximo Miller, in doubles. “It’s a toss-up. The freshmen are very even with Hunter and Maximo. They battled it out at the last challenge match. It’s hard to say who is #2 and two and who is #3,” Landes said. 5-2 loss to Campolindo At singles, Welch lost 6-1, 6-1 at No. 1. Moskovitz fell 6-1, 6-1 at No. 2, Collins lost 6-4, 6-2 at No. 3, and Van Den Bos lost 6-1, 6-0 at No. 4. At doubles, Davis and Assalian won 8-4 at the top spot. Misra and Fasteau won 8-4 at See Boys’ Tennis on page 27 Staff Photos Lucas Smolko looks for his third WACC singles title, and reach his third NCS singles final. Nate Welch is the team’s No. 2 singles starter. Boys Lacrosse team off to solid start under new coach Andy Kittler By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team is 2-1 through its first three games, They opened the season with a 6-3 victory over Miramonte at Witter Field on March 3, an 18-6 win over Northgate in Walnut Creek on March 5, and a a14-8 loss to Clayton Valley in Walnut Creek on February 26. The Highlanders are embarking on their first season under Andy Kittler, the school’s fourth coach since 2023. Former coach Al Yu led PHS to the NCS Finals in 2023, Jeff Lamb had a one-year stint in 2024, and then former PHS graduate Paul Pappas took the reins in 2025. “We want to reestablish the traditions of Piedmont High School. When you lack continuity in a coaching staff, you lost some of it. First and foremost, we want to rebuild the pipeline from JV. It’s about inspiring a love of the game by seniors down to freshmen,” Kittler said. Kittler served as assistant coach under Lamb in 2024. He played collegiately for Princeton in 2008, and served as an assistant coach at Stanford for five years from 2010-2014. “You can never overemphasize fundamentals, and I think that goes all the way up to professional sports. Passing, catching, footwork, communications – we really want to emphasize things that are basic to every sport. We want to build a really positive culture,” Kittler said. Through three matches, Kittler is pleased with what he’s seeing. He’s focused on revitalizing the entire program. “It’s a small team, we have 21 on the varsity roster and 11 on the JV, which is quite a bit smaller than teams we play in terms of numbers. We have a really good core group of juniors and seniors. We have all the tools of a team that can make a good playoff run,” Kittler said. The squad has some key returners, like junior Connor Fredericks, a talented faceoff specialist. Senior Timmy Kalamas was the leading scorer on the squad last season, and senior Staff Photos New head coach Andy Kittler (right) pictured in 2024 alongside former coach Jeff Lamb. Ian Nguyen is another returning attacker. Junior Milo Stevenson is also expected to make an impact. “Those are the big contributors. Those guys are pivotal for us and Milo is on the verge of a breakout year, I think he’ll be a big player for us this and next year,” Kittler said. P.J. Brayer returns as the team’s top defender, while sophomore Jax Thayer also got time last season. Fischer Veltri is another key defender. “The defense has been strong. In high school lacrosse, it’s easier to be good at defense. Our defense is really solid; Jax, Fischer, and P.J. are a very athletic and talented group,” Kittler said. Piedmont faces the task of replacing four-year starting goalie Gus Von Metzsch. Senior Luke McAuliffe, who was a three-year starting goalie for the water polo team, has made the jump from the pool to the field. McAuliffe will split halves with junior Denis Radzik. 6-3 win over Miramonte Piedmont led 1-0 through the first quarter, while Miramonte See Boys’ Lacrosse on page 26 Connor Fredericks (left) and Timmy Kalamas are two key returning players from last year. articles.text: Piedmont High competed in two events on Saturday, March 7, including the K-Bell Classic at Westmont HS in San Jose and the Dan Gabor Invitational at Amador Valley HS in Pleasanton. It was a strong performance by Piedmont’s sprinters at the K-Bell. The 4x100 relay team of Noah Hussein, Maddox Ma, Diego Hurwitz, and Rehan Mumtaz won their event with a time of 44.36 seconds in a field of 15 teams. They narrowly beat Piedmont Hills High School by .32 of a second. “The sprint squad is red hot right now and it’s really fun to watch,” said coach Pouyan Assadi. “Our workouts are really resonating with the athletes, and for the most part they’re not skipping the weight room, which is key. They truly believe they’re a championship squad and they’re holding each other accountable for the effort they give in practice.” It was also a strong run by standout sprinter Claire Aubrecht, who placed second out of 98 runners in the 100 meter dash with a personal record time of 12.70 seconds. She topped her previous best by .19 of a second, set just one week prior at the Skyline Invitational. “I’m loving watching Claire’s technical adjustments in her race. She earned that 12.7 mark and there’s more to come,” Assadi said. Dan Gabor Invitational In Pleasanton at the Dan Gabor Invitational, senior Skylar Best had an impressive 11th-place finish in the 800 meters in a field of 155, clocking a personal record time of 2:23.44. which she set at last year’s WACC Championship. “Skylar had her first big leap of the season. That was a seven second drop on her season best to hit a new personal best which happened at the end of last season in May. She has a crazy high ceilPhotos by Aaron Aubrecht, @csevenstudios Rehan Mumtaz was a key part of the 4x100 relay team taking second at the K-Bell Classic. He also had strong runs in the 100 and 400 meters. Claire Aubrecht placed second of 98 sprinters in the 100 meter dash at the K-Bell Classic. ing and we’re hoping she keeps pushing herself. Other K-Bell Classic results In the boys’ 100, Mumtaz placed ninth of 161 in the 100 meter dash with a time of 11.26. Ma finished 13th in 11.36, while Hurwitz was 34th in 11.73. articles.text: Piedmont High’s softball team recently beat University 11-9 at the Witter Softball Field on Friday, March 6 to improve its record to 2-1 through three games. The Highlanders’ bats were alive, scoring runs in all but one inning, including five runs in the bottom of the first. “We didn’t get a lot of batting practice before the season, so it’s nice to see. We’ve been doing a lot of tee work, so I guess it’s paying off,” coach Gene Denard said. It was a big game for sophomore Edie Elmquist, who was 2-for-2 at the plate with three runs, two RBIs, plus three stolen bases. She was also the winning pitcher, throwing for four innings and struck out four. “Edie is one of our main players; she’s a leader of this team. As the season carries on, she’ll keep getting more comfortable with her role,” Denard said. 11-9 victory over University Piedmont took a 5-0 lead after the bottom of the first inning and led 6-1 through two innings. University scored four in the top of the third, while PHS added one in the bottom half, 7-5. The Red Devils went up in the top of the fourth with three runs, 8-7, but Piedmont answered with two runs in the bottom of the fifth to take a 9-8 lead. University tied in the top of the sixth, but the Highlanders scored the game’s final two runs in the bottom of the sixth and held the Red Devils scoreless in the top of the seventh to win it. Piedmont’s big first inning, Elmquist and Kajsa Benson led off with walks. Teah Suhr went 2-for-4 with a run, RBI, and stolen base against University. thrown out at third, leading to Rosemary Dickinson hitting a two-RBI double. Teah Suhr followed with an RBI single, Talia Perl reached first on an error, while Penelope Hopper had an RBI in a fielder’s choice. After Samanthe Schey and Kaolee Talati drew walks to load the Hannah Joerger went 2-for-4 with two runs and two RBIs against the Red Devils. bases, the lineup went all the way around to Elmquist, who was hit by a pitch to score Perl. In Piedmont’s go-ahead bottom of the fifth, PHS loaded the bases with a walk by Schey, a single by Elmquist, and a walk by Benson. Joerger then hit a 2-RBI single to score Elmquist and Schey, making it 9-8. With the game tied 9-9 in the bottom sixth, Hailey Navarro and Schey drew one-out walks. After Navarro stole third, Elmquist hit an RBI single for a 10-9 lead. With two outs, Elmquist ran in to score on a passed ball, 11-9. In the final inning, Elmquist retired the first two batters with ground outs, but University loaded the bases with two singles and a walk. That’s when Elmquist forced a fly out to Schey in right field. Final stats: Navarro scored a run, drew a walk and had a stolen base. Joerger went 2-for-4 with two runs scored, two RBIs and a walk. Elmquist went 2-for-2 with three runs scored, two RBIs, two walks, and stole three bases. Suhr went 2-for-4 with a run scored, an RBI, a walk and a stolen base. Hopper had an RBI. Benson went 1-for-2 with a run scored, an RBI and three walks. Schey scored a run and drew three walks. Perl scored a run, had one RBI, walk and stolen base. Dickinson went 2-for-3 with a run scored, two RBIs, two doubles, two walks and a stolen base. Elmquist was the winning pitcher with four innings of work, striking out four. Perl pitched three innings, striking out three and allowed just one earned run. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-1 overall) hosts San Rafael at Witter Field today, March 11, at 4:00 p.m. They also host American on Friday, March 13 at the same time.

articles.text: The international photography exhibition Ocean Photographer of the Year will make its United States debut April 24 inside a historic World War II aircraft hangar at Alameda Point. The exhibition, presented by Oceanographic Magazine and Blancpain, will run for one month and feature a selection of winning and finalist images from the global Ocean Photographer of the Year competition. The show is hosted locally by West End Arts District in partnership with Bay Photo Lab. Now in its fifth year, the competition received more than 15,000 submissions from photographers worldwide. The exhibition includes images from categories such as wildlife, fine art, adventure, conservation, human connection, and young photographer of the year, along with the Female Fifty Fathoms Award recognizing women in ocean photography. “We’re thrilled to bring Ocean Photographer of the Year to Alameda Point and to invite the community to experience this powerful ode to the ocean in such a unique setting,” Tara Pilbrow, executive director of West End Arts District, said in a press release. “By breathing new life into Alameda Point’s military history, we’re also expressing our commitment to the kind of future we want to see: one rooted in creativity, environmental awareness, and shared cultural experiences.” Alongside the international exhibition, visitors can explore “Bay Perspectives,” a gallery featuring ocean photography focused on the San Francisco Bay and the California coast. The space will also include interactive marine science exhibits presented by the Sailing Science Center. “The stories behind these photographs are as compelling as the visuals themselves – they challenge us to see the ocean not just as a place of wonder, but as a world in need of our care,” said Daryl Karp, director and chief executive officer of the Australian National Maritime Museum. Public hours will run Saturdays and Sundays from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., with additional programs scheduled on Thursdays and Fridays. An opening gala hosted by Bay Photo Lab will also mark the company’s 50th anniversary. “Our mission is to share the ocean with non-ocean goers and photography is the most awesome conduit to do that,” said Will Harrison of Oceanographic Magazine. “Underwater photography is one of the most powerful allies in our fight to preserve and protect the ocean,” added Gaël Nicolle of Blancpain. For more information and to purchase tickets to the exhibition and events, visit www.westendartsdistrict.org.
articles.title: Ocean Photographer of the Year exhibition debuts at Alameda Point April 24

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oakland Museum of California OMCA’s popular “Friday Nights” series of events kicks off the spring season. The Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) free community-gathering evening event series “Friday Nights” returns next month, kicking off the spring season with live performances and weekly food concessions. OMCA hosts free, family-friendly community events every Friday at 5 p.m. throughout spring and summer, featuring live music, immersive arts activities and late-night museum access with the purchase of a museum ticket. Bring a blanket and lawn chairs to relax on the museum’s large lawn, where live music and entertainment takes place throughout the evening. Guests can bring their own food and refreshments or purchase from a stationed food truck on-site. A rotating list of vendors will be parked on 10th Street between Oak and Fallon Streets adjacent to the museum. No outside alcohol is permitted. Friday Night events are always free and open to the public, but late-night museum access requires a ticket purchase. Visit https://museumca.org/about-friday-nights-at-omca-with-off-thegrid/ to learn more.
articles.title: “Friday Nights” returns to Oakland Museum of California next month

articles.text: Opera San Jose performs March 17 - 19 Spring blooms are beginning to appear at Filoli, where tens of thousands of tulips, daffodils and hyacinths are coming into season. The historic estate features more than 16 acres of formal gardens and a collection of native and exotic plants. In March, orchids, magnolias and citrus blossoms begin to open across the property. Visitors may also see tulips, irises, wisteria, peonies and seasonal wildflowers. Spring is considered the estate’s signature season. Gardeners plant more than 130,000 bulbs each year, filling garden beds and containers throughout the grounds. Opera San Jose will present a preview of its 2026–27 season at Filoli with selections from La Traviata. Performances are scheduled March 17–19 in the estate’s ballroom. Evening performances begin at 7 p.m., with tickets priced from $75 to $105. Guests may also purchase champagne for an additional fee. Filoli is open daily from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Evening tickets allow visitors to tour the house and gardens beginning at 5 p.m. and remain on the grounds until closing at 8 p.m. Evening tickets are released weekly for the following four weeks. Food and drinks are available on-site at the Quail Cafe and the Vegetable Garden Bar. More information is available at Filoli’s website at https://filoli. org/ or by calling (650) 364-8300. Filoli in spring

articles.text: A previous year’s performance of Don Quixote. San Francisco Ballet will present Don Quixote, inspired by the novel of the same name by Miguel de Cervantes, at the War Memorial Opera House from March 19 - 29. The production is based on the 19th-century choreography of Marius Petipa and Alexander Gorsky and was restaged for the company in 2003 by former artistic director Helgi Tomasson and choreographer Yuri Possokhov. The ballet features music by Ludwig Minkus. The story follows the romance between Kitri and Basilio and is known for technically demanding choreography, including the Act III pas de deux and a jump associated with the character of Kitri. The production includes 152 roles performed across four casts. Principal dancers scheduled to perform Kitri include Sasha De Sola, Nikisha Fogo, Wona Park and Madeline Woo, along with first soloist Katherine Barkman. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse recently announced that it is extending the Tony Award-winning musical Once, playing onstage now through March 29. Featuring a book by Enda Walsh and music and lyrics by Glen Hansard and Markéta Irglová, Once is based on the 2007 film that earned the Academy Award for Best Original Song for “Falling Slowly.” Set in Dublin, the story follows an Irish busker and a Czech immigrant who form a deep connection through music during a life-changing week of songwriting and collaboration. The production is directed by Josh Marx, with music direction by Michael Patrick Wiles and choreography by Erin Rose Solorio. Actors perform their own instruments onstage, creating a pub-style atmosphere that underscores the show’s themes of community and artistic partnership. “I’ve always loved Once because it digs into something I think about a lot: what music really is and how it connects us as human beings,” Marx said. “I loved the movie Once when I first saw it — and then the Broadway production pulled me in even deeper, especially the way it evoked a sense of community; similar to drinking a pint of Guinness in an Irish pub while patrons play music together. For Berkeley Playhouse’s production, we’re looking to put something truly special together; each actor plays their own instrument (sometimes more than one!), and we want to create an unforgettable experience that capitalizes on the amazing talent that we’re bringing into the room.” Jake Gale and Gillian Eichenberger lead the cast as Guy and Girl. For tickets or more information, call (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org. Photo by Ben Krantz Jake Gale and Gillian Eichenberger perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Once. articles.text: Sentimental Value, written and directed by Joachim Trier, who is well known for his cinematic exploration of family relationships (The Worst Person in the World). The film has received nine Oscar nominations to include Best Picture, Best Actress, Best Director, Best Supporting Actor, and Best Supporting Actress (both Elle Fanning and Inga Ibsdolder Lilleass). The story focuses on the fractured relationships between renowned Norwegian film director Gustav Borg (Stellan Skarsgard) and his daughters Nora (Renate Reinsve) and Agnes (Inga Ibsdolter Lilleaas). Central to their backstory is the choice Gustav made early in their lives to use his divorce from his wife, Sissel, as a reason to leave Norway and pursue a career writing and directing. That impactful decision has caused years of estrangement from his daughters. Unexpectedly their mother dies, and Gustav returns to Oslo where he awkwardly attempts to reconnect with Nora and Agnes who now have separate lives. Nora is a fragile stage actress and Agnes is married with a son. Gustav meets with Nora and inelegantly tells her he has written a script about his mother, Karin, and would like her to portray her grandmother. It is set during WWII, and will be filmed in their multigenerational family home where the sisters grew up. Karin was captured by the Nazis, charged with belonging to the Norwegian resistance, and tortured, something she refused to talk about after the war. Agnes, who is an historian, discovers, later in the film, the trauma her grandmother endured. When Gustav was seven, Karin committed suicide. Nora, absent any real discussion with Gustav about the script or about her deep resentment due to his long absence from their lives, refuses the part and abruptly leaves. In her wake, the distance tween the two remains Stellan Skarsgård and Elle Fanning in Sentimental Value unresolved, and seems to come as a surprise to Gustav. Without the detachment of the camera lens, and his inherent Nordic reserve, he seems incapable of engaging with either Nora or Agnes. The first two acts of Sentimental Value almost feel like a prologue to what follows. Gustav finds an American actress, Rachel Kemp (Elle Fanning), who does not speak Norwegian agrees to take the role, yet soon begins to feel that the essence of Karin is ever elusive. I experienced the abrupt cuts from scene to scene puzzling. Was it the absence of connecting exposition? The film is character-driven, yet I found myself having to work to understand certain scenes. For example, the film cuts to Nora, in bed with, I assumed, a fellow actor. But this relationship is unexplained and quickly dropped. And there’s vagueness or continuing distance that are never resolved between the daughters and their father. And yet, there is a scene with Rachel who is comforted by Gustav when she sadly explains she cannot continue in her portrayal of Karin. There were also moments when I realized I had left the story, which is a red flag, a signal perhaps, that though I wanted to care about and understand these people and their nuanced history, I often felt lost. But clearly, Sentimental Value has been praised by the voting Academy, as have the actors. Sentimental Value. Norwegian film with subtitles. Written and directed by Joachim Trier. Starring Stellan Skarsgard, Renate Reinsve, Elle Fanning and Ilse Ibsdotler. Rated R. 2hrs 13mi. Released 2025. Streaming on Prime/Fandango/Apple tv

articles.text: Opera was the most popular form of entertainment for a very long time. Usually in opera lots of people get killed. So many in fact that opera could have been a morticians’ desideratum. Curiously, in Mozart’s marvelous opera Cosi fan tutte no one dies. This is very surprising. And the opera is a comedy nonetheless. Mozart was ingenious. The plot of the opera is ridiculous. That’s the way opera stories are. In some ways Mark Twain could have been one of the inspirations. Cosi fan tutte has many of the characteristics of Mark Twain plot and it is centered around the social mores of men and women. Perhaps I should say “men versus women.” That alone makes it both ridiculous and realistic. Mozart took these things into account and produced an extremely melodious opera. One beautiful aria is followed by other beautiful arias, one after another. The recent production by the Livermore Valley opera company was memorable. The small orchestra began with an energetic overture. In general the musicians were very polished. Conductor Alexandra Katzman led a very spirited performance. The curtain rose, and the singers took command of the story. The cast was evenly divided featuring three women, notably Meryl Dominguez, Courtney Miller, and Megan Potter and male leads Sid Chand, Samuel Kid and Eugene Brancoveanu. Erie Mills deserves credit for her general direction as do Bruce Olstad and Robert Harriot. This opera is popular for good reason. The audience is encouraged to consider many possibilities of social mores. Despite the turmoil, everything ends happily. Shakespeare would have summed it up by saying “all’s well that ends well.” Have a look at the schedule for the next series of operas presented by the Livermore Valley opera Company. You’ll be happy you did. Sunday in Piedmont An outstanding cello and piano recital was presented Sunday evening in the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Miles Reed is an outstanding young cellist and a laureate of the most recent Klein International Competition. For this program, he was joined by the acclaimed pianist Amy Zanrosso. Their program was notable for its diversity and high spirits. A song without words by Mendelssohn began the program. What followed was a miniature suite for unaccompanied cello composed by Paul Wiancko which Miles Reed introduced Mozart’s opera Cosi fan tutte as presented by the Livermore Valley Opera Company was as proficient as it was colorful.

The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The cellist told the audience that he was very much inspired by this particular work… And the composer was inspired in part by Bach. Virtually every aspect of cello technique is presented in a very condensed manner. It really got the attention of the audience. Concluding the first half of the program was another modern composition entitled Variations on a Slovakian Theme by Bohuslav Martinu. The title states that it is a Slovakian theme but it sounds more Hungarian to me. Nonetheless, the piece is excellent. There were sections which sounded like a Hungarian cymbalom. The finale is truly brilliant, and the performance by the cellist and the pianist was very convincing. Concluding the program was my favorite cello Sonata – Sonata No 3 by Ludwig van Beethoven. This is a very ingenious work often sounding like two young animals having fun. The audience responded enthusiastically and the artist presented a brilliant encore. I have heard the pianist Amy Zanrosso perform many times. Brava! Miles Reed, the cellist, is an outstanding young performer. His personality is charming in addition to his lofty talent. I told him that I had only one suggestion. One of the things that I have noticed with modern string players is that they put their finger on the string and then add the vibrato afterwards. In the words of one of the greatest performers of all time, this creates an unnatural crescendo which interferes with the flow of the music. Overall, his playing is outstanding – technically, tonally and musically. He is a worthy laureate of the Klein International String Competition. articles.text: A smooth collie stands stacked in the ring, ready for Best in Show Judging. Many dog owners wonder at some point whether their furry friend has what it takes to strut their stuff at a show. The purebred dog show world is a very unique one which demands not only a very healthy animal, but specific training designed to demonstrate to a judge that your dog is the ideal version of its breed. Hence, mixed breed dogs cannot compete.The breed standard is a written description of a perfect canine individual, typically mentioning the desirable body structure, coat, and gait. It may also include things like temperament or a specific facial expression desired for the breed. Show dogs are compared to this breed standard in the ring. Whether you decide to show your own dog or not, attending an all-breed AKC show is a great way to start off your dog show education. Handlers and breeders alike are typically happy to explain what is happening in the ring as well as what the judge is looking for in their specific breed. When attending your first show, make sure that you always ask permission before petting any dogs and avoid carrying around food as it may distract dogs. Take some time to watch your preferred breed in the ring. You’ll notice that they typically start with the youngest dogs and move upwards in maturity. It is well worth it to stay until the end when the first place dogs from all seven groups compete for Best in Show. Interestingly, these dogs are not being compared to each other, but rather against their individual breed standards. Needless to say, a judge must have a great deal of knowledge to make this decision! Curious about showing your own dog? A great way to test the waters is to enter your puppy in the beginner puppy competition (B-Pup). This is a low stakes show where puppies get to practice. This may give you an idea of whether your dog has a show career in their future based on how they place. Before committing to a show career, consider a couple pros and cons of the conformation show life. Shows may take up many of your weekends and require significant funding for travel and supplies. Additionally, your dog must remain intact (not neutered or spayed) in order to participate in breed shows. For many owners, this is a dealbreaker, as hormone-driven behaviors can quickly get out of hand and lead to lifelong behavioral problems. When making this decision, consider your individual lifestyle and, after attending a few shows, whether you feel this is truly a passion for you. Above all, dog shows should be joyful for both you and your canine companion! Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.

articles.text: On Monday, March 2, the First Mondays Reading Group drew an excellent turnout of 21 participants for its monthly discussion at Piedmont Community Hall. The group met to discuss their March selection, Harlem Shuffle by Colson Whitehead. A two-time Pulitzer Prize winner for The Underground Railroad (2017) and The Nickel Boys (2020). This is his 2021 novel that takes place in Harlem between 1959 and 1964. It is a crime fiction, a family saga, a morality play, a social novel about race and power, and is also an homage to Harlem. Whitehead’s Ray Carney lives in Harlem with his wife, with whom he is expecting their second child. Although Ray comes from a family with a criminal history, he makes his living working as an upstanding furniture store owner and salesman. Ray has steered his life toward an honest living, but his cousin Freddie is descending into Harlem’s criminal underworld. But money is tight for Ray, especially with his sales of sofas on installment plans, so when Freddie occasionally drops off a ring or necklace, Ray doesn’t ask where they came from, and he knows a jeweler downtown who doesn’t ask questions either. Freddie sets up a robbery and volunteers Ray to fence the stolen goods, but the heist goes wrong. This sends a cast of criminals into Ray’s life and forces him into a personal struggle between doing what is right/legal and getting ahead. The novel is divided into three parts and covers three separate capers that are set in 1959, 1961, and 1964, and ends with the Harlem riot of 1964. Harlem Shuffle was almost universally well-received by the readers. It was an easy, fast, and fun read. The readers felt like they were really in NYC and unfortunately, strongly influences the world. The flavor of Harlem and New York City at the time was one that the readers could relate to. Some reflected on their own 1960s NYC experiences and also considered what Harlem is today. It may have changed some, but its energy and demographics are still vibrant, diverse, and a little scary. While some readers felt Whitehead’s characterizations were rich, others wished he had developed supporting characters, like Ray’s wife. And there were a few readers who were not at all enamored with the book. They could not get invested in the characters and were disappointed with the subject matter. Additionally, the action seemed repetitive. The book may be a good social novel, as well as a crime, relationship story, but there was not enough in the book to capture their emotions and hold their interest. Readers were interested in reading more about Ray and Freddie in Whitehead’s trilogy and reading his other award-winning novels, but everyone seemed interested in having more First Mondays Reading Group discussions like this one. The group has selected Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets, a 2013 book by Belarusian Nobel laureate Svetlana Alexievich, for its April book and The God of the Woods by Liz Moore for May. The readers chose Barbarian Days: A Surfing Life by William Finnegan for their June read. With all their business done, they took a group photo at the back of the Community Hall. The readers will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion on April 6 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https://bit. ly/3R86PP4. Harlem Shuffle by Colson Whitehead marveled at Whitehead’s writing skills. He is a highly accomplished wordsmith and thinks in ways that most people cannot imagine. His language is vivid, and he can bring his thoughts to the page in rich and captivating prose. The readers got the idea and understood why Whitehead was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship (genius grant) in 2002 at the age of 32. Whitehead vividly paints the picture of New York City in the 1960s. It is a vibrant, dynamic place with an elite set of upperclass African Americans, but also more common people, like Ray and Freddie, who are just trying to survive. The group could understand how a guy like Ray could become a “little bent” while trying not to be a crook. The 1960s in Harlem were tough. The group could imagine themselves in Ray’s situation, being presented with shady dealings and rationalizing behaviors that were a slippery slope into criminality. The group felt this was not just a Harlem thing. It was and still is everywhere. It is often a matter of survival and a part of human behavior that, March 2026 discussion group: Pat McMahon, Robert White, Ken Young, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Adrienne Hamlin, Melba Yee, Alicia Rivera, Tim Weishahn, Lois Price, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Mary Carter, Peggy Shultz, Sue Backer, Mike Henn, Nancy Henn, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased to have Margaret Wade with them for the first time.

articles.text: Forty-five walkers and four K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra last Wednesday morning for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays outing. The group set out to revisit several of Piedmont’s parks and take a closer look at some of the city’s Heritage Trees. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created in 2018 by the City Council based on a recommendation from the Park Commission. Since then, more than 30 trees across the city have been designated as Piedmont’s “Heritage Trees.” The intent of the program is to recognize noteworthy and distinctive trees located in Piedmont’s parks and open spaces, encourage residents to visit those spaces, and promote the study and appreciation of nature. Walker and Park Commissioner Jack Fischrup told the group that the commission has been working for several years to install signs marking the existing Heritage Trees. The cost of the markers has now been approved and included in the City’s budget. The signs are expected to be installed by Arbor Day in April. Members of the Wednesday walking group have played a role in the program’s history. In 2023 the walkers nominated the mulberry trees in front of the Piedmont Play School at Hampton Park as a Heritage Tree candidate. With the enthusiastic help of the school’s young students— who also submitted the nomination—the trees won designation. The following year the walkers had another success when a Park’s Cherry Walk and Tea House area. At the bottom of the steps the walkers encountered several more Heritage Trees. Japanese maples added delicate color and form to the landscape, and nearby stood a group of Akebono cherry trees. In front of Community Hall, the walkers paused at a Yulan magnolia, known for its striking white blossoms in the spring. Continuing past Community Hall, the group stopped beside a large, twisting Coast live oak that has served as a backdrop for countless family photos over the decades. It is also a Heritage Tree and provided a good setting for the walkers’ group photograph. Nearby, behind the Exedra’s tot lot, the walkers saw another grouping of Coast live oaks. From there the group climbed Highland Avenue to Vista Avenue and City Hall, where a group of Evergreen dogwoods stands at the entrance. The walkers then continued down Vista and Bonita Avenues, passing the city’s new pool. The group will have an opportunity to visit the facility on March 25 during a tour with Recreation Director Chelle Putzer. At the Recreation Center on Hillside Avenue the walkers paused to admire a palm tree standing to the left of the building. The tree was a 2023 Heritage Tree winner nominated by Recreation staff and Hillside Preschool students. Known as a Canary Island date palm, the species is popular because its trunk stays relatively narrow while the canopy forms a symmetrical crown. The group then continued up Hillside Avenue to Blair Avenue Walter Blair grove of eucalyptus trees in lower Piedmont Park received Heritage Tree status. Their submission last year did not make the podium, but 2026 brings another opportunity. Nominations are due March 20, and the winners will be announced before Arbor Day on April 23. The group decided to revisit some past winners and begin thinking about what tree they might nominate this year. The first Heritage Trees were close at hand. Surrounding the Exedra Plaza is a grove of ten Highland poplars that have been designated Heritage Trees. From there the walkers headed up to the Community Hall parking lot to admire a community favorite that is not covered with lights this time of year. The Coast Redwood that serves as Piedmont’s holiday tree is also a Heritage Tree. The group then made its way up and down the Highland-Guilford Steps, a project completed by the City in 2023 with support from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. The group then made its way up and down the Highland-Guilford Steps, a project completed by the City in 2023 with support from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. The steps create a welcoming entrance to Piedmont Map of route and entered Dracena Park. Commissioner Fischrup guided the walkers to see several more Heritage Trees: another mature Coast live oak, a California buckeye, a native bigleaf maple, and a grove of six dawn redwoods located toward the back of the park on the site of Walter Blair’s 1850s quarry. Along the park’s upper path the walkers stopped at Storyteller Bridge, which crosses the park’s ravine. Max Becker shared how his younger brother rebuilt the bridge as an Eagle Scout project with help from family members, the City, and community volunteers. The group emerged from the park on Park Way and walked down to the bend where the street becomes Monticello Avenue. Along the way Sherry Jacobs joked that Park Way might more accurately be called Magnolia Avenue because of the many magnolia trees lining the street— even though Magnolia Avenue itself has none. A hidden path at the end of Park Way led the walkers back into Dracena Park to see the grove of dawn redwoods more closely. These remarkable trees once grew widely in California about one million years ago and were long believed extinct until they were rediscovered in central China in 1948. Today they are one of three living redwood species, along with the Coast Redwood and the Giant Sequoia. From the park’s play area the group looked down toward a stand of Southern magnolias with dramatic exposed roots—trees the walkers themselves nominated last year as a Heritage Tree candidate. The walkers then climbed the stairs near the play area to El Cerrito Avenue and continued up to Blair Avenue. Along the way it was noted that Walter Blair and his brother introduced eucalyptus trees to the Piedmont area in the late 19th century. The trees were planted as a boundary between what is now Mountain View Cemetery and Piedmont and were once known locally as “Blair’s Gum Trees.” They were removed in 1936 when the road was widened. The group had hoped to see several more Heritage Trees on streets to the south, but the morning had passed quickly. It was time to return to the Exedra via Carmel, Oakland, and Highland Avenues. The walkers had seen a number of Piedmont’s beautiful and historic trees—and there were more waiting to be discovered on future walks. They will also have to decide which tree deserves the group’s nomination for the 2026 Heritage Tree. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. pages.text: Wednesday, March 11, 2026 23 The Wine Corner Festival of Undiscovered Grapes: Featuring California’s rare wines Part 2 By Pierre DuMont (If you read Part 1 of this article in last week’s paper you can skip to the new wine reviews sown below.) On January 31, 2026, wine lovers gathered in downtown San Jose for the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes, an immersive wine-tasting celebration highlighting the world’s rare and lesser-known grape varieties. The event drew local residents and visitors eager to explore beyond familiar varietals like Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and Pinot Noir. Instead, guests sipped wines made from “underdog” grapes — including Semillon, Teroldego, Tannant, Bourbolenc, Cinsault, and Trousseau — representing more than 110 unique winegrape varieties grown in California. With dozens of wineries pouring their distinctive selections, attendees wandered the room sampling bold reds, aromatic whites, and intriguing blends that many had never encountered before. Wine producers from across the state were on hand to share stories of their vineyards and the heritage of these lesser-known grapes, offering insight into the diversity of California’s wine landscape. Participants could choose between general admission and VIP tickets. VIP guests enjoyed early access, a pre-tasting discussion focused on Lodi wine varietals with experts, a commemorative wine glass, and complimentary delivery of bottles ordered at the event. General admission ticket holders joined the tasting after the VIP session and had the option to have their wine purchases delivered for a flat fee. A food vendor on site offered small bites and snacks to pair with the wines, creating a festive atmosphere throughout the afternoon. Conversations flowed as easily as the pours, with many oenophiles excited to discover new favorites and broaden their palates. Organizers said the festival aimed not just to entertain but to educate, spotlighting vinicultural diversity and supporting small producers whose bottles might otherwise go unnoticed. For many attendees, the event succeeded in turning curiosity into appreciation, underscoring that California’s wine story extends far beyond its most popular grapes. The following wines were the standouts of the huge tasting. They are the cream of the crop and are worth searching out. WHITE WINES • 2024 Tansy Fiano, $36 This interesting grape is originally from the Taurasi region in southern Italy. The wine opens to fine, dusty, mineral aromas, followed by sweet citrus, lemon peel and apricot. This lean-bodied white ends with zippy acidity and a touch of zesty spice. Very foodfriendly it would go with seafood of any kind. In the mouth there are easy layers of apple, stone fruit and crushed stone that add depth and character. The finish is clean and satisfying. Beautiful wine! • 2024 Vigo Picpoul Blanc, $45 Picpoul, a minor grape from the south of France, seems to be gaining popularity in California. The name in French means “lipstinger” and it is known for its bracing acidity. This version from Paso Robles balances out that acidity with abundant melon, apple and pear fruit. It has aromas of lime zest and slate, is medium bodied and has a smooth, clean finish. Perfect aperitif. • 2024 Andis Semillon Bill Dillian Vineyard, $25 Coming from a 45-year-old vineyard in the Shenandoah Valley this grape is predominantly grown in southwest France and Australia. It is grassy and intense, with apple, straw, vanilla and wax. The palate follows with a stream of juicy acidity that flows through the fruit. The mouthfeel is weighty and round with a long lingering finish. The world needs a little less Sauvignon Blanc and a little more Semillon. • 2024 Perlegos Assyrtiko, $29 Usually, you must go to Santorini to taste this wine but leave it to the Greek-owned Perlegos winery in Lodi to import Greece’s best white grape and give it the old California try. It is succulent and fleshy, with brine, apple, pear and vanilla wafer aromas. It is complex and impressively layered, with texture and flavor in profusion. A great foodfriendly wine it would go with a wide range of meals from fish to chicken to cheese. The Assyrtiko grape is Greece’s finest white. RED WINES • 2023 Giornata Aglianico, $40 Aglianico is the most noble grape from southern Italy and is used to make sturdy, dense, longaged reds. This version from Paso Robles Giornata Winery is a gentle giant with dark fruit, earth, leather and warm spice. I could imagine lamb chops on the grill as a delicious food match. The wine ends with firm tannins, but the effect is not bitter because plenty of dark fruit remains throughout. • 2018 Kinetic Tinto Moderno, $15 (Best Value) This is a field blend of five Portuguese varietals Tinta Roritz, Touriga Nacional, Touriga Francesca, Souzao and Alvarelhao. It is a light and fruity wine with lots of finesse and style. Redolent of blueberries and red currants it is fresh and vibrant on the palate with a touch of acid on the finish. A remarkable value, this wine should be drunk now. Kinetic Cellars red blend was the best value of the tasting. • 2019 Post & Vine Carignane Contra Costa County, $24 This wine comes from one of the greatest, most overlooked vineyard areas in California. Tucked away in Contra Costa County near the town of Oakley are some sandy loam vineyards that are home of gnarly, century-old vines of Carignane and Mourvedre producing wines of great character. The wine is medium ruby in color and prettily perfumed, with fresh plum and blueberry fruit with notes of earth and a streak of graphite. The palate offers bright, fresh fruit character with loads of uplift and a long, floral-laced finish. Beautiful stuff to drink over the next 7-8 years. The Fiano grape from Italy shines in this Russian River wine. • 2023 Intercostal Wines Pinotage Bianco $35 This could be the rarest wine of all at the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes. As far as I know Lodi’s Intercoastal is the only winery to make a white version of this famous South African grape anywhere. The nose has aromas of honeysuckle, melon and citrus. DEREK McBREARTY PLUMBING Residential Plumbing Services Sewer line repair Gas lines Water heaters Earthquake shutoff valves Plumbing repair service 415-377-3841 Lic #795277 Contra Costa County is the home of this Old Vine wine. • 2020 Ambyth Portuguese Petite Grenache, $54 Hailing from Paso Robles. this is a blend of seven, yes seven Portuguese varietals. It is beautiful, velvety, beefy, complex and well-balanced. The tannins are present but not overpowering with layers of cassis, raspberries, and earth. It is round and full in the mouth with a savory complex finish. Would make a great partner to grilled BBQ ribs. • 2022 Starfield Tannat, $50 The Tannat grape is originally from the Madiran region in southwest France and has made a home in Uruguay. This example from the El Dorado Hills AVA is ripe, dense and personable, with some nuances of anise, roast beef and blackberries. This is an expressive Tannat that shows fine structure and even better concentration. This big blockbuster of a wine begs for a grilled ribeye steak. • 2024 Marchelle Cinsault Bechtold Vineyard, $54 Cinsault is one of the main blending grapes used in the south of France but is seldom bottled on its own there. I am glad to see some American wineries are starting to correct that as it is delightful on its own. Sort of like a cross between Pinot Noir and Grenache the bouquet reveals pure cherry fruit, with currants and pomegranate. It is light and vibrant on the palate; fairly simple but juicy, refreshing and satisfying. • 2022 Comunita Schioppettino, $55 What a fun discovery – another grape I have not only never tasted but never even heard of! The winemaker explained that it originally comes from the Friuli region of northern Italy with these grapes coming from a small vineyard in the Russian River Valley. The wine opens to a rustic bouquet of tart cherries, smoke, tar and earth. The bouquet is totally offbeat, but it is also bursting with authentic personality. The mouthfeel is bright, crisp and refreshing. Really interesting wine worth seeking out. • 2023 Alta Colina “Sun Worshipper”, $68 A blend of 61% Mouvedre and 30% Syrah from Paso Robles the Sun Worshipper is a blockbuster of juicy goodness. Aromatically, it leads with lashings of black fruits and berries, exotic spices and almost no hint of oak. In the mouth, the wine is a mirror image, with the added experience of fine tannins. This lovely wine, opulent yet nimble with great balance, finishes long and savory. ]• 2019 Anaya Nebbiolo, $48 Nebbiolo is famously hard to grow anywhere except in its homeland of Northern Italy so it is rarely attempted in California. This bottling from Lodi has some of the classic roses and tar nose the grape is known for. It delivers flavors of cherries, herbs and cranberries in the medium bodied style. The finish combines a bright, high-toned energy with assertive yet refined tannins and a lovely perfume. • 2024 Camin Dreams Mencia, $40 Sourced from a vineyard in San Benito County this rare grape from the north of Spain is rarely seen in the US. It produces a light-bodied, finesse style wine similar to Pinot Noir. Pale in color it has a young, fruit-driven nose with some floral notes, with an herbal touch and nice cherry fruit. The palate is juicy and tender, with very fine tannins, very clean and precise. The perfect wine to go with any preparation of salmon. • 2023 Trail Marker Trousseau Petites Joies, $28 Perhaps the lightest in color of all red wines, Trousseau originally from the Jura region of France, looks like a Tavel rose. This bottling from the Russian River Valley has lots of sediment showing it was made naturally and unfiltered. The wine is clean and bright, with a perfumed nose with notes of violets and a light bodied palate with subtle fine tannins. There’s balance and a certain earthiness. Delicious now it should be drunk in the next one to two years. • 2024 Derby Counoise, $46 Paso Robles’ Derby Winery has taken a grape that seldom escapes the blending bench in France and given it a star turn. It gives up lively cherry, violets, dried spices and a kiss of earth to go with the medium-bodied, supple and lively feel on the palate. Eminently quaffable this is a beautiful example of the variety to drink over the next 3-4 years.

Reader Question This week’s reader question sent me to hunt for something appropriate and… I refuse to join any club that would have me as a member. –Groucho Marx Question: I belong to a local HOA, a small monthly fee, that seems to exist for the sole reason to police landscaping. I am trying to be pro-active and update my yard to save money on my homeowner’s insurance, but it seems this is anathema to the HOA. Any advice? A: The best approach is to talk with your HOA board first. Let them know you’re planning updates to reduce wildfire risk and lower your insurance costs— hopefully they’ll appreciate the safety benefits for the whole neighborhood and might work with you on any concerns. Before making any changes, check your HOA’s CC&Rs to see what landscaping rules or restrictions might apply. Knowing the guidelines upfront saves headaches and helps you plan within the community’s standards. Potentially do a cost/benefit to see if the HOA fines are less than or equal to the insurance savings. And kudos to you for knowing many insurers offer discounts when you create defensible space, fire hardening, and clearing brush and making your yard more fire-resistant. These savings can range from a small percentage up to 50%, depending on your insurer and how much mitigation you do. This turnover underscore sustained demand for more accessible properties. While new listings are sparse, construction activity is robust. The city issued 17 building permits between February 14 and 21, totaling over $371,000 in job value. She learns that this shocking change was brought about by a witch named Yubaba (Suzanne Pleshette) who runs a bathhouse for tired spirits. Haku warns Chihiro to avoid the witch, but she is told she must serve the malevolent hag in order to return her parents to their original forms. And so begins Chihiro’s extraordinary journey through the park, meeting a host of demons and strange creatures. There are dragons, frogmen, a giant and very cranky baby, a spidery furnace stoker and other inhabitants that take her breath away. And so, this once fearful, contrary girl must face the museum-like, harrowing, spirit-filled place and learn to be brave for the sake of herself and her parents. Ultimately, it is her transformation that is at the center of Spirited Away. The animation, as expected, is dazzling, rich and lush and soft, each frame a hand drawn work of art. Of course, the story is unusual, steeped in Japanese mythology, and may be more appealing to young girls; however, boys will also enjoy the spectrum of mysterious spirits, especially Yubaba. articles.text: Early Bird Registration now open Piedmont Food Fest is turning five this year! The Bay Area’s most vibrant multicultural festival returns to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 25, from 11 a.m. - 4 p.m. Since launching in 2022, this volunteer-run event has become a community tradition of building shared experiences through food, drink, music, and arts. By connecting over 2000 attendees with 50 local businesses and community organizations, Piedmont Food Fest sets the stage for a day full of new experiences and memories for visitors of all ages. With its wide variety of sights, sounds, and tastes, Piedmont Food Fest has evolved into an event for the greater Bay Area, with many guests visiting from San Francisco, Marin, Fremont, and Danville. Piedmont residents often seize the opportunity to invite friends and family to spend the day together at the festival. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest. org to sign up for event updates as well as check out Early Bird specials for discounted drink packages & KidZone bracelets through March. This event is free to the public, and all are encouraged to invite friends and family to enjoy this day together. This year, Piedmont Food Fest will feature: • Food and dessert vendors: Casablanca Moroccan & Mediterranean, Aburaya Japanese Fried Chicken, Momolicious, BBtea, Hint of Desi, Cousins Maine Lobster, Aloha Aria’s Shave Ice, Swahili Spot, Arthur Mac’s, Lola’s Spanish Cuisine, Sunrise Deli, Bonito Poke, Lizetta’s Southern Soul Food, Crazy Empanadas, Pintoh Thai, and 3 Brothers Kitchen. • Local breweries and wineries: Oakland United, Farmstead Wines, P. Herrell Winery, and Covenant Wines – plus a rotating sangria and frosé station. • Live performances: Wilbert McAlister’s Cowboy and His Sometimes Blues Band, DJ HeyLove, the Purple Silk Youth Orchestra, Beloved Aerial Arts, Piedmont Middle School, Han Martial Arts, and a special performance by the Cal Band! • The KidZone: features ten carnival booths, a kid-favorite sno-cone station, and a multicultural crafts table. • Community groups & local retailers including PHS for Alameda Food Bank, No Immigrant No Spice, Immedium Books, Porschia’s Henna Tattoos, and Heather’s Face Painting. The installation and expansion of cameras in Oakland, San Leandro, Emeryville and other cities has also helped the region address vehicle theft. “The camera alerts our officers receive enable them to quickly identify whether those vehicles are coming in or out of our city,” Chief Shavies added. “And even in those that we don’t recover, we’re able to contact Oakland and let them know that they have one coming.” Through the continued use of ALPR cameras, Chief Shavies said residents’ privacy remains an important priority. The department works with Flock Safety to ensure the system complies with state requirements and community expectations. “I think it’s important that we feel the same concerns, and we have certain guardrails in place that will ensure that our entire community, and those that travel through, their privacy is respected,” said Chief Shavies. PPD continues to maintain direct authority over who is granted access to the city network. “Not only will we, but Flock Safety also will not share any of our data with anyone for any immigration reasons, or for any reproductive care reasons,” he said. In 2025, PPD continued its community outreach programs, including Cop on the Block and Coffee, Cars, and Cops. Youth engagement also continued through the department’s partnership with the Piedmont Unified School District for campus safety planning, drills and day-to-day coordination. “I think that in seeing me in the community, it’s not just about being visible, it’s also about listening and understanding the needs, the wants, and the desires of our community,” he said. The year 2026 will be PPD’s first full year under Chief Shavies. His priorities include increasing staffing and dispatch operations, continuing investments in training, maintaining proactive policing strategies and strengthening internal systems and accountability. “I want us to be one of the top police departments in the region in the way that we are addressing and reducing crime, the way that we’re responding to the members of our community, and in a way that we’re trained,” said Chief Shavies. articles.text: Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC) hosted its Annual Lunar New Year Celebration at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse this past Friday, February 27, to welcome in the Year of the Horse. The event featured food, drinks, crafts, games, musical performances from PHS and PMS students, and a Lion Dance as the highlight. Guests enjoyed a bento box dinner with specialty drinks from Tea on Piedmont and artisanal pastries from BakeSum. Piedmont High School’s Troubadours provided a musical performance, and Piedmont Middle School’s karate club showcased their moves on stage. The Lion Dance had drummers providing the musical backdrop as the lions danced across the stage, showcasing their impressive balance. Lunar calendar is based on a combination of lunar and solar movements, with the second new moon after the winter solstice marking the beginning of the new year. The Year of the Horse symbolizes vitality, speed, and perseverance. People born in the Year of the Horse are believed to possess similar traits, such as being hardworking, warm-hearted, and independent. articles.text: David B. Oppenheimer, a Piedmont resident for nearly 40 years, recently published his 10th book, The Diversity Principle, after 14 years of work and collaboration with more than 100 Berkeley research assistants. Oppenheimer, a clinical professor of law at the University of California, Berkeley School of Law, argues that the modern understanding of diversity began in the late Enlightenment era. Published by Yale University Press, the book reaches beyond law students and legal scholars, the audience for his previous nine publications, to readers interested in the idea, application and history of diversity. “I tell the story through the work and lives of a remarkable group of people who taught us that we make better decisions when we include people with different backgrounds, experiences, and viewpoints,” said Oppenheimer. He sets out to show that when diverse people are brought David B. Oppenheimer is a Clinical Professor of Law at Berkeley Law, the Co-Director of Berkeley Center on Comparative Equality & AntiDiscrimination Law. Faculty Co-Director of the Pro Bono Program. together and encouraged to engage with one another, results improve across fields. “They make better decisions in a classroom, [and] they generate more ideas. In a science lab, they make more significant discoveries. In government, they develop more innovative public policy proposals. In business, they will make more money. Diverse juries make more accurate, factual findings,” Oppenheimer told the Post.
articles.title: Cal Law Professor, David Oppenheimer, finishes 14-year labor of love, publishes The Diversity Principle

articles.text: Editor: The proposed Dearing memorial elicits all the wrong messages: • It’s different. • It doesn’t fit in. • It looks like a broken shaft. • It invites graffiti. • It could be used as a urinal. • The mail box is out of reach for a delivery. • The future for Blacks is through a glass darkly. • It’s an expensive hiding place. If you agree with any of the above, please write The Post or Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen. –Leigh Sorensen, Piedmont resident
articles.title: Dearing memorial – all the wrong reasons

articles.text: Editor: I was walking my old bones up to the Exedra from Baja Piedmont and sweating like I ate at that one curry restaurant down by the lake on Grand. Since I live at the lowest part of Baja I was quite overheated in the 77 degree weather that is so unseasonal for March let alone February. Who could have imagined that global warming would be so effective? I turned the corner on Magnolia and caught sight of the gleaming new Piedmont Pool, which is going to be ready any month now. I could not stop grinning as I imagined stripping down to the swimsuit I got in southern France back in 1973 and vaulting the fence. Cannonball! Kudos to everyone involved for planning the opening this spring while my health seems to be holding. As I type this with sweaty fingers on my iPhone in Piedmont Park — and recuperate with a $5 sundae as the buzzards look on approvingly from a nearby tree — I am so thankful that I have almost lived to see the new Piedmont Pool open. I can’t wait to dive in! –Ricardo Shibeewah
articles.title: Piedmont’s gleaming new pool

articles.text: Editor: Gray Cathrall’s 90th birthday is more than a personal milestone – it is a civic milestone for everyone who has benefited from his steady, principled presence in our City’s journalism. Plainly said: Piedmont is a better city because of Gray. Not metaphorically better. Concretely better. More honest about itself. More difficult to govern in a good way. More capable of the kind of informed civic argument that healthy communities depend on. These things don’t happen by accident. They happen because someone shows up, year after year, and does the unglamorous work of paying attention on behalf of everyone else. For over two decades, that someone has been Gray. Consider what his presence has meant. When a development project or a budget allocation or a school board policy deserves scrutiny, the Post has provided it. When neighbors needed a common ground — not social media’s battlefield, but a genuine civic commons where ideas meet and facts are checked — the Post has been that place. Without it, Piedmont would be navigating its own affairs with far less transparency and light. Local journalism of this quality is, in much of the country, gone. Piedmont has been spared that. Not because it was lucky, but because Gray chose to build something durable and then protect it. There is also the human dimension of his legacy — the writers he mentored who went on to careers shaped by his example, the readers who came to trust that what they held in their hands was accurate, the sources who learned they could speak to him and be treated fairly. Trust of that kind accumulates slowly. It dissipates quickly. Gray spent 27 years earning it and never a day squandering it. To reach this milestone is remarkable. To reach it having spent a third of it in genuine service to a community — having made that community more transparent, more informed, more capable of self-governance — is something even more rare. Piedmont has been shaped by many people over many decades. Few have shaped it as quietly, as consistently, or as well as Gray Cathrall. Happy 90th birthday, Gray. We are grateful for you every day. (See 90 Things About Gray in the box on page 3.) –Connie & Mark Herrick
articles.title: Celebrating Gray’s 90th

Right conduct controls the greater one.” – Mark Twain 1835 - 1910 American writer, humorist, essayist Dearing memorial – all the wrong reasons Editor: The proposed Dearing memorial elicits all the wrong messages: • It’s different. • It doesn’t fit in. • It looks like a broken shaft. • It invites graffiti. • It could be used as a urinal. • The mail box is out of reach for a delivery. • The future for Blacks is through a glass darkly. • It’s an expensive hiding place. If you agree with any of the above, please write The Post or Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen. –Leigh Sorensen, Piedmont resident Piedmont’s gleaming new pool Editor: I was walking my old bones up to the Exedra from Baja Piedmont and sweating like I ate at that one curry restaurant down by the lake on Grand. Since I live at the lowest part of Baja I was quite overheated in the 77 degree weather that is so unseasonal for March let alone February. Who could have imagined that global warming would be so effective? I turned the corner on Magnolia and caught sight of the gleaming new Piedmont Pool, which is going to be ready any month now. I could not stop grinning as I imagined stripping down to the swimsuit I got in southern France back in 1973 and vaulting the fence. Cannonball! Kudos to everyone involved for planning the opening this spring while my health seems to be holding. As I type this with sweaty fingers on my iPhone in Piedmont Park — and recuperate with a $5 sundae as the buzzards look on approvingly from a nearby tree — I am so thankful that I have almost lived to see the new Piedmont Pool open. I can’t wait to dive in! –Ricardo Shibeewah Welcome to Spring; welcome to the new pool Editor: The warm weather last week reminded me how excited I am for our pool. I am so grateful to be in a community that has made this investment. I wanted to express my excitement with a haiku: Oh, welcoming pool! You swim laps in my mind’s eye; Your deep end awaits! With towels ready, –Jay Bohanion Celebrating Gray’s 90th Editor: Gray Cathrall’s 90th birthday is more than a personal milestone – it is a civic milestone for everyone who has benefited from his steady, principled presence in our City’s journalism. Plainly said: Piedmont is a better city because of Gray. Not metaphorically better. Concretely better. More honest about itself. More difficult to govern in a good way. More capable of the kind of informed civic argument that healthy communities depend on. These things don’t happen by accident. They happen because someone shows up, year after year, and does the unglamorous work of paying attention on behalf of everyone else. For over two decades, that someone has been Gray. Consider what his presence has meant. When a development project or a budget allocation or a school board policy deserves scrutiny, the Post has provided it. When neighbors needed a common ground — not social media’s battlefield, but a genuine civic commons where ideas meet and facts are checked — the Post has been that place. Without it, Piedmont would be navigating its own affairs with far less transparency and light. Local journalism of this quality is, in much of the country, gone. Piedmont has been spared that. Not because it was lucky, but because Gray chose to build something durable and then protect it. There is also the human dimension of his legacy — the writers he mentored who went on to careers shaped by his example, the readers who came to trust that what they held in their hands was accurate, the sources who learned they could speak to him and be treated fairly. Trust of that kind accumulates slowly. It dissipates quickly. Gray spent 27 years earning it and never a day squandering it. To reach this milestone is remarkable. To reach it having spent a third of it in genuine service to a community — having made that community more transparent, more informed, more capable of self-governance — is something even more rare. Piedmont has been shaped by many people over many decades. Few have shaped it as quietly, as consistently, or as well as Gray Cathrall. Happy 90th birthday, Gray. We are grateful for you every day. (See 90 Things About Gray in the box on page 3.) –Connie & Mark Herrick

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council formally adopted an updated Local Hazard Mitigation Plan at their meeting on March 2. The plan provides a roadmap showing what Piedmont could do in the coming five years to reduce or avoid potential damages from natural hazards like earthquakes, wildfires, and severe weather. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP) identifies the natural hazards that pose the greatest risk to Piedmont and documents how each hazard would impact Piedmont if it were to occur. The plan identifies and prioritizes actions the City and community could take now that would prevent or reduce those potential impacts. The plan updates Piedmont’s first Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, which was adopted in 2019, to address evolving hazard threats and local conditions. The updated LHMP identifies 30 total actions, 9 that were included in the 2019 LHMP, and 21 new additions that could help reduce risk to Piedmont. The plan’s risk mitigation strategy is to strengthen the resilience of IT infrastructure, retrofit or replace critical facilities to meet modern seismic safety codes, provide annual fire fuel mitigation on city property, and strengthen local building and fire codes to require wildfire-resistant construction. Some of the identified actions, such as strengthening building codes and fire fuel mitigation on City property, have already been completed or are underway. Including an action in the LHMP does not guarantee that it will happen. Rather, it positions the City to apply for state and federal mitigation grants that could support implementing that project. Crafted over a year of research, discussion, and public engagement, the LHMP was submitted to the California Governor’s Office of Emergency Services and the Federal Emergency Management Agency for review in fall 2025. The City received notification in January 2026 that the document had passed review and was now eligible for Council adoption. “We are going to take care of problems before the disaster hits, hardening buildings, fixing storm drain infrastructure, working on vegetation management, so we’re all better prepared when a disaster hits, the impact is lower, and we’re able to respond and recover quicker,” said Fire Chief Dave Brannigan. Learn more about the Local Hazard Mitigation Plan update process and read the adopted plan at piedmont.ca.gov/LHMP. The Local Hazard Mitigation Plan community workshop that occurred in March 2025. articles.title: City Council adopts updated Local Hazard Mitigation Plan

articles.text: Teen Sidekicks recognized by the City Council for their work on 2025’s Sidekicks program. The Piedmont Recreation Department is looking for teens who have a passion for working with children to make a difference as a summer volunteer with PRD’s Sidekicks program. The Sidekicks program offers adaptive classes, workshops, and summer camps specifically designed for neurodiverse children. Teen Sidekicks assist experienced instructors in ensuring a safe, fun, and inclusive recreation experience for adaptive programming participants. As a summer Teen Sidekick, you’d help campers navigate an environment that they may at times find overwhelming. Serving as a Teen Sidekick is a way for teens to complete required volunteer hours and build experience for college applications. Sidekicks program staff ensure that each Teen Sidekick has the tools they need to succeed, offering guidance, training, feedback, and one-on-one consultations throughout their volunteer experience. To apply to be a Summer 2026 Teen Sidekick, submit your appliLocal children learn how to play tennis at the 2025 Sidekicks adaptive tennis event. cation online by Sunday, March 29. Volunteers must: • Complete an interview with PRD staff • Attend a required training and orientation on May 13, 6 p.m. (if accepted) • Commit to volunteering at least one week during the summer (morning or afternoon) • Have a genuine commitment Local kids playing in the Sidekicks adaptive soccer camp. to helping children enjoy recreational activities Sidekicks must turn 14 by June 1, 2026, or be entering 9th grade in the fall. Experience working with elementary-aged children is a bonus, but not required. The application is available at piedmont.ca.gov/SummerSidekick. PRD’s Sidekicks program began in 2021 to provide a “whole child” experience for neurodiverse kids, offering opportunities to create connections with peers, feel welcomed, and thrive in recreational interests outside of school, just like their classmates and siblings. Adaptive programs are meticulously designed to meet the unique needs of neurodiverse children. Each class and camp is held in a facility carefully chosen to limit distractions, while the curriculum and pace of activities are modified to support kids and build confidence as they learn new skills. For more information, visit piedmont.ca.gov/Sidekicks. With questions, contact Recreation Supervisor Eva Phalen at ephalen@piedmont.ca.gov.
articles.title: Teen volunteer opportunities with PRD’s Sidekicks program

articles.text: If you love big, sweet cats, Buster is for you! This beefy, 4-year-old brown tabby proves that first impressions don’t tell the whole story. Once marked as a working cat after arriving at a local shelter as a shy stray with an ear wound, he’s blossomed into an affectionate, cuddly companion who loves a warm lap. Buster may be timid in new environments, but if you can give him a little time, his confident, cheeky side shines. He enjoys soft pets in short sessions, likes being brushed to keep his coat soft and shiny, and will happily settle in close once he trusts you. He can become a little overexcited with too much petting, so he’ll thrive with an adopter who can read his body language and respect his signals. This sweet boy would do best in a calm, indoor-only home with a feline buddy he can wrestle with. Buster may Adopt Buster through Cat Town. be a great match for first-time adopters who appreciate a sensitive, loving cat and are open to going at his pace. Buster is neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. He’s ready for a patient home that will celebrate how far he’s come. Want to meet Buster? This three-year-old female participates in doggy playgroups at Oakland Animal Services shelter and is dog friendly. Tokyo is 53 pounds, and is elegant and graceful.
