articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery will host its 18th Annual Tulip Exhibition at the cemetery’s Tower Chapel, Friday through Sunday, March 20-22, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The free event welcomes in Spring with striking floral arrangements by Bay Area florists, garden clubs, and students from college floral design class. Photographers, florists, flower enthusiasts, and nature and art lovers are welcome. Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s annual tulip exhibit has become a cherished community tradition. This year is the exhibit’s third year back after a hiatus due to COVID-19 restrictions. Mountain View Cemetery (5000 Piedmont Avenue) is an historic garden cemetery in the foothills of Oakland and Piedmont. One of the oldest cemeteries in the Western U.S., it has served the community since 1863 and even includes a section for Civil War soldiers. The cemetery was established by a group of East Bay pioneers “Tulips and Dots in Motion” by Agnes Kang from the 2024 Tulip Exhibition under the California Rural Cemetery Act of 1859. Mountain View was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect who also designed New York City’s Central Park, Brooklyn’s Prospect Park, and much of UC Berkeley and Stanford University. For more information on the annual Tulip Exhibition, visit www.mountainviewcemetery. org.
articles.title: 18th Annual Tulip Exhibition returns March 20-22

articles.text: Piedmont Education Foundation’s Spring Fling season, themed Palm Royale, is dedicated to the “A” in STEAM, the arts. Enhancements to visual and performing arts programs at Beach, Havens and Wildwood are planned and can be supported at the Palm Royale event on April 25. Piedmont children deserve to learn with musical instruments and art supplies in good repair. As fourth and fifth graders prepare for music theory and string instruction, Spring Fling funds will help ensure there is sufficient sheet music and enough violins. Mountain View Cemetery (5000 Piedmont Avenue) is an historic garden cemetery in the foothills of Oakland and Piedmont. Mountain View was designed by Frederick Law Olmsted, the landscape architect who also designed New York City’s Central Park, Brooklyn’s Prospect Park, and much of UC Berkeley and Stanford University. articles.text: Piedmont Middle School (PMS) was named a “2025 California School to Watch” by the California League of Middle Schools (CLMS) with support by the California Department of Education. PMS was one of 90 middle schools selected for the designation, and there are 246 schools of all levels in California with the title. “This program recognizes model middle-grades schools that are academically excellent; developmentally responsive; socially equitable; and led through strong, collaborative leadership,” stated State Superintendent of Public Instruction, Tony Thurmond in a release. The current list includes 46 schools who were added this year and 44 existing Schools to Watch who reapplied. Piedmont Unified School District Superintendent Jennifer Hawn will travel to Long Beach on March 5 for a two-day “Schools to Watch” awards ceremony and district leadership reception. “This prestigious designation reflects the collective efforts of dedicated staff, engaged students, supportive families, and a deeply committed community. At Piedmont Middle School, a shared focus on belonging, high expectations, and student well-being creates an environment where all students are known, supported, and challenged to grow,” said PMS Principal Karyn Shipp. Shipp will make way for current Vice Principal Jamie Van Kleeck to take over the Principal role in July, pending board approval in tonight’s March 4 school board meeting. The statewide 2026 Schools to Watch List will be released later this month.

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District will continue to accept nominations for the 2026 Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award until March 13. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. Previous recipients include: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000); Lisa Lomenzo (2001); jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002); jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003); Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004); Cynthia Gorman (2005); Grier Graff (2006); Julia Burke (2007); Maude Pervere (2008); jointly to Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009); Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010); Andrea Swenson (2011), June Monach (2012), Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013), Ray Perman (2014), Jennifer Fox (2015), Katie Korotzer (2016), Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018), Cathy Glazier (2019), Sue Smegal (2020), Ken Li (2021), Eileen Ruby (2022), David Ragones (2023), Sarah Pearson (2024) and most recently, Cory Smegal in 2025. Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982. Art also was very active with the Piedmont Continuation High School (now called Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established in his memory by School Board member Dewey Watson. Nominations for this award are now being sought and will be kept strictly confidential. The deadline for nominations is March 13. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 6, Board of Education meeting, where the honoree’s good works will be acknowledged. Nomination forms are available on the bottom of the Superintendent’s webpage Piedmont. k12.ca.us/ref/superintendent, in the District Office (760 Magnolia Avenue), or by calling Rosalina Barrios, Executive Assistant to the Superintendent, at 594-2614.

We held a productive discussion about the importance of our athletics program and how our community comes together to support our athletes. What I appreciated about our discussion was the focus on how to help our already outstanding program get even better. We discussed such topics as safety, how we model behavior for visiting teams/fans, and how we can promote positive sportsmanship in our students. Thanks also to Jean Takazawa for sharing important perspectives about sports culture at the middle and high school levels. The presentation deck is linked HERE, including the notes we took during the meeting based on community input. If you have additional ideas on how we can continue to improve and support our athletics programs related to sportsmanship and spectator conduct, please reach out to Tyler Small, Dr. Yoshihara, or me. articles.text: Piedmont High’s Advanced Acting class will present the acclaimed play Eurydice, by Sarah Ruhl, in the Alan Harvey Theater on Friday, March 6, and Saturday, March 7 at 7:00 p.m. each night. Eurydice is a comedic drama that reimagines the classic myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, focusing on Eurydice’s journey through the Underworld. Reunited with her deceased Grette Willats (left) and Sparrow Lieu prepare for this weekend’s performances of Eurydice during a rehearsal. Mother, Eurydice must grapple with forgotten memories of her past life while facing a life-altering choice. With contemporary characters and plot twists, Eurydice is a fresh look at love and loss. The play is directed by senior Amelia Addington, and the cast includes Yiyou Fang, Kirstin Fedor, Jack Herrlinger, Nico Kaltenecker, Sparrow Lieu, Lila Schwab, and Grette Willats. Addington has been excited to direct the show because of its creative and poetic natures. “Its abstract storytelling and emotional depth allow both the cast and the audience to interpret the story in different and personal ways,” she said. With nearly 20 plays and a MacArthur Genius Grant to her name, author Sarah Ruhl is one of the most important American playwrights of our time. The Advanced Acting Class has previously produced her shows, Dead Man’s Cell Phone and The Clean House. Eurydice has been produced from high schools to Broadway, and it has been translated into 14 languages. In 2021, Ruhl adapted Eurydice into an Opera that ran during the New York Metropolitan Opera Season. Eurydice is recommended for most audiences, though some material may not be suitable for younger audience members. This production explores themes of love, loss, memory, and the afterlife. It is always encouraged that audiences use their best judgment based on the show’s themes and the child’s age and maturity level. Contact producer Kimberly Taylor, at ktaylor@ piedmont.k12.ca.us, with any questions. Tickets are $5 for students and $10 for general admission. Tickets can be purchased at phsacting. ludus.com.

articles.text: & Kaito Ciammaichella Piedmont’s Troop 1 Scouts received a behind the scenes look at how local news is made - from the use of robotic cameras to the teamwork involved in getting video and news on the air. On February 14, fifteen Scouts took a tour of the KTVU studios in Oakland’s Jack London Square. At the start of the tour, the Scouts were invited onto the set of KTVU’s “Take 2 This Morning” streaming show. The Scouts were interviewed by anchors Allie Rasmus and Frank Mallicoat. Mallicoat told the troop members he is an Eagle Scout—the highest ranking one can earn in scouting. He talked to the troop about all the beneficial skills he gained from his scouting experience. “I learned so much, like leadership, working as a team, cooking, camping, taking care of myself and others, reaching goals, and being responsible,” said Mallicoat. “I’m still friends with a number of my fellow Scouts even 50 years later.” Members of the troop also toured the KTVU control room. They learned how the audio, video, and other equipment operate and spoke with news producers and directors about their roles. “The most surprising thing I learned is that the cameras in the studio were unmanned and moved by themselves,” said Scout, Kian Spina. “The studio was like a finetuned machine, with everyone depending on everyone,” added Scout Ozzie Edelson-Evans. Some Scouts had the opportunity to sit in the director’s chair and change all the different camera angles, backgrounds, and screen editing. Afterwards, some Scouts read from the teleprompter to experience part of the job of a news anchor. “We learned about the role of the producer and how they must crunch all the different interviews and squeeze all the times together, so it all fits into the one news report,” said Scout Adrien Messina. The Scouts learned had the chance to observe how the green screen works. The screen is a chromakey software program used by meteorologists to display weather satellite maps and 5-day forecasts. If someone wears the color green in front of the screen, the satellite image will appear on their clothing. Scouts used a green tablecloth to see what it was like to “disappear” into the green screen. “Everything green showed weather on it, so Allie gave us a green piece of fabric and everything under it disappeared!” said Troop 1 Scout Kaito Ciammaichella. “It showed me it takes a lot of work to put on the news.” The Scouts had a revelatory experience into the innerworkings of television. “It really opened my eyes, and it’s something I would have never seen without Scouts,” said Troop member Cormac Hoffmam. articles.text: Assistant Scoutmaster Troop 1 Piedmont Scouts in Troop 1 set out on their Urban Backpacking/ Kirby Cove Service Project outing on February 27. The annual trip takes place one week before Kirby Cove Campground opens for the 2026 season. Given the mid-winter timing, this adventure often unfolds under gray skies, gusty winds, and occasional rain. Not this year. The skies were blue, the sun was out, and barely a breeze, making for a perfect day for a hike. Getting to Kirby Cove Recreation Area, one of the crown jewels of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area, makes up most of the adventure. Starting in Piedmont, the troop rode AC Transit’s Route 88 bus to downtown Oakland, then walked a mile to Jack London Square to board the ferry to the San Francisco Ferry Building. This year, with the Pier 41 Short Hop Ferry no longer in service, Scouts added an extra mile to their route, hiking from the Ferry Building to Pier 39. A favorite tradition soon followed: a stop at Boudin Bakery at Fisherman’s Wharf, where Scouts refueled with sourdough bread, cheese bread, and other well-earned treats. From there, the group continued on foot through Fort Mason and Crissy Field, pausing at the Golden Gate National Parks Conservancy’s Warming Hut before making the climb to the Golden Gate Bridge. For several Scouts and adult leaders, it was their first time crossing the bridge on foot, accompanied by sweeping views of the bay. After taking in the scenery at Vista Point in Marin County, the troop began the final descent down the trail to Kirby Cove near the base of the Golden Gate Bridge. In total, the Scouts covered eight miles of stunning vistas, varied terrain, and the kind of camaraderie that turns shared miles into shared memories. Upon arrival at Kirby Cove, Scouts were greeted and briefed on their Service Project by the National Parks System MainteJulia Bencher and Patrol Leader Susannah Cantrill on the ferry Asst. Senior Patrol Leaders Cade Ogles and Ciaran Gallagher with Senior Patrol Leader Theo Cost on the ferry Sammy Labauch, Dylan Frazier, and Solomon Gur enjoy the ferry ride through the Oakland Estuary. Scouts Ben Calloway, Zubin Sen, and Ben Cole hike across the Golden Gate Bridge. Scouts Graham Grippando and Ben Mittan clean a campsite fire ring. Troop 1 Scouts enjoy the Kirby Cove beach near the base of the Golden Gate Bridge.

articles.text: Here’s a question worth asking at your next family dinner: What do a bike wheel, a clock, and a pizza have in common? The answer is a number your older kids have probably met in math class—one that’s been quietly running the show all around them since before they could count. That number is Pi. Pi (written as the Greek letter π) is the ratio of any circle’s circumference (the distance around it) to its diameter (the distance across). This means if you divide the distance all the way around a circle by the distance across it through the center, you’ll always get a number around 3.14 (or Pi). It works for every circle, everywhere, without exception, whether pizza, plate, or planet. That consistency is what makes Pi remarkable. It’s one of the most important numbers in mathematics, art, nature, technology, and so many other industries. Because Pi is a number specific to circles, it comes up in the mathematics of circles in a variety of ways. When your kid spins around on a merry-go-round, Pi helps describe the path they’re traveling. When they ride a bike, Pi helps determine how far they go with every single rotation of the wheel. When they toss a basketball through a hoop, Pi helps define the circle they’re aiming for. And here’s what I love most about Pi for kids: it’s irrational. Literally! Pi is an example of a type of number in mathematics we call “irrational,” a number that cannot be expressed as the ratio of two integers. This means their decimal digits continue on forever without ever repeating. Mathematicians, computers, and people all over the world (including kids) have calculated Pi out A young visitor beams with delight as he enjoys a slice of pie during last year’s Pi Day celebration at the Exploratorium. to trillions of digits—and it just keeps going. For most everyday math, we round Pi to 3.14, but certainly part of the magic of Pi is its infinite tail. To make this tangible at home, try this Cutting Pi activity: gather a few circular objects from around the house—a mug, a plate, a jar lid—and use a piece of string to measure around each one, then across. For each circle, divide its circumference by its diameter and write down what you find. What do you notice? With younger kids, invite them to try to find a circular object that breaks the pattern, and test it together. With older kids, invite them to explain why some Pi estimations are so close or far from the actual ratio– why was that plate’s ratio about 3, when that clock’s ratio was 3.13?... And if you want to go all in: Pi Day was invented right here at the Exploratorium, and we’ve been celebrating it every March 14 for nearly 40 years. This year, join us on Saturday, March 14, for a full day of math-inspired activities and presentations, a Pi Parade, and a free slice of pie. Come for the STEAM, stay for the slice—and see Pi in action all around you. For complete instructions on the Cutting Pi activity, visit the Exploratorium’s Science Snacks collection at exploratorium.edu/ snacks. Dr. Megan Taylor leads a team of educators, teacher educators, and scientists as Chief Teaching & Learning Officer at the Exploratorium. A Nationally Board Certified Teacher with over two decades of experience in the San Francisco Bay Area, Dr. Taylor earned her MA and PhD in Mathematics Education from Stanford University. Before joining the Exploratorium, she founded Trellis Education, a nonprofit dedicated to ensuring California public school students have exceptional math and science teachers who share critical identities with them. An enthusiastic Exploratorium visitor for over four decades, Dr. Taylor champions the power of hands-on discovery.

articles.text: Highlanders receive No. 3 seed in CIF State Division 1 Piedmont High’s No. 3 seeded girls’ basketball team took home third-place in the North Coast Section Open Division, beating No. 4 Clayton Valley Charter 58-53 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, February 27. Two days earlier, the Highlanders lost 52-39 to No. 2 Carondelet, which went on to beat No. 1 San Ramon Valley for the title. On Tuesday, March 3, PHS received the No. 3 seed in the CIF State Division 1 bracket and faced No. 14 Antelope for the third time this season Results were not complete by Post time. “We’re working hard right now and the girls are doing what we ask. The bigger games we’re in, the higher the stakes; you realize every possession is important. We need every point and rebound we get,” coach Bryan Gardere said. There were 16 total lead changes in the game with Clayton Valley. Piedmont trailed 53-49 lead with 2:45 left in the game. But from that point on, the Highlanders didn’t allow another basket. “The energy in the room changed, My teammates and I knew what we had to do to get the win. Our competitiveness changed, we just wanted it more,” junior Taylor White said. Converting shots at the free throw line proved to be a critical piece of the win. The Highlanders converted 21 of 26 free throws, including 11 of 12 in the fourth quarter. “Free throws are something we’ve been crying about as coaches. We had them try to Staff Photos Jenelle Solis celebrates with coach Bryan Gardere after Piedmont’s win over Clayton Valley Charter. shoot at lunch time, after practice, and we shot a lot in yesterday’s practice. The more reps, the better,” Gardere said. “We have set goals and we always try to get above 70 percent. That’s something we’ve been working toward all year,” sophomore guard Jenelle Solis said. 58-52 victory over Clayton Valley Charter Piedmont led 17-16 through the first quarter, including five lead changes when Solis landed a shot with five seconds left. The back-and-forth scoring continued in the second quarter with five lead changes through the opening three minutes. CVC pushed its lead to 30-24, but PHS closed with baskets by Andrea Martin and White to cut the deficit to 30-28 at halftime. In the third quarter, Piedmont went up 36-35 at the 3:52 mark. Taylor White logged 21 rebounds in Piedmont’s win over Clayton Valley Charter. Andrea Martin led with 25 points on Clayton Valley. Clayton Valley scored the final four points of the quarter to tie up the game 39-39 going into the fourth. There were three more lead changes in the fourth until Piedmont took control with 1:15 left. CVC went up 50-45 midway through the quarter, but PHS chipped away to 50-49. Clayton Valley hit a 3-pointer with 2:45 left, 53-49, but the Highlanders followed with a 9-0 scoring run to end the game. It started with White grabbing an offensive rebound and assisting Martin, a free throw by Martin, and a bucket by Solis to take the lead 54-53 with 1:15 left. From there, Solis and Alexa Ba closed the game with two free throws apiece. Final stats: Martin led with 25 points and also had nine rebounds. Solis had 13 points, two rebounds, one assist, and a steal. Ba had nine points, four rebounds, two assists, and a steal. White had nine points, 21 rebounds, six assists, and four steals. Saniyah Johnson had two rebounds and two steals. 52-39 to Carondelet Piedmont led 12-5 through the first quarter and 22-14 by halftime. But Carondelet exploded for 20 points in the third quarter and held Piedmont to five points, jumping ahead 34-29. Carondelet outscored Piedmont 18-10 in the fourth. Final stats: Martin had 13 points, seven rebounds, one assist. Be had 11 points, four rebounds, one assist, and one steal. Johnson had six points, three rebounds, and two steals. White had five points, three rebounds, two assists, and two steals. Solis was held to two points, one rebound, three assists, and a steal. Tuesday vs. No. 14 Antelope Piedmont hosted No. 14 Antelope of Roseville for the first round of the Division 1 CIF State tournament on Tuesday, March 3. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP With a victory on Tuesday, No. 3 Piedmont (21-4 overall) will host the winner of No. 6 Central East and No. 11 Pinewood on Thursday, March 5

pages.text: 12 Wednesday, March 4, 2026 Sports Piedmont girls take third in NCS Open Division Highlanders receive No. 3 seed in CIF State Division 1 By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s No. 3 seeded girls’ basketball team took home third-place in the North Coast Section Open Division, beating No. 4 Clayton Valley Charter 58-53 at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, February 27. Two days earlier, the Highlanders lost 52-39 to No. 2 Carondelet, which went on to beat No. 1 San Ramon Valley for the title. On Tuesday, March 3, PHS received the No. 3 seed in the CIF State Division 1 bracket and faced No. 14 Antelope for the third time this season Results were not complete by Post time. “We’re working hard right now and the girls are doing what we ask. The bigger games we’re in, the higher the stakes; you realize every possession is important. We need every point and rebound we get,” coach Bryan Gardere said. There were 16 total lead changes in the game with Clayton Valley. Piedmont trailed 53-49 lead with 2:45 left in the game. But from that point on, the Highlanders didn’t allow another basket. “The energy in the room changed, My teammates and I knew what we had to do to get the win. Our competitiveness changed, we just wanted it more,” junior Taylor White said. Converting shots at the free throw line proved to be a critical piece of the win. The Highlanders converted 21 of 26 free throws, including 11 of 12 in the fourth quarter. “Free throws are something we’ve been crying about as coaches. Clayton Valley hit a 3-pointer with 2:45 left, 53-49, but the Highlanders followed with a 9-0 scoring run to end the game. articles.text: Photos by Mark Aikawa Diego Delventhal embarks on his senior season. He slugged two doubles against Skyline. Piedmont High’s baseball team got its season underway in big fashion with a dominant 10-1 win over Skyline on the Titans’ home field in the Oakland Hills on Friday, February 27. Piedmont undergoes big changes from last year’s team that reached the North Coast Section quarterfinals as the No. 2 seed. Still, coach Eric Olson is excited about the returning team. “I looked around and we have some new guys in starting roles, but we also have guys who are back and guys who have bigger roles than last year,” Olson said. Piedmont’s infield is among the reasons for Olson’s optimism. The middle of the infield will have senior Diego Delventhal at shortstop having the rare opportunity to play alongside his younger brother, Lucas Delventhal, at second base. “It’s always been a dream of mine. To get out there and train with him every day is a dream come true. He deserves the opportunity and works just as hard as I do,” Diego said. “Since I was in middle school, I’ve been dreaming about teaming up with my brother. It’s really cool. I’ve been prepared to play and I let my play do the talking today. Hopefully I can stay hot,” mentioned Lucas. Pitcher Massimo Mittone started Friday’s win over Skyline, throwing four innings with three strikeouts and an earned run. George Bishop logged two innings and struck out two, while Thomas Moision struck out all three in one inning. Along with three-year starter Jack Meyjes, Olson also feels the pitching staff is among the strongest part of the team. “We got off to a start last year like we’ve never seen before; something like no runs allowed in 21 innings. We also have confidence in Jack. George pitched great today and we saw Thomas Moison, who has some great stuff too,” Olson said. “What really set our team apart this year is how many guys who can come in and confidently throw strikes. articles.text: As things go in youth sports in Piedmont, kids build friendships and connections on the fields and in gyms that they may take with them for the first of their lives. With this year’s Piedmont High baseball team, seniors Diego Delventhal and Jack Meyjes embark on their final season playing together before graduating with the Class of 2026, ending a tradition they’ve largely continued since their tee-ball days when they were five-years-old. Delventhal and Meyjes have been teammates on Piedmont High’s varsity baseball team for four years. Delventhal has been a second baseman and shortstop, while Meyjes has been an infielder and pitcher. Following graduation this spring, Meyjes will be off to continue his baseball career at Bates College while Delventhal will head to Pitzer College. “It started back in tee-ball; he was the first person I made friends with,” said Meyjes. “Throughout our elementary school years, we were always on the same team. We always stuck together.” They’ve seen success both on the school’s team and during their little league days. Playing on the Piedmont Baseball and Softball Foundation’s Pinto league for ages 7-8, the two won a championship game where Meyjes hit the walk-off winner to lift the trophy. “We were in Pinto and he came up with the bases loaded in a tie game. He hit a walk-off to win the championship down the right field line,” Delventhal recalled. “We won a couple of Piedmont championships. It was our second year in Pinto That was probably in the second grade, I just remember celebrating with him, his dad, and my dad,” Meyjes said On the high school team, the pair has been a key part of recent success. The Highlanders reached the 2023 North Coast Section semifinals as the No. 8 seed as freshmen. As sophomores, they were runners up in the 2024 NCS championship and CIF State D4 championship after winning the WACC Foothill regular season title, They were last year’s No. 2 seed in the NCS Div. 3 postseason and reached the quarterfinals. In 2024 as sophomores, Meyjes was the winning pitcher when Piedmont wpm the league championship (WACC Foothill), clinching a 7-5 win over Berkeley. “I remember when he closed it out to win league and we all congregated at the mound to celebrate. That was dope,” Delventhal said of his favorite high school memory of Jack. Diego Delventhal (left) and Jack Meyjes reflect on their many years playing baseball alongside each other, and now for the final time in 2026. Diego Delventhal (left) and Jack Meyjes have largely been teammates ever since their days in tee-ball.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team has returned for its 2026 season, having already played its first two matches of the season. The Highlanders lost 15-8 at Foothill on Tuesday, February 24 and fell 10-7 to Campolindo at Witter Field two days later. PHS is back after reaching last year’s Division 2 North Coast Section championship game, finishing as runners up to College Park in an 8-7 overtime loss. That team featured 14 seniors from the Class of 2025, meaning this year’s squad inherently has some huge changes. “We’ve barely had a week of practice and played a decent Foothill team. From that game to Campolindo, these girls really figured it out,” coach Carlton Chan. Piedmont has to replace Friedie Schickedanz, whose role was to hold up the ball near the net as a playmaking scorer and assister. Still, PHS brings back the Post’s honorable mention for Athlete of the Year, Peyton Watson. Hallie Burden is another returning player poised for a big role after missing the entire 2025 season due to an injury. “It’s a whole new roster. Hallie didn’t play all last year and is now taking the draw. We have Peyton, and most of our girls were on JV last year. We basically have a few seasoned varsity girls who are pulling along their younger teammates,” Chan said. Last season, Piedmont faced struggles during the early portion of the schedule in moving the ball up field as they transitioned defense into attack. There was a similar tone in 2026’s opening two games, but PHS found its groove in the second quarter against Campolindo. “We told them that the Campolindo game was going to be a lot faster. What we did was go back to fundamentals, spread out, make the back pass, and trust each other,” Chan said. 10-7 loss to Campolindo Campolindo led 5-1 through the first quarter and Piedmont trailed 8-4 by halftime. Campo extended its lead to 9-4 through the third quarter, while the Highlanders scored three in the fourth and only conceded one. Piedmont scored the game’s opening goal after a minute and a half, but the Cougars went on to score five straight goals. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont Unified School District hosted a meeting to examine fan conduct at games following a brawl after a basketball game on January 30. On January 30, a shocking altercation between Piedmont High’s students and the visiting San Leandro boys’ basketball team players and coaches made the KTVU News. It was a moment that preceded two other incidents from high school athletics to make larger headlines; a racial slur being hurled at an Arizona high school basketball game on February 20, and De La Salle in Concord announcing on February 25 that they are suspending their baseball team for the first five games of its season based on conduct violations. To call attention to appalling behavior at sports events throughout the country, Piedmont Unified School District hosted a fan conduct meeting on Thursday, February 26 to talk with Piedmont parents about concerns regarding the January 30 brawl. “This is a topic that is certainly in the news.; we know school districts run into problems, whether it be the athletes themselves or spectator conduct. We’ve had some bumps in the road as well, so we want to get out in front of this issue,” Superintendent Jennifer Hawn said. Piedmont High athletic director Tyler Small and principal David Yoshihara discussed certain models and protocols they would like to use going forward, noting that accountability for adults in attendance is also important. “A lot about this is us as a district and high school holding a high standard. Tyler and I are at a lot of events and see student interactions, as well as adult interactions. It’s one thing to work with students, but it’s also difficult to see how some adults behave, because I do know the students are watching,” Yoshihara said. Yoshihara made sure to mention that their goal is to have great play appreciated, regardless if the team is the home or away side. “We want to acknowledge great play regardless of what team. We want it to be exciting, we want it to be loud. Loudness is okay, it’s what we choose to say. “Go Highlanders” is okay, but if we’re antagonizing the other team, we have to figure out where we draw those lines,” Yoshihara said. Yoshihara listed things that will no longer be acceptable. include students or fans calling out opposing players by name, number, hair styles, attire, or anything identifying a specific player. Tyler later mentioned that there could be some collaboration with Western Alameda County Conference schools to streamline new rules to help prevent students from rushing the fields or courts after wins. Hawn acknowledged that the conduct of Piedmont’s players has been stellar, evident by the boys’ basketball team completely avoiding the fracas on January 30. The issue, as evident on that January night, was with spectators and coaches of the opposing team. “The conduct of our athletes are typically excellent. I think it’s the fan conduct, both the adults and sometimes students, where we have some work to do. But we can do it, we can absolutely do it. That’s why we’re here, to reset expectations and bring in the community to help us with this,” Hawn said. One topic of debate has been whether the school will bring in additional security for night games. When asked if it’s important to have more security at big events, knowing kids storming onto fields of play to celebrate is a typical tradition in sports, Hawn responded: “I don’t think it is a dramatic safety issue. I think it’s probably a communication of expectations and maybe some amount of an accountability issue.” PUSD is examining preventing fans from rushing fields of play following a notice from the State.
articles.title: PUSD hosts “Fan Conduct” meeting

NEXT UP Piedmont (0-2 overall) hosts Miramonte at Witter Field on Thursday, March 5 at 7:00 p.m. Staff Photos Piedmont Unified School District hosted a meeting to examine fan conduct at games following a brawl after a basketball game on January 30. By Jonathan Comeaux On January 30, a shocking altercation between Piedmont High’s students and the visiting San Leandro boys’ basketball team players and coaches made the KTVU News. It was a moment that preceded two other incidents from high school athletics to make larger headlines; a racial slur being hurled at an Arizona high school basketball game on February 20, and De La Salle in Concord announcing on February 25 that they are suspending their baseball team for the first five games of its season based on conduct violations. To call attention to appalling behavior at sports events throughout the country, Piedmont Unified School District hosted a fan conduct meeting on Thursday, February 26 to talk with Piedmont parents about concerns regarding the January 30 brawl. “This is a topic that is certainly in the news.; we know school districts run into problems, whether it be the athletes themselves or spectator conduct. We’ve had some bumps in the road as well, so we want to get out in front of this issue,” Superintendent Jennifer Hawn said. Piedmont High athletic director Tyler Small and principal David Yoshihara discussed certain models and protocols they would like to use going forward, noting that accountability for adults in attendance is also important. “A lot about this is us as a district and high school holding a high standard. Tyler and I are at a lot of events and see student interactions, as well as adult interactions. It’s one thing to work with students, but it’s also difficult to see how some adults behave, because I do know the students are watching,” Yoshihara said. Yoshihara made sure to mention that their goal is to have great play appreciated, regardless if the team is the home or away side. “We want to acknowledge great play regardless of what team. We want it to be exciting, we want it to be loud. Loudness is okay, it’s what we choose to say. “Go Highlanders” is okay, but if we’re antagonizing the other team, we have to figure out where we draw those lines,” Yoshihara said. Yoshihara listed things that will no longer be acceptable. include students or fans calling out opposing players by name, number, hair styles, attire, or anything identifying a specific player. Tyler later mentioned that there could be some collaboration with Western Alameda County Conference schools to streamline new rules to help prevent students from rushing the fields or courts after wins. Hawn acknowledged that the conduct of Piedmont’s players has been stellar, evident by the boys’ basketball team completely avoiding the fracas on January 30. The issue, as evident on that January night, was with spectators and coaches of the opposing team. “The conduct of our athletes are typically excellent. I think it’s the fan conduct, both the adults and sometimes students, where we have some work to do. But we can do it, we can absolutely do it. That’s why we’re here, to reset expectations and bring in the community to help us with this,” Hawn said. One topic of debate has been whether the school will bring in additional security for night games. When asked if it’s important to have more security at big events, knowing kids storming onto fields of play to celebrate is a typical tradition in sports, Hawn responded: “I don’t think it is a dramatic safety issue. I think it’s probably a communication of expectations and maybe some amount of an accountability issue.” PUSD is examining preventing fans from rushing fields of play following a notice from the State.

articles.text: The Piedmont High School Mountain Bike Team opened the 2026 NorCal League season at Fort Ord with two podium finishes and a 4th-place overall team standing in a field of 435 high school racers. On a fast, sandy 4-mile course that grew looser throughout the day, riders had to balance power with patience. Senior Jasper Schuetz finished 2nd in Varsity Boys in 1:09:31, delivering five steady laps and averaging over 300 watts in a powerful early-season performance. Sophomore Josephine Schuetz won the JV2 Girls race in 59:14, breaking the one-hour mark and claiming the leader’s jersey with a margin of more than two minutes. Piedmont also saw strong finishes from Zachary Carter (6th, JV1 Boys D2), Rose Reining (6th, JV2 Girls), and Caleb Canada (10th, JV2 Boys D2), contributing to a deep and balanced team result. The team’s strength ran deep, with Mina Herrgott, Olivia Bailey, Kai Hsu, Gabriel Barbosa, Asher Villarreal, Henry Call, Emilio Roberts, and Chase Mellers all delivering determined efforts in highly competitive divisions. The strength of Piedmont MTB extends beyond the high school team. Piedmont DEVO (the middle school development program) is one of the largest and fastest-growing youth sports programs in the community, introducing riders in grades 6–8 to skills training, teamwork, and Jasper Schuetz, a Piedmont High School senior, led the Varsity race in a tight pack of seven that swapped positions with Payton Shoresman of San Luis Obispo for five laps. Josephine Schuetz takes the win, joined on the podium by Hannah Slattery-Weisberg of Berkeley High, Naomi Bair (San Luis Obispo Composite), Kaity Bugsch (Sonora MTB Granite Grinders Composite), and Haley Wilson (San Luis Obispo Composite). articles.text: Treasure Island Museum is adding a second public art gallery including works by artists featured at the 1939 and 1940 Golden Gate International Exposition. The new gallery opens this Saturday, March 7, in the museum’s historic Building One and includes paintings, drawings, sculptures, lithographs and more by California artists, displayed publicly for the first time in decades since the groundbreaking exposition. The gallery will feature rotating exhibitions showcasing artwork preserved by the Spencer Jon Helfen Collection, offering visitors a glimpse into the island’s unique past and significance in the San Francisco Bay Area’s history and future. The museum was established in 1975 and opened to the public in 1976. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and has served as a Pan American Airways terminal and naval headquarters in addition to an exposition hub. Treasure Island Museum’s mission is to preserve and interpret the island’s Pacific-themed heritage, educate residents and visitors on its historical relevance to contemporary issues, support community partnerships and inspire future generations through programs, exhibitions and events. The gallery opening is held on March 7, 12 p.m. to 3 p.m. at 39 Treasure Island Rd #111 in San Francisco. The event is free but registration is required. Visit https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/event-details/gallery-opening to learn more and to register online. articles.text: Local florist participates for 26th year J.Miller Flowers and Gifts arrangement at Legion of Honor For 26 years, sisters Valerie and Robin Lee have marked the arrival of spring not just with blossoms in their shop windows, but with an installation at one of the Bay Area’s most anticipated museum traditions. The co-owners of J.Miller Flowers and Gifts are once again among more than 120 floral designers participating in the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s annual Bouquets to Art exhibition, which runs through Sunday, March 8. The weeklong event pairs arrangements with works from the permanent collections and architecture of the de Young Museum and the Legion of Honor. Proceeds help underwrite exhibitions, conservation projects and education programs at the museums. “It truly is one of my favorite weeks of the year,” Valerie Lee said. “I love being able to share my passion for flowers, art and nature with my friends, customers, garden clubs and museum visitors.” This year, the sisters chose a quieter, more contemplative work than in years past: Miss Eve Fairfax, a marble bust by French sculptor Auguste Rodin, on view in Gallery 8 at the Legion of Honor. “Auguste Rodin is my favorite artist and sculptor of all time,” Lee said. “All of his art evokes wonder, calm and joy when he encompasses nature into his art.” Lee said the gallery itself influenced her direction. “It was a very calming space and sculpture,” she said. “So I wanted something very calming to complement that.” Rather than bold or highly manipulated materials, Valerie said she opted for “a restrained palette of whites and greens.” Drawing inspiration from the sculpture’s ivory tones and delicate veil, the Lees created an arrangement in layered whites designed to echo its form. “That was my intention,” Lee said of the symmetrical lines that mirror the veil. “If you look at the close-up, those white alabaster anthuriums depict her face, because I felt like her face just looked like porcelain. Very delicate.” The anthuriums were sourced directly from a specialty grower in Hilo, Hawaii. The hybrid variety, developed in collaboration with the University of Hawaii and Green Point Nursery, is known for its refined shape and soft coloration. “It’s such a unique, delicate anthurium,” Lee said. “That’s Valerie Lee preps her arrangement. Photos courtesy of Valerie Lee what I wanted for her face, because she’s a really beautiful, delicate face in contrast to the harshness of just marble.” Additional white dendrobiums and phalaenopsis orchids, along with makara leaves and curly willow, complete the arrangement. Lee designed and installed the piece herself, taking into account the scale of the gallery and the need for the flowers to last the duration of the weeklong show. “My absolute favorite part of the week is being able to share my creative ideas through flowers and interpret different art through the years,” she said. “It’s always a challenge that I embrace, and I truly love sharing the Bouquets to Art experience with our art- and flower-loving community.” Lee will also participate in the museum’s Meet the Designer program on Thursday, March 5, and Friday, March 6, from noon to 1 p.m. in Gallery 8 at the Legion of Honor, where she will discuss her inspiration, floral selections and history with the exhibition. Bouquets to Art continues through Sunday, March 8, at the de Young and Legion of Honor. Two related programs round out the weekend: On Friday, March 6, at 2 p.m. in the Koret Auditorium at the de Young, “Bloom Where You’re Rooted: Culture and Floral Design” will feature florist Gina Lett-Shrewsberry and author Teresa J. Speight discussing the African American experience in floriculture. Tickets are $55 and include admission to Bouquets to Art at both museums. Seating is limited and first come, first served. On Saturday, March 7, at 1 p.m., Bay Area artist Kija Lucas will present an artist talk in the Koret Auditorium exploring themes of home, heritage and inheritance in her photography. Admission is included with a Bouquets to Art ticket. Doors open 30 minutes before the program; seating is limited and unassigned.
articles.title: J. Miller Flowers showing at FAMSF’s Bouquets to Art

articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse presents the Tony Award-winning musical Once opening February 21 and running through March 8. Featuring a book by Enda Walsh and music and lyrics by Glen Hansard and Markéta Irglová, Once is based on the 2007 film that earned the Academy Award for Best Original Song for “Falling Slowly.” Set in Dublin, the story follows an Irish busker and a Czech immigrant who form a deep connection through music during a life-changing week of songwriting and collaboration. The production is directed by Josh Marx, with music direction by Michael Patrick Wiles and choreography by Erin Rose Solorio. Actors perform their own instruments onstage, creating a pub-style atmosphere that underscores the show’s themes of community and artistic partnership. “I’ve always loved Once because it digs into something I think about a lot: what music really is and how it connects us Photo by Ben Krantz Jake Gale and Gillian Eichenberger perform in Berkeley Playhouse’s production of Once. as human beings,” Marx said. “I loved the movie Once when I first saw it— and then the Broadway production pulled me in even deeper, especially the way it evoked a sense of community; similar to drinking a pint of Guinness in an Irish pub while patrons play music together. For Berkeley Playhouse’s production, we’re looking to put something truly special together; each actor plays their own instrument (sometimes more than one!), and we want to create an unforgettable experience that capitalizes on the amazing talent that we’re bringing into the room.” Jake Gale and Gillian Eichenberger lead the cast as Guy and Girl. For tickets or more information, call (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org.
articles.title: Berkeley Playhouse premieres Once on Feb. 21

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Cal Performances The opera merges Jean Cocteau’s 1946 romantic fantasy with Philip Glass’ 1994 score. Opera Parallèle will present two major productions this Spring, with a revival of its critically-acclaimed production of La Belle et la Bête showing Friday, March 13, and Saturday, March 14, both at 8 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. Based on Jean Cocteau’s 1946 film and set to Philip Glass’s 1994 score, the production fuses live performance with film imagery in a surrealist retelling of the classic fairy tale. Nicole Paiement conducts, with direction and production concept by Brian Staufenbiel. The creative team also includes projection designer and director of photography David Murakami, lighting designer Jessica Ann Drayton, costume designer Natalie Barshow, hair and makeup designer Y. Sharon Peng, and sound designer Jay Cruz. Sung in French with projected English supertitles, the approximately 90-minute opera runs without intermission. The cast features Hadleigh Adams as La Bête, Le Prince, Avenant and l’Officier; Chea Kang as La Belle; Aurélien Mangwa as Le Père, Ludovic and L’Usurier; and Sophie Delphis as Félicie and Adélaïde. Tickets start at $55. Later in the season, Opera Parallèle presents the West Coast opera debut of Doubt, with music by Douglas Cuomo and a libretto by John Patrick Shanley. The opera will be staged in partnership with Presidio Theatre, with performances Friday, May 29, and Saturday, May 30, at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, May 31, at 3 p.m., at Presidio Theatre in San Francisco. Based on Shanley’s Pulitzer Prize- and Tony Award-winning play, Doubt is sung in English with projected English supertitles and runs approximately 100 minutes without intermission. These performances introduce a new chamber orchestra version created by the composer and an abridged libretto by Kevin Newbury. Paiement conducts with Staufenbiel directing. The cast includes Matthew Worth as Father Flynn, Rhoslyn Jones as Sister Aloysius, Naomi Steele as Sister James, and Deborah Nansteel as Mrs. Miller. Tickets start at $66.
articles.title: Opera Parallèle performs La Belle et la Bête at UC Berkeley March 13 & 14

articles.text: Festival held at War Memorial Opera House May 9 & 10 San Francisco Ballet School will celebrate decades of artistic leadership this spring with a galastyle festival at the War Memorial Opera House, marking the first time the school’s Spring Festival will be staged in the historic venue with live orchestral accompaniment. The 2025 Spring Festival, set for May 9 and 10, features works by past and present artistic directors of San Francisco Ballet, including Helgi Tomasson, Michael Smuin, Lew Christensen and current San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo. Students will perform to live music by the Grammy Award-winning San Francisco Ballet Orchestra under Music Director and Principal Conductor Martin West. The program, curated by School Director Grace Holmes, includes excerpts from Rojo’s “Raymonda,” Tomasson’s “Handel – A Celebration,” Smuin’s “Quattro a Verdi,” Christensen’s “Vivaldi Concerto Grosso” and August Bournonville’s “La Sylphide.” “This program is a testament to the legacy, evolution, and enduring artistry that defines San Photo by Lindsay Thomas San Francisco Ballet School Students in 2024 Spring Festival Francisco Ballet and San Francisco Ballet School,” Holmes said in a press release. “It is an honor to celebrate the innovation and creativity that continue to inspire generations of dancers and audiences on a global scale. We are proud to be able to give these students the opportunity to perform in a venue with such a rich legacy alongside the unparalleled SF Ballet Orchestra as our students continue to develop artistically and strive toward professional careers in ballet.” Additional works include a world premiere by company member Davide Occhipinti and the West Coast debut of Esteban Hernández’s “1941,” both commissioned through the organization’s Creation House initiative supporting emerging choreographers. Performances are scheduled for 7 p.m. May 9 and 4 p.m. May 10. Tickets start at $29, with discounted children’s tickets available. Proceeds will support scholarships and education programs serving more than 40,000 community members annually. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ support-engage/special-events/ to purchase tickets online. Photo by Lindsay Thomas San Francisco Ballet School Spring Festival will be held at the War Memorial Opera House on May 9 & 10.
articles.title: San Francisco Ballet School announces 2025 Spring Festival

Works from Purcell, Schubert, Dowling, Schumann and Ralph Vaughn Williams will be followed by a composition by the 19th Century Romantic composer Massenet. Kander and Ebb’s song, Razzle Dazzle, from Chicago will be followed by Leonard Cohen’s iconic Hallelujah. Romanza by the beloved Italian R&B, Jazz, and Disco composer Malavasy will round out the evening’s presentation. The Konverg Duo has toured throughout Asia and Europe. For an uplifting evening indulgence don’t miss this concert at 7 p.m. on Friday, March 13. Reception to meet the artist to follow. $20 at the door. ®

For Berkeley Playhouse’s production, we’re looking to put something truly special together; each actor plays their own instrument (sometimes more than one!), and we want to create an unforgettable experience that capitalizes on the amazing talent that we’re bringing into the room.” Jake Gale and Gillian Eichenberger lead the cast as Guy and Girl. San Francisco Ballet School announces 2025 Spring Festival Festival held at War Memorial Opera House May 9 & 10 By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Ballet School will celebrate decades of artistic leadership this spring with a galastyle festival at the War Memorial Opera House, marking the first time the school’s Spring Festival will be staged in the historic venue with live orchestral accompaniment. The 2025 Spring Festival, set for May 9 and 10, features works by past and present artistic directors of San Francisco Ballet, including Helgi Tomasson, Michael Smuin, Lew Christensen and current San Francisco Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo. Students will perform to live music by the Grammy Award-winning San Francisco Ballet Orchestra under Music Director and Principal Conductor Martin West. Opera Parallèle performs La Belle et la Bête at UC Berkeley March 13 & 14 Photo courtesy of Cal Performances The opera merges Jean Cocteau’s 1946 romantic fantasy with Philip Glass’ 1994 score. By Allyson Aleksey Opera Parallèle will present two major productions this Spring, with a revival of its critically-acclaimed production of La Belle et la Bête showing Friday, March 13, and Saturday, March 14, both at 8 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. Based on Jean Cocteau’s 1946 film and set to Philip Glass’s 1994 score, the production fuses live performance with film imagery in a surrealist retelling of the classic fairy tale. Nicole Paiement conducts, with direction and production concept by Brian Staufenbiel. The creative team also includes projection designer and director of photography David Murakami, lighting designer Jessica Ann Drayton, costume designer Natalie Barshow, hair and makeup designer Y. Sharon Peng, and sound designer Jay Cruz. Sung in French with projected English supertitles, the approximately 90-minute opera runs without intermission. The cast features Hadleigh Adams as La Bête, Le Prince, Avenant and l’Officier; Chea Kang as La Belle; Aurélien Mangwa as Le Père, Ludovic and L’Usurier; and Sophie Delphis as Félicie and Adélaïde. Tickets start at $55. Later in the season, Opera Parallèle presents the West Coast opera debut of Doubt, with music by Douglas Cuomo and a libretto by John Patrick Shanley. The opera will be staged in partnership with Presidio Theatre, with performances Friday, May 29, and Saturday, May 30, at 7:30 p.m., and Sunday, May 31, at 3 p.m., at Presidio Theatre in San Francisco. Based on Shanley’s Pulitzer Prize- and Tony Award-winning play, Doubt is sung in English with projected English supertitles and runs approximately 100 minutes without intermission. These performances introduce a new chamber orchestra version created by the composer and an abridged libretto by Kevin Newbury. Paiement conducts with Staufenbiel directing. The cast includes Matthew Worth as Father Flynn, Rhoslyn Jones as Sister Aloysius, Naomi Steele as Sister James, and Deborah Nansteel as Mrs. Miller. Tickets start at $66. articles.text: Concerts held March 22 - May 31 Berkeley Symphony will open its 2026 Chamber Series with four curated programs highlighting contemporary voices and classical masterworks, all held at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The series begins with “Roots and Resonances” on February 22 at 4 p.m., curated by composer Samuel Adams. The program features percussionist Haruka Fujii and a string quartet from the symphony in works exploring texture and timbre, including music by Salina Fisher and Osvaldo Golijov, as well as Adams’ “Sundial” and Fujii’s “Divisions.” On March 22, “French Connections,” curated by Dianne Nicolini of Classical California KDFC, will feature works by Francis Poulenc, Lili Boulanger and Gabriel Fauré. Composer Juan Pablo Contreras curates “The Music of Muses” on April 12, with music by Reena Esmail, Jennifer Higdon and Bedřich Smetana, alongside his “Musas Mexicanas.” The series concludes May 31 with “I, Too, Sing America,” curated by James Parrish Smith, featuring works by Brian Raphael Nabors, Anna Clyne and Antonín Dvořák. The symphony closes its 2025/26 season following the conclusion of Music Director Joseph Young’s successful sixyear tenure. “This season represents an exciting new chapter for Berkeley Symphony,” said Berkeley Symphony Executive Director Marion Atherton in a press release. “We’re thrilled to welcome some of today’s most compelling conductors, each bringing their unique artistic vision to our stage.” This season “shines a light on stirring masterpieces from the classical canon alongside groundbreaking contemporary works,” Atherton added. “From Dvorák’s lyrical Eighth Symphony to Shostakovich’sspirited Ninth and Haydn’s vivid ‘Military’ Symphony, we’re exploring rich musical territory beyond the standard repertoire while showcasing the versatility and excellence of our orchestra.” Chamber Series subscriptions are $120 and available through the symphony’s box office and website. Subscriptions can be purchased by calling the box office at (510) 841-2800 or visiting berkeleysymphony.org. The symphony returns to the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Spring. pages.text: 18 18 Wednesday, March 4, 2026 The Musical Gourmet Heroes and hero worship By Joseph Gold A philosopher famously observed: “From the genius we learn what to do. From the fool, we learn what not to do.” This is a paraphrase from the philosophy of the great American tenor Jerry Hadley (1952-2007). In case you don’t recognize the name, he was one of the great singers from the recent past, and he always advised to study the greats of the distant past. Parallel to this is constant self-analysis based on the principles of the great minds and logic. Many times the principles expressed in another sphere apply in music as well as in our personal lives. I always think of the philosophy of the great football coach Vince Lombardi who observed, “The team that controls the line of scrimmage wins the game.” Let’s apply that philosophy across the board. My father spoke frequently of the great tenor Enrico Caruso. He might have been the greatest singer of all time, but he was also one of the finest people of all time. His generosity, both on the The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet stage and off, was exemplary. Using the philosophy of Vince Lombardi once again we get advice from the legendary Spanish violinist Pablo de Sarasate. He told my first violin teacher that it is important to keep the fingers directly above the strings of the violin. All musicians would be advised to follow this philosophy. Additionally, he said that if you look good, you will sound good. I was fortunate to have known some stellar figures of the past who offered advice. Van Cliburn was one of them. His generosity was similar to that of Enrico Caruso. Ditto for opera star Brian Sullivan. The Duke of Baena (Spanish diplomat) was a brilliant representative from another sphere. He was a diplomat for the ages. For example, he even knew how to deal with Generalissimo Franco. That was quite an accomplishment. Another outstanding character from Spain is the noted guitarist and composer Jaume Torrent. He has taken the guitar to a new realm which is light years beyond “standard guitar thinking”. I have often wished that guitarists would open their minds to the musical compositions of Jaume Torrent, and it seems that a few guitarists have opened their minds. Most guitar music is rooted in one or two keys only. How myopic. But… Jaume Torrent has opened the universe by composing pieces in every key available. As always, the words of Rocky Marciano ring true. “The bigger they are, the nicer they are”. Jaume Torrent is a forward-looking guitarist and composer. In this respect, he is unique in the world of music. It is a quiet beat, played without dialogue by Niv Sultan. It is also when the series makes its intentions clear. This is not just a thriller about intelligence agencies. It is a story about identity, memory, and the thin line between home and enemy. Watching Tehran while realworld tensions with Iran fill the headlines adds an uneasy charge. The show, now in its third season on Apple TV+, unfolds like a psychological pressure cooker. Writer Moshe Zonder and director Daniel Syrkin build a narrative that compresses time and emotion. Missions unravel in minutes. Loyalties shift quickly. Decisions carry immediate, personal consequences. At its core, the show explores an ancient antagonism sharpened by modern radicalism. It understands that conflict between Israel and Iran is not only strategic but historical and ideological. Yet what gives Tehran its power is its refusal to flatten anyone into a symbol. The enemies are fully human. They love their families. They make mistakes. They doubt themselves. The antagonism is real, but so is the shared fragility of the people caught inside it. The engine of the series is not flawless tradecraft but human fallibility. Characters are driven by rage, fear, pride and loyalty as much as by policy. The pacing is relentless. There are no indulgent flashbacks or narrative detours. The compression of time is deliberate. This is clearly a show, not a documentary about spy work. articles.text: Mason Thames in How to Train Your Dragon There are stories that endure because they tap something we recognize before we can name it — the outcast, the misunderstood creature, the friendship that costs something. How to Train Your Dragon, now reimagined in live action, knows exactly what kind Adapted from the animated franchise, itself drawn from Cressida Cowell’s books, the film returns us to the Viking village of Berk, where dragons are feared, hunted and poorly understood. At the center is Hiccup, a slight, thoughtful boy born into a culture that prizes brute strength. He is the chief’s son who cannot become his father. Into this comes Toothless — a Night Fury, the most feared dragon in the skies — injured, grounded, and just as stranded from the world as the boy who finds him. What begins as secrecy becomes friendship. What begins as fear becomes trust. When Hiccup looks into a dragon’s eyes and sees something like himself, he cannot go through with the kill. That moment of recognition — quiet, almost accidental — is where the film lives. The dragon who has every reason to destroy humans learns, slowly, to depend on one. What DeBlois has always understood — as the writer-director of the original trilogy, now returned to remake his own work — is that Hiccup is not learning to tame a dragon. He is learning to see one. His village’s hatred is not mere superstition; it is inherited identity, passed down so long it feels like instinct. To question it is to become a stranger in your own home. DeBlois never lets Hiccup off easily, and never lets the audience mistake recognition for resolution. The live-action finds textures the animation could only suggest. The flying sequences are exhilarating, but it is the stillness that lingers — a wordless early encounter where Hiccup and Toothless circle each other, neither willing to look away, each unsure whether to run. Wind moves through Viking fur cloaks. Scales catch real light. Berk feels inhabited rather than constructed. The outsider, this film keeps insisting, sees what the tribe has trained itself not to. It is an old idea. DeBlois makes you feel it anyway. How to Train Your Dragon. Directed by Dean DeBlois. Starring Mason Thames, Nico Parker, Gerard Butler. Released in 2025. 1 hr., 56 min. Rated PG. articles.text: Flow is one of those films I genuinely regret not seeing sooner. It won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature in 2025, and once I finally sat down with it, I understood why. The film is built on a technology called Blender, a free, open-source 3D creation suite that gives animators a painterly, almost impressionistic visual style. I’ll be honest: when people start explaining “core animation technology,” my eyes glaze over. But none of that matters once the film begins. What unfolds on screen is lush, detailed, and immediately absorbing. The story follows a black cat living alone in an abandoned house deep in the forest. There’s no dialogue, no narration, just sound. Animal noises. Barking. The cat’s soft mewing. The filmmakers have to make you care about this creature without a single spoken word, and somehow, they pull it off. Things get moving when a massive flood tears through the forest, almost Biblical in scale. The cat, who we come to know as Flow, is swept up along with everything else. The hope, such as it is, becomes finding dry land. What Flow finds instead is a small sailboat carrying an odd collection of survivors: lemurs, a dog, a large white stork-like bird, a capybara. None of them especially want to share the space. All of them have to do it. There’s an environmental undercurrent running through the whole film, though it never turns preachy. More striking is what the filmmakers chose not to do. The animals aren’t anthropomorphized. They don’t speak or reason like humans. articles.text: The Oakland Zoo has welcomed a new red-tailed monkey baby boy! The Zoo’s resident red-tailed guenons, Nonami the mother and Marley the father, welcomed a male offspring in February. The milestone marks the first birth of a guenon monkey at Oakland Zoo. Nonami and her baby boy, named Tumbili, are thriving. He is nursing and bonding normally with Nonami, and she is ensuring the baby stays close. As a veteran mom, Nonami has successfully given birth at her previous Zoo to two other females who also live at Oakland Zoo: Ikea and Skittles. Nonami and her baby have joined the rest of the troop in their habitat, and the baby’s sister, Ikea, has shown strong interest in her brother and wants to help Mom with grooming while Nonami supervises. Mom and baby frequently spend time in the habitat, where visitors can see them every day, but sometimes Mom may prefer to retreat to a cozy, warm bedroom space with her baby. Nonami and Marley were recommended for breeding by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) within the Guenon Red-tailed Monkey Species Survival Plan (SSP). The SSP was created by the AZA (which accredits Oakland Zoo) to promote the sustainability of a healthy, genetically diverse, and demographically varied AZA population. Keepers are thrilled about the Nonami, one of Oakland Zoo’s resident red-tailed guenons, and her new baby boy, Tumbili.

articles.text: One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing one with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what the Piedmont Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and a lively discussion afterward. The Flix Fest’s March selection is 400 Blows, directed by Francois Truffaut. This film was his first New Wave film as a director and is considered an autobiographical portrayal of his own adolescent years. The film takes place in 1959 in the urban cityscape of Paris. Using a hand-held camera, Truffaut follows the adventures of 12-year-old Antoine Doinel, with a mixture of outdoor and static scenes of his apartment and classroom. Antoine’s artistic interests are curtailed by a rigid French curriculum focused on the written word, and his emotional development is stunted at home by unloving parents, who treat him as a nuisance in their adult lives. These restrictions lead Antoine to rebel against his teacher in class and his parents at home with acts of mischief and truancy, as he searches for freedom of expression with his best friend from school. The theft of a typewriter from his father’s office results in a night in jail and a 2-month stay at a juvenile detention center for boys, requested by his parents, who no longer know how to control his behavior. Antoine’s escape from this center leads him for the first time to the seashore, where he stands in the film’s final scene to face the camera in a frozen frame, staring back at us to ponder his future, and ours. 400 Blows will be screened on Thursday, March 12, at the Piedmont Center of the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45 p.m, and the movie is free to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis and can bring snacks. The next movie will be Enchanted April, a 1991 romantic comedy directed by Mike Newell, to be shown on April 9. Please note that due to a venue conflict, the film will be shown at 4 p.m.

articles.text: Last Wednesday morning brought 46 walkers and three K-9 companions to the Exedra, ready to finish what a rainy week had interrupted. The mission: complete a tour of Piedmont’s Victorian homes drawn from Ann Swift’s 2007 book, Cottages and Castles – The Centennial Houses of the City of Piedmont. Swift served as Piedmont City Clerk for 22 years and became the city’s unofficial historian. Written for Piedmont’s centennial, her book documents 173 homes that were already over 100 years old at the time of publication. On this walk, her historical research was shared along the route, and architect Jim Kellogg returned to offer architectural commentary on each house. The prior week’s rain had cut the tour short before reaching two Victorians on Oakland Avenue. This Wednesday, the group would see those and more, swinging through the western side of the city. The walkers set off down Magnolia Avenue, crossed Hillside to Oakland Avenue, and headed down to Jerome Avenue. At 29 Jerome, a dog named Moose made the group’s arrival unmistakable. His barking brought out the homeowner, Christopher, who came down to greet everyone. The house Robert Gray built in 1894 is a compact Victorian cottage, and Kellogg described its standout features: a large front bay window beneath a projecting roof gable, fish-scale shingles, and a sunburst detail at the ridge. By 1901, the property belonged to John Spring, who died a multi-millionaire with a 16-acre Berkeley estate. In 1895 he had sued the Piedmont Consolidated Cable Company and won $14,000, seed money he invested in land across Berkeley, Alameda, and Piedmont that surged in value after the 1906 earthquake. Swift speculated the cottage served as a weekend escape from his San Francisco residence. The group posed for a photo on the entry steps with Christopher and Moose before moving on. From Jerome, the walkers wound through Cambridge Way, across Grand Avenue, and up Greenbank to Rose Avenue, a street with a quirk worth pausing over. The houses on the north side are in Oakland; those on the south are in Piedmont. The reason goes back to the city’s rushed incorporation in 1907, when Piedmont residents voted to break away from Oakland. To file the paperwork in Sacramento quickly, city founders grabbed the only detailed map available, one from the Piedmont Sanitary Sewer District. Sewer lines follow geography, not streets, which is why roughly 136 parcels are split between the two cities today. Rose Avenue holds a cluster of notable Victorians. At 950 Rose, the sewer district assessed the property at $250 and the house at $400 when it was built in 1901. The earliest records describe just one bedroom; a Rose family owned it by 1926, and the street appears to be named for them, not the flower. The tall Queen Anne turret on the right was added in the 1970s, and basement expansion added bedrooms over time. Kellogg noted the house sits at the tail end of the Victorian era; the homes built on Rose just a few years later already reflect 20th-century tastes: Bungalow, Craftsman, American Foursquare, and various Revival styles. At 934 Rose, Peter and Christine Nelson, Norwegian immigrants who arrived in 1881, built their Queen Anne cottage in 1895. Peter drove a water cart; Christine raised their children and, by 1907, ran a catering business from home. That same year they built 938 Rose next door, and the contrast tells the story of a style falling out of fashion. The 1895 house is ornamented with sunburst patterns, wood spindle supports, dentil trim, bay windows, and the original white picket fence. The 1907 house is straightforward clapboard with Participating were Mike Gallant, Joanne Larson, Dan Scdonis, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Sarah Johnson, Noemi Alvarado, Melba Yee, Lori Austin, Nadeen Guffanti, Bill Ahern, Ken Moy, Tina Shum, Alissa Quan, Jim Kellogg, Mary Ann Barnes, June Yee, Edith Lee, Stella Houston, Betsy Lim, Chuck Oraftik, Regina O’Connor, Sean Brient, Sherry Jacobs, Kat Lang, Marcia Arthurs, Max Becker, Jim Kellogg, Mark Davis, Peggy Shultz, Denny McGee, Pat Nicholas, Marianne Jakas, Irene Thompson, Mary Carter, Albert Chen, Alicia Rivera, Brian Hamlin, Jeff Kasmar, Nancy Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Mike Henn, Rick Eigenbrode, and Dick Carter. The 1895 house is ornamented with sunburst patterns, wood spindle supports, dentil trim, bay windows, and the original white picket fence. The 1907 house is straightforward clapboard with Map of the walk Doric columns, a hip roof, and none of the ornament. A decade was all it took. Next door at 930 Rose, Welsh immigrant Hugh Davies built his house the same year as the Nelsons. A carpenter at Mountain View Cemetery, Davies supported a wife and eventually five children in the home. Before 1926 he divided it into two units. The Queen Anne details survive: fishscale gable shingles, decorative corner brackets, dentils over the bay windows, and the original stained glass entry door. The group navigated past tree trimmers working the Piedmont side of Rose but not the Oakland side, then looped back via Linda and Kingston Avenues to Greenbank. At 225 Greenbank, Ole Berg built a one-story cottage in 1907. A 45-year-old Norwegian stevedore working in the Oakland docks, Berg may well have done much of the construction himself. The house lacks some details that would have required a finish carpenter but carries the Queen Anne hallmarks: fishscale shingles, turned posts, and spindlework. He added a garage in 1926, and the house was raised in the 1990s to add a second floor. Back on Oakland Avenue, the group noted 1138 Oakland, a late Victorian built by C. H. Hawley in 1901, with bay windows on each side, multiple gables, and an original lot that once extended through to what is now 85 Fairview Avenue. Then it was time to head home via upper San Carlos and Magnolia. A longer walk than usual, but a rewarding one. Ann Swift’s Centennial homes on Sunnyside Avenue and beyond are waiting for a future Wednesday. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest is back for a fifth year! The Bay Area’s most vibrant multicultural festival returns to Piedmont Park on Saturday, April 25, from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. for a one-day celebration of global flavors, live music, and community connection. Festivalgoers can enjoy live performances including Wilbert McAlister’s Cowboy and His Sometimes Blues Band, DJ HeyLove, the Purple Silk Youth Orchestra, Beloved Aerial Arts, Han Martial Arts, Piedmont Middle School, and even a special performance by the Cal Marching Band. For Avantika Prabhakara and her husband Vishwas, Lafayette parents of three, that idea wasn’t on the radar… until their neighbors gave them a chance. “Building a home maintenance company with my wife, Avantika, was never the plan,” Vishwas says. “But after an irrigation specialist took a hefty deposit and completely ghosted us, we realized how common and frustrating that experience was. With a small group of neighbors willing to take a chance on something new, that’s how Honey Homes got started.” Back in 2022, 15 Beta members in Lafayette said yes to a brand-new concept: a dedicated handyman for your home. Not a one-off contractor, but someone reliable, consistent, and invested in your house year-round. Those early families helped shape everything — from dependable scheduling to thoughtful, family-friendly service designed specifically for busy households. Four years later, Honey Homes now supports over 400 families in Piedmont and over 3,000 families across the Bay Area, Los Angeles, Dallas, Austin, and Chicago. For Piedmont homeowners, that means help with everything from mounting garage racks, hanging blackout shades in sunny rooms, tightening loose fixtures, or pressure-washing front walkways along Highland Avenue. Honey Homes is all about helping families reclaim time, energy, and peace of mind. In a community known for beautiful historic homes and full family calendars, Honey Homes is designed to help families protect their homes — and reclaim their time. “What started as a neighborhood experiment has become a community of families counting on us for more comfort, more joy, and a lot less stress at home,” Avantika says. Thank you to Piedmont To celebrate the community that has embraced Honey Homes, the team is giving back. Ten Piedmont neighbors will receive a complimentary Honey Homes trial — including a personalized planning walk-thru and 1.5 hours of dedicated handyman help to tackle those lingering to-dos. It’s their way of saying thank you to the neighbors who continue to support local, family-founded businesses. articles.text: Part 1 Earlier this year on January 31, wine lovers gathered in downtown San Jose for the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes, an immersive wine-tasting celebration highlighting the world’s rare and lesser-known grape varieties. The event drew local residents and visitors eager to explore beyond familiar varietals like Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and Pinot Noir. Instead, guests sipped wines made from “underdog” grapes — including Semillon, Teroldego, Tannant, Bourbolenc, Cinsault, and Trousseau — representing more than 110 unique winegrape varieties grown in California. With dozens of wineries pouring their distinctive selections, attendees wandered the room sampling bold reds, aromatic whites, and intriguing blends that many had never encountered before. Wine producers from across the state were on hand to share stories of their vineyards and the heritage of these lesser-known grapes, offering insight into the diversity of California’s wine landscape. Participants could choose between general admission and VIP tickets. VIP guests enjoyed early access, a pre-tasting discussion focused on Lodi wine varietals with experts, a commemorative wine glass, and complimentary delivery of bottles ordered at the event. General admission ticket holders joined the tasting after the VIP session and had the option to have their wine purchases delivered for a flat fee. A food vendor on site offered small bites and snacks to pair with the wines, creating a festive atmosphere throughout the afternoon. Conversations flowed as easily as the pours, with many oenophiles excited to discover new favorites and broaden their palates. Organizers said the festival aimed not just to entertain but to educate, spotlighting vinicultural diversity and supporting small producers whose bottles might otherwise go unnoticed.
