pages.text: 24 24 Wednesday, March 4, 2026 The Wine Corner Festival of Undiscovered Grapes: Featuring California’s rare wines Part 1 By Pierre DuMont Earlier this year on January 31, wine lovers gathered in downtown San Jose for the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes, an immersive wine-tasting celebration highlighting the world’s rare and lesser-known grape varieties. The event drew local residents and visitors eager to explore beyond familiar varietals like Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and Pinot Noir. Instead, guests sipped wines made from “underdog” grapes — including Semillon, Teroldego, Tannant, Bourbolenc, Cinsault, and Trousseau — representing more than 110 unique winegrape varieties grown in California. With dozens of wineries pouring their distinctive selections, attendees wandered the room sampling bold reds, aromatic whites, and intriguing blends that many had never encountered before. Wine producers from across the state were on hand to share stories of their vineyards and the heritage of these lesser-known grapes, offering insight into the diversity of California’s wine landscape. Participants could choose between general admission and VIP tickets. VIP guests enjoyed early access, a pre-tasting discussion focused on Lodi wine varietals with experts, a commemorative wine glass, and complimentary delivery of bottles ordered at the event. General admission ticket holders joined the tasting after the VIP session and had the option to have their wine purchases delivered for a flat fee. A food vendor on site offered small bites and snacks to pair with the wines, creating a festive atmosphere throughout the afternoon. Conversations flowed as easily as the pours, with many oenophiles excited to discover new favorites and broaden their palates. Organizers said the festival aimed not just to entertain but to educate, spotlighting vinicultural diversity and supporting small producers whose bottles might otherwise go unnoticed. For many attendees, the event succeeded in turning curiosity into appreciation, underscoring that California’s wine story extends far beyond its most popular grapes. The following wines were the standouts of the huge tasting. They are the cream of the crop and are worth searching out. (Part 2 will follow next week). White Wines An enticing blend off Picpoul and Chenin Blenc offers peachy, grapefruit and floral flavors. It has a silky texture, vibrant acidity and a refreshing finish. The perfect aperitif. • 2024 Oxlee Graham Chenin Blanc/Picpoul “Elinor’s Blend” $39 Picpoul a tart, astringent grape from the south of France is here paired with one of my favorite white grapes Chenin Blanc. The combination brings out the best of both varietals. Its aroma is of apricots, peaches and fresh baked bread. The medium-bodied palate The rare Bourboulenc from the Rhone Valley performs well in California • 2024 Acquiesce Bourboulenc $37 This is one of the 13 grapes that are permitted for use in Chateauneuf du Pape in the Rhone Valley. Hints of melon, almond, and graphite accent notes of lime zest, peach and tangerine on the nose. It’s medium bodied to full-bodied, somehow broad and crisp at the same time, with a velvety texture and a savory finish. • 2024 Pali Orange Muscat “Enz Vineyard” $35 It may be hard to track this wine down as only 35 cases were made and it is stunning. A charming nose of honeysuckle, gardenia and orange blossoms jumps out of the glass. You anticipate a sweet wine but on the palate, it is bone dry with apple, mango and citrus flavors. It is deeply layered and complex finishing long, savory and satisfying. This is a delicious grape that deserves to be more widely vinified. • 2024 Rideau Roussanne $52 Roussanne is one of the main white grapes from the Southern Rhone region in France and is used to make white Chateauneuf du Pape. This version from the Santa Ynez Valley starts with a powerful bouquet of jasmine, peach and pears, followed by a satiny seamless palate. It finishes with a balanced, uncommonly bright and tangy finish enlivened by a persistent undertone of minerality. Perfect to accompany roast chicken. • 2023 Acorn Gruner Veltliner $32 Hailing from the Allegria Vineyard in the Russian River Valley this is a noble effort to replicate the national grape of Austria here in California. The wine is textural and floral, with orange blossom, lavender, slate and lemon rind. The wine is structured and chalky, with a savory drift through the middle palate, which draws out the fruit and exotic spice through the finish. Great acidity keeps the wine fresh and inviting. Red Wines Grown on limestone soils the Brosseau Grenache shows great character • 2023 Brosseau Grenache $40 Hailing from a limestone vineyard in the remote Chalone appellation in the Gavilan Mountains, the Brosseau Grenache is a stunning example of the varietal. The wine boasts wonderfully pure cherries on the nose plus hints of herbs and dried spices. Medium-bodied it manages to be both firm and silky-textured at the same time, demonstrating great length and adding seductive shadings of anise and cloves on the finish. This lovely wine, reminiscent of a Chateau Rayas Chateauneuf de Pape, is ready to drink now but will last for at least a decade in the cellar. • 2023 St. Amant Alicante Bouschet $26 (Best Value) Alicante Bouschet was once widely planted in California often mixed with Zinfandel in a field blend. This comes from a Lodi vineyard originally planted in 1922. The wine is dark, almost opaque and feels young and lively. It is textbook Alicante This beautiful Alicante Bouschet from Lodi is the best value wine Bouschet with notes of wild berries, herbs and spices, an earthy and rustic touch and oodles of character. This underappreciated grape deserves more exposure and will continue to improve in the cellar for a long time. • 2023 Ottavino St. Laurent Ricci Vineyard $60 This wine epitomizes what the Festival of Undiscovered Grapes is all about. I have not only never tasted the St. Laurent grape, and I have never even heard of it. It originated in Austria and is grown only at the Ricci Vineyard in the Carneros region. It has a heady, sharp, boysenberry aroma and a bright cherry fruit flavor, light and fruity sort of like a beefy Pinot Noir. Delightful! • 2023 JMC Cellars Teraldego $37 Hailing from the Alto Adige region in northern Italy the Teraldego grape offers a bright and punchy profile with wild cherry, tart plum, leather and rose scents. It has a fragrant and delicate personality with a light supple body and a tart clean finish. This foodfriendly wine would be a perfect partner to grilled salmon. • 2023 Madrona Petit Verdot $38 A glass-coating opaque purple color, the wine sports an impressive bouquet of exotic spices, violets and blackberry. This sets the stage for a concentrated, robust, intense, nicely proportioned wine that will benefit from 4-5 years of additional cellaring. It should see its 20th birthday in peak form. • 2023 Cairjn Red Table Wine $80 This Paso Robles wine is styled after the powerful red blends of Priorat Spain. Primarily Carignan with some Mourvedre, Cab and Syrah thrown in for complexity. It leads with a darkfruited bouquet with anise, baking spices and a touch of leather. The palate strikes a midpoint between plush generosity and vibrant energy, culminating in a lively, juicy finish underpinned by gentle yet persistent tannins, savory flavors, smoke and a sturdy core of mineral notes. • 2023 Lyons Mourvedre $68 This relatively new winery from the Santa Ynez Valley specializes in Rhone varietals. The 2023 Mourvedre reveals an abundance of flowers (violets?) overlaid with nuances of dark cherries, wild berries, tobacco, spices and what the French affectionately call “animal” (wet dog). Built around full-bodied bright acids and deep blueberry fruit, it features a supple layered texture with ultra refined tannins. It recalls for me some of my favorite Mourvedres from the Bandol region in France. Delicious now it will easily last for a decade. A Rhone style blend from Paso Robles • 2021 Thacher “Relative Strangers” $65 A red field blend from Paso Robles this reminds me of a Grenache/Syrah/Mouvedre blend. It’s scented of blueberries and cherries, baking spices, earth and leather. The full-bodied palate features restrained, earthy flavors framed by juicy acidity and soft tannins with a spicy finish. Great partner to a slab of ribs fresh off the grill. • 2018 CrossHatch Winery “Shading” $50 The Shading is a blend of 50% Grenache, 25% Syrah, and 25% Mourvedre from the Los Olivos District in Santa Ynez Valley. Inky dark in color, the wine shows dusty earth, cherries and licorice on the nose, while the full-bodied palate is supple with a silky texture from the Grenache and an underpinning of black olives from the Syrah. Showing ample richness and length, it is a fun, ebullient wine.

What used to be viewed as a backyard cottage is becoming a strategic financial tool. State and local regulations have made it significantly easier to build ADUs, and many properties can now accommodate more than one unit. Even more impactful, lending guidelines now allow projected rental income from an ADU to be used to help qualify for a mortgage. That changes the math. For Buyers, it can increase purchasing power. For homeowners, it can create income flexibility. For investors, it can materially improve property performance. ADUs are no longer a niche feature. They are increasingly influencing valuation, demand, and how lenders evaluate risk and opportunity. As housing affordability continues to dominate the conversation, expect ADUs to move from the “nice bonus” to a mainstream strategy. Her husband, Jerome Herrick, and daughters, Marianne Canori and Meredith Johnson, were at her side. Born on August 25, 1944 at Alta Bates Hospital in Berkeley, she was the daughter of Dr. Thomas Richard Hofmann and Mary Hofmann. She attended Anna Head School in Berkeley and graduated from Berkeley High School in 1962. She attended the University of the Americas in Mexico City and later graduated from San Jose State University, specializing in the education of children with autism spectrum disorder. Susan met her husband, Jerome “Jerry,” at Berkeley High School; however, their love story did not begin until several years after graduation when they reconnected through mutual friends. Sue and Jerry were married on May 12, 1973. They soon moved to Piedmont and welcomed daughters Marianne and Meredith. Susan devoted countless hours volunteering in Piedmont schools den Club and the Hoe and Hope Garden Club, continuing her lifelong commitment to preserving and enhancing the beauty of the city she loved. Susan maintained a vibrant community life and was a member of the Town and Country Club, Claremont Country Club, the East Bay Auxiliary of the de Young Museum, the Hill Branch of UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland, the National Charity League, and The Cancer League. Her most cherished role was that of a devoted mother and adoring “Nana” to her five grandchildren. Her loved ones describe her as elegant and refined, thoughtful, creative, and loving. She was the heart of her family and will be profoundly missed. A private celebration of her life is planned in Hawaii, the birthplace of her mother, Mary, and a place filled with some of her happiest memories. Donations in memory of Susan Herrick may be made to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation at www.piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org. Sultan anchors the series as Tamar, born in Iran and raised in Israel. She trained in Krav Maga for the physical demands of the role and spent months studying Farsi. The language training matters. Tamar does not merely recite lines in another tongue. She shifts between Hebrew and Farsi with the ease and tension of someone navigating two identities. Her accent, her hesitation, the way she listens before responding, all signal that language itself is part of the battlefield. Sultan never lets Tamar’s competence erase her vulnerability. That balance keeps the show grounded even when coincidence occasionally nudges the plot forward. Opposite her is Shaun Toub as Faraz Kamali, the Iranian intelligence officer determined to catch her. Faraz is nominally the antagonist, yet he is written and performed with depth and restraint. He is not a caricature of repression but a man of principle who pays a personal price for his convictions. When Tamar and Faraz circle each other, the tension is electric precisely because neither tle lessons. They just behave like animals, and that restraint makes everything feel more urgent and more honest. I did find myself wondering whether younger kids would stay with it. Israeli critics have praised the series for portraying Iranian characters as complex individuals rather than stereotypes. Some international viewers have accused it of advancing an Israeli perspective. The show does not neatly resolve that tension. Instead, it sits inside it. That willingness to dwell in ambiguity is one of its strengths. The production design reinforces the mood. Filmed in Athens and carefully dressed to resemble Tehran, the city feels dense and claustrophobic. Street markets, apartments and intelligence offices are rendered with a tactile realism. Dialogue flows in Hebrew, Farsi and English. The trilingual structure adds authenticity and also suspense. Misunderstandings are not simply plot devices. They are embedded in the reality of people thinking and feeling in different languages. Later seasons expand the world without losing focus. The additions of internationally known actors signal the show’s growth, but the heart of the story remains the same. Personal choices under impossible circumstances. Private doubts inside public conflicts. Tehran became the first Israeli series to win an International Emmy for Best Drama Series, and the recognition feels earned. It is not flawless. Tamar sometimes survives on luck that stretches plausibility. Certain plot turns move at breakneck speed. But that acceleration is part of the design. The compression of events forces the emotional truth to the surface. In a world that often reduces geopolitics to slogans, Tehran offers something more unsettling and more honest. It shows how long histories and modern radicalism collide inside individual lives. It insists that even in the most polarized conflicts, the people on both sides remain recognizably human. Tehran is streaming on Apple TV+. Tehran. Created by Moshe Zonder, Dana Eden and Maor Kohn. Directed by Daniel Syrkin. Starring Niv Sultan, Shaun Toub, Glenn Close and Hugh Laurie. Premiered in 2020. Approximately 45–60 minutes per episode. TV-MA. Streaming on Apple TV+. and a story told entirely through image and behavior, it asks something of its audience. Whether a seven-year-old stays locked in when Flow finds himself in danger, I’m not sure. For tweens and teens, though, especially those ready for something that trusts them a little more, Flow is a remarkable film. Fully deserving of its Oscar, and then some. Flow. articles.text: Olsen does what she does best, carrying impossible knowledge lightly. When she first encounters Turner’s character, the moment could collapse into melodrama. Instead, it lands as pure physical recognition — something that bypasses thought entirely. Turner, who has often seemed slightly displaced in time in his earlier roles, uses that quality to leave you wondering whether he has stumbled into an old pattern or has always been part of it. Director Tran Anh Hung, best known for The Scent of Green Papaya, understands how to film faces. There are no rules here, no cosmic flowcharts. He simply watches recognition happen and trusts we will feel its pull. The camera lingers a beat longer than expected; a glance carries more weight than any special effect

articles.text: The book traces a two-century history of diversity as both an intellectual and institutional principle, beginning in 1810 with Wilhelm von Humboldt’s University of Berlin, where participation by Jews and Catholics was encouraged. The Diversity Principle follows the spread of the idea from person to person since then. Oppenheimer does not plan to celebrate the publication with time off. “I don’t take vacations,” he said. “I don’t think I would have written the book without the help of these remarkable students.” He has two hopes for the book’s impact. First, he wants to broaden the historical understanding of diversity. “I hope that when people are discussing the value of diversity and someone says, this is just a new psychology idea invented in the 1970s to support affirmative action, that other people in the conversation will say, ‘No, no, you’re wrong about that. It goes all the way back to the 19th century. You haven’t read The Diversity Principle, you have a false premise’.” His second goal is to encourage dialogue across political lines. “I hope that this allows me to talk with diversity opponents as well as diversity proponents, that it allows me to be in conversation with people from across the political spectrum.” In a review for Forbes, Marybeth Gasman wrote, “One of the most striking interventions in the book is historical. From Oppenheimer’s perspective, diversity did not begin as a corrective to discrimination. It began as a thePiedmont resident and Cal Law Professor, David Oppenheimer, published The Diversity Principle on February 24. ory of knowledge.” Oppenheimer said that while compiling the book, he uncovered the stories of influential but often overlooked figures, including Pauli Murray, a 20th century civil rights lawyer whose work challenging race and gender segregation was largely excluded from the historical narrative. Although some of Oppenheimer’s own diversity-related work dates back to the Discrimination Law Clinic in 1982, he said this project unearthed the existence of important people he had never heard of. Next, Oppenheimer plans to assemble a research team to examine the legal legacy of Pauli Murray. The Diversity Principle is available wherever books are sold, including Bookshop.org. pages.text: 32 32 Wednesday, March 4, 2026 Eternity Continued from page 19 Olsen does what she does best, carrying impossible knowledge lightly. When she first encounters Turner’s character, the moment could collapse into melodrama. Instead, it lands as pure physical recognition — something that bypasses thought entirely. Turner, who has often seemed slightly displaced in time in his earlier roles, uses that quality to leave you wondering whether he has stumbled into an old pattern or has always been part of it. Director Tran Anh Hung, best known for The Scent of Green Papaya, understands how to film faces. There are no rules here, no cosmic flowcharts. He simply watches recognition happen and trusts we will feel its pull. The camera lingers a beat longer than expected; a glance carries more weight than any special effect could. The dialogue is genuinely funny and feels lived-in. There is a running argument about furniture that should not work but does, and Parker’s script understands that humor gives romance oxygen. Without it, eternal love would suffocate under its own seriousness. Where the film strains is in its final act. Parker is asking what choice means if you have already made it before, whether patterns of love become their own prison. The movie edges toward something genuinely unsettling, then leans into near-future technology and explicit explanations just when it had worked best leaving the metaphysics mysterious. Still, there is something quietly defiant about Eternity’s faith in performance. The film finds surprising emotional force in scenes that are nothing more than two people talking across a table. It works because these actors are allowed to inhabit moments rather than illustrate them. Not everything needs to reinvent cinema. Sometimes it is enough for a film to remember what movies used to do well: let actors act, let dialogue breathe, trust that small human exchanges might matter more than spectacle. In an age when romantic leads are often little more than well-lit props moving through digital set pieces, watching three talented actors simply perform feels quietly radical. Eternity. Directed by Tran Anh Hung. Written by Nathan Parker. Starring Miles Teller, Elizabeth Olsen and Callum Turner. Released in 2025. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated PG-13. Streaming on Apple TV+. articles.text: The Piedmont Scout Council held its annual Pinewood Derby Race on February 7 in Piedmont’s Community Church Gymnasium. Under the guidance of the Derby’s master of ceremonies, Robert Dickinson, the Derby hosted more than 130 Cub Scouts. As per tradition, the derby hosted its racing on the Council’s historic wooden track. Originally built in 1967 by James H. Obando and later restored by Bill Meckel and Gary Hartsock in 1995, the track continues to symbolize the time-honored tradition of a derby full of creativity, friendly competition, and sportsmanship by the Scouting ideals. “The 2026 derby was another amazing success thanks to fantastic scout and adult volunteers who helped get Cubs checked in, and manage the ‘pit crew’, shuttling cars and keeping track of every win and loss as cars go through the heats,” said District Executive Eris Turner. The races were divided into three groups by age: Lions (Kindergarteners) & Tigers (1st), Wolves (2nd) & Bears (3rd), Webelos (4th) & Arrow of Lights (5th). The first race, combining the Lions and Tigers, was the Model cars raced down the ramp in sets of four toward an electronic finish line.

articles.text: The Superior Court of Alameda County is seeking residents to serve on the Alameda County Civil Grand Jury. The jury’s primary responsibility is to examine and report on the operations of local government agencies and to investigate citizen complaints, acting as the public’s watchdog. As a member of the Civil Grand Jury you would work with 18 other panel members to investigate citizen complaints and examine the operations of local government agencies across Alameda County. This work involves reading and analyzing investigative materials, questioning witnesses, and writing reports. Serving on the Grand Jury is a significant commitment. The jury meets twice a week (Wednesday and Thursday mornings) for a year. Most jurors devote additional time beyond this to their service. Grand jurors are paid $15 a day plus mileage and/or public transportation reimbursement. Applications for the 2026- 2027 term (starting July 1) are due by April 1. To apply, visit the Alameda County Grand Jury website at https://grandjury.acgov. org/join-us/. For more information, you may contact Piedmont resident Michael Henn (calstep2@aol. com), a current member of the Grand Jury. special ways,” she said. Before 2018, Cub Scouts were only open to boys. In the fall of 2018 and the spring of 2019, those two programs opened up to girls as well as boys. “That’s something that our council has done really well. During the time that I’ve been here, we have now had our first, Katherine Benson, the Scout Executive of Piedmont Council, is taking a new position at the Scout National office. and then many subsequent, young ladies who earned the rank of eagle,” emphasized Benson. As the Cub Scout Director for the National Council, Benson will be heavily involved in developing training for Cub Scout volunteers to make it easier and help bring more new families into the Scouts. “Right now in our movement, Cub Scouting is a really important program. Cub Scouts is where most families first join scouts, and we want to make sure we’re doing a good job,” said Benson. “Cub Scouts is one of the avenues that allows us to do activities as a family and have a really positive multi-generational impact. I’m excited to be focusing on this program, working with volunteers across the country to make it better, and to make people aware of the resources available to figure out how to do this with their kids in our neighborhoods.” As Benson reflected on her time in Piedmont, she said she is incredibly thankful to the community and their welcoming nature. “It has been such a sweet season of life to be a part of the Piedmont community, and specifically the Piedmont Scouting community. articles.text: Born on February 2, 1944 in San Francisco, John Speakman passed away on December 23, 2025, at the age of 81 due to the effects of a stroke. A resident of Alamo, he was the Fire Chief in Piedmont from 1997 to 2010. John served in both the Oakland and Piedmont Fire Departments. After serving 29 years in the Oakland Fire Department, he was appointed Fire Chief of Piedmont in 1997, and served ably until his retirement in 2010, bringing 42 years in the fire service to a close. During his tenure, he provided excellent fire protection and emergency medical services to both the Oakland and Piedmont residents, as well as disaster preparedness, CPR, and first aid classes in conjunction with the cities’ changing needs. John spent his retired years occupied by his love of sailing, golfing, cooking, John Speakman and spending time with his two grandchildren, Keoni and Emiko. John is survived by his son, Matthew; daughter-in-law, Cheryl; and his grandchildren, Keoni and Emiko. He is predeceased by his wife, Susan. At his request, there will be no service.
articles.title: Former Piedmont Fire Chief John Speakman dies at 81

articles.text: Shaggy is an 8-month-old German Shepherd mix who weighs about 51 pounds. He’s a happy, relaxed boy full of puppy enthusiasm, curiosity, and a genuine desire to connect with people. Like most Shepherds, Shaggy is smart. He loves showing off his mastery of commands in exchange for snacks. Eager to please and treat-motivated, he is easy to train. Shaggy is social and playful and attends a doggie playgroup. Check out the video of him playing with his friends on Oakland Animal Services website. Still a puppy Shaggy can get excitable, but he is easily redirected with treats. When he isn’t exploring, he enjoys getting pettings and soaking up attention. Shaggy would grow into a wonderful companion with appropriately matched dogs or as a solo dog with dog friends. Come meet Shaggy and see if he is a fit for you. Shaggy is Shaggy is a bouncy puppy with a big heart available to see you at Oakland Animal Services this Thursday from 12 - 7 p.m., or this Friday, Saturday, or Sunday between 12 and 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12 or a dog that weighs 25 pounds more or less than Shaggy must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about adoption or how to temporarily foster a puppy or dog, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@ gmail.com.

During the time that I’ve been here, we have now had our first, Kate Benson and fellow scoutmasters hiking Lassen Peak during troop 11’s outing to Lassen National Park Katherine Benson, the Scout Executive of Piedmont Council, is taking a new position at the Scout National office. and then many subsequent, young ladies who earned the rank of eagle,” emphasized Benson. As the Cub Scout Director for the National Council, Benson will be heavily involved in developing training for Cub Scout volunteers to make it easier and help bring more new families into the Scouts. “Right now in our movement, Cub Scouting is a really important program. Cub Scouts is where most families first join scouts, and we want to make sure we’re doing a good job,” said Benson. “Cub Scouts is one of the avenues that allows us to do activities as a family and have a really positive multi-generational impact. I’m excited to be focusing on this program, working with volunteers across the country to make it better, and to make people aware of the resources available to figure out how to do this with their kids in our neighborhoods.” As Benson reflected on her time in Piedmont, she said she is incredibly thankful to the community and their welcoming nature. “It has been such a sweet season of life to be a part of the Piedmont community, and specifically the Piedmont Scouting community. articles.text: This year, the City is reviving the Volunteer of the Year award for the first time since 2019. The City is also introducing a new award: Young Volunteer of the Year (under age 25), intended to uplift the meaningful contributions young people make across Piedmont. Piedmont has long been known as the “City of Volunteers.” This award, first introduced in 2014, recognizes community members whose volunteer service helped strengthen Piedmont in 2025 – whether through neighborhood improvement, arts and culture, direct community support, or building a more welcoming and inclusive community. Nominations open through March 13 To nominate a volunteer, complete the online nomination form by Friday, March 13: https://form. jotform.com/260417487348162. Volunteer service can take many forms – from a long-running commitment to a concentrated effort that made a real difference in a single year. Nominations may recognize service that strengthened Piedmont through areas such as: • Community enrichment: improving neighborhoods and shared spaces, from beautification and clean-ups to public safety and neighborhood initiatives • Culture & Heritage: preserving local history, celebrating Piedmont’s diverse community, and supporting cultural events • Arts: strengthening the community through the visual and performing arts, arts educa- • • tion, events, and mentorship Social: direct community support and humanitarian service, including work with seniors, children, individuals with disabilities, families, and community health and safety Allyship: fostering belonging and solidarity, challenging bias, and helping make Piedmont a safe and welcoming community for everyone Nominations will be reviewed using a blind scoring process that considers measurable impact, service dedication, innovation and leadership, and character and values. Top-scoring nominees are then forwarded to a City Council subcommittee for final selection. Awardees will be recognized at the City’s annual Volunteer Appreciation Reception on April 20, 2026.

articles.text: Piedmont Asian American Club is hosting a Lunar New Year celebration this Friday, February 27, at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, providing an evening of performances, food, and community celebration. The annual event will run from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. and feature performances by Piedmont High School students, crafts, a raffle, and a traditional Lion dance. Food and drink will include dim sum, boba drinks, and panang curry. Gourmet desserts and specialty drinks will be provided by Bakesum and Tea on Piedmont. “I encourage all to recognize the contributions of the Asian American community to the community of Piedmont,” said Mayor Betsy Andersen. PAAC representatives Jean Takezawa and Cassindy Chao spoke at the February 17 council meeting, thanking the council for their support of the event. “This proclamation matters, representation matters, public recognition matters. When a city names and honors a community’s tradition, it signals belonging and tells our children that their cultures are not peripheral; they are part of the civic fabric of this place. Thank you for honoring this holiday,” said Takezawa, the Director of Diversity, Equity, Inclusion & Belonging, at PHS Affinity Mentorship Program. PAAC’s Lunar New Year Celebration is open to all community members. “I wanted to invite everybody again to our Lunar New Year event,” said Chao. “What’s nice is that it brings young and old together, and it really shares our community and our culture with everybody.” Tickets are limited and expected to sell out. General admission is $25 and includes dinner. Tickets can be purchased at https://bit.ly/4rlmA6K or by scanning the QR code in the poster. Pictured are City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore (left), City Attorney Deepa Sherma, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, PAAC representative Cassindy Chao, Councilmember Jennifer Long, PAAC representative Jean Takezawa, Councilmember Lorrel Plimier, amd Councilmember Tom Ramsey.
articles.title: Piedmont celebrates Lunar New Year this Friday, Feb. 27

articles.text: Bennett and Tommy are a pair of cats ready to show just how rewarding patience can be. At about 10 months and 1 year old, they are playful, curious, and seeking a calm, indoor-only home with someone who understands shy cats. Tommy is a striking gray tabby with green eyes. He startles at sudden noises and keeps his distance at first, but with time his sweet personality emerges through adorable mealtime “honks” and mews, and his love of catnip, silvervine, treats, and playtime. With patience, and Bennett by his side, Tommy continues to soften and relax. Bennett, a petite tuxedo cat, is affectionate and expressive with a sweet, playful streak. He enjoys gentle pets and will even curl up in your lap late at night, offering slow blinks. He is still polishing his manners around food and play but is eager to learn. This pair is ready for a patient home that will celeAdopt Bennett and Tommy through Cat Town. brate every small step forward. They could join a quiet household with older children or teens and would do best with an adopter who can read body language and go slow. Bennett and Tommy are neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV/FIV negative. Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@ cattownoakland.org. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) Superintendent Jennifer Hawn will host a community meeting on Thursday, February 26, at 4:30 p.m. in the District Office Board Room, 760 Magnolia Avenue. to discuss sportsmanship and spectator conduct following the January 30 varsity boys basketball game that ended in violent altercations. Community members are invited to attend and participate as the district reviews what occurred following the game between Piedmont and San Leandro High. Hawn will present PUSD’s current conduct rules and recent actions. Time will be reserved at the end for community input. Hawn indicated that this is an important conversation and that sportsmanship must extend beyond the players on the court to include fan behavior. “The energy of our student sections can be one of the most joyful parts of high school athletics, but we also recognize that we have important work to do in developing consistently positive approaches to student fan behavior. School spirit should encourage our team while showing respect for opponents, officials, and visiting families,” Hawn wrote in her Piedmont Pulse newsletter on February 9. It is available at Smore.com/n/tu493. As a result of the fight in the PHS gym, Piedmont’s basketball team played without fans in attendance on February 4. In his February 13 Parent Newsletter, PHS Principal David Yoshihara shared his hopes of turning the page on the regrettable incident. “Three of our teams should make playoffs, which start next week,” Yoshihara said. “Feel free to come support our Highlanders if you’re in town and want to help us farm aura in the gym or on the field. It should be a lot of fun ... emphasizing FUN.” Hawn’s meeting is not the first action taken by district leadership. Yoshihara also led a discussion about the January 30 boys basketball game and its aftermath during the PHS Parents’ Club morning meeting on Friday, February 13. In her most recent Piedmont Pulse newsletter, Hawn applauded the role model efforts that were made that night in the face of the chaotic scene. “Thank you to Ben Spencer, Shamaree Worley, all of our basketball coaches, David Yoshihara, and especially Tyler Small for their remarkable leadership and steady presence in keeping our players and students safe during Friday night’s basketball game. Their professionalism and care reflect the very best of our district,” she said. “However, district staff shall not obstruct, interfere with, or otherwise impede an officer or employee of an agency conducting immigration enforcement who nonetheless enters district-provided transportation, a nonpublic area of any district property or facility, or a nonpublic area where any district-sponsored program or activity is occurring.” PUSD’s policy also requires the Superintendent, or a designee, to report to the Board in a timely manner any requests by an officer or employee of an agency conducting immigration enforcement. The requirement is in effect if the requests are about: a student or their household’s information, personnel records of employee, or permission to enter district provided transportation, and district non-public areas. To view the current policy visit: Docs.google.com/document/d/1YJmtSZ-dszkgylsKdYfBIvJ4mrQqyCti0OKUkaPuryo/ edit?tab=t.0

articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center Chabotspace.org 10000 Skyline Boulevard, Oakland 336-7300 Chabot is open Friday-Sunday, 10:00 a.m.-5:00 p.m., for a full day of fun and exploring the out of this world exhibits. Older kids will love the shows in the planetarium and megadome, the boldest way to experience space and science, on the biggest of big screens. Every Friday and Saturday night the Chabot Observatory Deck has a free telescope viewing as well, weather permitting, check their website for visibility status. Exploratorium Exploratorium.edu Pier 15, San Francisco, (415) 528-4444 The Exploratorium is a favorite destination for young science loving guests. Come check out the interactive exhibits that require active participation. The kids will be amazed at the dozens of exhibits ready for discovery. Amongst the center’s mind-blowing exhibits are the Aeolian Harps, Anamorphic Benches, the Bacteriopolis, and the Chaotic Pendulum. The Exploratorium has more exhibits, features and activities than can be seen in one day, so consider a membership. Lawrence Hall of Science Lawrencehallofscience.org 1 Centennial Drive, Berkeley 642-5132 The Hall is open for visitors to come explore the wonders of science and the universe Wednesday–Sunday, 10:00 a.m.- 5:00 p.m. For more than 50 years the Hall has enabled kids to discover something new, and get hands-on, with exhibits for all ages. Catch a show in the planetarium or the 3-D Theater for larger than life wonder and education. Meet real life mammals, bugs, and reptiles in the Animal Discovery Zone as well. Oakland Zoo Oaklandzoo.org 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland 632-9525 The Oakland Zoo sets the standard for world-class animal care in captivity. Guests will marvel at the many species taking residence at the zoo, while learning about conservation in the wild. The Zoo is open every day from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Take the gondola to the amazing boardwalk of the California Trail, for viewings of wolves, buffalo and bears. Amusement rides and a brand new electric train are open as well. Make sure to buy tickets in advance for timed-entry. The personnel records of any district employee, personal information of any district employee as defined in Civil Code 1798.3, or any other confidential employee information (Education Code 234.7; Government Code 7285.2) 4. Grant permission to an officer or employee of an agency conducting immigration enforcement to enter any transportation provided by the district, a nonpublic area of any district property or facility, or a nonpublic area where any district-sponsored program or activity is occurring (Education Code 234.7; Government Code 7285.1) The policy goes on to state “However, district staff shall not obstruct, interfere with, or otherwise impede an officer or employee of an agency conducting immigration enforcement who nonetheless enters district-provided transportation, a nonpublic area of any district property or facility, or a nonpublic area where any district-sponsored program or activity is occurring.” PUSD’s policy also requires the Superintendent, or a designee, to report to the Board in a timely manner any requests by an officer or employee of an agency conducting immigration enforcement. The requirement is in effect if the requests are about: a student or their household’s information, personnel records of employee, or permission to enter district provided transportation, and district non-public areas. Come check out the interactive exhibits that require active participation. The kids will be amazed at the dozens of exhibits ready for discovery. Amongst the center’s mind-blowing exhibits are the Aeolian Harps, Anamorphic Benches, the Bacteriopolis, and the Chaotic Pendulum. The Exploratorium has more exhibits, features and activities than can be seen in one day, so consider a membership. articles.text: Piedmont High’s Advanced Acting class will present the acclaimed play Eurydice, by Sarah Ruhl, in the Alan Harvey Theater on Friday and Saturday, March 6-7 at 7:00 p.m. each night. Eurydice is a comedic drama that reimagines the classic myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, focusing on Eurydice’s journey through the Underworld. Reunited with her deceased Mother, Eurydice must grapple with forgotten memories of her past life while facing a life-altering choice. With contemporary characters and plot twists, Eurydice is a fresh look at love and loss. The play is directed by senior Amelia Addington with a cast that includes Yiyou Fang, Kirstin Fedor, Jack Herrlinger, Nico Kaltenecker, Sparrow Lieu, Lila Schwab, and Grette Willats. Addington said she is excited to direct the show because of its creative and poetic natures. “Its abstract storytelling and emotional depth allow both the cast and the audience to interpret the story in different and personal ways,” she said. With nearly 20 plays and a MacArthur Genius Grant to her name, author Sarah Ruhl is one of the most important American playwrights of our time. The Advanced Acting Class has previously produced her shows, Dead Man’s Cell Phone and The Clean House. Eurydice has been produced from high schools to Broadway, and it has been translated into 14 languages. In 2021, Ruhl adapted Eurydice into an opera that was performed during the New York Metropolitan Opera season. Eurydice is recommended for most audiences, though some material may not be suitable for younger audience members. This production explores themes of love, loss, memory, and the afterlife. For more information contact producer Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Tickets are $5 for students and $10 for general admission. Tickets may be purchased at phsacting. ludus.com or with cash at the door.

articles.text: Piedmont for Inclusive Education (PIE) will host its second annual benefit concert supporting the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Sidekicks program on February 27. The concert will feature We Are Leaves, formerly The Date Nights, a band made up of Piedmont parents, at Piedmont Community Hall from 7 to 9 p.m. The band, consisting of Beach Elementary parents, describes its music as “indie pop.” Lead singer and guitarist Matthew Zapruder said the group writes “songs that have recognizable melodies and structures but are maybe a little quirkier than those you might hear in your car on the radio.” “We write songs about our local community: they mention Dracena Park and its audible owls, as well as a local ghost who lives in Dracena named Celeste,” said Zapruder. Proceeds from the concert will benefit the Sidekicks program, led by Larisa Martiniak. The program pairs neurodiverse children with a dedicated teen sidekick to help them navigate activities, build social connections and participate more fully and confidently in summer camps and other programs. Through the experience, teen sidekicks develop communication skills, patience, adaptability and emotional intelligence. Photo by Sasha Przybyla We Are Leaves will play live music at the Sidekicks Benefit Concert, with Matthew Zapruder (left) (lead vocals and guitar), Peter Jaeschke (bass), and Supina Mapon (violin and vocals). Steve Pearson (drums) and Miles Boison (guitar) not pictured. “Having older kids help neurodivergent kids in after-school and other programs makes inclusion actually happen, by supporting families and kids who wouldn’t otherwise be able to participate in those activities,” said Zapruder. The Sidekicks program trains Piedmont teens to support safe, fun and inclusive after-school classes and summer programs for neurodiverse school-aged children. Last year, Sidekicks supported more than 60 Piedmont participants, and 45 teen sidekicks were trained. “The Sidekicks program has changed my kid’s life. He has so much more confidence having a buddy help him through what could easily be overwhelming experiences,” said one Piedmont parent. Sidekicks program offerings, new classes and camps, and increased staff training will be supported by the concert. Learn more about the Sidekicks program at Piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ recreation/adaptive_programs__ sidekicks. To buy tickets for the Sidekicks Benefit Concert visit: Piedmontstore.org/products/ pie-piedmonters-for-inclusive-education-copy?

articles.text: In spring, Piedmont Council’s five troops (youth groups for all kids, boys and girls, in 5th grade and up) open their doors to families interested in the scouting program. Open house meetings are an opportunity for kids and their parents to visit a specific scout troop, meet youth and adult leadership, and learn about that troop’s unique brand of scouting. Troops also share highlights from recent campouts, and discuss upcoming activities. Scouting is a time-honored tradition in the community of Piedmont, with 20% of Piedmont youth involved in the program. Scouting provides youth with hands-on leadership experiences and allows them to practice life skills while serving their community. It instills citizenship and character, fosters communication, and builds a self-reliance in youth as they organize events and take on challenges together. Our middle son, George, balanced Scouting with water polo throughout high school and discovered something just as powerful as competition: community. He built friendships across age groups while camping and participating in high adventure trips to Sea Base and Northern Tier. Now playing club water polo at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, he continues to enjoy the outdoors along the Central Coast. His journey to team captain began with teaching younger Scouts how to tie knots – skills he later perfected in pursuit of catching the next big fish on trips to Kirby Cove and Dillon Beach. Henry, our youngest, is currently a Life Scout in Troop 11 and a dedicated water polo player. After years of learning alongside his older brothers, he is finishing his Eagle requirements and final merit badges – building confidence, perseverance, and the readiness to step forward and guide others when it counts. Because Scouting is Scoutled, older Scouts teach and guide younger ones—sometimes it’s messy, but that’s where real growth happens. The leadership, resilience, and accountability practiced in Scouts now guide our boys in school, athletics, friendships, and the fields they are pursuing. Just as importantly, they learned how to balance multiple commitments – sports, academics, and service – without giving up one passion for another. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team got the job done in its first game of the North Coast Section Open Division playoffs as the No. 3 seeded team, beating No. 6 Cardinal Newman 66-45 on Thursday, February 19 at Binks Rawlings Gym. They will advance to visit No. 2 Carondelet in the semifinals tonight, February 25, in Concord. Thursday’s win over the Cardinals marked the return of sophomore guard Jenelle Solis, who was last year’s Western Alameda County Conference Player of the Year and The Post’s Freshman of the Year. It was her first game in the lineup since January 13 when she was injured in a game against Bishop O’Dowd. “I was dealing with the injury, got an x-ray, and felt worse after playing. I had to get a CT scan and it revealed a fracture. I started rehab on Saturday [Feb. 14], I’m honestly surprised I lasted the whole game without Staff Photos Taylor White (left) and Savannah Dennig celebrate after beating Cardinal Newman in the first round of the North Coast Section Open Division. getting subbed out. I just kept pushing,” Solis said. Piedmont went 9-1 without Solis, creating an up-tempo style as she dealt with a fracture in her foot. Now that she’s back, coach Bryan Gardere is aware that Jenelle Solis returned to the lineup after recovering from a lingering injury. keeping their fast-paced system is important toward their continued success. “In the beginning, it was 7-1 Cardinal Newman, and we kept walking it up. I told Jenelle that we have to play faster, we’ve got to pick up the pace,” Gardere said. During Solis’ absence everyone around her gained more responsibility as ball handlers as she recovered. “We got better. We forced other teams to worry about other players as options to score and move the ball around,” junior Taylor White said. The win over Cardinal Newman avenges last year’s NCS Open Division first round game which Piedmont lost 51-45. PHS beat CN earlier this season 64-50 on December 13, continuing that standard with an even larger win. Freshman Alexa Ba watched last year’s game from the sidelines, but scored 16 points in Thursday’s win. “It was especially good because I was just watching last year. It’s great to come back and take the win,” Ba said. Carondelet will be a tough opponent. The Cougars are 23-5 and had one common opponent with Piedmont, Iolani. PHS beat the Raiders 48-46 on December 29, while Carondelet beat them 60-46 on December 12. “I know their coaches from playing AAU. Carondelet hits a bunch of threes, so we have to lock that up. It’s going to be a tough match, but they need to watch out for us too,” White said. 66-45 win over Cardinal Newman Cardinal Newman opened with a 7-1 lead, but Piedmont came back to tie with 4:05 left. In the quarter. PHS took a 14-13 lead at the 2:04 mark when Solis converted two free throws. The Cardinals hit a 3-pointer with 50 seconds left to take a 16-14 lead to end the first quarter. In the second, Piedmont scored the first 11 points of the quarter to jump ahead 25-16, holding Cardinal Newman 0-for-6 with four turnovers before finally getting on the board with 3:27 left. CN chipped away at the lead, making it 31-29 Highlanders at halftime.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to a close, falling to No. 5 Albany in the NCS Quarterfinals. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team’s season came to an end on Saturday, February 21, when they were upset by No. 5 Albany, 58-49, at Binks Rawlings Gym. Piedmont was seeded No. 4 in the Division 2 North Coast Section postseason playoffs. It defeated No.13 Urban 55-46 in the opening round at home on Wednesday, February 18. It marks the first time Piedmont hasn’t reached the semifinal round of the NCs playoffs since 2018. “The better team won tonight,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. “Of our five keys to the game, we didn’t do three of them. It’s the earliest we’ve exited the postseason in seven years, so that feels pretty weird.” Second-chance points and missed opportunities told the story for the Highlanders, getting outrebounded 47-25. Piedmont finished 4-of-25 for 3-pointers and missed nine free throws on the night, including six in a row in the third quarter. “On top of second-chance points, we were miserable cold from the floor. We started 1-for- 13 from three, and missed six free throws in a row in the third quarter. Sometimes that’s just how the night goes, but give credit to Albany. They beat us fair and square,” Spencer said. The result comes as a bit of a surprise after the Highlanders closed its regular season in stellar form with four straight wins over strong opponents – Bishop O’Dowd, Berkeley, Alameda, and Castro Valley. “We were really on a hot streak. There were stretches where I thought we’d get back in the game and figure things out, but it didn’t come to fruition,” Spencer said. “I can’t say I noticed anything bad in practice throughout the week. We just got beat,” mentioned senior captain Dillon Casey. Casey closes his Piedmont High career among the school’s best all-time scorers. He finished No. 4 on the school’s list with 1,392 points behind No. 1 A.J. Harris (1,581), No. 2 Sean Rodriguez (1,541), No. 3 Eric Flato (1,402), and ahead of No. 5 JoJo Murphy (1,355). PHS will see several key players depart with the Class of 2026, including Casey, P.J. Brayer, Akash Bornstein, and Cash Panico. Carrying the torch will be Beach Lorin, who was the team’s second leading scorer behind Casey, and Lucian Fang-Ring. “Beach was killer this year, there’s not much that’s going to stop him next year. We have Lucian, and those two will be the dynamic duo,” Casey said. 58-49 loss to No. 5 Albany Albany led 12-9 through the first quarter, but Piedmont took a lead at the 5:55 mark of the second quarter with five straight points via Casey assisting FangRing for a 3-pointer, while FangRing stole a ball and then assisted Casey for a layup to make it 14-12. However, the Cougars took the lead with a 9-3 run to end the quarter leading 21-16. Albany maintained the fivepoint lead through the midway Dillon Casey finished his Piedmont career No. 4 on the school’s All-Time scoring list with 1,392 points in four years.

articles.text: It was a rough ending for Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team. The Highlanders, the No. 5 seeded team, traveled to No. 5 Sonoma Academy in Santa Rosa on a cold Saturday, February 21, falling 2-1 in extra time in the North Coast Section Division 2 quarterfinals. To get there, PHS beat No. 12 Acalanes 3-nil at Witter Field on Tuesday, February 17. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 10-2-8 (W-T-L) to end coach Matt Spencer-Harty’s first year at the helm. Their Div. 2 NCS berth marked a two-division jump from last year, when they were the top seed in Div.4. “I’ve enjoyed every minute of it. The girls were great, the personalities were good fun. I’m excited to get it started again because it’s such a great group,” coach Matt Spencer-Harty said. Leaving a sour taste from Saturday’s loss was the way Sonoma Academy scored its opening goal, where a Sonoma striker clearly corralled the ball with the bicep area of her arm before scoring. If the proper call was made, the Highlanders’ could have walked out with a 1-nil victory. “Without a doubt it was a handball. The center referee is 40 yards behind the play, so he couldn’t see it. The linesman is 20 yards back, so he couldn’t see it as well. I asked for an explanation, but they couldn’t explain why. That should’ve ended 1-nil to us, so that was really frustrating,” Spencer-Harty said. Regardless, there is a lot to be proud of from this year’s girls’ soccer team. Spencer-Harty made inroads on an aggressive style in his first year as head coach, while young stars emerged: freshmen Olivia Nealon, Olivia Kan-Miller, Olivia Lucaccini, and Makenna Small, and sophomores Ayla Blanford and Teah Suhr. Looking ahead to next year, the team could have some solid leadership along its back line with Chloe Toyama, Erica Smith, and Daniella Lucaccini as senior defenders. “One person I’d like to highlight is Olivia Nealon,” Spencer-Harty said. “She’s been unbelievable this season. She was probably our best player against Acalanes and she’s only a freshman. We’re losing some important players, but there’s a core group of freshman and sophomores who can step up.” 2-1 loss to Sonoma Academy Sonoma Academy’s goal in the 52nd minute came after a slow pass was played back to PHS goalkeeper Rachel Young. The Coyotes’ forward tried to chip the ball past Young rushing off her line, causing the ball to hit off the Highlanders’ keeper and skip upward. Then, the striker brought the ball down off of her extended arm before slotting in a shot. Young repeatedly signaled to the referee for a handball, but no call was made. Piedmont answered just three minutes later on some terrific interplay and a finish by Miranda Liu for her final goal as a Highlander. It started with Elia Kwong playing a pass to Blanford, who sent a pass back to Kwong on her first touch. Kwong chipped the ball over the defense to Liu Olivia Nealon had two assists against Acalanes. Staff Photos Miranda Liu scored once against Sonoma Academy, and twice against Acalanes in her final two appearances for Piedmont High. charging into the box, leading to Liu wrapping her left foot around the ball on its second bounce. PHS had shots from Nealon and Arden Sorensen-Wald go wide in the 60th, but both teams traded possession for the final 20 minutes of regulation. Five minutes into extra time, Daniella Lucaccini cleared a near goal off the line that led to a Sonoma corner kick, where a defensive header looped the ball toward the right post. A Coyotes’ forward lifted a looping pass to the opposite post, leading to her teammate rising for a header in close distance to score the golden goal. 3-0 shutout of Acalanes Piedmont got its first goal of the game at the 10 minute mark, when Kan-Miller sent in a shot following a corner. It started with Sorensen-Wald sending a cross toward the net, leading to the Dons’ keeper parrying the ball. It fell to Liu, who fired a shot that deflected off a defender. KanMiller was opportunely in position to slot in a shot. After that, a lightning delay stopped play for about an hour. Liu got the second goal in the 31st minute. It started with Blanford playing a pass off the right sideline centrally to Nealon. The freshman took one touch around a charging defender, playing a pass through Acalanes’ back line to Liu in behind. Liu sent a shot from a couple of yards outside the box to the right post for the goal. PHS’ last goal came in the 45th by Liu, once again. This time, Nealon gained possession in the attacking third, rolling a pass to Liu in the box. With her first touch, Liu chipped the ball past the charging Dons’ GK.

pages.text: Wednesday, February 25, 2026 13 No. 5 Piedmont falls to No. 4 Sonoma Academy in extra time By Jonathan Comeaux It was a rough ending for Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team. The Highlanders, the No. 5 seeded team, traveled to No. 5 Sonoma Academy in Santa Rosa on a cold Saturday, February 21, falling 2-1 in extra time in the North Coast Section Division 2 quarterfinals. To get there, PHS beat No. 12 Acalanes 3-nil at Witter Field on Tuesday, February 17. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 10-2-8 (W-T-L) to end coach Matt Spencer-Harty’s first year at the helm. Their Div. 2 NCS berth marked a two-division jump from last year, when they were the top seed in Div.4. “I’ve enjoyed every minute of it. The girls were great, the personalities were good fun. I’m excited to get it started again because it’s such a great group,” coach Matt Spencer-Harty said. Leaving a sour taste from Saturday’s loss was the way Sonoma Academy scored its opening goal, where a Sonoma striker clearly corralled the ball with the bicep area of her arm before scoring. If the proper call was made, the Highlanders’ could have walked out with a 1-nil victory. “Without a doubt it was a handball. The center referee is 40 yards behind the play, so he couldn’t see it. The linesman is 20 yards back, so he couldn’t see it as well. I asked for an explanation, but they couldn’t explain why. That should’ve ended 1-nil to us, so that was really frustrating,” Spencer-Harty said. Regardless, there is a lot to be proud of from this year’s girls’ soccer team. Spencer-Harty made inroads on an aggressive style in his first year as head coach, while young stars emerged: freshmen Olivia Nealon, Olivia Kan-Miller, Olivia Lucaccini, and Makenna Small, and sophomores Ayla Blanford and Teah Suhr. Looking ahead to next year, the team could have some solid leadership along its back line with Chloe Toyama, Erica Smith, and Daniella Lucaccini as senior defenders. “One person I’d like to highlight is Olivia Nealon,” Spencer-Harty said. “She’s been unbelievable this season. She was probably our best player against Acalanes and she’s only a freshman. We’re losing some important players, but there’s a core group of freshman and sophomores who can step up.” 2-1 loss to Sonoma Academy Sonoma Academy’s goal in the 52nd minute came after a slow pass was played back to PHS goalkeeper Rachel Young. The Coyotes’ forward tried to chip the ball past Young rushing off her line, causing the ball to hit off the Highlanders’ keeper and skip upward. Then, the striker brought the ball down off of her extended arm before slotting in a shot. Young repeatedly signaled to the referee for a handball, but no call was made. Piedmont answered just three minutes later on some terrific interplay and a finish by Miranda Liu for her final goal as a Highlander. It started with Elia Kwong playing a pass to Blanford, who sent a pass back to Kwong on her first touch. Kwong chipped the ball over the defense to Liu Olivia Nealon had two assists against Acalanes. Staff Photos Miranda Liu scored once against Sonoma Academy, and twice against Acalanes in her final two appearances for Piedmont High. charging into the box, leading to Liu wrapping her left foot around the ball on its second bounce. PHS had shots from Nealon and Arden Sorensen-Wald go wide in the 60th, but both teams traded possession for the final 20 minutes of regulation. Five minutes into extra time, Daniella Lucaccini cleared a near goal off the line that led to a Sonoma corner kick, where a defensive header looped the ball toward the right post. A Coyotes’ forward lifted a looping pass to the opposite post, leading to her teammate rising for a header in close distance to score the golden goal. 3-0 shutout of Acalanes Piedmont got its first goal of the game at the 10 minute mark, when Kan-Miller sent in a shot following a corner. It started with Sorensen-Wald sending a cross toward the net, leading to the Dons’ keeper parrying the ball. It fell to Liu, who fired a shot that deflected off a defender. KanMiller was opportunely in position to slot in a shot. After that, a lightning delay stopped play for about an hour. Liu got the second goal in the 31st minute. It started with Blanford playing a pass off the right sideline centrally to Nealon. The freshman took one touch around a charging defender, playing a pass through Acalanes’ back line to Liu in behind. Liu sent a shot from a couple of yards outside the box to the right post for the goal. PHS’ last goal came in the 45th by Liu, once again. This time, Nealon gained possession in the attacking third, rolling a pass to Liu in the box. With her first touch, Liu chipped the ball past the charging Dons’ GK. articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team is back, competing in its first two events of the season on Saturday, February 21 at the Grizzle Invitational at San Lorenzo HS and the 27th Annual Pittsburg Relays at Diablo Valley College. The Highlanders are undergoing big changes atop its roster after the graduation of the Post’s 2026 Athletes of the Year, Miguel Long and Nia Kim. However, track coach Pouyan Assadi thinks the Western Alameda County Conference is ripe for the picking. “The WACC has almost fully turned over in the last year. On the boys’ side, about a dozen guys between Berkeley, O’Dowd, Castro Valley and us who were varsity mainstays all graduated,” Assadi said. For the boys’ team, Assadi looks ahead to sprinters like Eric Venner, Maddox Ma, and Rehan Mumtaz making their mark. “The boys have had an incredible offseason. Eric, Maddox, and Rehan are the stars of the show on the sprinters side. Eric has a chance to be the bonafide sprint leader on the team, I wouldn’t be surprised to see him hit elite marks,” Assadi said. Also poised to return this spring is the Post’s honorable mention for 2025 Athlete of the Year, Sebastien Swain, who missed the entire cross country season as he recovered from surgery. “Seb is still in his ramp-up period. He’s doing the workouts and looks good. The question is when can he become healthy enough to race at a competitive level,” Assadi said. On the girls’ team, sprinter Claire Aubrecht is looking toward a big spring after helping the 4x100 and 4x400 relay teams reach last year’s NCS Meet of Champions. “Claire opening up the season with a PR in the 200 was nice to see. The question is if she can bring down her 100 or 400 time as well,” Assadi said. On the distance team, junior Leighton Mand will continue being a major factor after reaching the 2025 CIF State Cross Country Championship last fall—where she finished 96th of 205. Skylar Best, a senior, is also poised for a strong season. “Leighton and Skylar are really keen on taking the 4x800 team as far as they can. Leighton has some pretty high goals and Photos by Jenni Tsoi-Best Eric Venner looks ahead to a strong campaign in the sprint categories. Sebastien Swain returns to the track in 2026 after missing a year while recovering from surgery. Claire Aubrecht will lead the girls’ sprint teams. Skylar is pretty similar. Those two have been training really hard and are coming off a nice finish in the CIF State meet,” Assadi said. Grizzly Invitational results Piedmont filled the field at the Grizzly Invitational with several winning marks on the afternoon. On the boys’ side, Rehan Mumtaz won the 100 meter dash with a time of 11.69 seconds in a field of 18. Also competing was Jason Shum, finishing third in 12.32. Mumtaz also won the 200 meters in 23.53 against 17 other athletes while Shum finished fourth in 25.05. Mumtaz won the long jump at 18 feet, 6.5 inches in a field of six, and Shum was second at 18 feet-0. Claire Aubrecht came away with two wins on the day. She won the 100 in 13.19 against nine other runners, and also claimed the 200 in 26.96 in a field of six. Freshman Akunna Iroh was one of two competing in the long jump, finishing on top with a distance of 16 feet, 8.25 inches. It marked her very first long jump event. Senior Uzoma Iroh was also one of two in the shot put. She logged a winning distance of 29 feet, 9.5 inches. Pittsburg Relays results Piedmont brought its distance runners to the Pittsburg Relays. For the girls, Mand finished third of 20 runners in the 1600 with a time of 5:38.19. Also competing was Amalia Gray, placing seventh in 5:49.39. PHS boys had four competing in the 1600. Dresden Schulte-Sasse was 12th of 36 runners with a time of 4:56.59, Ian Chung was 14th in 4:57.47, Aaron Bennett was 15th in 4:57.48, and Devon Thai rounded things out in 21st, 5:07.90. NEXT UP Piedmont competes in the Farmer Throws & Jumps Carnival at Hayward HS on Thursday, March 5 at 3:30 p.m. They also compete in three events on Saturday, March 7: the Dan Gabor Invitational at Amador Valley in Pleasanton, the K-Bell Track and Field Classic at Westmont HS in San Jose, and the Ugly Eagles Relays in Concord.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Slate.com Alysa Liu of Oakland has risen to star status after winning a gold medal at the Olympics. The 2026 Winter Olympics has officially concluded. The United States finished second place in the medal count with six gold, 10 silver, and five bronze medals. Norway, once again, led the Winter Olympics with 31 medals. Oakland’s Alysa Liu becomes a star 20-year-old Alysa Liu captured Olympic gold in the women’s free skate event, becoming a star in the process. Her gold medal marked a moment of personal triumph for the Bay Area talent, who trains at Oakland Ice Center, after retiring from skating following the 2022 Olympics for her own mental health. It marked Team USA’s first gold medal in the women’s event since 2002. Making the moment even more special for those in the Bay Area was how Liu paid tribute to Oakland, shouting out The Town on multiple occasions, saying she was glad to bring Oakland to Milan. Fenton’s Creamery on Piedmont Ave. declared Liu has “ice cream for life.” Oakland mayor Barbara Lee announced that the city is planning a celebration for Liu. “The City of Oakland is planning a community-wide celebration to honor Olympic gold medalist and Oakland’s hometown hero Alysa Liu! Her achievement has filled our city with pride, and we are coordinating with her team now to finalize a date so the community can celebrate her together,” Lee wrote on Instagram. Team USA women’s hockey edges by Canada in overtime Team USA won the women’s hockey gold medal by defeating rival Canada 2-1 in a thrilling overtime victory on February 19. The Americans went undefeated through the tournament, outscoring opponents 33-2, but struggled to find the same fluidity in the gold medal match. In the game, Canada took a 1-0 lead on a shorthanded goal in the second period, but the U.S. responded late when veteran captain Hilary Knight tipped in a shot with just over two minutes left to tie the score and force overtime. Knight’s goal set new U.S. Olympic records for most career goals. Four minutes into a 3-on-3 sudden-death overtime, Megan Keller scored the golden goal, making a wicked deke by a defender before finishing with a backhand finish into the net. It marked the United States’ third Olympic gold. U.S. men’s hockey stuns Canada Much similarly to the women’s side, Team USA’s men’s hockey team captured an historic gold medal, defeating rival Canada 2-1 in overtime on February 22. It was the U.S.’s first gold medal since the famed “Miracle on Ice” in 1980, ending a 46-year drought. The Americans jumped ahead early with a goal from Matt Boldy in the first period, but Canada responded to tie the game. Goalie Connor Hellebuyck was monumental, stopping 41 of 42 shots. In the 3-on-3 overtime period, Jack Hughes delivered the dramatic golden goal one minute and 41 seconds in, ripping the puck past Canadian goalie Jordan Binnington to seal the victory.

articles.text: Piedmont Council is digging up adventure for its annual Cub Scout Day Camp. Piedmont Cub Scouts and all youth (rising 1st to 5th graders) will be returning to Dracena to journey back in time for camp’s prehistoric “Dinos” theme. During Day Camp, June 15 – 18, campers will take part in a wide range of activities including Scout Skills which showcase the Scouting program. Sports and games will get campers active, arts and crafts will challenge creativity, STEM activities will promote simple scientific thoughts. Day Camp will end on Thursday with its traditional egg drop in partnership with the Piedmont Fire Department. Day Camp is planned by a collaborative team of youth from Piedmont Council’s five Scout BSA troops and Community Service Crew. Those Scouts not only plan the camp activities, but also spend the week as staff, guiding the campers through all the fun things they planned. Coming onboard as 2026’s Program Advisor is Rebecca Fisher, former Pack 5 Cubmaster and current Troop 11 parent. The Council is putting on its archaeological gear and getting ready to run a program full of adventure at Dracena, “The tradition of day camp continues for longtime attendees and new campers alike,” said District Executive Eris Turner. “It brings together youth from across our community for an experience they rarely get and even brings the neighborhood and past Scouts out for the egg drop. It’s truly a special week for everyone involved.” Interested youth can register for Day Camp through the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Community Pass catalog (piedmont.ca.gov/activityguide). articles.text: When we picture summer camp, we tend to imagine the highlights: the lake at sunset, kids on a ropes course, a campfire under the stars. And when we evaluate camps, we usually ask the sensible questions — safety, staff ratios, medical coverage, All are important. But if you talk to teens or adults about what shaped them at camp, they rarely describe the zip line. They describe the counselor who helped them navigate conflict, the tone of the cabin at night, the feeling of belonging, or the way adults responded when something went wrong. Those elements don’t always show up in brochures. They live in the culture. Here are five questions that may gently reveal that culture. 1. What is your philosophy around discipline? Most camps today aren’t punitive. The deeper question is how they understand behavior. When a child struggles — socially, emotionally, or impulsively — is the response primarily corrective, or developmental? In my work around coaching children’s behavior (parCampers at Camp Augusta enjoy a healthy meal around the table with their counselors. entingtuneup.org), discipline is framed as skill-building: emotional regulation, perspective-taking, responsibility, and repair. A camp that thinks this way will speak about growth, coaching, and restoring relationships — not just enforcing rules. You’re listening for how adults guide, not how they correct. 2. What does staff training focus on beyond the required basics? Every camp must cover safety procedures and personnel policies. That’s foundational. But what else fills the training days? Do they prepare counselors to understand child development? Group dynamics? Homesickness? Conflict mediation? Inclusive practices? Emotional coaching? How to notice the quiet child who isn’t asking for help? A detailed schedule may be hard to parse, and what matters is what leaders emphasize. If they speak thoughtfully about belonging, guiding peer relationships, creating community, communication skill building, that tells you something. If you really want to deep dive, ask for some of the lesson plans. Activities are visible. Adult preparation is not — yet it shapes nearly everything your child experiences. 3. In the last decade, how many campers have required emergency services — and for what general reasons? This isn’t about expecting perfection. It’s about transparency and learning. No meaningful residential program operates for years without incidents. What matters is whether the camp tracks patterns, speaks calmly about them, and adapts. articles.text: On a summer morning at Walker Creek Ranch, music brings everyone together before breakfast. Sunlight glimmers through the trees, voices rise from cabins, and campers head outside, greeting each other and the rising sun with song. This is the setting for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s (PEBCC) Summer 2026 sleepaway camps, returning to Marin County this summer. Spread across 1,700 acres of forest, grassland, and trails, Walker Creek Ranch gives young singers a rare chance to step away from screens and school schedules, to spend their days learning, exploring, and making music together. Campers splash at the pond, hike the trails, and discover the beauty of the outdoors. Everyone is accepted for who they are, creating a community where singing and being together are at the heart of each day. PEBCC offers two summer camp experiences. Camp Joyful Voices, a six-day program for singers ages 7 to 11, is designed with younger campers in mind. Days balance rehearsals and musicianship classes with crafts, spirit days, swimming, and games. Colorful friendship bracelets appear on wrists within days, and campers sing on hikes, at mealtimes, and around the campfire. No prior experience is required, so every child can join and experience the joy of singing. Choir Camp, PEBCC’s flagship twelve-day program for singers ages 10 to 15, adds deeper musical focus while keeping the same sense of shared adventure. Campers rehearse daily, study music theory, and participate in vocal lessons, while also hiking to the lake, kayaking, and gathering under the redwood trees for evening songs. Repertoire introduced at camp continues into the school-year season starting in the fall, giving singers a shared foundation and lasting friendships. Many PEBCC singers say Choir Camp is the highlight of their year and that they wait all year for the chance to return. The camp experience extends beyond rehearsal into shared The friendships singers form are some of the best parts of PEBCC’s summer camps is. They last a lifetime! Our campers have fun and make memories while hiking, swimming, crafting, and living through music. No previous singing experience is required! articles.text: defined by the absence of challenges, but by how they respond to them. 4. If you removed the fun activities, what would still make this camp valuable? Zip lines and sailing are wonderful. But if you subtract the activity list, what remains? Is the camp’s value rooted in belonging, mentorship, independence, responsibility, and living in community? Or is it primarily in facilities? How does the camp “operationalize” or make real those values and intentions? This question helps reveal whether the heart of the program runs deeper than the schedule. 5. How are campers awakened — and how are the quiet margins of the day handled? Brochures show the highlights. Growth often happens in the transitions. • Is wake-up playful or functional? • What happens before breakfast? It’s often about 30 minutes – what’s that look like? • How is wind-down guided before and just after lights out? After the evening program and before lights out, there’s often a good hour, or even two. What most commonly happens? What else? • Are those moments intentional and relational — or simply supervised? The tone of the morning and the calm of the evening often say more about a camp’s culture than the biggest events. None of these questions are about catching anyone off guard. They’re about understanding the emotional climate your child will live inside. They’re about how adults coach, how they respond to struggle, and how they shape the small, repeated moments that quietly form character. The big activities create excitement. The invisible structures create growth. Randall Grayson is the director of Camp Augusta. A camper meets a new friend at Camp Augusta are built on the belief that singing together helps young people grow: not only as musicians, but as listeners, collaborators, and friends. Summer 2026 is the next chance for voices to echo along the trails and across the creek, carrying connections far beyond camp. Be part of the chorus, and come sing with us at camp!
