articles.text: Shotgun Players will open its 34th season on March 21 with The Goat or, Who is Sylvia? by Edward Albee at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. The Tony Award-winning play centers on Martin Gray, a successful architect whose personal life unravels after he tells his wife and son that he is in love with a goat named Sylvia. The disclosure leads to conflict within his family and raises questions about morality, loyalty and acceptance. The production is directed by Shotgun Players company member Kevin Clarke. In a statement, Clarke said the play “tests the limits of permissiveness” and asks audiences to consider the characters’ perspectives. William Giammona plays Martin Gray. Erin Mei Ling Stuart portrays his wife, Stevie Gray. Kevin Singer appears as Ross, a longtime family friend, and Joel Ochoa plays the couple’s son, Billy. The play premiered on Broadway in 2002 and won the Tony Award for best play. It was also named a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for drama in 2003. Performances run March 21 through April 19. Showtimes are 7 p.m. Wednesdays and Thursdays, 8 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays, and 2 p.m. Sundays. Preview performances are scheduled for March 21, 22, 25, 26 and 27. Opening night is March 28. A masked matinee is planned for March 29. A haptic tour and live audio-described performance will be offered April 12, with the tour at 1 p.m. and the performance at 2 p.m. Post-show discussions will follow Thursday and Sunday performances. A special event for theatergoers 25 and younger is scheduled for April 2. The Ashby Stage is located at 1901 Ashby Ave. Tickets are available at shotgunplayers.org or by calling 510-841-6500 ext. 303.
articles.title: Shotgun Players presents The Goat opening March 21

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony ushers in the Year of the Horse with a special Lunar New Year concert held Saturday, February 28. The symphony’s annual Lunar New Year event occurs each February at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco, drawing upon Asian customs and musical heritage to mark one of the most important holidays across East, South and Southeast Asian cultures. This year’s concert is conducted by Mei-Ann Chen, a Taiwanese-American orchestra conductor who has been Music Director of the MacArthur Award-winning Chicago Sinfonietta since 2011. She also serves as Chief Conductor of Austria’s Recreation Grosses Orchester Graz at the Styriarte festival, making her the first female Asian conductor in that role. The program features both traditional and modern music, including Huan-Zhi Li’s Spring Festival Overture, Liu ChiaChang’s Alone Ascending the West Chamber, Che-Yi Lee’s Mei-Ann Chen conducts this year’s annual Lunar New Year concert. music from Dancing Strings, Tyzen Hsiao’s The Angel from Formosa, Huang Ruo’s Flower Drum Song from Feng Yang from Folk Songs for Orchestra and more. The symphony is joined by clarinetist Yuhsin Galaxy Su and Erhu player George Gao. An erhu is a traditional Chinese twostringed bowed instrument, often described as a type of spike fiddle, and is one of the most prominent instruments in Chinese classical, folk, opera, and contemporary music. The concert begins at 5 p.m. Attendees may purchase a VIP ticket for admission to the event’s preconcert reception at 4 p.m. as well as a celebratory postconcert banquet dinner. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/.
articles.title: SF Symphony performs Lunar New Year concert on Feb. 28

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet presents The Blake Works, a full evening-length exploration of choreographer William Forsythe’s ongoing collaboration with Grammy Award-winning musician James Blake, beginning this Friday, February 27. The program marks the company premiere of Forsythe’s latest works and brings together new material with audience favorites in a first-of-its-kind North American presentation. The Blake Works is a dynamic collection that reimagines ballet through Forsythe’s signature deconstructed aesthetic. Set to Blake’s layered, atmospheric soundscapes, the evening features Prologue, The Barre Project, and Blake Works I. Originally developed during the pandemic, The Barre Project draws inspiration from traditional ballet barre training, transforming foundational exercises into striking performance material. Together, the works form a high-energy, rhythmically charged journey that pushes classical technique into thrilling contemporary territory. The program also reflects a broader movement in ballet, as choreographers continue to explore the expressive possibilities of Blake’s music. At New York City Ballet, choreographer Kyle Abraham has similarly harnessed Blake’s pop sensibility. Building on the momentum of 2018’s The Runaway, Abraham’s Love Letter, his fourth work for the company, features music by Blake and premiered at the 2022 Fall Fashion Gala. The ballet for Photo courtesy of San Francisco Ballet The program highlights choreographer William Forsythe’s ongoing collaboration with Grammy Award-winning musician James Blake. 16 dancers pairs classical virtuosity with contemporary swagger, complemented by bold costumes from British fashion designer Giles Deacon and lighting by Dan Scully. While distinct in style, both Forsythe and Abraham demonstrate how Blake’s evocative sound world can inspire ballet artists to new physical and emotional heights. With The Blake Works, San Francisco Ballet celebrates Forsythe’s enduring innovative spirit and offers audiences a powerful vision of ballet’s future. “As SF Ballet’s repertoire continues to evolve and expand, we invite audiences to experience a season representing the best ballet has to offer, with our worldclass dancers bringing to life a dynamic range of classical and contemporary choreography and stories capturing everything from the drama of the everyday to the mythic and ethereal,” said Tamara Rojo, Artistic Director of SF Ballet. “We will continue to share this spirit of innovation and excellence beyond the Opera House stage as we bring the company across the country and the world.” The Blake Works shows at The War Memorial Opera House this Friday through March 8. Tickets for upcoming performances by San Francisco Ballet are available through the company’s official website, https://www.sf ballet. org. Patrons can purchase single tickets, season packages or buildyour-own series directly online by selecting a performance and clicking the ticket link. Tickets are also available by phone at 415-865-2000, Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. On performance days, the box office at the War Memorial Opera House opens approximately four hours before curtain.

articles.text: The Fort Mason Center for Art The exhibition, on view now In Line Describing a Cone, a single point of light gradually traces a circle over the course of the projection. Conical Solid projects a rotating blade of light from a fixed central axis. Cone of Variable Volume alters the size of a complete circle across four movements. The works begin as film animations and are experienced through projection in a darkened gallery. McCall developed the series after moving from London to New York in 1973. He described the works as films that exist in the moment of projection with an audience, rather than as objects with a fixed form. The “solid light” works are associated with developments in avant-garde cinema, Minimalism and Structural Film of the 1970s. The exhibition organizers said the pieces also anticipate later immersive and participatory installation practices. Anthony McCall: First Light continues a collaboration between the Kramlich Art Foundation and Fort Mason Art that began in 2015-16 with a presentation of Janet Cardiff’s Forty-Part Motet. Additional programming includes a related film series titled “Do You See What I See.” Exhibition dates, hours and admission information are available through Fort Mason Center for Art and Culture. Visit https:// fortmason.org/event/anthony-mccall-first-light-2/2026-02-19/ to learn more. 8 80 01 1 M MA AG GN NO OL LI IA A A AV VE E. ., , P PI IE ED DM MO ON NT T, , C CA A 9 94 46 61 11 1 P PR RE ES SE EN NT T: : Out of Time, Out of Place … a look at displacement and self-discovery through the eyes of artists in the diaspora. Hellenic-American artists explore these concepts through the convergence of music and poetry. The cornerstone of the program is Malis’ original song cycle Another Shore, Another Country set to the poetry of C.P. Cavafy, commissioned by ProMusica Detroit and premiered in February, 2024. Cavafy, who lived most of his life in Alexandria, Egypt, is the quintessential voice of the Greek diaspora and a prominent figure among 20th-century poets . The Kombos Collective is a champion of Greek composers, shedding light on the rich musical repertoire coming out of Greece and the Greek diaspora by presenting captivating programming in intimate concert settings inspired by the Hellenic World. Kombos has released several full-length albums and performed at the Kennedy Center for Michael Malis Constantine Novotny Ellie Falaris Ganelin (piano) (baritone) (flute) the Performing Arts, the Library of Congress, and cultural centers and universities across the U.S. and Canada. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, February 25, 2026 By Allyson Aleksey The Fort Mason Center for Art and Culture and the Kramlich Art Foundation presents the Bay Area premiere of works by British artist Anthony McCall in a current exhibition titled Anthony McCall: First Light. The exhibition, on view now through March 8, features three works from the early 1970s, including Line Describing a Cone (1973), Conical Solid (1974) and Cone of Variable Volume (1974). The pieces are part of McCall’s “solid light” series, which uses projected light and theatrical haze to create three-dimensional forms in space. In Line Describing a Cone, Anthony McCall: First Light exhibit now at Fort Mason a single point of light gradually traces a circle over the course of the projection. Conical Solid projects a rotating blade of light from a fixed central axis. Cone of Variable Volume alters the size of a complete circle across four movements. The works begin as film animations and are experienced through projection in a darkened gallery. McCall developed the series after moving from London to New York in 1973. He described the works as films that exist in the moment of projection with an audience, rather than as objects with a fixed form. The “solid light” works are associated with developments in avant-garde cinema, Minimalism and Structural Film of the 1970s. The exhibition organizers said the pieces also anticipate later immersive and participatory installation practices. Anthony McCall: First Light continues a collaboration between the Kramlich Art Foundation and Fort Mason Art that began in 2015-16 with a presentation of Janet Cardiff’s Forty-Part Motet. Additional programming includes a related film series titled “Do You See What I See.” Exhibition dates, hours and admission information are available through Fort Mason Center for Art and Culture. Visit https:// fortmason.org/event/anthony-mccall-first-light-2/2026-02-19/ to learn more. The colonel has intelligence that could prove catastrophic if it falls into Russian hands. It’s a suicide mission dressed up as a rescue operation. They set off into no man’s land, and things immediately feel wrong. Not in the conventional war-movie sense of escalating danger but wrong in a more fundamental way. The forests are too quiet. The corpses they pass seem oddly decomposed. Time behaves strangely—their watches stopped when they cheated death in the first battle. Encounters with the enemy take on a ritualistic, almost mythological quality. The crew, pumped full of Wehrmacht-issued methamphetamine, can’t trust their own perceptions anymore. Schüt ter’s per for mance anchors the growing unreality. He plays Gerkens as a man who has built his entire identity around the chain of command, around the idea that orders flow downward and responsibility flows upward. It’s a seductive bargain: do what you’re told, and you’re absolved of moral weight. Each time he repeats his mantra – we follow orders – you can see him reinforcing the walls of this prison he’s built for himself. The rest of the cast sketches out alternative responses. pages.text: Wednesday, February 25, 2026 21 MOVIES FOR ADULTS The Tank when orders aren’t enough By Erik Wurgaft There’s a moment early in Dennis Gansel’s The Tank when Lieutenant Philip Gerkens, played with clenched-jaw precision by David Schütter, repeats what sounds like a personal motto: “We follow orders, and that’s all there is to it.” He says it to reassure a younger crew member. He says it, one suspects, to reassure himself. The phrase becomes a kind of incantation throughout the film, spoken with increasing desperation as the mission deteriorates and reality itself seems to buckle. By the time the credits roll, that simple sentence has been turned inside out and ultimately revealed as the most dangerous lie a soldier can tell himself. The Tank arrives on Prime Video disguised as something audiences already know: a World War II tank thriller in the vein of Brad Pitt’s Fury, complete with claustrophobic interiors, muddy Eastern Front landscapes, and the tension of men sealed inside a metal coffin while death circles outside. Gansel, who directed episodes of Das Boot and made his reputation with Die Welle (The Wave), understands how to wring suspense from confined spaces. When Gerkens’s Tiger tank submerges in a river to hide from Soviet forces, the sequence rivals anything in Wolfgang Petersen’s submarine masterpiece. The premise is straightforward; Autumn 1943, occupied Ukraine. Gerkens and his fiveman crew receive orders to peneLaurence Rupp, Sebastian Urzendowsky, Yoran Leicher, and Leonard Kunz in The Tank trate deep behind Soviet lines and extract a Lieutenant Colonel von Hardenburg from a secret bunker. The colonel has intelligence that could prove catastrophic if it falls into Russian hands. It’s a suicide mission dressed up as a rescue operation. They set off into no man’s land, and things immediately feel wrong. Not in the conventional war-movie sense of escalating danger but wrong in a more fundamental way. The forests are too quiet. The corpses they pass seem oddly decomposed. Time behaves strangely—their watches stopped when they cheated death in the first battle. Encounters with the enemy take on a ritualistic, almost mythological quality. The crew, pumped full of Wehrmacht-issued methamphetamine, can’t trust their own perceptions anymore. Schüt ter’s per for mance anchors the growing unreality. He plays Gerkens as a man who has built his entire identity around the chain of command, around the idea that orders flow downward and responsibility flows upward. It’s a seductive bargain: do what you’re told, and you’re absolved of moral weight. Each time he repeats his mantra – we follow orders – you can see him reinforcing the walls of this prison he’s built for himself. The rest of the cast sketches out alternative responses. Sebastian Urzendowsky’s Keilig, a former teacher, keeps asking “why” even when answers would be dangerous. Laurence Rupp’s Weller has achieved a kind of brutal honesty about what they’re actually doing. Young Yoran Leicher’s Michel still believes in something like innocence, though you can watch it draining out of him scene by scene. For a German filmmaker making a World War II movie, there’s no redemptive arc available. American war films can end with victory over evil. But what does a German director do with the Eastern Front, where his grandfather’s generation committed horrors that still echo? Those burning Ukrainian villages in the background aren’t just atmosphere. They’re evidence. The film never lets you forget that these men, sympathetic as they might be individually, are part of an occupying force engaged in a war of annihilation. This is where The Tank becomes genuinely uncomfortable. Gansel forces you to spend two hours inside the heads of Wehrmacht soldiers, to understand their fear and exhaustion, and then refuses to let any of that erase what they’re complicit in. The German press hasn’t quite known what to do with it. Andreas Kilb in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung called it “technically brilliant, but morally problematic,” noting that the victims remain largely invisible. The Süddeutsche Zeitung suggested tank enthusiasts might enjoy it but everyone else should probably stay away. While criticism is partially justified, the focus on perpetrators rather than victims is precisely the point. Gansel is asking a question Germans have been asking for eighty years: what do you do with the knowledge that ordinary people, not monsters, just ordinary people following orders, committed extraordinary evil? The film’s answer arrives in its final act when Gerkens completes his mission. What Gerkens faces in those final moments isn’t a tribunal or a battle. He meets his commanding officer again, the man who gave him those orders he’s been hiding behind. But they’re not standing at heaven’s gate. They’re somewhere much hotter, somewhere final, and the officer who commanded him can offer no protection now, instead of orders come questions. It’s an image of almost medieval directness: two men who followed and gave orders, standing together at the edge of consequences they can no longer deflect to higher authority. articles.text: Dear Jim I’ve been noticing a lot of issues at my home, such as drainage problems in my basement and crawlspace, more cracks inside on the walls and ceilings that are getting bigger, and I have a sloping floor in my dining room. I have had several contractors out to help me solve these issues, but they all have very different opinions and prices for the work. How can I understand who to hire and the right approach for the work? In the Bay Area, foundation and drainage issues are more than an inconvenience — they threaten your home’s structural integrity. Unfortunately, many homeowners find themselves overwhelmed by a sea of conflicting opinions from contractors. To protect your investment, it is critical to distinguish between a quick fix and a permanent engineering solution. 1. Prioritize Diagnostics Over “Eyeballing” The most important step in any foundation or drainage repair is a thorough inspection. If a contractor provides a bid based solely on a walk-around of your exterior, be cautious. A true specialist should perform a deep subsurface inspection, including physically entering the crawl space to identify the root cause of the issue. This includes reviewing the condition of the foundation, soils, moisture patterns and potential structural defects. In many cases, reputable firms recommend low-cost diagnostic steps first, ensuring homeowners do not spend unnecessarily on major work if a simpler diversion solution will resolve the problem. 2. Specialization vs. Generalization While a general contractor or landscaper may understand how Drainage problems lead to foundation deterioration and mold in the crawlspace. to move water, they often lack the structural expertise required to diagnose and design deep drainage systems or evaluate older foundations. Bay Area soils are notoriously complex and require specific local experience. A foundation and drainage specialist should be able to diagnose, design and clearly explain the proposed approach without immediately deferring to a thirdparty engineer or architect who is not on site and may miss critical details. The best specialists bring in engineering support when appropriate, but their field experience in defining the proper scope of work is essential. 3. Decoding the “Different Opinions” When bids vary widely, there are usually important reasons. Lower bids often omit critical longevity measures such as highgrade waterproof membranes, properly engineered French drains or adequate foundation reinforcement. Less expensive solutions may be easier to install but can create new problems, particularly with simplified drainage “fixes.” Ask every bidder: How will this system handle a 50-year storm event? Climate change has intensified and accelerated foundation and drainage risks. A comprehensive approach remains the most reliable way to address these challenges. 4. Why Experience Matters In construction, longevity is one of the clearest indicators of quality. Choosing a contractor with decades of experience and hundreds of comparable projects significantly increases the likelihood they will understand your home’s specific conditions and complete the work on time and on budget. Such firms are relatively rare, but investing time in proper due diligence may be one of the most important steps a homeowner can take. By focusing on diagnostic rigor and specialized local expertise, you can help ensure your home remains stable for decades to come. Conversations with Your Local Contractor is a feature by Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. If you have residential, homeowner questions OR ideas for an article you’d like Jim to highlight, please send an email to jim@jimgardnerconstruction.com. Jim is a long-time Piedmont resident and has been doing foundations drainage and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983.

articles.text: Tucked into the rolling hills of Sonoma County’s Russian River Valley, Dehlinger Winery marks its 50th anniversary this year as one of the region’s most respected and enduring family-owned wine estate. Founded in 1975 by Tom and Carole Dehlinger, the winery has remained dedicated to crafting small-lot, estate-grown wines that capture the character of its distinctive hillside soils and cool coastal climate. Tom Dehlinger was only 28 when he planted the first 14 acres of vines on what had been an old apple ranch near Vine Hill Road. At the time, the Russian River Valley appellation was not yet nationally recognized, and winegrowing infrastructure was sparse. With degrees in biochemistry and studies in viticulture and enology, Dehlinger combined scientific rigor with a hands-on pioneer spirit, planting classic varieties such as Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Syrah. Twenty years ago a wine friend of mine served me Dehlinger Pinot Noir from the High Plains Vineyard. I was enchanted by the Burgundian-like complexity and the supple power and grace of the wine. When I called up to try to buy some, I was told all their wines were sold to their waiting list. When I tried to get on the waiting list to buy some, I was told there was a waiting list to get on the waiting list. On my recent visit I was happy to find that, while scarce, it is now considerably easier to buy their wine. Over the decades the estate grew to roughly 45 acres of vineyards, and the family learned how different soils — from the sandy Goldridge to the denser Altamont soils — shaped the character of the fruit. Today, wines are often labeled not just by varietal but by site-specific expression, such as Goldridge and Altamont Pinot Noirs, reflecting the subtle influences of soil and sun on flavor. Dehlinger remains independent and family-run, with Tom and Carole’s daughters, Carmen and Eva Dehlinger, at the helm of 4101 Vine Hill Road, Sebastopol, CA 95472 707 823-2378 tastings by appointment Eva Dehlinger is in charge of winemaking and viticulture.

In 2017 the winery expanded its estate with the acquisition of the neighboring Stiling Vineyard, a move that broadened its vineyard holdings and reinforced its dedication to estate-grown production. Today, Dehlinger wines remain elusive favorites, sold primarily through a dedicated mailing list and served in top restaurants, a testament to five decades of craftsmanship, continuity, and fidelity to a singular Russian River Valley site. articles.text: Dick Carter Last Wednesday morning was cold by Piedmont standards, and rain fell steadily shortly before the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking Wednesdays group gathered at the Exedra. With weather uncertain, the walkers opted to stay in central Piedmont for their weekly outing. Despite the drizzle, about 30 water-resistant participants arrived with umbrellas in hand, along with two canine companions. Before setting off, the group reflected on the work of Ann Swift, who served as Piedmont city clerk for 22 years, from 1988 to 2010, and became the city’s unofficial historian. As a gift for Piedmont’s centennial in 2007, Swift authored Cottages and Castles – The Centennial Houses of the City of Piedmont, documenting 173 historic homes that were more than 100 years old at the time. According to Deputy City Clerk Lisa Argue, copies of the book remain available at City Hall for $30. Swift begins her survey with Piedmont’s “First Generation Houses.” In the late 1870s, the East Bay hills began attracting European settlers, many of them middle-aged Forty-Niners seeking cleaner air and open land across the bay from San Francisco. Some early arrivals, including Isaac and Sarah Requa, constructed large estates and mansions on expansive tracts. The pace of development accelerated after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, when demand for housing in the East Bay surged. Large estates were subdivided, creating sites for new homes and setting the stage for the architectural character that still defines much of Piedmont. Walker and architect Jim Kellogg provided the group with historical context on Victorian architecture, the dominant residential style from the mid-19th century through about 1900. Victorian design encompassed several variations, including Queen Anne, Italianate “Stick style,” and American Gothic. In Piedmont, Queen Anne became especially prevalent, characterized by wraparound porches, steep gabled roofs, corner turrets, decorative drip moldings, ornate wood trim, spindlework and turned posts. torian homes often displayed an eclectic mix of details. Factory-produced millwork, widely circulated pattern books and the expansion of the American railroad system allowed builders and homeowners to order decorative components from afar, contributing to increasingly elaborate designs. Many of Piedmont’s Victorians remain concentrated on the city’s western side along Rose and Sunnyside avenues, but the Walking Wednesdays group focused on homes closer to the civic center. Following Swift’s guide, the walkers could view several “Centennial Houses” while staying within easy reach of shelter should the rain intensify. The group began by heading up Highland and Mountain avenues to visit 55 Craig Ave., one of the two oldest remaining homes in Piedmont. Built around 1880 by Hugh Craig, the elaborate Stick-Italianate Victorian originally stood on what was then Vernal Avenue. The street was renamed Highland Avenue in 1910 to honor “The Highlands,” the massive 22-bedroom mansion of mining and banking figure Isaac Requa. Craig was born in Sydney, Australia, in 1841 to Scottish parents and spent part of his youth in New Zealand before moving to California. In 1874 he joined the New Zealand Insurance Company and soon opened a San Francisco office, working in fire and marine insurance until his death in 1919. Though successful, Craig was not among the mining and lumber magnates who built Piedmont’s grandest estates. He grew barley and oats for his horses at home and commuted to San Francisco by streetcar and ferry. Craig also played a civic role, helping incorporate Piedmont in 1907 and serving as mayor from 1907 to 1914. When Highland Avenue was widened in 1912, his house was famously placed on rollers and pulled by horses to its present location. When Highland Avenue was widened in 1912, his house was famously placed on rollers and pulled by horses to its present location. Kellogg noted that the Craig House Walking route remains Piedmont’s best example of Victorian Italianate style. It was designed by prominent West Coast architect Charles L. Bugbee, whose clients included Leland Stanford, Charles Crocker, David Colton and R.J. Tobin. Continuing up Craig Avenue, the group paused at 311 Highland Ave. The exact construction date of this Victorian is uncertain, but Captain William Lawrence is listed at the address in the 1894 city directory. After the death of Lawrence’s wife, Mary, her two sisters remained in the home as housekeepers. Lawrence later left them the property, but financial hardship followed. According to local accounts, the sisters eventually took their own lives in the home after turning on the stove gas — one of the more somber stories in Piedmont’s residential history. At the Highland stoplight stands 1900 Oakland Ave., a classic Queen Anne built in 1899 by John Rackliffe at age 73. The home features a wraparound porch, cross-gabled roof, octagonal turret and intricate shingle detailing typical of the style. Rackliffe and his wife Ellen built the house for their two adult children and a grandchild. The current owners, the Coffin family, later commissioned archiOn hand were Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Jasmine Cai, Mary Carter, Marcia Arthurs, Mike Gallant, Mary Ann Barnes, Bill Ahern, Judy Sokoloff, Lori Austin, Lisa Euphrat, Tyler Johnson, Alicia Rivera, Jim Kellogg, Melba Yee, Noemi Alvarado, Chuck Oraftik, Sherry Jacobs, Jack Fischrup with K-k best friend Kojak, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Leigh Sorensen, Mark Davis, Joyce Ahren, Rick Eigenbrode, Brian Hamlin, Adrienne Hamlin, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, and Dick Carter. The group was please Audrey Sung brought her husband Matt Truesdell to walk with them for the first time. tect Greer Graf to design a second-story addition that carefully matches the original Victorian detailing, earning a Piedmont Design Award. Farther along at 225 Highland Ave., walkers noted a house with an unusually deep front setback. Kellogg explained that although the structure dates to the Victorian era, its restrained wood detailing gives it more of a California Ranch character. Annie Hendry originally built the home in 1898 at 1905 Oakland Ave., across from the Rackliffe residence, where it was surrounded by extensive gardens. When Highland Avenue was widened in 1912 and 70 street trees were planted, much of Hendry’s garden was lost. She responded by moving the house to 225 Highland and positioning it far back from the street to protect her remaining landscape. Hendry lived in Piedmont until 1930. The group then returned to Oakland Avenue and stopped at 1811 Oakland Ave., built in 1896 by Edward and Martha Elrod and purchased in 1901 by Hamilton and Olive Whitney. Originally a one-story Victorian cottage, the house was raised in a 1966 renovation to create a second floor. Notably, Queen Anne elements such as fish-scale shingles and a stained-glass window beneath the front gable were preserved. Turning north on Bonita Avenue, the walkers reached 227 Bonita Ave., where Swift highlights what she calls “a whimsical gargoyle” perched on the front gable. The Queen Anne home, built in 1895 by Paul and Johanna Berkenfeld, represents the later Victorian period. Kellogg noted its straightforward rectangular plan enhanced by exuberant pattern-book ornamentation — carved wood trim, decorative shingles, spindlework at the entry porch and the distinctive gable figure watching over visitors. By this point, the rain had intensified. Rather than continue farther down Oakland Avenue, the group chose to save additional Victorian stops for a drier Wednesday. The walkers returned to the Exedra via Bonita and Magnolia avenues. Though shorter than usual, the rain-soaked walk proved both enjoyable and informative — a fitting tribute to Ann Swift’s careful documentation and to the enduring architectural character of Piedmont’s Victorian homes. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information.

articles.text: This past week a Piedmont resident spotted a large great horned owl on the branch of a redwood tree on their property. The bird grew increasingly irritated as the residents drew closer to the base of the tree. The Post spoke with a representative from Lindsay Wildlife Experience to understand if there was reason to be concerned and to learn how to co-exist with the bird. “It is possible that the owl is resting during the day, and it feels that people are getting too close. If that’s the case, the bird will eventually move on. If it stays, it may be defending a nest,” said Peter Flowers, Wildlife Hospital and Rehabilitation Manager. Nesting season for the great horned owl is generally January through March. The total nesting period can last 4 to 5 weeks of incubation and 5 to 7 weeks until fledging of the young. They will use the nests of other raptors rather than building their own. Sometimes you can see their nest high up in the tree. Otherwise, you have to depend upon their defending the area as an indication. They will also hoot nightly to indicate their territory to other birds. “Great Horned owls are territorial but generally not a threat to people unless defending a nest, in which case they may hiss, raise their wings, clack their beak, but rarely dive at you,” said Flowers. Photo courtesy of Lindsay Wildlife Museum A great horned owl “If an owl is nesting nearby, it is best not to approach. Do not make eye contact, keep noise to a minimum, and keep pets away. Smaller pets should stay inside and be outside on leash or supervised,” Flowers said. Flowers advises residents who see an owl in their neighborhood to avoid using rodenticides, consider window decals to prevent potential window strikes, and remove hazards such as netting or fishing line. When not nesting, the great horned owl will patrol its normal territory and find its favorite spots to stop and rest. If there is a great horned owl in your neighborhood, it can be quite beneficial in keeping the rodent population under control. If residents want to learn more about local raptors, veteran raptor biologist Allen Fish will discuss the raptors living in the East Bay and share stories of high-speed chases, family drama, and near miraculous survivals. His talk will be at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Wednesday, March 11 at 6:30 p.m.

articles.text: One-hundred years later, the descendants of Piedmont’s first black family intend to file a lawsuit against the city seeking to rectify the loss of their property and generational wealth 100 years ago. The lawsuit was filed by the Legal Defense Fund, the nation’s first civil rights law firm, on February 2, in Alameda County Superior Court on behalf of the descendants of Sidney and Irene Dearing. The Dearings faced a sustained campaign of intimidation, including threats of lynching, cross burnings, brick-throwing, and attempted bombings. “It’s deeply painful, but necessary, to confront the trauma and other harms my family continues to face because of governmental action to take my great-grandparents’ home solely because they were Black homeowners,” said a descendant of the Dearings and plaintiff in the lawsuit. The family is asking for a remedy for the loss of generational wealth, educational access, and other resources that come with a home in Piedmont. The suit seeks damages related to the long-term value of the lost property, an official apology, and other remedies. Mortimer is an 8-month-old puppy To meet him, submit your adoption questionnaire online at the shelter’s website, and you will be contacted by his foster to arrange a meet and greet. articles.text: This year, the City is reviving the Volunteer of the Year award for the first time since 2019. The City is also introducing a new award: Young Volunteer of the Year (under age 25), intended to uplift the meaningful contributions young people make across Piedmont. Piedmont has long been known as the “City of Volunteers.” This award, first introduced in 2014, recognizes community members whose volunteer service helped strengthen Piedmont in 2025 – whether through neighborhood improvement, arts and culture, direct community support, or building a more welcoming and inclusive community. Nominations open through March 13 To nominate a volunteer, complete the online nomination form by Friday, March 13: https://form. jotform.com/260417487348162. Volunteer service can take many forms – from a long-running commitment to a concentrated effort that made a real difference in a single year. Nominations may recognize service that strengthened Piedmont Past Winners of Piedmont’s Volunteer of the Year: 2014 – Allen “Doc” Gardner 2015 – Susan Herrick 2016 – Carla Betts 2017 – Marilyn Weber 2018 – Susan Hill 2019 – Lyman Shaffer 2025 – Stan Silverman (Police Volunteer of the Year) 2025 Police Volunteer of the Year, Stan Silverman, accepting his award next to former Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. through areas such as: • Community enrichment: improving neighborhoods and shared spaces, from beautification and clean-ups to public safety and neighborhood initiatives • Culture & Heritage: preserving local history, celebrating Piedmont’s diverse community, and supporting cultural events • Arts: strengthening the community through the visual and performing arts, arts educa- • • tion, events, and mentorship Social: direct community support and humanitarian service, including work with seniors, children, individuals with disabilities, families, and community health and safety Allyship: fostering belonging and solidarity, challenging bias, and helping make Piedmont a safe and welcoming community for everyone Nominations will be reviewed using a blind scoring process that considers measurable impact, service dedication, innovation and leadership, and character and values. Top-scoring nominees are then forwarded to a City Council subcommittee for final selection. Awardees will be recognized at the City’s annual Volunteer Appreciation Reception on April 20, 2026.

articles.text: Applications are now open for appointed volunteer positions on the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee, Recreation Commission, and as the City’s representative to the Mosquito Abatement District Board of Trustees. For most bodies, members are appointed to three-year terms, with a limit of two consecutive terms. Serving in these volunteer positions is an excellent opportunity to learn more about the inner workings of City government. As a Commissioner, you’d help shape City programs, policies, and services by providing a valuable resident perspective on upcoming and proposed projects. Learn more about the work Commissioners do by watching past meetings on the City’s online video archive. https://piedmont.ca.gov/news/kcom-tv/ live_content_and_video_archive Apply online by March 13 at piedmont.ca.gov/Commissioner. Key Dates for Applicants Applicants must be available for a pre-appointment interview with the City Council and a mandatory in-person training at City Hall before assuming their position. • Applications Due: Friday, March 13, 5 p.m. • Mandatory interviews: Monday, March 23 (evening) • Required Brown Act Training: Monday, March 30 (evening) • Appointments effective: Tuesday, April 1 Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee • 3 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Studies and provides recommendations on annual budget, long-term financial projections, mid-year budget adjustments, and the City’s municipal services tax rate and renewal. Meets as needed Civil Service Commission • 1 Vacancy (1 incumbent eligible to reapply) Deals with personnel issues, including classification, and serves as the hearing board in disputes between the City and employees. Meets as needed. Mosquito Abatement District • 1 Vacancy (0 incumbent eligible to reapply) Reviews and approves District policies, annual budget, and expenditures. Meets monthly on second Wednesdays, 5:00 p.m. Park Commission • 2 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to public parks and street trees. Meets monthly on first Wednesdays, 5:30 p.m. Parking Hearing Officer • 2 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Serves as an Administrative Hearing Officer for appeals of parking tickets issued by the City of Piedmont. Meets as needed. Planning Commission • 2 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to planning and building. Makes decisions regarding proposed modifications or construction to homes. Requires approximately 4 hours per month in addition to meeting time. Meets monthly on second Mondays, 5:30 p.m. Public Safety Committee • 2 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues related to crime reduction and disaster preparedness Meets bi-monthly Recreation Commission • 4 Vacancies (2 incumbents eligible to reapply) Advises on issues regarding recreation programs, sports field development, allocations of field space, and other issues. Meets monthly on third Wednesdays, 7:30 p.m. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: On February 22, from 2 to 4 p.m, the Pardee Home Museum will host Gene Anderson, the author of Legendary Locals of Oakland. Anderson will give a lecture about mid-19th-century Oakland, historic events, and high-profile neighbors when the Pardee family came to town. There will be a champagne reception following the lecture with sweets & savories. This will prove to be an educational and enjoyable program for all to experience. Anderson is a fourth-generation Oakland resident. His great-grandparents lived in West Oakland, and his great-grandfather worked for the South Pacific Company on a ferry boat, the only way to cross the Bay before there was a bridge. Gene was born in Long Beach but raised in Michigan, where his mother was from, and the family would visit the Bay Area every spring. He eventually moved to the Bay to attend college and ended up staying. Mr. Anderson’s interest in Gene Anderson Gene Anderson’s Legendary Locals of Oakland Pardee Home Museum Oakland history took off in 2009, at a time when the city was in the national spotlight following the killing of Oscar Grant. That’s when he started a blog called “Our Oakland.” He would ride his bike around town and take pictures of old signs he’d come across during his rides. The more photos he posted, the more readers of the blog would comment with personal stories connecting them to those old forgotten signs. It was through those comments and the discovery of local stories that Gene realized Oakland’s history was little known outside of small circles of residents. Tickets are $25 with all proceeds going to Pardee Home Museum. Save your seat on Eventbrite or call Richelle Lieberman at 510.381.1973. https://bit. ly/4tHzKwk
articles.title: Gene Anderson presents: “Old Town Oakland in the mid-19th Century”

articles.text: Every spring Piedmont Scout Council’s five troops open their doors to families interested in the scouting program. Open house meetings are an opportunity for kids and their parents to visit a specific scout troop, meet youth and adult leadership, and learn about that troop’s unique brand of scouting. Troops also share recent and upcoming activities. In advance of the open houses the Council is hosting informational sessions this week. These sessions will explain the basics of the scouting program, talk about what scouting looks like in Piedmont, assist in deciding which troop to visit, and provide a safe space to have your questions about scouting answered. Scouting is a time-honored tradition in the community of Piedmont in which 20% of Piedmont youth are involved. Scouting provides youth with hands-on leadership experiences and allows them to practice life skills while serving their community. It instills citizenship and character, fosters communication, and builds a self-reliance in youth as they organize events and take on challenges together. For more information contact Piedmont Council’s Program Coordinator Eris Turner: eturner@piedmontbsa.org – (510) 844- 4752

articles.text: Chabot Space & Science Center to celebrate splashdown Incredible advancements are made every day in the pursuit of space exploration. This year marks an especially exciting milestone in space travel with the launch of Artemis II. As early as March, the Orion spacecraft will travel around the moon and back. For this incredible mission, NASA astronaut Victor J. Glover has been selected to be the Pilot. Glover’s role in Artemis II will help pave the way for future space travel and explorers alike. The path of an astronaut Born and raised in California, Victor J. Glover attended Cal Poly where he earned a Bachelor of Science in General Engineering. While attending Cal Poly, Glover was a NCAA Division-I wrestler and football player. He also led efforts to establish the first student-funded outreach and retention center in the California Public University system. After graduating from Cal Poly in 1999, Glover joined the U.S. Navy. While serving in the Navy, Glover earned a Master of Science in Flight Test Engineering, a Master of Science in Systems Engineering, and a Master of Operational Art and Science. In the Navy, Glover was a test pilot in the F/A-18 Hornet, Super Hornet, and EA-18G Growler. Over the course of his career, Glover has garnered 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 different aircrafts, completed over 400 carrier arrested landings, and 24 combat missions. NASA astronaut Victor Glover has been selected as the Pilot of Artemis II. Out of more than 6,000 candidates, Glover was selected in 2013 to be one of eight members of the 21st NASA astronaut class. In 2018, Glover was assigned to his first spaceflight mission as Pilot of the Crew Dragon spacecraft. Glover also served as Expedition 64/65 Flight Engineer aboard the International Space Station. Glover’s extensive education and experience in science, engineering, and flying made him the perfect candidate to be selected in 2023 for Artemis II Pilot. Looking to the future Victor J. Glover is helping to lay the foundation for future space exploration and travel. The successful completion of Artemis II will send Glover and his fellow crew members into the next phase of the Artemis program: the exploration of the lunar South Pole. If the mission is successful, Glover will be the first person of color to walk on the surface of the Moon. Astronauts like Glover will help inspire generations of space explorers for years to come. Splashdown at Chabot Chabot Space & Science Center plans to host a splashdown party to celebrate this incredible achievement in space travel. This stellar event will include moonthemed crafts and snacks, special guest speakers from NASA Ames, and a livestream of the splashdown in Chabot’s planetarium, theater, and NASA Ames Visitor Center. For updates on this special event and more visit chabotspace.org. The date will be determined once a launch day has officially been selected for Artemis II, so keep an eye on our events calendar: chabotspace.org/ programs/events-listing.
articles.title: Victor Glover selected as Pilot for Artemis II

This year marks an especially exciting milestone in space travel with the launch of Artemis II. As early as March, the Orion spacecraft will travel around the moon and back. For this incredible mission, NASA astronaut Victor J. Glover has been selected to be the Pilot. Glover’s role in Artemis II will help pave the way for future space travel and explorers alike. The path of an astronaut Born and raised in California, Victor J. Glover attended Cal Poly where he earned a Bachelor of Science in General Engineering. While attending Cal Poly, Glover was a NCAA Division-I wrestler and football player. He also led efforts to establish the first student-funded outreach and retention center in the California Public University system. After graduating from Cal Poly in 1999, Glover joined the U.S. Navy. While serving in the Navy, Glover earned a Master of Science in Flight Test Engineering, a Master of Science in Systems Engineering, and a Master of Operational Art and Science. In the Navy, Glover was a test pilot in the F/A-18 Hornet, Super Hornet, and EA-18G Growler. Over the course of his career, Glover has garnered 3,000 flight hours in more than 40 different aircrafts, completed over 400 carrier arrested landings, and 24 combat missions. articles.text: Piedmont for Inclusive Education (PIE) will host its second annual benefit concert supporting the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Sidekicks program on February 27. The concert will feature We Are Leaves, formerly The Date Nights, a band made up of Piedmont parents, at Piedmont Community Hall from 7 to 9 p.m. The band, made up of Beach Elementary parents, describes its music as “indie pop.” Lead singer and guitarist Matthew Zapruder said the group writes “songs that have recognizable melodies and structures but are maybe a little quirkier than those you might hear in your car on the radio.” “We write songs about our local community: they mention Dracena Park and its audible owls, as well as a local ghost who lives in Dracena named Celeste,” said Zapruder. Proceeds from the concert will benefit the Sidekicks program, led by Larisa Martiniak. The program pairs neurodiverse children with a dedicated teen sidekick to help them navigate activities, build social connections and participate more fully and confidently in summer camps and other programs. Through the experience, teen sidekicks develop communication skills, patience, adaptability and emotional intelligence. We Are Leaves will play live music at the Benefit Concert, with Matthew Zapruder (left) (lead vocals and guitar), Peter Jaeschke (bass), Supina Mapon (violin and vocals), and Steve Pearson (drums). “Having older kids help neurodivergent kids in after school and other programs makes inclusion actually happen, by supporting families and kids who wouldn’t otherwise be able to participate in those activities,” said Zapruder. The Sidekicks program trains Piedmont teens to support safe, fun and inclusive after-school classes and summer programs for neurodiverse school-aged children. Last year, Sidekicks supported more than 60 Piedmont participants, and 45 teen sidekicks were trained. “The Sidekicks program has changed my kid’s life. He has so much more confidence having a buddy help him through what could easily be overwhelming experiences,” said one Piedmont parent. Sidekicks program offerings, new classes and camps, and increase staff training will be supported by the concert. Learn more about the Sidekicks program at Piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/recreation/ adaptive_programs__sidekicks To buy tickets for the Sidekicks Benefit Concert visit: Piedmontstore.org/products/ pie-piedmonters-for-inclusive-education-copy?

articles.text: On February 4, Piedmont High School welcomed 16 exchange students from Sant Celoni, a town near Barcelona, Spain. The students spent 12 days in Piedmont attending classes, living with host families, and experiencing American culture. Spanish students Montse Fradera and Noa Guirado shared their perspectives on the program. Both attend school in Sant Celoni and chose to participate in the exchange to improve their English language skill and better understand daily life in America beyond what they see in movies or online. The students described the Piedmont campus as beautiful and noticeably larger than their school in Spain. One of the biggest differences they observed is the variety of classes offered. Courses such as dance and other artistic electives stood out to them, as their school in Spain focuses more heavily on traditional subjects. Academically, they did find some similarities. After attending a biology class, one student noted that the material was comparable to what they are studying at home. However, learning English adds an extra challenge. Living with host families has been another highlight of the trip. They described their families as welcoming, generous, and eager to include them in daily activities. The experience has helped them feel more comfortable in a new environment. American food has also made an impression upon the group. Reese’s peanut butter cups have quickly become a favorite, as Spanish students and Piedmont host students gather at the Exedra. Visiting students from Spain took a trip to San Francisco’s Pier 39 and the Aquarium of the Bay. Foreign exchange students from Spain hop onto the Powell and Hyde Street cable car. Photo courtesy of Commons.wikimedia.org Pictured is the Plaça de la Vila or (main square) of the Spanish student’s hometown of Sant Celoni. After a 13-hour flight from Spain, guest students take the BART train to visit San Francisco. the American candy is not commonly found in Spain. At the same time, they mentioned that Americans are missing out on Lemon Fanta, a popular Spanish soft drink. Before making the 6,000-mile journey, they had heard stereotypes that Americans primarily eat unhealthy “junk food.” Their experience, however, has challenged that perception. They were surprised to see their host families eating balanced meals with plenty of vegetables. What has stood out most about Piedmont students is their openness and friendliness. In their first classes, many students approached them to introduce themselves and ask questions, making them feel welcome almost immediately. Post.

pages.text: 8 8 Wednesday, February 18, 2026 PHS welcomes exchange students from Spain By Evolette Mak On February 4, Piedmont High School welcomed 16 exchange students from Sant Celoni, a town near Barcelona, Spain. The students spent 12 days in Piedmont attending classes, living with host families, and experiencing American culture. Spanish students Montse Fradera and Noa Guirado shared their perspectives on the program. Both attend school in Sant Celoni and chose to participate in the exchange to improve their English language skill and better understand daily life in America beyond what they see in movies or online. The students described the Piedmont campus as beautiful and noticeably larger than their school in Spain. One of the biggest differences they observed is the variety of classes offered. Courses such as dance and other artistic electives stood out to them, as their school in Spain focuses more heavily on traditional subjects. Academically, they did find some similarities. After attending a biology class, one student noted that the material was comparable to what they are studying at home. However, learning English adds an extra challenge. Living with host families has been another highlight of the trip. They described their families as welcoming, generous, and eager to include them in daily activities. The experience has helped them feel more comfortable in a new environment. American food has also made an impression upon the group. Reese’s peanut butter cups have quickly become a favorite, as Spanish students and Piedmont host students gather at the Exedra. Photos by Deysi Sahagon Visiting students from Spain took a trip to San Francisco’s Pier 39 and the Aquarium of the Bay. Foreign exchange students from Spain hop onto the Powell and Hyde Street cable car. Photo courtesy of Commons.wikimedia.org Pictured is the Plaça de la Vila or (main square) of the Spanish student’s hometown of Sant Celoni. After a 13-hour flight from Spain, guest students take the BART train to visit San Francisco. the American candy is not commonly found in Spain. At the same time, they mentioned that Americans are missing out on Lemon Fanta, a popular Spanish soft drink. Before making the 6,000-mile journey, they had heard stereotypes that Americans primarily eat unhealthy “junk food.” Their experience, however, has challenged that perception. They were surprised to see their host families eating balanced meals with plenty of vegetables. What has stood out most about Piedmont students is their openness and friendliness. In their first classes, many students approached them to introduce themselves and ask questions, making them feel welcome almost immediately. The foreign exchange program was pioneered last year by PHS Spanish teacher Deysi Sahagon. Piedmont will send its own group of students to Spain again this year, during Spring Break. Although adjusting to the nine-hour time difference has been difficult, with early bedtimes and even earlier mornings, both students said they would highly recommend participating in an exchange program. For them, it is not only an opportunity to strengthen their English, but also a chance to build friendships and gain a deeper understanding of another culture. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern reporter for the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: The Post caught up with Piedmont High alum Trevor Fleshman and his wife Ana to learn about the couple’s history at UC Davis, their wedding in the mountains, and their recent move to Piedmont to start their next step in life together. Trevor and Ana met through a mutual friend at UC Davis in 2012. Ana originally attended Santa Barbara City College before transferring to Davis in her junior year, where her best friend was a part of the same friend group as Trevor. A year later, both of them were single and decided to give a relationship a try. The couple dated for six years before getting married in 2019 in Murphys, California in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains. The two moved to Piedmont a year ago into Trevor’s grandmother’s house, three blocks from his mom, Patty Dunlap. He grew up and went to school in Piedmont, graduating with the high school Class of 2009 from Piedmont High School. He now gets to introduce his wife and 19-month old daughter, Cleo, to the community as he and Ana celebrate their first Valentine’s Day in their Piedmont home. “I think I’ve never been a huge Valentine’s Day person, but when Trevor and I first got together, he was very sweet,” said Ana. “I remember he baked me a cake for Valentine’s Day, and he used to leave me little notes on my desk if he came over to the house and I wasn’t there. I feel like Trevor really brought me into the fold of being romantic on Valentine’s Day.” “Ana’s like the evil princess from Frozen. She had a cold, black heart when I met her, so now I’m trying to work her out,” said Trevor. The couple plans to keep their Valentine’s Day celebration low key. They’ll enjoy a home-cooked meal together and enjoy each other’s presence. “It’s nicer to be together than be out in a restaurant and have to run around with all the other people on dates,” he said. Ana appreciates Trevor’s positive attitude and his easy-going goofiness. On the other hand, Trevor appreciates Ana’s strength. “She holds it all together. It’s been really fun watching her become a mom. She hasn’t lost any of her sparkle for life. She is always down to have a good time,” he said. Trevor and Ana Fleshman have been married for four years. articles.text: Anne and Greg’s first trip together in 2013 to Jackson Hole, Wyoming. One could say that Anne and Greg Wheeler’s connection to Valentine’s Day started with the idea of a slow-cooked Italian meal. They met in San Francisco in 2011, while volunteering for the non-profit called Slow Food that protects traditional cooking and farming practices; the organization was founded when the first McDonald’s opened in Italy in 1986. Anne was still in a relationship when they met, so Greg, like good cooking, took things slow and built a good friendship with Anne over the next year. “Then we both stopped volunteering, and after a couple of missed opportunities to reconnect, finally — I was still trying to find my Anne — I saw her. She had just joined Match.com that day.” said Greg. “Literally that day I found her, we went out, and I just fell in love.” Greg still recalls being smitten upon finding Anne’s online dating profile, on which she included her chickens with names like Pollo Picasso, and Eggy Vedder. “I took my profile down the next day, I never even got a date out of it,” said Anne. The couple dated while living in San Francisco for a year and a half, before getting married on October 11, 2014 on Stinson Beach. Anne described the wedding as perfect, she grew up going to her family’s beach house in Stinson. A month after the wedding, Anne enrolled in a 12-month culinary school program, San Francisco Cooking School, before doing her stage at the Italian restaurant A16. “Anne was in her third trimester, with our first, standing up all day long, working in the restaurant. And I’m at home, with my head exploding, wondering, ‘when is my wife and our babyto-be, going to come home?’ She was walking backwards up a hill to get to her car, working so her husband wouldn’t starve at home,” he said with a smile. The couple lived in San Francisco’s Upper Haight district for four years, then moved to Crocker Highlands for five, before moving to Piedmont in 2022, where Anne grew up. The Wheelers started a cook book club with five other couples in 2017 upon moving to Oakland, which was a great way to reestablish their life together in the East Bay. The Wheelers have three daughters at Wildwood; Izzy is ten and their twins Millie and Bea are seven. Valentine’s Day is big in the Wheeler household, Anne is the founder of Saltysistersbakeshop.com and works overtime for a month leading up to Valentine’s Day filling cookie orders. “Valentine’s Day is our girl’s favorite holiday. Everyone makes Valentine’s for their classmates, and Izzy does very elaborate homemade Valentine’s. So we start that a month before. She made friendship bracelets one year for everyone, and then little clay statues specific for each person another year” said Anne. It’s not all Italian food and sugar cookies for the Wheelers, one of the first trips they took together was to Vietnam. There, they took three cooking classes one in the north, one in central Vietnam and then the south. “Those cooking classes, were no small affair,” remembered Greg. “Each one was about five, six hours long. You’re taken to the market, you buy all the food, bring it back, you prepare the meal, and then you get to sit down and eat it. It was amazing.” The Wheelers of Piedmont, provide the proof that the fastest way to the heart is through the stomach. Their love for one another goes beyond food however; Anne and Greg’s surely could endure hunger strikes of victuals in the name of their nuptials. Anne and Greg’s wedding picture

By Jay Russell One could say that Anne and Greg Wheeler’s connection to Valentine’s Day started with the idea of a slow-cooked Italian meal. They met in San Francisco in 2011, while volunteering for the non-profit called Slow Food that protects traditional cooking and farming practices; the organization was founded when the first McDonald’s opened in Italy in 1986. Anne was still in a relationship when they met, so Greg, like good cooking, took things slow and built a good friendship with Anne over the next year. “Then we both stopped volunteering, and after a couple of missed opportunities to reconnect, finally — I was still trying to find my Anne — I saw her. She had just joined Match.com that day.” said Greg. “Literally that day I found her, we went out, and I just fell in love.” Greg still recalls being smitten upon finding Anne’s online dating profile, on which she included her chickens with names like Pollo Picasso, and Eggy Vedder. “I took my profile down the next day, I never even got a date out of it,” said Anne. The couple dated while living in San Francisco for a year and a half, before getting married on October 11, 2014 on Stinson Beach. Anne described the wedding as perfect, she grew up going to her family’s beach house in Stinson. A month after the wedding, Anne enrolled in a 12-month culinary school program, San Francisco Cooking School, before doing her stage at the Italian restaurant A16. “Anne was in her third trimester, with our first, standing up all day long, working in the restaurant. And I’m at home, with my head exploding, wondering, ‘when is my wife and our babyto-be, going to come home?’ She was walking backwards up a hill to get to her car, working so her husband wouldn’t starve at home,” he said with a smile. The couple lived in San Francisco’s Upper Haight district for four years, then moved to Crocker Highlands for five, before moving to Piedmont in 2022, where Anne grew up. The Wheelers started a cook book club with five other couples in 2017 upon moving to Oakland, which was a great way to reestablish their life together in the East Bay. The Wheelers have three daughters at Wildwood; Izzy is ten and their twins Millie and Bea are seven. Valentine’s Day is big in the Wheeler household, Anne is the founder of Saltysistersbakeshop.com and works overtime for a month leading up to Valentine’s Day filling cookie orders. “Valentine’s Day is our girl’s favorite holiday. Everyone makes Valentine’s for their classmates, and Izzy does very elaborate homemade Valentine’s. So we start that a month before. She made friendship bracelets one year for everyone, and then little clay statues specific for each person another year” said Anne. It’s not all Italian food and sugar cookies for the Wheelers, one of the first trips they took together was to Vietnam. There, they took three cooking classes one in the north, one in central Vietnam and then the south. “Those cooking classes, were no small affair,” remembered Greg. “Each one was about five, six hours long. You’re taken to the market, you buy all the food, bring it back, you prepare the meal, and then you get to sit down and eat it. It was amazing.” The Wheelers of Piedmont, provide the proof that the fastest way to the heart is through the stomach. Their love for one another goes beyond food however; Anne and Greg’s surely could endure hunger strikes of victuals in the name of their nuptials. Anne and Greg’s wedding picture

articles.text: Piedmont High school students Katie Tran and Anna Szymanski published their new children’s book When Ken Needs A Minute on February 4. Tran, a junior, penned the text of the book, and Szymanski, a sophomore, created the illustrations. When Ken Needs A Minute is designed to help young kids, specifically those with neurodiversities like autism spectrum disorder, to better understand their emotions. The story brings Ken the Elephant to life in 25 pages. “As students who are passionate about mental health, inclusion, and education, we wanted to create a resource that could help make a positive impact in our community and beyond,” said Tran. The duo independently published the book and copies can now be purchased at Amazon. com/When-Needs-Minute-Neurodiversity-Self-Regulation/dp/ B0GMGDBQ3C/. “We especially enjoyed collaborating throughout the creative process, as well as receiving feedback from educators, parents, and individuals who work closely with neurodivergent children. Their insights helped shape the overall direction and purpose of the book,” said Tran. The story helps children explore feelings, practice self-regulation, and celebrate individuality. When Ken Needs A Minute is marketed to parents, teachers, and therapists of children threeeight years old. A moral of the story is that being yourself and taking a minute when you need it, is always enough. articles.text: Piedmont seeded No. 5 seed in NCS playoffs Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team closed its season on a high note, blanking Encinal 2-nil in Alameda for the regular season-finale on Thursday, February 12. The result brought Piedmont’s record to 9-2-7 (W-T-L) overall, giving them a berth in the Division 2 North Coast Section bracket as the No. 5 seed. Piedmont hosted No. 12 Acalanes in the first round of postseason playoffs on Tuesday, February 17. Results were not complete by Post time. Reaching the NCS Div 2 bracket marks a two tier promotion after competing in D4 last season. “We’re playing good football; it’s just creating chances in the final third and finishing those chances. We can’t be reliant on just one or two players,” said coach Matt Spencer-Harty. “Winning is a habit. The effort is there and we’ve seen what can happen when we try our hardest. With that knowledge, we’ll carry it forward into NCS,” senior center back Darcy McKee added. It was a monster performance by Piedmont’s senior midfielder Arden Sorensen-Wald. She had an assist to Stephanie Lee for the Highlanders’ opening goal, where she whipped in a perfect pass to Lee in the middle of a group. She then scored PHS’ second goal on a rocket shot from 35 yards. 2-0 shutout of Encinal Piedmont’s first goal came in the 11th minute at the end of a corner. After an initial pass was played from Sorensen-Wald, the ball ricocheted around the box leading to Miranda Liu assuming possession and playing a pass back to Sorensen-Wald. The Highlanders’ midfielder made one move around a Jets’ defender, sending an inch-perfect laser across the face of the net to find Stephanie Lee inside a crowd of players. articles.text: Piedmont receives No.3 seed in NCS Open Division Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team closed its season in stellar fashion, beating rival Bishop O’Dowd 44-40 to capture their fourth consecutive Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division title on Thursday, February 12. This year, PHS is the outright league champion after haring the title with O’Dowd in 2024 and 2025. As a result, Piedmont moves into the North Coast Section Open Division, the top bracket, with the No. 3 ranking. They will host No. 6 Cardinal Newman on Thursday, February 19, which marks a rematch of last year’s Open Division first-round, which PHS lost 51-45 to the Cardinals. This year the Highlanders beat Cardinal Newman handily, 64-50, on December 13. “I’m excited for playoffs. We work all year for this moment going back to open gyms and conditioning,” said coach Bryan Gardere. ”There’s preseason, regAndrea Martin led with 23 points against O’Dowd. Savannah Dennig drives in during Piedmont’s last possession of the game to find Andrea Martin. Staff Photos Piedmont celebrates after beating Bishop O’Dowd to capture its fourth straight WACC Foothill Division title. Pictured are Savannah Dennig (left), Andrea Martin, and Taylor White. ular season, and then postseason. Now we’re here, these are the moments we get ready for. We know it’s going to be tough, but the girls are excited for it,” Against Bishop O’Dowd, Piedmont led 40-29 in the fourth quarter, but the Dragons went on a 9-0 scoring run to cut the Highlanders’ lead to 40-38 with 2:36 left in the game. “Our approach was just to get the ball back, find a way to score, and avoid playing at their pace,” Taylor White said “They scored a few times and I said, “Okay, They are on a run.” But we’re taught to stay calm; everyone goes on a run – that’s basketball. We helped them with a few turnovers,” Savannah Dennig added. PHS stayed composed, scoring when Taylor White assisted Andrea Martin to make it 42-38 with 1:35 left. O’Dowd made it 42-40 with 36 seconds left on the clock, but Piedmont had the final word with six seconds remaining when Dennig drove to the hoop and laid off a pass to Martin for the game’s final bucket. “I was first going to pass it to Lex [Alexa Ba]. I got the ball and started driving. I saw Lex open, but a defender moved in at the last second while I was in the air. Andrea was there, so I threw it to her instead. Drea went up and made it, I was so happy,” Dennig said of the play. “We were trying to make a quick play, and I thought to cut through with Savannah driving. I got into the middle and she found me,” Martin added. 44-40 victory over Bishop O’Dowd Playing in their gym, O’Dowd led through most of the first quarter. Piedmont cut their lead to 13-12 as the quarter expired with Martin converting two free throws. In the second quarter, both teams traded points until the Highlanders went on a 5-0 run to end the quarter. They took the lead in the final second when Martin drew a foul and converted both free throws for an 18-17 lead at halftime. Piedmont opened the third quarter with an exhausting 13-0 run to take a 33-20 lead, and established a 15-point, 36-21 advantage to end the third quarter. But the Dragons weren’t done. O’Dowd scored the first eight of 10 points to open the fourth quarter, cutting the PHS lead to 38-29. White assisted Martin on another bucket, but BOD answered by going on its nine-point run to make it 40-38 with 2:36 left in the game. articles.text: Sam Shelby (left) and Jordan Alemania, PHS Class of 2025 graduates, both committed to play at Division 1 NCAA programs. Two former football players from Piedmont High’s Class of 2025 graduating class are off to play at the next level. Last month, Sam Shelby announced he signed on to continue playing at Williams & Mary, while Jordan Alemania is set to join Holy Cross. Both players departed from Piedmont without immediately joining a college program, instead opting to take a fifth year of high school at The Hun School, a prep school in Princeton, New Jersey. They recently sign with two Division 1 NCAA programs. “It was a discussion I had with the coaches both at Piedmont and The Hun. The coaches at Piedmont knew I had what it took to play at the Division 1 level and at a good school. Coach Todd Smith at The Hun said, ‘If you come here, you’ll earn what you deserve, you just have to prove it on the field.’” Shelby said. “I heard that some older Piedmont football players from the early 2000s took some postgraduate years on the East Coast and landed at some good Division 1 programs. Coach Smith reached out to me and talked about what they had to offer,” Alemania mentioned. The Hun School put Shelby and Alemania alongside a wealth of collegiate talent and athletes who could very well be in the NFL one day. In total, 21 students from Sam and Jordan’s class have signed with D1 college programs, including the No. 1 ranked edge rusher in the entire 2026 class, USC Trojan-bound Luke Wafle. The Raiders’ program took on some of the best nation’s schools. They traveled to Orlando, Florida to play No. 2 ranked school, St. Frances Academy. It was really fierce competition; we played some top- 10 schools in the nation,” Alemania said. “I’m a big believes in being the product of your environment. Up and down the roster is 40 guys that are likeminded and all have the same goals. You play alongside guys who are doing big things, you’re going to follow suit. The practice environment alone was huge,” Shelby mentioned. The pair traveled across the country to create new opportunities. “Coach Smith (at the Hun School) has been in the business a really long time. He has so many connections, especially on the East Coast. Coming to The Hun gave me geographically more exposure. On the East Coast, we’d have coaches come visit who were just a quick drive away, instead of having to fly in. It was really helpful,” “Recruiting is more difficult when you’re talking about schools that are all the way across the country. Football, especially, has less college programs overall in California compared to the East Coast. Being out there was super helpful because coaches were funneling in to see our team,” Alemania said. articles.text: The 2026 Winter Olympics are underway in Italy through February 22. As of Tuesday, February 17, the United States holds third place in the medal count with six gold, 10 silver, and five bronze medals. Norway leads both medal and gold categories with 31 and 14 respectively, Italy has 24 medals and nine gold, and Germany has 20 medals with five gold. Here’s a rundown of some of the best moments from this year’s Olympic Games. Jordan Stolz sets Olympic speed skating record Team USA’s star speed skater Jordan Stolz captured Gold in the 1,000 meter and 500 meter races. He clocked an Olympic record of 1:06.28 in the 1,000 meter on February 11, and followed up with a record time of 33.77 in the 500 meter on February 14. Team USA women’s hockey dominating Team USA is dominating the field in women’s hockey, Photo courtesy of TEAM USA Team USA speed skater Jordan Stolz set Olympic records in the 500 and 1,000 meter races. Photo courtesy of NCAA.com Team USA’s Women’s Hockey is one step away from winning Gold in a dominating run of games. Photo courtesy of E! News USA’s Ilia Malinin shocked the world by finishing eighth in the free skate with several falls after being the heavy favorite for Gold. currently outscoring opponents 31-1 in this year’s games. They are set to face Canada for the Gold Medal on February 19. They opened with a 5-1 win over the Czech Republic in group play, shut out Switzerland and Canada 5-0 in the preliminaries, routed Italy 6-0 in the quarterfinals, and beat Sweden 5-0 in the semifinals on February 16. Ilia Malinin struggles in free skate lia Malinin entered as the gold medal favorite but delivered an uncharacteristic performance in the February 13 free skate, finishing eighth overall. He failed to land his signature quadruple axel, falling twice on jumps. The gold went to Mikhail Shaidorov of Kazakhstan. Elana Meyers Taylor wins sixth medal in bobsled Team USA’s 41-year-old veteran Elana Meyers Taylor made history on February 16, winning the sixth medal of her bobsledding career, tying the United States’ record in all sports. She is now the most decorated bobsledder in the sport’s history. She took Gold in the women’s monobob with a time of 3:57.93, edging Germany’s Laura Nolte by just 0.04 of a second.
