articles.text: Annual fundraiser is April 29 The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is hosting Art Bash, the museum’s signature annual fundraiser, on Wednesday, April 29. Limited tickets are on sale now. Art Bash raises more than $2,500,000 annually to benefit the museum’s education and family programs, as well as community engagement events that benefit over 150,000 people every year. The event transforms the museum’s entire campus into a multi-layered experience of art, performances and social activities. This year’s celebration also marks the 10th anniversary of SFMOMA’s building expansion. Art Bash 2026 begins with a ticketed dinner featuring a live auction of works by contemporary artists in partnership with Sotheby’s. After the dinner phase, the event broadens to a museum-wide party with immersive art installations by Bay Area artists Rose D’Amato and Rupy C. Tut., live music and other creative activations across multiple floors, drawing thousands of attendees and often lasting into the morning hours. Live music is presented in partnership with Stern Grove Festival with featured artists to be announced at a later date. Tickets may be purchased at sfmoma.org/artbash. SFMOMA’s Art Bash returns this spring.
articles.title: Tickets for SFMOMA Art Bash 2026 on sale now

articles.text: Photo courtesy of American Conservatory Theater The new play is based on the Paranormal Activity films created by filmmaker Oren Peli. American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) in San Francisco presents the North American premiere of Paranormal Activity, a new stage production based on the film franchise from Paramount Pictures, premiering tomorrow, February 19 and running through March 15. The new play presents an original story set in the world of the Paranormal Activity films created by filmmaker Oren Peli. The stage adaptation is written by Levi Holloway, whose credits include Grey House, and is conceived with director Felix Barrett. Illusions are designed by Tony Award winner Chris Fisher. The story follows James and Lou, who relocate from Chicago to London in an effort to leave their past behind. They encounter a series of unexplained events that suggest a continuing supernatural presence. Cher Álvarez and Patrick Heusinger star as Lou and James. Álvarez’s previous stage credits include work with Goodman Theatre, Steppenwolf Theatre and Writers Theatre. Heusinger has appeared on Broadway in “Next Fall” and “Fiddler on the Roof.” Shannon Cochran plays Carolanne, James’ mother, and Kate Fry portrays Etheline Cotgrave, a medium. Understudies are Caroline Hendricks, Michael Holding and Carol Buinis. The creative team includes Fly Davis (scenic and costume design), Anna Watson (lighting design), Gareth Fry (sound design) and Luke Halls (video design). Casting is by Bob Mason. The production is presented by arrangement with Paramount Pictures and Melting Pot, in co-production with Chicago Shakespeare Theater, Center Theatre Group and Shakespeare Theatre Company. In conjunction with the run, A.C.T. will offer a series of InterACT events, including post-show conversations on select dates, a Pride Night event, a Tasting Night and a pre-matinee workshop. The production will run at A.C.T.’s Toni Rembe Theater at 415 Geary Street in San Francisco. Visit act-sf.org/interact for tickets and to learn more about subscribing to these events throughout the season. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday: 11 a.m. – 5:30 p.m. Sunday: 1 p.m – 5 p.m. Donations accepted at 2501 Harrison Street Tuesday & Wednesday: 9 a.m. – 12:00 p.m. Saturdays: 10 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.

articles.text: An exhibition at the Legion of Honor is shedding fresh light on the artistic partnership between two leading figures of French Impressionism. Manet & Morisot, on view now through March 1, is the first major exhibition devoted to the friendship and creative exchange between Édouard Manet and Berthe Morisot, both celebrated French Impressionist artists. Spanning 15 years from 1868 to 1883, the Manet & Morisot exhibition traces the evolution of the artists’ relationship in Paris at a pivotal moment in the development of modern art. Manet is widely regarded as a pioneer of modern painting, while Morisot was the only woman to exhibit under her own name in the original Impressionist group. Their story has often centered on Manet’s early portraits of Morisot, with her work framed as an extension of his influence. However, a new scholarship presented in the exhibition challenges that narrative. By the final years of his life, curators argue, Manet increasingly followed Morisot’s lead, adopting her choice of subjects, lighter palette and rapid, expressive brushwork. Though close friends and part of the same avant-garde circles, the two artists differed markedly. Manet, known for his charm and ambition, worked primarily in the studio, revising his canvases extensively to achieve a spontaneous effect. His paintings are noted for their bold graphic power and engagement with art history. Morisot, by contrast, was admired for her reserve and intelligence. Trained largely as a plein-air painter, she developed a style defined by light, atmosphere and swift execution under shifting outdoor conditions. Her compositions often shimmer with delicacy and immediacy. Through paired works and new research, Manet & Morisot reexamines their celebrated friendship and recasts their roles in shaping modern art. Visit https://www.famsf.org/ to learn more. The exhibition leaves the museum on March 1.
articles.title: Legion of Honor Manet & Morisot exhibition leaves March 1

By Allyson Aleksey American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) in San Francisco presents the North American premiere of Paranormal Activity, a new stage production based on the film franchise from Paramount Pictures, premiering tomorrow, February 19 and running through March 15. The new play presents an original story set in the world of the Paranormal Activity films created by filmmaker Oren Peli. The stage adaptation is written by Levi Holloway, whose credits include Grey House, and is conceived with director Felix Barrett. Illusions are designed by Tony Award winner Chris Fisher. The story follows James and Lou, who relocate from Chicago to London in an effort to leave their past behind. They encounter a series of unexplained events that suggest a continuing supernatural presence. Cher Álvarez and Patrick Heusinger star as Lou and James. Legion of Honor Manet & Morisot exhibition leaves March 1 By Allyson Aleksey An exhibition at the Legion of Honor is shedding fresh light on the artistic partnership between two leading figures of French Impressionism. Manet & Morisot, on view now through March 1, is the first major exhibition devoted to the friendship and creative exchange between Édouard Manet and Berthe Morisot, both celebrated French Impressionist artists. Spanning 15 years from 1868 to 1883, the Manet & Morisot exhibition traces the evolution of the artists’ relationship in Paris at a pivotal moment in the development of modern art. Manet is widely regarded as a pioneer of modern painting, while Morisot was the only woman to exhibit under her own name in the original Impressionist group. Their story has often centered on Manet’s early portraits of Morisot, with her work framed as an extension of his influence. However, a new scholarship presented in the exhibition challenges that narrative. By the final years of his life, curators argue, Manet increasingly followed Morisot’s lead, adopting her choice of subjects, lighter palette and rapid, expressive brushwork. Though close friends and part of the same avant-garde circles, the two artists differed markedly. Manet, known for his charm and ambition, worked primarily in the studio, revising his canvases extensively to achieve a spontaneous effect. His paintings are noted for their bold graphic power and engagement with art history. Morisot, by contrast, was admired for her reserve and intelligence. Trained largely as a plein-air painter, she developed a style defined by light, atmosphere and swift execution under shifting outdoor conditions. Her compositions often shimmer with delicacy and immediacy. Through paired works and new research, Manet & Morisot reexamines their celebrated friendship and recasts their roles in shaping modern art. articles.text: Jazz trumpeter Dave Rocha appears in concert with his trio Jazz trumpeter Dave Rocha will perform a free concert with his trio at the San Francisco Botanical Garden this Saturday, February 21. Rocha is a celebrated trumpeter who has been playing professionally for most of his adult life, having worked for years in the New York jazz scene performing alongside legendary bands of Lionel Hampton, Larry Elgart, and Machito. He also leads his own jazz combo in numerous club engagements across the United States. The concert, entitled Jazz Amongst the Magnolias, celebrates one of the most significant conservation collections of Magnolias in the United States. Magnolias bloom January through March at San Francisco Botanical Garden, offering a unique and magnificent concert background. In addition to playing the trumpet, Rocha will also perform with the flugelhorn, a cousin to the trumpet that has a deeper, more mellow tone. The concert program includes Dave Rocha compositions by Freddie Hubbard, Alan Onaje Gumbs, Ornette Coleman, Jackie McClean, McCoy Tyner and more. Guitarist Luke Schwartz and acoustic bassist Heath Proskin round out the trio. The concert begins at 1 p.m. on Saturday, February 21. No advance registration is required. Admission to the San Francisco Botanical Garden is free for all members, San Francisco residents, children under four-yearsold and military veterans. Rain cancels the event. articles.text: A new exhibition at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco highlights the bold experimentation reshaping contemporary Japanese ceramics. “New Japanese Clay” brings together modern and contemporary works that reimagine a centuries-old tradition. Infused with vivid color and sculptural ambition, the pieces range from rugged, earthbound forms that evoke stone and soil to delicate constructions that appear as light as paper or billowing fabric. Museum officials said the presentation reflects both Japan’s rich ceramic history and the increasingly global nature of contemporary art training and practice. The exhibition focuses on a new generation of Japanese potters who are expanding the expressive possibilities of clay. According to Chief Curator Dr. Robert Mintz, who organized the exhibition, the featured artists build on the legacy of the mingei, or folk art, movement while forging distinctly experimental paths. “The artists in New Japanese Clay are challenging the conventions of functional ceramics and pivoting toward a purely sculptural experience,” Mintz said in a statement. “Their creations are meant to intrigue and delight; the vessel form is just a point of departure for spectacular experimentation.” Through innovative materials and techniques, the artists move beyond traditional utilitarian forms, emphasizing texture, scale and abstraction. Many also share their creative processes through social media, offering audiences insight into the technical and conceptual development behind their work. All works on view are drawn from the collection of Dr. Phyllis A. Kempner and Dr. David D. Stein. The exhibition is made possible with support from Tania and Michael Stepanian, with sustained funding provided by the Akiko Yamazaki and Jerry Yang Endowment Fund for Exhibitions and the Kao/Williams Contemporary Art Exhibitions Fund. For more information, visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/ exhibitions/new-japanese-clay/. Discover oral care for the whole family. harmonyoralhealth.com/ scheduling (510)986-0220

articles.text: The White Elephant Sale, Oakland Museum of California’s (OMCA) decades-old, largest annual fundraiser, closes this weekend with an open warehouse sale. The White Elephant sale is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, a group of over 100 year-round members, to raise proceeds to support the museum in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements and more. The White Elephant Sale is touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale and garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The fundraiser has contributed over $23 million to the Museum since the Board’s inception in 1959. The sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. Volunteers sort, repair, and price items donated by the public, building a collective effort that benefits the museum and local residents alike. Browse without the crowds on select days between now and Saturday, February 21, between 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. New merchandise will be added throughout the sale. Spots can be reserved for $7 a day and should be made ahead of entry. No children under 12 (including infants in front carriers) will be allowed, and only service animals are permitted in the warehouse. Animals that solely provide companionship, comfort, or emotional support are not considered service animals and will not be allowed in the warehouse. No food or drinks, except water, are permitted inside the warehouse. The event is cashless. Visit https://museumca.org/ event/67th-annual-white-elephant-sale-open-warehouse-days/ for more information. The White Elephant Sale is OMCA’s largest annual fundraiser.

Superb local pianist Carl Blake was joined by an equally superb flutist William Underwood lll. Their program was a complete overview of flute and piano music. Dr. Blake told The phenomenon of a second wind me that flute and piano repertoire is immensely difficult. You would never know it from the way they performed. They began with a few brief By Joseph Gold The second wind is a phenomenon of sports. In addition, it can be a phenomenon of psychology. There are times when we need a second wind. Last week was a perfect example. Sometimes when exhaustion seems to overcome us, we are revitalized by something called the second wind. words and then got down to business. Their rendition of a Bach Sonata was eloquent. They were expressive when the music called for that and introspective when the music called for that aspect. These days musicians like to play loudly. What impressed me about the Blake/Underwood concert was their ability to play softly. Every once in a while, they used a very special musical technique called “Messa di voce” – a long note which begins very softly increasing in volume, and then ending softly again…all in a single breath. Most impressive! As the concert progressed, so did their artistry. I know that Dr. Blake had an active concert career in the past when he performed under the auspices of the State Department. William Underwood deserves an international career also. Busy weekend Many events crowded into Saturday’s schedule. It began with a musical demonstration-concert featuring Taiko drums. Many of the performers were very advanced in age. One is 92 years old… I should say 92 years young. Taiko drumming combines music with balletic movements. The drum ensemble was tireless. They also dressed in very colorful ethnic costumes. After the program, I spoke to the 92-year-old performer. She was not pleased with the performance, but no one in the audience realized it. After the concert my wife and I rushed over for a lovely Valentine’s lunch at Lavanta Greek restaurant in San Leandro. We really needed a second wind before attending the evening performance in Piedmont played by Richard Dowling. Dowling is another artist who deserves worldwide recognition. His biography is impressive but he is not a widely known concert artist in these parts. It was a perfect way to end Valentine’s Day. All of the music was intelligently chosen and ran the gamut from Chopin through Gershwin and Joplin. Every composition was preceded by a very amusing “spoken word”. Dowling is both a master pianist and a master of the spoken word. He keeps the speeches brief and amusing. There is humor in everything he says, and the information is …well… very informative. When he plays, the piano sings with a vocal freedom that tells a vivid story. Even though the concert concluded with a ragtime medley of pieces by Scott Joplin, Richard Dowling prepared the audience for an impressive knockout – with a wild encore. Ann is soon pregnant, gives birth in the forest to first-born Susanna (Bodhi Breathnach), the couple soon marry (sans ceremony), and find she is again pregnant. In a harrowing birth Agnes delivers not just a female child named Judith but a boy they call Hamnet. Eleven years pass. Judith and Hamnet (Olivia Lynes and Jacobi Jupe) have grown close. William has found success as a playwright and writes and directs his works in London. We watch him depart for the theater, embracing his family with affection while saying goodbye. And it is at this point the narrative takes an unexpected turn. What follows is a surreal, seemingly paranormal moment when Hamnet, who shares a loft bedroom with Judith, is unable to wake her. Finding he0r unresponsive he lies down next to his sister See Hamnet on page 28 Legends of the Fall worth seeing again Jessie Buckley and Paul Mescal in Hamnet Brad Pitt and Karina Lombard in Legends of the Fall By Chris Honoré Legends of the Fall is extraordinary. Nominated for three Oscars at the 67th Academy Awards, it is a sweeping family saga, set in the early 20th century, beautifully photographed using the stretching plains and snow-capped mountains of Montana as its backdrop and winning a gold statue for Best Cinematography. But what makes this film truly exceptional is its complex story, a compelling narrative based on the novella of the same name by Jim Harrison, and brackets love, war and tragedy. As well it is replete with a cast of consummate actors, each delivering exceptional performances. Brad Pitt stars as Tristan, the wild middle brother; Anthony Hopkins embraces the role of Col. William Ludlum, the patriarch; Aidan Quinn, portrays the oldest brother, Alfred; and Henry Thomas in the role of Samuel, the youngest. The story begins when Mr. and Mrs. Little (Hugh Laurie and Geena Davis) visit an orphanage where they meet and decide to adopt Stuart (Michael J. Fox). When they bring him home, he is not greeted all that warmly by the older son, George Little (Jonathan Lipki), who resents having a mouse for a brother. And there’s the family cat, Snowball (Nathan Lane), who takes one look at Stuart and views him as dinner. Clearly, things don’t get off to a good start for Stuart. George unintentionally throws him down the laundry chute along with the laundry. Mrs. Little manages to put him in the washing machine where Stuart swallows a mouthful of sudsy detergent. And thus begins Stuart’s adventure. He does end up bonding with George when he helps him win a remote-controlled sailboat race. articles.text: Ariana Grande and Cynthia Erivo in Wicked: For Good The second half of Universal’s ambitious adaptation of the Broadway phenomenon Wicked arrives with greater emotional weight and sharper political edges. Where last year’s first installment reveled in the spectacle of Shiz University and the effervescence of early friendship, Wicked: For Good steps into more complicated territory: betrayal, propaganda and the cost of choosing conscience over comfort. Directed again by Jon M. Chu and based on the stage musical by Stephen Schwartz and Winnie Holzman, the film completes the story of Elphaba and Glinda as the Wizard tightens his grip on Oz and dissent becomes dangerous. Cynthia Erivo deepens her portrayal of Elphaba, now fully embracing the mantle of the so-called Wicked Witch. Erivo’s performance is less about green makeup and flying broomsticks than about moral isolation. Her Elphaba is not defiant for sport but because she sees injustice and cannot look away. The film’s most powerful moments are quiet ones, when her resolve carries a cost visible only in her eyes. Opposite her, Ariana Grande gives Glinda unexpected complexity. In the first film, Glinda’s charm and comic timing dominated. Here, Grande allows doubt and ambition to coexist. Glinda is not a villain, but she is tempted by proximity to power. The tension between the two women becomes the emotional engine of the film, culminating in scenes that feel less like fantasy spectacle and more like a breakup between best friends who have chosen different futures. The supporting cast benefits from the darker tone. Jonathan Bailey brings steadier presence to Fiyero, no longer simply a romantic foil but a man forced to confront his own loyalties. pages.text: Wednesday, February 18, 2026 21 AMERICANS IN PARIS By Patricia Forsyth Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on January 22, 2020. Paris is the city for lovers. There’s undeniable romance wandering cobbled medieval streets ever branching to more crooked lanes, particularly in the Marais and Montmartre. Art is everywhere. A stroll along stately 19th c. boulevards is a delight of stunning shops and tony restaurants, where well-mannered staff and gastronomic foods await. It is never a bore. One may duck into any of the quaint shops where you are greeted by Madame or Monsieur who is happy to pleasantly engage. Partake in sidewalk café society and recharge with an afternoon espresso as you watch people go by – gaggles of people in the streets full of jaunty, hurried or ambling passersby in pairs clasping hands or arm-inarm. You’ll see parents clucking at toddlers, moms pushing tykes on scooters, youngsters on scooters sometimes in twos, in and out of slow walkers either elderly or lost and confused. These are the sidewalks of Love Locks No More Paris literally bursting with color and life. Through the ages, Parisians have trumpeted in design, art, culture, ideas, and science. Paris is itself a celebration of sorts, a leader in trends and cultural change. The remarkable architecture endures. This is a city of light, sky, and air, a city without skyscrapers. Parisian buildings may not be built taller than six stories. The French sensibility is embedded in art, movement, style, and perspective. “The historical ornately designed iron railings fell victim to too much love.” That is probably why Parisians strongly disliked it when tourists were placing sets of steel padlocks on bridge railings overlooking the Seine. The trend was spotted in Paris about 10 years ago; although the romance of locking hearts may date back to forlorn lovers during The Great Photo by Robbie Grant Close up glimpse on the pedestrian bridge Pont des Artes now known as the Lock Bridge and before the metal railings were removed for safety reasons. Two rail sections weighing 45 tons collapsed in 2015. Notre Dame Cathedral (left) is shown prior to April 2019 when a massive fire destroyed the roof and spire. In the foreground are padlocks on Pont de L’Archeveche (Bridge of the Archbishop). War (WWI) in Serbia. Couples on a visit to Paris would pledge a “forever love” sealed with a kiss, and intertwined a set of locks onto a railing and tossed the key into the Seine. Judging by sheer tonnage, the lovers were particularly attracted to footbridges in sight of Notre Dame Cathedral on Isle de la Cite. It wasn’t long before pedestrian bridge railings were groaning under the weight of literally hundreds of thousands of padlocks. Seemingly as quickly as teams of city workers armed with bolt cutters cleared the padlocks, the locks reappeared. The City of Paris was growing increasingly concerned about bridge safety, structural integrity and rail collapse. The Seine, a busy waterway for commerce and sightseeing barges, though not especially deep at 30 feet, was at very serious risk should a railing collapse from above. T he a e s t he t ic s a b out “adorned” bridge railings outraged Parisians who rallied around cries of disgraceful tourists defacing their beloved historical places: the masses of lovepadlocks. Then, in June 2015, two railing panels weighted down with 45 tons of locks fully buckled onto the pathway causing Pont des Artes to be evacuated and closed to pedestrians. Cue the full-throttle counter measures already underway in the lovelocks battle. The city’s Public Works department began to systematically remove the loaded-down railings and board up the missing rails with temporary wood panels for street art displays while permanent railings were fabricated. The historical ornately designed iron railings fell victim to too much love; and the railings are gone for good. In their place are thick plexiglas panels in flat metal frames that discourage padlocks. Paris being a socially conscious city put the million salvaged locks to good use for a scrap metal meltdown with proceeds to help humanitarian causes. articles.text: On past walks the group had walked the length of St. James Drive to Corpus Christi Catholic Church but had never gone inside the church or considered its history. St. James is a long, flat, easy-to-walk street. Going last Wednesday to the end of the street at Park Boulevard would reward the walkers with a tour of the church. However, when the walkers gather at the Exedra, the forecast had changed. Rain was to be coming early morning, but a group of over 40 walkers showed up, hoping for the best. The walkers went up Highland Avenue, past beautiful yellow daffodils and white azaleas at the top of Piedmont Park, to Sheridan, Wildwood, and Crocker Avenues, and Hampton Road to Hampton’s meeting with St. James Drive. St. James is seven tenths of a mile long to its end at Park Blvd. The group started their walk at the two white columns that mark one of the entrances to St. James Woods, a large, 1920s real estate neighborhood development. The walkers noted a very large, uprooted tree stump on a steep slope whose tree had obviously once blocked the street after a winter storm. There were also many lovely gardens in front yards. A mature cactus garden was especially appreciated. However, as they began walking a light rain started to come down. Some walkers decided to go back after the rain started, but over 30 walkers made it to Corpus Christi’s lower driveway where Father Leo Edgerly came out to greet them. Some church history was shared. The Corpus Christi Parish was founded in 1929 as part of what was then the archdiocese of San Francisco. Reverend Francis D. Ahern was appointed pastor effective November 4, 1929. He formally opened the parish on Sunday, November 24, when he celebrated the church’s first Mass. The new parish first operated from a rented cottage at 222 St. James Drive, which doesn’t exist today. In 1930 the archdiocese purchased the property at St. James Drive and Park Boulevard for the construction of a combined church and rectory that started in September of that year. On Sunday, January 11, 1931, Archbishop Hanna blessed the new church that seated 160 parishioners and the rectory. In November 1933, Father Edwin J. Keller began his three-decade tenure as pastor of the Corpus Christi Parish. There were then 250 families in the parish and Father Keller immediately began planning for the construction of the present-day church. The new church was dedicated on Sunday, March 8, 1936. The church building is often thought to represent California Mission architecture but it is actually based on the ecclesiastical architecture of the hills in Piemonte, Italy in the 10th Century. Shortly after the church’s completion, a parishioner commissioned Ansel Adams to photograph it. The parish continued to flourish and opened the Corpus Christi School in September 1956. It has a K-8 student body and is the fourth elementary school in Piedmont. In 1962, the church was renovated and extended by 55 feet, doubling its size. It now has a seating capacity of 1,000 parishioners. Construction of a new rectory commenced in August 1966 and was completed in May 1967. In 1997, the City of Piedmont required a seismic retrofit of the church building and pastor Father Albano Oliveira developed a master plan for the church. It included the renovation and improvement of the church building, an activity building, and improvements to the school. In June 1997, the parishioners moved to the school auditorium, where masses were celebrated until December when they were able to return to the church. The finished church was dedicated on Sunday, March 29, 1998. Between June and December of 1998, the church’s Gibson Center and Plaza were constructed next to the church, completing the master plan. Father Oliveira officially opened the center on December 27. However, to everyone’s sorrow, he died unexpectedly two days later. Father Leo Edgerly was appointed pastor in 1999. Twenty-seven years ago he summarized the church’s history in a single sentence, “They sowed the seeds; we reap the benefits.” Father Leo invited the walkers to come into the church where they sat in pews as he shared information about the church. He said the reason the church is on Piedmont’s border with Oakland border is that the city’s Among those who made it to Park Boulevard and Corpus Christi Church last Wednesday were Bill Ahern, Jasmine Cai, Jim Kuo, Dan Scdonis, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Vicki Trimbach, Judy Sokoloff, Joyce Ahern, Cathy Laymon, Mark Davis, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Chuck Oraftik, Jim Kellogg, Denny McGee, Mike Gallant, Judy Love, Claudine Bach, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Abha Kothari, Max Becker, Albert Chen, Sherry Jacobs, Mary Carter, Michelle Yang, Melba Yee, Peggy Shultz, Audrey Sung, Lori Austin, Rick Eigenbrode, Noemi Alvarado, and Dick Carter.

articles.text: Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on September 29, 2021. In my experience, the most difficult part of painting buildings is not finding the painting contractor, not the scraping, sanding or surface preparation, not dealing with the mess. The most difficult part is the selection of colors. Maybe this is because like most aspects of the architectural field, color selection is a curious mix of art and science, and…we A variation on the classical color wheel fashioned by Sir Isaac Newton in 1666 that we all learned in grammar school. Although modern physics reveals variants on the principles involved, they still hold true when mixing paint. Colorists continue to use the color wheel to determine harmonious color combinations. all experience colors differently. Balancing the main color attributes of hue (color: red, blue, etc.), intensity (saturation or purity), and value (lightness/ darkness i.e., tints/shades) with other associated variables is simply a difficult job. In the end, from the bold, emotion-evoking colors of Mexican architects such as the famous Luis Barragan, to the restrained, subtle colors we are most familiar with in the Bay Area, exterior colors on a building reveal, perhaps more than anything else, the attitudes, ideas and personality of the owners. Building colors should first respond to the character, style, and detailing of the architecture. Schemes with multiple colors require a natural stopping/starting point for color changes such as a different material or corners and offsets in wall planes. Certain interior colors need also be coordinated, most notably curtains and shades which are seen through the windows and have to work with the exterior colors. Because all urban buildings are surrounded by neighboring buildings, as well as landscape planting, paving, and other elements, exterior color selection necessarily also involves urban design considerations; each building is part of a larger neighborhood palate. Evaluation of color requires certain steps to be successful. Most importantly, although not nearly done often enough, is to allow enough time for color selection and approval before painting starts. Once an attitude and concept is settled upon, selection begins with little paint chips – only the first step. Many architectural offices specify that large (100 sf) samples then be painted on at least two different walls of the building with different natural light conditions. These must be allowed to dry for at least a few days before being evaluated. It is good for owners to then reflect on the samples at different times of the day for a good week before modifications are made or final approval given. Using somewhat similar colors, these two homes, after creative responses to the different architecture detailing, result in a very different feeling – both terrific! Many times, it is difficult to describe exactly why a color scheme is so attractive. But the important thing is to simply recognize it as good, and to know that you like it.

articles.text: Is your furry friend feeling a little off? Diarrhea and vomiting are common stressors for pet owners because our beloved canine companions tend to explore the world with their mouths. Digestive problems can be challenging for both dogs and their owners, but a few tips and tricks on what to feed and when can go a long way. First, it can help your dog a great deal if you withhold food for a couple hours after they have had an episode of vomiting or diarrhea. This allows the stomach to stabilize. Make sure plenty of water is available if the dog is thirsty, as digestive issues are often accompanied by dehydration. For dogs with mild stomach issues, veterinarians often recommend a “bland diet.” Many owners have heard this term but are unaware of the wide range of options on it. Rice is a classic soothing food; it is easy on the stomach and can help firm up stool. Boiled chicken breast is another great option, providing lean protein that’s gentle on the digestive system. Many owners will combine chicken and rice for a few days until symptoms improve. But these aren’t the only options. Scrambled eggs (with no seasoning) are also a good choice, offering another easily digestible protein source. Further, plain pasta is a simple carb dogs can enjoy which is easy on the tummy. To add some extra hydration or to tempt a dog who finds their very plain diet unappetizing, consider adding low-sodium chicken broth. A tablespoon or two of plain Greek yogurt can also go a long way, providing probiotics to support gut health. If your dog is particularly ill, feed these new band diet options in small freScooter the Great Dane checks out his bowl, eager to feel better on the bland diet. quent meals to ease digestion. Although not strictly on the bland diet, adding some plain canned pumpkin to your pup’s food can assist with necessary fiber to ease digestion. This is a good option for dogs who have ongoing issues with stool that is too firm or too soft, but who are not sick. If your dog has a pre-existing health condition, such as kidney disease, it is crucial to consult with your veterinarian before making any changes to their diet. These dogs may require a special diet, such as restricted protein, and sudden changes can be harmful. For dogs on prescription diet, it is often best to continue this diet to avoid tummy upset from sudden changes. If your dog’s symptoms persist or worsen after a couple days on the bland diet, consult with your vet to rule out underlying issues. With a little patience and the right foods, your pup should be back to their playful self in no time. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. articles.text: Frederic Vignobles On a sunny afternoon in the Pacific Northwest, the ferry ride from Seattle to Bainbridge Island offers stunning views of the snowcapped Olympic mountains to the west and majestic Mount Ranier to the southeast. The crossing of the Puget Sound takes about a half hour, and it’s a short walk to the quaint main street. After perusing the local bookstore and small shops, one can stop in the downtown tasting room that pours some of the wines of the Eagle Harbor Wine Co. For a richer experience we recommend making the short drive to the winery located on what used to be a Christmas tree farm. It’s in a contemporary light industrial building adjacent to a distillery, a sculptor’s gallery, and the Bainbridge Island’s artist cooperative known as BARN. Most days, you can taste a full range of wines, tour the facility, and often have the chance to speak with the folks making the wine. Eagle Harbor Wine Co. is owned and operated by Emily Parsons, who grew up drinking European wines. Like many of us, she embraces the “wine is food” and “good wine is part of a good life” philosophy. Unlike most of us, she went on mid-career to pursue studies through UC Davis, apprentice with founding Eagle Harbor winemaker Hugh Remash, and, a dozen years ago, purchasing the winery outright. Her vision was to meld the high-quality fruit grown in eastern Washington with carefully selected oak barrels from single forests in France and a minimalist approach to winemaking that respects the intrinsic qualities of the grapes. Early on, she emphasized Bordeaux varietals and blends, and in more recent years has broadened the offering as more high-quality varietals are available within the state. We tasted virtually the full range of Eagle Harbor wines and selected five that we particularly enjoyed. Available through the winery at www.eagleharbor.wine. • 2024 Eagle Harbor Viognier, $30 Viognier is a white varietal from the northern Rhone in France, known for its bouquet. The Eagle Harbor Viognier opens with hints of spring blossoms, gingery spice, pineapple and apricot. Medium-bodied, it’s plump and rounded, with a silky texture and a long tropical fruit-tinged finish. Viognier is a difficult varietal to grow, and this wine shows off the region as a promising place for the grape. • 2019 Eagle Harbor Condor, $45 This is a left bank Bordeaux blend consisting of 50% Cabernet Sauvignon, 35% Merlot and 15% Hugh Remash founder and consulting winemaker with Emily Parsons

Recent scholarship reveals that, by the final years of his life, Manet increasingly followed Morisot’s example — her choice of subjects and colors, and even her rapid, fluttering brushstrokes. Rich in new research, the exhibition recasts this celebrated artistic friendship and, by extension, the story of modern art. Also on display was an extraordinary Auguste Rodin collection. Approximately 50 objects in bronze, marble, and plaster — all from the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s permanent collection — are being presented in a new context as the exhibition examines the artist’s influential work and his celebrated life, from his early days courting controversy with sculptures that bore unexpected levels of naturalism, to his later prestige and lasting influence. Each of the Piedmont Seniors was given an audio tape so that they could each explore throughout the museum at their own pace and have the background and history of the art pieces narrated to them. pages.text: 26 26 Wednesday, February 18, 2026 Seniors By Janet Epstein The Piedmont Seniors recently ventured to San Francisco on a misty and slightly rainy day to visit the Legion of Honor Museum, located in Lincoln Park. It was founded in 1924, and was opened to the public on Armistice Day, November 11, 1924, in dedication to the memory of the 3,600 Californians who perished in World War I. On display was the first major exhibition dedicated to the artistic exchange between French Impressionists Edouard Manet (1832-1883) and Berthe Morisot (1841-1895). Manet was the era’s great pioneer of modern painting, and Morisot, the only woman to exhibit under her own name in the original Impressionist group. Unfolding over a period of 15 years (1868–1883), this exhibition traces the evolution of a friendship between two groundbreaking artists. The story of their relationship has often been told through Manet’s early portraits of Morisot, with Morisot’s own work treated as an offshoot Piedmont Seniors visit Legion of Honor in SF of Manet’s. Recent scholarship reveals that, by the final years of his life, Manet increasingly followed Morisot’s example — her choice of subjects and colors, and even her rapid, fluttering brushstrokes. Rich in new research, the exhibition recasts this celebrated artistic friendship and, by extension, the story of modern art. Also on display was an extraordinary Auguste Rodin collection. Approximately 50 objects in bronze, marble, and plaster — all from the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco’s permanent collection — are being presented in a new context as the exhibition examines the artist’s influential work and his celebrated life, from his early days courting controversy with sculptures that bore unexpected levels of naturalism, to his later prestige and lasting influence. Each of the Piedmont Seniors was given an audio tape so that they could each explore throughout the museum at their own pace and have the background and history of the art pieces narrated to them. articles.text: Last month I wrote about my friend Jackie. This is part two of her story, still unfolding in real time. I wish I could tell tell you everything turned out smoothly. I can’t. Like many life transitions, this one has been layered, emotional and far more complicated than anyone expected. After years of thinking about it, Jackie made the move to Merrill Gardens. Leaving her home of 35 years was no small decision, but the stairs had become too much. I constantly worried about her falling. She lived alone and rarely had visitors. Something had to change. Still, choosing a senior community meant more than a new address. It meant being surrounded by people after a lifetime of independence and solitude. Jackie is a bit of a loner, so this was going to take adjustment. The move itself was stressful, but the real hurdle came after the boxes arrived. Unpacking became overwhelming. Finding a place for everything felt impossible to her, and she would not accept help. Not even putting away a single plate, because then she “wouldn’t know where it was.” A plate. A stapler. Toilet paper. Five months later, she still isn’t settled. Both her financial planner, who had recently moved his own mother, and I offered professional organizers. She refused. Pride, fear, control. It’s rarely just one thing. Then, about a month ago, Jackie fell. She landed in the emergency room. After a short stay, she was sent back to her apartment, though it was clear she couldn’t safely manage on her own. Getting to the bathroom, managing medications, arranging meals. All of it was too much. Somehow, she ended up back in the ER again. I’m still unclear on the details, but it seemed like the only way to trigger the next level of care. Kaiser transferred her to an assisted living facility, where she remained mostly bedridden. I’m her friend, not family or an official advocate, but I could see things weren’t right. I asked a nurse about physical therapy. “She’s getting it daily,” they told me. Jackie said she wasn’t. That disconnect became the norm. “That’s not true,” she’d say. It became hard to know what was accurate and what wasn’t. Jackie has since returned to her independent living community, but she is no longer independent. She needs assistance now. And this is where we are today: facing the reality of care needs, resistance to help, and the very real concern about cost. We plan for college. We plan vacations. We make lists for holiday meals. But do we truly plan for aging? For the day errands become exhausting. When driving feels unsafe? When managing medications gets confusing? Ask yourself: • Will I keep my car? • How will I get to the bank? • Who will pick up prescriptions? • How will I get to doctor’s appointments? • Who will help with taxes, bills, laundry and meals? • Do loved ones know my passwords and how to access medical information? • The list goes on. Tasks that once felt simple can quickly become overwhelming. Often, these transitions happen suddenly. A fall. An illness. A moment that changes everything. Please start the conversation now, while you’re healthy and clear-minded. It’s one of the greatest gifts you can give your family and yourself. A lifetime of memories, belongings and decisions doesn’t sort itself out in a crisis. Just as we use professionals to plan travel or manage finances, there are caregivers, advocates, organizers and senior service experts ready to help with this stage of life. Planning is the key to making an emotional transition as smooth as possible. It’s never too early to begin. And one day, you’ll be grateful you did. Debbi DiMaggio, SRES, Senior Real Estate Specialist Real Estate Advisor | Author | Podcast Host Mastering the Art of Success

articles.text: It is intended to be a time of repentance, prayer, fasting, self-discipline, charity and giving. Many people give up something for Lent, like cookies or beer. There are charming stories of children – not quite clear on the concept – saying they will give up making their beds or eating Brussels sprouts. Lent begins on Ash Wednesday, which falls 40 days before Easter. In many places, the day before Ash Wednesday is a day of feasting and partying before the more sober period of Lent begins. It is called Mardi Gras, Carnival or Fat Tuesday. On Ash Wednesday, Christians go to church and receive ashes on their foreheads in the shape of a cross, symbolizing mortality, repentance and a time of spiritual reflection; some fast that day or abstain from eating meat. The last week of Lent is Holy Week, which includes Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday, Good Friday and Easter Sunday. You are invited to learn more and to worship at Piedmont Church Sundays at 10am, in person or online. Christians receive ashes on their foreheads on Ash Wednesday to symbolize death, repentance and a desire to live in Christ’s image. Unlike Christmas, which is always on December 25, Easter – the most important celebration in Christianity – falls between March 22 and April 25. The actual date each year is determined by solar and lunar timing as it is the first Sunday after the first full moon that occurs on or after the March 21st Spring equinox. This formula was established by the Council of Nicea (AD 325) and ties loosely to Jewish Passover, since that is when scripture says the crucifixion and resurrection occurred. Lent is a 40-day period of preparation leading up to Easter. The 40 days reflects the 40 days that Jesus spent in the wilderness before beginning his ministry. 2026 LENTEN SERVICES Ash Wednesday tonight at 7pm Palm Sunday, March 29 at 10am Maundy Thursday, April 2 at 6pm Good Friday, April 3 at 7:30pm Easter Sunday, April 5 at 8:30 and 10am

articles.text: At its February 2 meeting, the City Council unanimously adopted revised Objective Design Standards that will govern new housing construction in Piedmont. The standards update existing rules for ADUs, mixed-use projects and multifamily development. City staff said the revisions clarify language and remove ambiguity, based on staff review and community feedback. “We’ve reviewed it several times, from staff internally to the city attorney’s office, the subcommittee and planning commissioners, to make sure the standards are measurable and that we’ve removed subjectivity,” said Planning and Building Director Kevin Jackson at the meeting. The City received 241 responses to public surveys seeking input on which standards mattered most to residents. The most common concerns centered on neighborhood character, including tree canopy and landscaping (65%), building height and massing (61%), and spacing between homes (54%). Jackson said staff and the city attorney spent about two and a half hours reviewing public comments to determine whether changes were needed. “The comments provided additional clarity and wordsmithing to standards that were already in place,” he said. After about 18 months of development, the Objective Design Standards establish clear, measurable and enforceable rules for design elements such as articulation and massing, aiming to give residents, property owners and developers consistent expectations for new housing in Piedmont. Objective Design Standards cover open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm
articles.title: City Council adopts revised Objective Design Standards

articles.text: Piedmont’s Park Commission met on Wednesday, February 4, to review the findings of the Sustainable Park Management Plan. Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent and WRT consultants delivered a presentation to the Commission summarizing their work so far, what they heard from the community at various pop-up events, and insights from an online survey. The project’s engagement efforts received 580 responses, with 82% of respondents being Piedmont residents. They found that most respondents use the parks for exercise (65%), walk their dogs in off-leash areas (61%), and to socialize (50%). The community was asked about their values for the parks, and the top two results were offleash dog areas (51%) and natural beauty (50%). Sixty-five percent of respondents strongly support the management of dog areas. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, February 11, 2026 Local Items City Council adopts revised Objective Design Standards By Jake Lannon At its February 2 meeting, the City Council unanimously adopted revised Objective Design Standards that will govern new housing construction in Piedmont. The standards update existing rules for ADUs, mixed-use projects and multifamily development. City staff said the revisions clarify language and remove ambiguity, based on staff review and community feedback. “We’ve reviewed it several times, from staff internally to the city attorney’s office, the subcommittee and planning commissioners, to make sure the standards are measurable and that we’ve removed subjectivity,” said Planning and Building Director Kevin Jackson at the meeting. The City received 241 responses to public surveys seeking input on which standards mattered most to residents. The most common concerns centered on neighborhood character, including tree canopy and landscaping (65%), building height and massing (61%), and spacing between homes (54%). Jackson said staff and the city attorney spent about two and a half hours reviewing public comments to determine whether changes were needed. “The comments provided additional clarity and wordsmithing to standards that were already in place,” he said. After about 18 months of development, the Objective Design Standards establish clear, measurable and enforceable rules for design elements such as articulation and massing, aiming to give residents, property owners and developers consistent expectations for new housing in Piedmont. Park Commission discusses Sustainable Park Management Plan findings By Jake Lannon Piedmont’s Park Commission met on Wednesday, February 4, to review the findings of the Sustainable Park Management Plan. Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent and WRT consultants delivered a presentation to the Commission summarizing their work so far, what they heard from the community at various pop-up events, and insights from an online survey. The project’s engagement efforts received 580 responses, with 82% of respondents being Piedmont residents. They found that most respondents use the parks for exercise (65%), walk their dogs in off-leash areas (61%), and to socialize (50%). The community was asked about their values for the parks, and the top two results were offleash dog areas (51%) and natural beauty (50%). Sixty-five percent of respondents strongly support the management of dog areas. During the public forum period after the presentation, multiple residents shared their thoughts on off-leash dog areas, emphasizing their importance to the community. When asked what they hope will still be true in 20 years, respondents emphasized: • Preservation of natural beauty, trees, and the parks’ essential character • Continued high standards of maintenance and care • Parks remain fundamentally as they are today • Continued access to off-leash dog areas • Spaces that serve children and future generations The project team will continue their work, considering the Commissioner’s comments as they refine the recommendations. They’ll return to the Commission to share the changes made to the Sustainable Park Management Plan this spring. articles.text: Every spring Piedmont Scout Council’s five troops open their doors to families interested in the scouting program. Open house meetings are an opportunity for kids and their parents to visit a specific scout troop, meet youth and adult leadership, and learn about that troop’s unique brand of scouting. Troops also share recent and upcoming activities. In advance of the open houses the Council is hosting informational sessions this week. These sessions will explain the basics of the scouting program, talk about what scouting looks like in Piedmont, assist in deciding which troop to visit, and provide a safe space to have your questions about scouting answered. Scouting is a time-honored tradition in the community of Piedmont where 20 percent of Piedmont youth are involved. Scouting provides youth with hands-on leadership experiences and allows them to practice life skills while serving their community. It instills citizenship and character, fosters communication, and builds a self-reliance in youth as they organize events and take on challenges together. For more information contact Piedmont Council’s Program Coordinator Eris Turner: eturner@piedmontbsa.org – (510) 844- 4752

articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff: Our high school athletic programs are a point of deep pride for our community and for me personally. We are fortunate to have extraordinary student athletes who compete with heart, coaches who model leadership and integrity, and administrators who work hard to ensure that every event is safe and well-run. At the same time, sportsmanship extends beyond the players on the court; it includes the conduct of our fans. The energy of our student sections can be one of the most joyful parts of high school athletics, but we also recognize that we have important work to do in developing consistently positive approaches to student fan behavior. School spirit should encourage our team while showing respect for opponents, officials, and visiting families. I will be hosting a community meeting on February 26 at 4:30 p.m. at the District Office Board Room to discuss sportsmanship and spectator conduct, and I welcome your partnership in this important conversation. I also want to express my deep gratitude to our staff during what has, at times, felt like a chaotic stretch. Thank you to Ben Spencer, Shamaree Worley, all of our Basketball coaches, David Yoshihara, and especially Tyler Small for their remarkable leadership and steady presence in keeping our players and students safe during Friday night’s basketball game. Their professionalism and care reflect the very best of our district. If you have a moment, I encourage you to view the Instagram post of our players “taking a stand” against poor spectator behavior. It is a strong reminder that our students are capable of leading the way in creating a climate of respect. Together, we can ensure that our athletic events reflect not just competitive excellence, but the fine character that defines our community. In Community, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Previous recipients include: Hunter McCreary (1998); Ann Chandler (1999); Ruth Cuming (2000); Lisa Lomenzo (2001); jointly by Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002); jointly by Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003); Elizabeth (Betsy) Gentry (2004); Cynthia Gorman (2005); Grier Graff (2006); Julia Burke (2007); Maude Pervere (2008); jointly to Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009); Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010); Andrea Swenson (2011), June Monach (2012), Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013), Ray Perman (2014), Jennifer Fox (2015), Katie Korotzer (2016), Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018), Cathy Glazier (2019), Sue Smegal (2020), Ken Li (2021), Eileen Ruby (2022), David Ragones (2023), Sarah Pearson (2024) and most recently, Cory Smegal in 2025. Art Hecht was a tireless community volunteer, and was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1982. Art also was very active with the Piedmont Continuation High School (now called Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established in his memory. Nominations for this award are now being sought and will be kept strictly confidential. The deadline for nominations is March 13, 2026. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 6, 2026, Board of Education meeting, where the honoree’s good works will be acknowledged. Curling ice is bumpy, mimicking ice that forms naturally in the outdoors, which increases friction as the stone slides across it. Team members use “brooms” to frantically sweep (polish) the ice to speed up or curl (alter the trajectory of) the stone towards the house. Scouts on the ice after the end of the lesson. The team leader, the skip, directs the team members in aiming the stone and sweeping the ice. After a short lesson the Scouts assembled into teams to face each other on the ice. articles.text: We live in a world that rewards constant expansion. Add more contacts, engage in more conversations, expand your reach! So, when connection feels thin, it’s easy to assume the answer is that you aren’t doing enough. You need to add more people and make more of an effort to “enhance your network.” But I’ve been noticing something else, most of us already have people in our lives we like and trust. There are plenty of people we see or talk to regularly. And still, the connection can feel flat, not because anything is specifically wrong, but because it stays on the surface. We check in, exchange updates, smile and move on. I’ve been wondering what might happen if, instead of reaching wider, we went just a little deeper. Not in a big, huge dramatic way. Just a small shift in how we show up to every opportunity to engage. Asking a follow-up question and actually waiting for the answer. Sharing one honest detail instead of a polished summary. Letting a conversation linger thirty seconds longer than usual instead of rushing to wrap it up. Taking the time to really notice what’s behind someone’s eyes. Here’s a simple way to try it: the next time someone asks, “How are you?” pause before giving your default answer. Say one thing that’s actually true, even if it’s small. Or, if you’re the one asking the question, pick one person you already know and ask a second question, like “What’s been taking up a lot of your energy lately?” and then listen. Don’t interrupt, don’t fix, and don’t hurry them along. When you do this, something subtle often changes because the pace has to slow. The interaction can feel less transactional. There’s a moment where you can feel the connection deepen. And it’s not because you said something deep and profound, but because you stayed present a beat longer than usual. What I like about this experiment is that depth doesn’t require intensity. It doesn’t ask for oversharing or emotional excavation. It just asks for you to choose to pay attention. You might try this once or twice this week with someone who’s already in your life. It doesn’t have to be someone impressive, just someone familiar who you genuinely want to connect with. We don’t always need to widen our circles to feel more connected. Sometimes we just need to meet the people we already have a little more fully. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Connection experiment: going deeper instead of wider

articles.text: 2nd victory of season vs. Roseville-based team Staff Photos Piedmont is one step closer toward an NCS Open Division berth. They close the regular season at Bishop O’Dowd on February 12. Alexa Ba hit the tying basket to force overtime against Antelope, and scored the eventual go-ahead points in overtime. Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team continued its stellar play, beating Antelope in Roseville 61-56 on Saturday, February 7. They also bashed San Leandro 64-15 on Monday, February 9 at the Pirates’ gym, improving their record to 17-3 overall with just two games left in the regular season. The Highlanders’ win over Antelope marked their second victory over the school this season after beating the Titans 57-37 on January 24. Antelope is currently the No. 3 team in the San Joaquin Section and No. 33 team in California. PHS, meanwhile, is No. 17 in the state and No. 3 in North Coast Section. “Antelope made 11 threes. We held on and got the win, but it was a tough game. It was gut-checking,” coach Bryan Gardere said. Their win over the Titans came in overtime. Piedmont trailed by eight points in the fourth quarter and were down 52-47 with 1:22 left in the game. That’s when sophomore Jaden Jones hit a critical 3-pointer with one minute left to make it a 52-50 deficit. After a defensive stop, Alexa Ba hit a floater with 25 seconds remaining to tie it up at 52-52. In overtime, PHS’ defense stood stout by allowing just four points. “We started chipping away with four minutes left and forced overtime. We locked in defensively and stopped turning the ball over. Second-half, we tightened up,” Gardere said. Saniyah Johnson returned from her injury, leaving Piedmont patiently waiting for point guard Jenelle Solis to get back as well. PHS will face O’Dowd in the season-finale on February 12, and the two sides could meet once again in the North Coast Section Open Division if Piedmont and BOD keep the No. 3 and No. 4 seeds respectively. The Open Division first round is set for Thursday, February 19. “We’re still a bit shorthanded, Jenelle coming back changes a lot of things for us. Everyone is getting experience and live reps, but we need someone who is arguably a top three point guard in the state,” Gardere said. 61-56 win over Antelope Piedmont led 16-9 through the first quarter and 26-21 by halftime. Antelope battled back to take a 41-37 lead in the third quarter and led by eight, 49-41, with 4:34 left in the fourth quarter. From there, Piedmont went on a 6-0 run to make it a 49-47 deficit after a free throw by Andrea Martin, a 3-pointer by Ba, and a layup by Martin. Antelope hit a 3-pointer with 1:22 left, 52-47. That’s when Savannah Dennig found Jones left unmarked beyond the arch, hitting an important 3-pointer to make it 52-50 with one minute remaining. After a defensive stop with 39 seconds left, Ba hit a running floater off the backboard to knot it up at 52-52 with 25 seconds remaining. A final heave by Antelope clanged off the rim. In overtime, Dennig found Jaden Jones, a sophomore, hit an important 3-pointer in the fourth quarter against Antelope to help force overtime. Martin driving to the rim on a nifty behind the back bounce pass, leading to the go-ahead layup 12 seconds in with 3:48 left. Antelope tied it 54-54 on its next possession. Ba grabbed an offensive rebound after Jones missed a 3-pointer, leading to a put-back basket, 56-54 with 2:44 left. A defensive stop led to Taylor White grabbing an offensive board and drawing a foul to hit both free throws, 58-54 with 1:57 to go. Antelope made its last basket with 1:43 remaining, leading to a long Piedmont possession that finished with Martin hitting a running shot in the paint with 55 seconds left. After White grabbed a rebound on a failed 3-pointer, Antelope fouled to send her to the line—hitting Piedmont’s last free throw, 61-56. Final stats: Martin had 23 points, 12 rebounds, two assists, and four steals. Ba had 15 points, eight rebounds. Dennig had nine points, nine rebounds, and four assists. White had seven points, 12 rebounds, four assists, and two steals. Johnson had four points, 10 rebounds, and a steal. Jones had three points, one rebound. 64-15 blowout over San Leandro Piedmont led 13-0 through the first quarter and didn’t allow a point until the 7:40 mark in the second quarter. PHS extended the lead to 25-7 in the second quarter, 48-11 in the third, and added 16 more points in the fourth. Final stats: Martin had 21 points, Dennig and Ba had 15 points, Johnson had six points, Jones had three points, and Nia Jackson scored one. Tuesday vs. Alameda Piedmont visited Alameda on Tuesday, February 10. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (17-3 overall, 4-0 league) visits Bishop O’Dowd tomorrow, February 12, at 6:30 p.m.
articles.title: Highlanders win a thriller against Antelope

articles.text: Big week includes win vs. Berkeley In a monumental week for Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team. The Highlanders , avenged two losses against Western Alameda County Conference foes. Piedmont first defeated Bishop O’Dowd 64-62 on Wednesday, February 4 inside a closeddoor game with no spectators at Binks Rawlings Gym. They also defeated Berkeley 61-52 at the Yellowjackets’ home on Friday, February 6. Walking into Wednesday’s game against O’Dowd, Piedmont’s season was at a crossroads after the incident against San Leandro, where a brawl spilled out onto the court that made the KTVU news. As a response, PHS and Bishop O’Dowd condemned poor fan behavior and elected to play the game with no spectators. “It’s been a helluva week, I couldn’t be more proud of this team,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. “The reliance and urgency they’ve shown over the last seven days has been phenomenal. After the San Leandro incident, I told the boys this could be a breaking point in the season, where we can come together and play our best basketball. You find out who you are when things are going bad,” coach Ben Spencer said. The incident is serving as a rallying point for Piedmont, building a sense of camaraderie amongst the group after what could’ve been a destructive moment. It culminated in the school’s first victory over the Dragons since 2016 and avenges a mid-January 63-56 loss to Berkeley. “To beat O’Dowd for the first time in 10 years and get a bounceback win over Berkeley is a testament to our team. One thing we talked about is how you respond to adversity. You have to put your head down and go to work,” senior guard Dillon Casey said. Piedmont had to play critical defense in the fourth quarter of both games, limiting both the Dragons and Yellowjackets to nine points. Their win over Bishop O’Dowd featured a critical block by P.J. pages.text: 12 Wednesday, February 11, 2026 Sports PHS boys beat O’Dowd for first time in 10 years Big week includes win vs. Berkeley By Jonathan Comeaux In a monumental week for Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team. The Highlanders , avenged two losses against Western Alameda County Conference foes. Piedmont first defeated Bishop O’Dowd 64-62 on Wednesday, February 4 inside a closeddoor game with no spectators at Binks Rawlings Gym. They also defeated Berkeley 61-52 at the Yellowjackets’ home on Friday, February 6. Walking into Wednesday’s game against O’Dowd, Piedmont’s season was at a crossroads after the incident against San Leandro, where a brawl spilled out onto the court that made the KTVU news. As a response, PHS and Bishop O’Dowd condemned poor fan behavior and elected to play the game with no spectators. “It’s been a helluva week, I couldn’t be more proud of this team,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. “The reliance and urgency they’ve shown over the last seven days has been phenomenal. After the San Leandro incident, I told the boys this could be a breaking point in the season, where we can come together and play our best basketball. You find out who you are when things are going bad,” coach Ben Spencer said. The incident is serving as a rallying point for Piedmont, building a sense of camaraderie amongst the group after what could’ve been a destructive moment. Highlanders win a thriller against Antelope 2nd victory of season vs. Roseville-based team By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team continued its stellar play, beating Antelope in Roseville 61-56 on Saturday, February 7. They also bashed San Leandro 64-15 on Monday, February 9 at the Pirates’ gym, improving their record to 17-3 overall with just two games left in the regular season. The Highlanders’ win over Antelope marked their second victory over the school this season after beating the Titans 57-37 on January 24. Antelope is currently the No. 3 team in the San Joaquin Section and No. 33 team in California. PHS, meanwhile, is No. 17 in the state and No. 3 in North Coast Section. “Antelope made 11 threes. We held on and got the win, but it was a tough game. It was gut-checking,” coach Bryan Gardere said. Their win over the Titans came in overtime. Piedmont trailed by eight points in the fourth quarter and were down 52-47 with 1:22 left in the game. That’s when sophomore Jaden Jones hit a critical 3-pointer with one minute left to make it a 52-50 deficit. After a defensive stop, Alexa Ba hit a floater with 25 seconds remaining to tie it up at 52-52. In overtime, PHS’ defense stood stout by allowing just four points. “We started chipping away with four minutes left and forced overtime. We locked in defensively and stopped turning the ball over. Second-half, we tightened up,” Gardere said. Saniyah Johnson returned from her injury, leaving Piedmont patiently waiting for point guard Jenelle Solis to get back as well. PHS will face O’Dowd in the season-finale on February 12, and the two sides could meet once again in the North Coast Section Open Division if Piedmont and BOD keep the No. 3 and No. 4 seeds respectively. The Open Division first round is set for Thursday, February 19. “We’re still a bit shorthanded, Jenelle coming back changes a lot of things for us. Everyone is getting experience and live reps, but we need someone who is arguably a top three point guard in the state,” Gardere said. 61-56 win over Antelope Piedmont led 16-9 through the first quarter and 26-21 by halftime. Antelope battled back to take a 41-37 lead in the third quarter and led by eight, 49-41, with 4:34 left in the fourth quarter. From there, Piedmont went on a 6-0 run to make it a 49-47 deficit after a free throw by Andrea Martin, a 3-pointer by Ba, and a layup by Martin. Antelope hit a 3-pointer with 1:22 left, 52-47. That’s when Savannah Dennig found Jones left unmarked beyond the arch, hitting an important 3-pointer to make it 52-50 with one minute remaining. After a defensive stop with 39 seconds left, Ba hit a running floater off the backboard to knot it up at 52-52 with 25 seconds remaining. A final heave by Antelope clanged off the rim. In overtime, Dennig found Jaden Jones, a sophomore, hit an important 3-pointer in the fourth quarter against Antelope to help force overtime. Martin driving to the rim on a nifty behind the back bounce pass, leading to the go-ahead layup 12 seconds in with 3:48 left. Antelope tied it 54-54 on its next possession. Ba grabbed an offensive rebound after Jones missed a 3-pointer, leading to a put-back basket, 56-54 with 2:44 left. A defensive stop led to Taylor White grabbing an offensive board and drawing a foul to hit both free throws, 58-54 with 1:57 to go. Antelope made its last basket with 1:43 remaining, leading to a long Piedmont possession that finished with Martin hitting a running shot in the paint with 55 seconds left. After White grabbed a rebound on a failed 3-pointer, Antelope fouled to send her to the line—hitting Piedmont’s last free throw, 61-56. Final stats: Martin had 23 points, 12 rebounds, two assists, and four steals. Ba had 15 points, eight rebounds. Dennig had nine points, nine rebounds, and four assists. White had seven points, 12 rebounds, four assists, and two steals. Johnson had four points, 10 rebounds, and a steal. Jones had three points, one rebound. 64-15 blowout over San Leandro Piedmont led 13-0 through the first quarter and didn’t allow a point until the 7:40 mark in the second quarter. PHS extended the lead to 25-7 in the second quarter, 48-11 in the third, and added 16 more points in the fourth. Final stats: Martin had 21 points, Dennig and Ba had 15 points, Johnson had six points, Jones had three points, and Nia Jackson scored one. Tuesday vs. Alameda Piedmont visited Alameda on Tuesday, February 10. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (17-3 overall, 4-0 league) visits Bishop O’Dowd tomorrow, February 12, at 6:30 p.m.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Stanford Athletics Claire Dean, PHS Class of 2022, is a senior on Stanford’s gymnastics team. In this week’s edition of Piedmont athletes in college, we take a look at Claire Dean of Stanford’s gymnastics team, Parker Terrill of UC Berkeley’s track team, and Nico DeFazio of Howard Christian University’s baseball team. Terrell also set a new personal record at the Cal Opener on March 8. 2025, where he recorded a vault of 17 feet, 2.75 inches, finishing third of eight athletes. CLAIRE DEAN Stanford Claire Dean, PHS Class of 2022, is currently competing as a senior on Stanford’s gymnastics team. So far this season, the Cardinal are 4-1 with Dean appearing in all five events. She competes primarily in the beam events and the floor exercises. She had scores of 9.825 on the beam and 9.875 on the floor in Stanford’s 197.1-194.65 win over Pittsburgh on February 6. She also had a 9.875 score on the beam and 9.750 floor in their 196.97-196.825 win over Cal on January 30. She helped the Cardinal win the 2025 ACC Championship and reach the second round of the NCAA Regional Championships, finishing with a 19-6 overall record. For the ACC Championship, Dean recorded a score of 9.850 on the balance beam and a 9.900 on the floor exercise. In 2024, Dean helped her school finish fourth in the Pac-12 Championships and reach the NCAA Championships semifinals. Photo courtesy of Howard Christian University Nico DeFazio, PHS Class of 2022, is a redshirt junior on Howard Christian University’s baseball team. NICO DEFAZIO Howard Christian University Nico DeFazio, PHS Class of 2022, is entering his redshirt junior year on Howard Christian University’s baseball team after transferring from Chabot College in Hayward. He previously played at University of the Pacific after high school and started all 42 games for the Gladiators, helping them go 28-14. He was among Chabot’s best players with a .329 batting average on 53 hits, 15 doubles, six triples, four home runs, 37 RBIs, and 53 runs scored. In 2024 at University of the Pacific, DeFazio finished with 29 appearances and started 21 times, recording 13 hits, four doubles, six runs scored, and four RBIs. With Piedmont, DeFazio was named the WACC Shoreline’s Player of the Year in 2022 with a .408 batting average with 29 hits, 10 doubles, three triples, and a home run. Photo courtesy of Cal Athletics Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, is a senior on California’s track and field team. PARKER TERRILL California Parker Terrill, PHS Class of 2022, is a senior on the University of California’s track and field team. He was our 2022 Co-Athlete of the Year as a record-setting pole vaulter at Piedmont High. He finished his 2025 campaign strongly, reaching the NCAA Division 1 West First Round on May 28-31. Parker placed 26th of 37 athletes in the pole vault at the event, recording a height of 16 feet, 5.5 inches. To get there, he made it to the 2025 ACC Championship, finishing eighth of 17 in 16 feet, 7.25 inches.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Fox News The U.S. women’s hockey team has three straight 5-0 wins, including an historic shutout of Canada. The 2026 Winter Olympics are underway in Italy through February 22. As of Tuesday, February 10, the United States holds fourth place in the medal count with two gold, three silver and two bronze medals. Norway leads both medal and gold categories with 12 and six respectively, Italy has 11 medals and two gold, Japan has eight medals with two gold, while three other nations have three gold medals including Germany, Sweden, and Switzerland. Here’s a rundown of some key moments as we churn through the opening week this year’s Winter Games. USA women’s hockey team dominates Canada The United States women’s hockey team had an unprecedented 5-0 win over Canada on Tuesday, February 10 in the preliminary round. It marked the first time the Canadians have been shut out in the Olympics. It was the largest margin of victory for any USA-Canada hockey match, men or women’s. It also marked USA’s third straight 5-0 win after beating Switzerland and Finland by the same score on February 9 and February 7. The quarterfinals are set for February 13-14, the semifinals are on February 16, and finals on February 19. Bay Area’s Alysa Liu takes Gold Alysa Liu, a 20-year-old who graduated from Oakland School of the Arts, recently won the gold medal Gold as a member of the USA team ice skating event. She Photo courtesy of E! News Alysa Liu of Oakland won the gold medal in women’s figure skating. took second in the short program behind Kaori Sakamoto of Japan. Liu began her Olympic journey as a child at the Oakland Ice Center. She’s drawn attention for her dyed hair and “smiley” piercing on her lip, bringing a quintessential Oakland and Bay Area flair to the Olympic games. Ilia Malinin back in lead of men’s figure skating The “Quad God” is back on top for Team USA. Ilia Malinin was behind Japan’s Yuma Kagiyama following the Team event, but jumped ahead after winning Tuesday’s short program. As things stand, Malinin leads with a score of 108.16 going into Friday’s free skate. He leads Kagiyama’s 103.07, while France’s Adam Siao Him Fa is third in 102.55, Italy’s Daniel Grassl is fourth with 93.46, and Kazakhstan’s Mikhail Shaidorov rounds out the top five with 92.94. Lindsey Vonn suffers broken leg We may have seen the last of Team USA’s great alpine skier, Lindsey Vonn. On Sunday, February 8, Vonn suffered a complex tibia fracture just 13 seconds into her run after clipping a gate. It required her to be airlifted from the course. Vonn’s injury has caused some backlash after entering the Winter Olympics with a torn ACL in the same leg. Vonn contends that the injuries are separate and unrelated. Her father, Alan Kildow, told the Associated Press that he wants to prevent Vonn from racing ever again. “She’s 41 years old and this is the end of her career. There will be no more ski races for Lindsey Vonn, as long as I have anything to say about it,” Kildow said. Photo courtesy of Variety Downhill skier Lindsey Vonn had to be airlifted off the course after suffering a broken leg.
