articles.text: As winter winds down, spring has a way of arriving all at once – longer days, fuller calendars, and a fresh wave of home to-dos. For Piedmont families, February is the ideal moment to get ahead before sports schedules, spring break plans, and outdoor activities take over. A little preparation now can save time, stress, and surprise repairs later. Here are a few smart, handyman-approved ways to prepare your home for spring: 1. Check drainage around your home. After winter rains, make sure downspouts are clear and directing water away from your foundation. In older Piedmont homes, poor drainage is one of the most common – and preventable – causes of long-term damage. 2. Tune up doors and windows. If doors stick or windows feel drafty, it’s often a hinge or alignment issue – not a full replacement. A quick adjustment improves comfort and can lower energy bills as temperatures rise. 3. Refresh outdoor lighting. Days are getting longer, but early evenings and fog still roll in. Replace burned-out bulbs and consider warm-tone LED fixtures near walkways and play and entertaining begin. A pro tip most homeowners miss: Check caulking around exterior windows and doors before the rainy season tapers off. Small gaps are far easier to seal now than after moisture works its way inside. Eleanor must decide whether to selfishly remain in the Good Place, knowing she is causing the problems, or make the ultimate sacrifice for her new friends and surrender herself to the Bad Place. The Good Place is a delightful blend of philosophy and sitcom storytelling and was nominated for multiple Primetime Emmys over its four-season run. All six of the main characters bring distinct personalities to the show, and while they are wildly different, their group dynamic is what makes the series work. On her own, Eleanor isn’t especially likable or redeemable, but paired she goes to St. Kits with her new husband. And so begins what becomes a road trip to Boston, one that includes the school’s food manager/cook, Mary, played by D’Vine Joy Randolph, nominated for Best Actress in a Supporting Role; sharp-tongued Angus, feeling abandoned; and Paul, driving his worn, nondescript sedan. Angrily, wracked by loneliness, his plan to escape once again ruined, he turns the massive turtle upside down and leaves it in the hot sun. What happens next is magical and I am reluctant to explain more. But suffice it to say that it is then that the narrative arc of the film is revealed and it beckons the audience to step into a reverie that is so quietly offered up it can only be called a meditation on life. Using a palette of vibrant and muted colors, it is all but impossible not to be drawn in, pulled like a gentle out-going tide swirling around your ankles, the sand slipping from under your feet. articles.text: Piedmont Community Church is committed to nurturing the next generation. The heart of NextGen is partnering with parents to help kids and teens develop a faith that truly sticks - one that shapes identity, builds resilience and guides everyday decisions as they grow up in a very challenging world. We want kids to know that they belong and are loved, supported and accepted for who they are. Adult leaders bring the stories of the Bible to life and connect scripture to kids’ lives. In small Life Groups, relationships grow, questions are welcomed and faith becomes personal. NextGen is lots of fun, with special holiday events for all ages as well as overnights, retreats and mission trips for older kids as part of our program. NOT JUST FOR KIDS It’s no secret that parenting today is more challenging than ever. Our NextGen Parent Life Group meets throughout the year to offer encouragement, connection and practical support. For more NextGen information, contact Kerry Perschitte at kerry@piedmontchurch.org Ultimately, we want all children and students to understand how God’s Word fits into their lives. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) test scores in English Language Arts (ELA) and Mathematics ranked the third highest among unified school districts in California on the California Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) for the 2024- 2025 school year. The CAASPP system is a collection of computer-based assessments in English Language Arts/ Literacy, Mathematics, and Science. Students in grades 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 11 take the ELA and Math tests. This standardized test program replaced the STAR testing program in 2014. “We are incredibly proud of our students for their remarkable achievements on the CAASPP assessments this year,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “These results are a testament to the hard work and rigor applied by our students, the unwavering commitment of our educators, and the strong partnership with our families.” For ELA, 85% of PUSD students met or exceeded the state standard. In Mathematics, 82% of students met or exceeded the state standard. The District’s performance achieved the #1 ranking in Northern California for both ELA and Math performance. A total of 92 Piedmont students achieved a perfect result in at least one of the CAASPP exams. articles.text: The mechanical room of the new community pool The setbacks of Piedmont’s community pool have tested the community’s patience, but the upgrades are a critical part of a larger shift toward sustainability. Once complete, the electrical infrastructure is expected to significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions, making the long wait not just a matter of finishing a project, but an investment in a cleaner, more environmentally responsible future for the city. According to the former Piedmont Community Pool Committee, the old facility’s natural gas use may have accounted for nearly two-thirds of all gas consumption across Piedmont’s municipal buildings. The CAASPP system is a collection of computer-based assessments in English Language Arts/ Literacy, Mathematics, and Science. Students in grades 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 11 take the ELA and Math tests. This standardized test program replaced the STAR testing program in 2014. “We are incredibly proud of our students for their remarkable achievements on the CAASPP assessments this year,” said Superintendent Jennifer Hawn. “These results are a testament to the hard work and rigor applied by our students, the unwavering commitment of our educators, and the strong partnership with our families.” For ELA, 85% of PUSD students met or exceeded the state standard. In Mathematics, 82% of students met or exceeded the state standard. The District’s performance achieved the #1 ranking in Northern California for both ELA and Math performance. A total of 92 Piedmont students achieved a perfect result in at least one of the CAASPP exams. articles.text: Do you know a Piedmonter who’s inspired you to rethink how you heat your home, save water, or go all-electric? Nominate them for the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Awards. Now in their third year, Piedmont’s Sustainability Awards recognize up to four residents each year, whose home improvements, water-wise choices, or commitment to green living have helped move sustainability forward in Piedmont. The goal is to showcase real-world examples of climate-friendly upgrades right here in our community – and to celebrate the residents who are helping move Piedmont toward its climate action goals. To submit a nomination, complete the online nomination form by February 18, 2026. https://form.jotform. com/260258202453147 City staff will review nominations, confirm that nominees want to participate, and select award recipients. Selected awardees will be recognized at the Planning Commission Design Awards Gala on April 15, 2026. Awardees will be featured in City communications, such as case studies or video profiles. Sustainability leadership can look different from household to household. A nomination might highlight a single project or a longer series of improvements. Examples include: • Electrification and clean energy upgrades, from heat pumps and induction cooking to solar and battery storage • Energy-efficiency improvements, such as insulation, air sealing, or windows • Wat e r-w ise la nd scap e s and systems, including • drought-tolerant planting, smart irrigation, rainwater capture, or greywater Community leadership, such as sharing lessons learned, hosting tours, or helping neighbors get started. Past Sustainability Award honorees have shown what’s possible in Piedmont – from deep electrification and solar, to water-saving landscapes and habitat-focused yards, to sharing knowledge with other residents who are just getting started. • 2024 honorees: Shannon and Rob Bloemker; Hope and Larry Salzer; Cass Caulfield and Any Hempeck; Russell and Amy Griffith • 2025 honorees: James Glabuer and Tracy Lieu; Susan Miller-Davis and Jonathan Davis; and the owners of 335 Sea View Avenue. Planning Commissioner Michael Beuselinck (left), 2025 sustainability awardees Jonathan Davis & SusanMiller Davis, and Planning and Building Director Kevin Jackson from left to right.

articles.text: Noctis is an adorable, intelligent, 4-year-old cat with a curious mind and a playful spirit. He loves interactive wand play and will happily jump, pounce, and stalk toys with impressive focus—it’s a bit like watching a nature documentary unfold in your living room! You’ll be smitten by his adorable trills (when he’s pleased) and grunts (when he’s displeased). He’s on a special diet to support his digestive health and will need to remain indoors because he has feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV), which is easily managed and doesn’t shorten his lifespan. Affectionate and social, this little house panther enjoys soft petting and cuddles in moderation. He’s confident, and loves attention, but he can become overstimulated if petting goes on too long. An adopter with some cat experience who’s comfortable reading body language and redirecting him with toys will help him thrive. Adopt Noctis through Cat Town. When he’s not playing, Noctis enjoys following his people around and keeping a close eye on everything you’re doing. This sweet black cat will greet you at the door when you come home! Noctis would do best in a household where he has space to explore, plenty of daily stimulation, and he may do well with another cat. He’s neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and FeLV-negative, Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@ cattownoakland.org. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Three months ago, the city of Piedmont welcomed its new Climate Action Fellow, Emma Grossman. Over the next 11 months, she will be focused on helping the city meet its climate goals and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Grossman grew up in Seattle, Washington, surrounded by nature. She and her father would go camping and hiking in their spare time bonding over nature. Her love for the environment has become a huge part of who she is today. “From a very young age, I was taught to really love nature,” she said. “I see nature as a really intrinsic part of who I am, and that love has never gone away.” Grossman pursued her passion at New York University, where she graduated with degrees in environmental studies and global public health. It was at NYU where Grossman realized she could turn her love of nature into a career. “I think when I got to college, I realized that loving the environment was something that I could actually put into my work and become professionally important to me as well,” Grossman said. Grossman spent her college career working as a sustainability consultant and a food waste & recovery intern for companies in New York City. After graduation this past May, she found Piedmont’s fellowship through the Sustainability Service Corps and was drawn to the idea of working in government. Climate action fellow Emma Grossman in front of City Hall “I was immediately drawn to working for city governments. It’s something I really haven’t done before, but I had an inkling that I might like it,” Grossman added. “As I read through the city of Piedmont’s profile and their job description, it immediately caught my eye, and that went to number one on my list.” As a Climate Action fellow, her primary role is to assist in the implementation of Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan. A plan that was passed in 2018 to support statewide climate efforts and provide a pathway for Piedmont to reduce greenhouse gas emissions 40% by 2030, and be on track to reduce emissions 80% by 2050. “I’m mainly involved in our electrification strategy and decarbonization work,” Grossman added. She is the current lead on the rebate program in Piedmont, helping residents switch from fossil fuel-burning home appliances to electric. It’s only been three months, but she’s already making an impact on the program. “I took a look at the program and its reach in the last two years, and I made a report about that. We have some potential changes to the program coming soon, based on my recommendations and what we talked about as a department,” said Grossman. Over the remaining eight months of Grossman’s fellowship, she’ll be dedicated to helping Piedmont become a sustainable, green community. “I want residents to be able to experience the full benefits of electrification and of meeting our climate action goals,” she added, “I want residents to breathe healthier air, drink cleaner water, and experience cleaner parks.”
articles.title: Profile: Climate Action Fellow Emma Grossman

articles.text: The Piedmont Asian American Club will ring in the Lunar New Year with an evening of performances, food, and community celebration on Friday, February 27, at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. The annual event will run from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. and feature performances by Piedmont High School students, crafts, a raffle, and a traditional Lion dance. Food and drink will include dim sum, boba drinks, and panang curry. Gourmet desserts and specialty drinks will be provided by Bakesum and Tea on Piedmont. “In times when many immigrants question their place in this country, cultural celebrations like Lunar New Year offer a welcoming space to gather, share, and be recognized,” said event organizer Della Chow. “For many Asian children, this event is especially meaningful, giving them the chance to celebrate their identity and proudly showcase their cultural heritage amid everyday pressures to fit in.” The event is open to all community members. “Come together, share joy, and honor the rich traditions of Lunar New Year with family, friends, and the vibrant spirit of our community,” Chow said. Tickets are limited and expected to sell out. General admission is $25 and include dinner. Tickets can be purchased at https://bit.ly/3O4kKbs. The Lion Dance performance at the 2025 PAAC Lunar New Year reduce energy usage to 1.1 gigawatt-hour while emitting no greenhouse gases. The shift is also expected to generate substantial financial benefits. “The energy consultant estimated a $1.5 million savings in energy costs over 20 years by going all electric, which will offset the higher initial costs of the hardware,” said Keating. Piedmont isn’t the first city to design a fully electrified pool. The City of Mountain View was the first electrified municipal aquatics center in California. It included more than 10,000 square feet of pool area. The facility uses solar panels on the roof and an all-electric hot water system with heat pumps to generate all its energy without greenhouse gases. That project served as a model for Piedmont’s clean-energy pool design. While the delays have been difficult for residents, the former pool committee members maintain that the environmental benefits and long-term operational savings make the wait worthwhile.

pages.text: Wednesday, January 28, 2026 5 PAAC Lunar New Year Preview Feb. 27 By Jake Lannon The Piedmont Asian American Club will ring in the Lunar New Year with an evening of performances, food, and community celebration on Friday, February 27, at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse. The annual event will run from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. and feature performances by Piedmont High School students, crafts, a raffle, and a traditional Lion dance. Food and drink will include dim sum, boba drinks, and panang curry. Gourmet desserts and specialty drinks will be provided by Bakesum and Tea on Piedmont. “In times when many immigrants question their place in this country, cultural celebrations like Lunar New Year offer a welcoming space to gather, share, and be recognized,” said event organizer Della Chow. “For many Asian children, this event is especially meaningful, giving them the chance to celebrate their identity and proudly showcase their cultural heritage amid everyday pressures to fit in.” The event is open to all community members. “Come together, share joy, and honor the rich traditions of Lunar New Year with family, friends, and the vibrant spirit of our community,” Chow said. Tickets are limited and expected to sell out. General admission is $25 and include dinner. Tickets can be purchased at https://bit.ly/3O4kKbs. The shift is also expected to generate subThe Activity Pool stantial financial benefits. “The energy consultant estimated a $1.5 million savings in energy costs over 20 years by going all electric, which will offset the higher initial costs of the hardware,” said Keating. Piedmont isn’t the first city to design a fully electrified pool. The City of Mountain View was the first electrified municipal aquatics center in California. articles.text: Superintendent Jennifer Hawn delivered her second annual “State of the District” report at the Jan. 21 school board meeting. Hawn’s presentation outlined the strategic plan of the Piedmont Unified School District and highlighted the district’s recent focus on academic investment. “We have accomplished a lot, and we should just take a moment to just enjoy the fact that we have an incomparable team of administrators, of teachers, of classified staff. They provide expert service every day,” Hawn said. Hawn highlighted a significant change at the elementary level this year as a story of success. “We moved away from a curricular program, an English language arts program, that we didn’t feel really reflected that science of learning focus. And we moved toward Fish Tank learning, which is a new English language arts adoption,” she said. Creating an environment where students can thrive is another district priority. One metric the district uses to assess this is the California Healthy Kids Survey. Hawn said there were some inconsistent survey results at the middle school, which prompted a review of the school’s climate and culture. “Piedmont Middle School being named a California School to Watch this year is really exciting. There’s an award ceremony that will happen in March, and I’m just super excited to see PMS recognized for the great work that they do,” Hawn said. The Schools to Watch program is a national network of hundreds of schools in 20 states. Schools apply in the fall and submit an application following a validation visit. Piedmont Middle School was found to meet the program’s qualifications. Hawn also addressed the district’s cell phone policy, which she described as a work in progress. The district is currently implementing a one-year cell phone policy and plans to adopt a more restrictive permanent policy next year to align with state directives. “We made the bold and innovative move to adopt Latin, we are super excited about that,” Hawn said, referring to plans to introduce Latin to fifth graders next year. Hawn also reported strong interest in AP Business and Personal Finance, a new course to be added next year. Earlier in the evening, Elise Marks said that 130 students had expressed interest, which would require five separate course offerings. Hawn noted that reviewing and updating the district’s mathematics programming would be a focus in the near future. “Math has been a conversation. We have a [math] board policy that is actually out of date, so we really do need to take a look at math pathways,” Hawn said. “The secret sauce in Piedmont is really community engagement,” Hawn said when introducing the topic of partnering outside the classroom. Hawn said she has started holding “student lunches” this year so she can hear directly from students. The district has also placed a renewed focus on adding more meaningful field trips. Hawn acknowledged that there has been significant change in the district in recent years and signaled that the pace of change may slow. “We have accomplished a lot in the last several years, and so I think moving forward, a lot of the work that we’ll be doing is thinking about how we might refine what we are currently working on, rather than adding something significantly new,” she said. “I wish we could print this and put this in the Piedmont Post,” board member Susy Struble said following Hawn’s report. articles.text: Dear PUSD Families & Staff: At a time when our broader world may feel uncertain and, at times, volatile, the importance of safety, care, and connection within our school community cannot be overstated. Piedmont Unified School District remains firmly committed to ensuring that our schools are places where students and adults feel safe, supported, and cared for, and where we look out for one another as a shared responsibility of our community. Thank you for supporting our efforts to create safety in our schools. This year’s State of the District report reflects the collective work of teachers, principals, staff, students, families, and community partners who continue to elevate Piedmont Unified School District. Guided by our Vision, Mission, and Core Values, we have strengthened our programs, deepened student support, launched major instructional initiatives, and advanced the goals outlined in our District Strategic Plan, LCAP, and 2025– 26 District Goals. We have invested deeply in outstanding academics, student wellness, operational systems, and community partnerships. Our success is driven by organizational coherence, including a strategic plan that drives our priorities and goals at all levels of our organization. Our actions are intentional in building a district that is more aligned, more transparent, and more responsive to the students and families we serve. I am grateful for our Board of Education, whose wise leadership and clear direction guide our progress; for our certificated and classified staff who care for, teach, and inspire students each day; for our families and community partners whose investments sustain our programs; and for our students, whose curiosity, courage, and compassion give meaning to our work. Together, we continue to build a district we are proud of today and tomorrow. In Community, Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent

articles.text: Understanding dyslexia and language-based learning differences As a speech-language pathologist, one of the most common pieces of advice I hear given to struggling readers is well-intentioned but incomplete: “They just need to read more.” For many children, increased reading practice does help. But for a significant number of students, reading more—without the right support—only leads to frustration, fatigue, and declining confidence. The reason is simple: reading is not a natural skill. Unlike spoken language, which most children acquire through exposure, reading requires the brain to make very specific connections between sounds, letters, and meaning. When those connections don’t develop easily, practice alone is not enough. Dyslexia is one of the most well-known language-based learning differences. It is not a problem with intelligence or motivation. Children with dyslexia often have difficulty with phonological processing—the ability to hear, identify, and manipulate the sounds in spoken words. This makes learning sound-letter relationships and decoding words especially challenging. Other children may struggle with oral language skills, such as vocabulary, sentence structure, or understanding complex language. These students may learn to decode words but have trouble with reading comprehension, written expression, or retaining what they read. In both cases, telling a child to “just read more” is like asking someone to run farther without first teaching them how to walk efficiently. Why does more practice sometimes backfire? When reading is effortful, children expend so much mental energy decoding words that little is left for comprehension. Repeated failure can lead to avoidance, anxiety, and the belief that they are “bad readers.” Over time, this can affect academic performance across subjects and impact self-esteem. This is why some children read nightly, attend school faithfully, and still fall further behind. The issue is not a lack of effort: it’s a mismatch between the child’s learning needs and the instruction they are receiving. Research is clear about what supports struggling readers. Effective intervention is explicit, systematic, and structured. It targets the underlying skills that support reading, including phonemic awareness (hearing and manipulating sounds in words), sound-symbol relationships, decoding and encoding (reading and spelling), vocabulary and language comprehension, working memory and language organization. Approaches grounded in the science of reading help children build what researchers call orthographic mapping, the process by which words become stored in long-term memory for automatic recognition. Once this happens, reading becomes faster, smoother, and more enjoyable. Speech-language pathologists often play a key role in this process, particularly when reading difficulties are tied to broader language weaknesses. Intervention is most effective when it is individualized and based on a child’s specific profile of strengths and needs. If your child dislikes reading, avoids it, or seems to work much harder than peers, trust your instincts. More reading is helpful after the right skills are in place—not before. With proper assessment and evidence-based support, struggling readers can make meaningful progress and, just as importantly, regain confidence in their ability to learn. Reading success isn’t about trying harder. It’s about teaching smarter. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. She can be reached at kathryn.pengilly@speechinc. com. More information can be found at www.speechinc.com.

Hop along the trails, stones and shoreline in this truly unique to the Bay Area environment. Take the dogs and older kids capable of bouldering on a shoreline. articles.text: Winnie Pickavance holds up her Pinewood Derby car. Niko Kobylczak works on a derby car. On Saturday, January 24, 9th Grade Girl Scout Troop 33587 hosted a Pinewood Derby Workshop to help racers build their cars from start to finish. The workshop, held for the 21st time at the Piedmont Middle School shop, helped more than 60 racers build their cars. As pinewood cars took form from a variety of racers it became apparent some aimed for just speed, some aimed for design and some aimed for design and speed. Everyone got to flex their engineering and design skills to create their cars. Eight-year-year old Cora Pickavance admitted “I want to win the race, but I also just really like my car” about her BART train-inspired car. Nine-year-old sister, Senior Girl Scout Maya Evans sets up a decorating station at the workshop. Elena and Sorcha Campbell work on their cars at the sanding station. Winnie, described the workshop as “a fun way to hang out with my friends, learn about power tools, and get creative.” There are still racing spots for kids and around five spots left for adults. The big race day will be Saturday, February 7; this will be the third time that Troop 33587 has hosted the official race. Registration is open until February 3 at https://forms.gle/iCTpsdhFSci8VFuu7. For more details, visit https:// sites.google.com/view/girlscouttroop33587/home. If you need your car cut, please email carolynpan@yahoo.com to schedule a time to cut your car. • • Trial Run Day January 31, 10 a.m.-12 p.m. at the Piedmont Community Church Race Day February 7, 3-6 p.m. at the Piedmont Community Church

articles.text: In spring, Piedmont Council’s five troops (youth groups for all kids, boys and girls, in 5th grade and up) open their doors to families interested in the scouting program. Open house meetings are an opportunity for kids and their parents to visit a specific scout troop, meet youth and adult leadership, and learn about that troop’s unique brand of scouting. Troops also share recent and upcoming activities. In advance of the troop’s open houses, Council leaders will host informational sessions during the week of February 9th. These sessions will explain the basics of the scouting program, talk about what scouting looks like in Piedmont, assist in deciding which troop to visit, and provide a safe space to have your questions about scouting answered. To receive information about the time and location of the info sessions, please fill out the Google form here: https://forms.gle/WwPS4SkHRhoEwuro6 Scouting is a time-honored tradition in the community of Piedmont, with twenty-percent of Piedmont youth involved in the program. Scouting provides youth with hands-on leadership experiences and allows them to practice life skills while serving their community. It instills citizenship and character, fosters communication, and builds a self-reliance in youth as they organize events and take on challenges together. Have questions about the info sessions or open houses? Reach out to Piedmont Council’s Program Coordinator Eris Turner: eturner@piedmontbsa.org – (510) 844-4752

ADVERTISE IN THE POST Girl Scouts Pinewood Derby workshop By Girl Scout Troop 33587 On Saturday, January 24, 9th Grade Girl Scout Troop 33587 hosted a Pinewood Derby Workshop to help racers build their cars from start to finish. The workshop, held for the 21st time at the Piedmont Middle School shop, helped more than 60 racers build their cars. As pinewood cars took form from a variety of racers it became apparent some aimed for just speed, some aimed for design and some aimed for design and speed. Everyone got to flex their engineering and design skills to create their cars. Eight-year-year old Cora Pickavance admitted “I want to win the race, but I also just really like my car” about her BART train-inspired car. Nine-year-old sister, Senior Girl Scout Maya Evans sets up a decorating station at the workshop. Elena and Sorcha Campbell work on their cars at the sanding station. Winnie, described the workshop as “a fun way to hang out with my friends, learn about power tools, and get creative.” There are still racing spots for kids and around five spots left for adults. The big race day will be Saturday, February 7; this will be the third time that Troop 33587 has hosted the official race. Registration is open until February 3 at https://forms.gle/iCTpsdhFSci8VFuu7. For more details, visit https:// sites.google.com/view/girlscouttroop33587/home. If you need your car cut, please email carolynpan@yahoo.com to schedule a time to cut your car. • • Trial Run Day January 31, 10 a.m.-12 p.m. at the Piedmont Community Church Race Day February 7, 3-6 p.m. at the Piedmont Community Church Which Troop Will Choose? articles.text: As the Lighting Ceremony in Piedmont Park approaches each year, Piedmont residents are invited to send holiday greetings to friends and neighbors through donations to the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF). This year, in addition to PBF’s ongoing funding initiatives, donors also had the opportunity to support the replacement of swings in the Main Park. PBF is delighted to report that the community responded with remarkable generosity. Contributions will be directed in accordance with donors’ wishes, supporting not only the replacement swings, but also the Dearing Family Memorial Project, and the Reforest Piedmont, Neighborhood-by-Neighborhood effort. PBF extends its heartfelt thanks to all who contributed and is pleased to recognize donors whose gifts were made since July 1, 2025. More than $200,000 has been received, which includes a generous bequest from long time community volunteer Carl Anderson. Special appreciation is also extended to the underwriters who financed the citywide mailing that invited the entire community to participate in the annual Piedmont Lights Up! event. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team continued its stature as one of the best teams in California with two wins at Binks Rawlings Gym over the past week. They recently beat Antelope 57-37 on Saturday, January 24 and won 76-55 over Alameda on Thursday, January 22. Their 20-point victory over Antelope was quite the statement. The Highlanders entered as the No. 16 ranked team in California while the Titans were ranked No. 18. Without star PHS point guard Jenelle Solis, who remains out with an ankle injury, the win represents a critical result toward Piedmont’s postseason seeding. “Everyone is continuing to grow. The ball handling department is going to be really important over the next three weeks. We all know how good of a playmaker Jenelle is, so everyone has to be a point guard and take on those responsibilities,” coach Bryan Gardere said. Losing Solis for the last three Savannah Dennig had 12 points and 13 rebounds against Alameda, along with seven points and seven boards in a victory over Antelope. Staff Photos Taylor White kicks out a pass against Alameda. She had 12 points and 14 rebounds against Alameda and 13 points and 11 rebounds against Antelope. games means the Highlanders require nearly its entire lineup to take more responsibility as ball handlers. Forward Saniyah Johnson, a key rebounder, has also been out. “We have to step up and play for our teammates, because we’re missing Jenelle and Saniyah. Everybody has a new role, I feel like as the games go on, things are improving,” Taylor White said. “We don’t have a second Jenelle or Saniyah, so we all have to add things to our game. We have to dribble more, talk more, and come together as a team,” Savannah Dennig mentioned. With seven games left in the regular season, it marks an important time for the Highlanders to ramp up toward the North Coast Section playoffs. They are on track for an Open Division berth for a second straight year, which would give them an automatic berth in the CIF State tournament. “We could clean up our free Freshman Alexa Ba drives in against Alameda. She had 13 points against Alameda and 11 points against Antelope. throw. We. can’t have as many misses as we did tonight [against Alameda]. We need to keep working on our free throws and our defense, being able to switch defenses mid-game, and talking on the floor without miscommunicating,” Dennig said. “When a team presses us, we need to be more comfortable and let the press come to us without rushing through it. As coach says, we have to grow fast because playoffs are coming quickly,” White said. 57-37 win over Antelope Piedmont led 17-12 through the first quarter and extended its lead to 34-23 by halftime. PHS stepped up their defense in the second half, outscoring the Titans 11-5 in the third quarter and 12-9 in the fourth. Final stats: Andrea Martin led with 24 points, 16 rebounds, and three blocks. White had 13 points, 11 rebounds, six assists, one steal, and one block. Alexa Ba had 11 points and three rebounds. Dennig had seven points, seven rebounds, two assists, and one block. Nia Jackson had two points. Jaden Jones had eight rebounds and an assist. 76-55 victory over Alameda Piedmont got out to a commanding 24-10 lead in the first quarter and pushed the lead to 43-25 by halftime. The Hornets inched closer in the third quarter to trail 62-46 entering the fourth quarter, while Piedmont put up 14 more points in the final going and conceded nine. Alameda made things a little bit closer in the fourth quarter, shaving away at Piedmont’s lead to put itself back 14 points, 68-54 with six straight points. But it was no-sweat for the Highlanders, closing with eight of the final nine points. Final stats: Martin led with 36 points, 10 rebounds, and two assists. Ba had 13 points, two rebounds, and four assists. White had 12 points, 14 rebounds, and six assists. Dennig had 12 points, 13 rebounds, and four assists. Jackson had four points. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont looks to pick itself up after tough losses to Alameda and University. Their loss to Alameda marked the fifth time they relinquished a fourth-quarter lead. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team had a frustrating week with two losses, bringing its record to 13-7 overall and 1-3 against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division teams. They lost 67-58 to Alameda in the Hornets’ home gym on Thursday, January 22 and fell 83-62 to University at Binks Rawlings Gym two days later. Piedmont held a 53-46 lead with 3:30 left in the game with Alameda, but was held to five points in the remaining time. The loss marked the Highlanders’ fifth defeat after holding a fourth-quarter lead. “We’re 13-7, but easily could be 18-2,” said coach Ben Spencer. “We had five games where we had a fourth quarter lead; Acalanes, we had a 12 point lead with two minutes to go. Berkeley, we had a five point lead. Alameda, we had an eight point lead. We just haven’t found a way to close games.” Alameda and University had a common trend where the opponent’s press caused problems for the Highlanders’ offense. “The press seemed to give us a lot of trouble against Alameda. I thought we did well tonight against University’s press when we ran it correctly. University is just deep with 12 guys who are all great shooters. But, I’m proud of how we battled,” Spencer said. 12 to jump ahead 52-30. PHS crept closer in the third, 66-47, but University outscored Piedmont 17-15 in the final going. There were four lead changes in the first quarter. Lorin scored on a put-back offensive rebound to lead 8-6 after two minutes, but University went up 12-10 on its own offensive board a couple of minutes later. PHS then went ahead 15-14 after Will Hinman converted a pair of free throws with 56 seconds left, but University scored on its next possession on a 3-pointer. They never relinquished the lead from then on. Final stats: Lorin led with 19 points, Casey had 13, Brayer scored seven, Panico had six, Ollie Dougan scored five, Hinman and Fang-Ring had four, while Ruben Cohen scored two. NEXT UP Piedmont (13-7 overall, 1-3 league) hosts Castro Valley tonight, January 28, at 7:00 p.m. and will also host San Leandro on Friday, January 30 at the same time. The Highlanders held Alameda to just nine points in the third quarter while scoring 18 to take a 43-40 lead going into the fourth. However, the Hornets piled on 27 points in the final going, while Piedmont put up 15. Final stats: Beach Lorin led with 25 points, Dillon Casey had 12, P.J. Brayer scored 10, Lucian Fang-Ring scored eight, while Cash Panico had three. 83-62 loss to University Piedmont kept things close through the first quarter, trailing 21-18, but the Red Devils turned up the heat in the second quarter with an aggressive press that kept the Highlanders off balance— scoring 31 points to Piedmont’s Beach Lorin led with 25 points against Alameda and 19 points against University. articles.text: Beats San Leandro 3-1, falls 2-0 to top-ranked O’Dowd Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team is rolling through its final regular season matches, beating San Leandro 3-1 at Witter Field on Tuesday, January 20 while losing 2-0 at Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland on Friday, January 23. The results bring Piedmont’s record 6-2-4 (W-T-L). Despite the loss to O’Dowd, the Dragons are currently the No. 13 ranked team in California and No. 55 in the entire nation. Piedmont, meanwhile, is No. 174 in the state, making Friday’s result encouraging. Bishop O’Dowd is currently undefeated at 8-0-0 without conceding a single goal this year, and fields talented players like freshman Sadie Siedel, who competes semi-pro on Oakland Soul’s W League team. “We were very much looking forward to Bishop O’Dowd. They are a very good team and is a really good test to see where we’re at,” coach Matt Spencer-Harty said. Piedmont now has six matches left in its season against Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division foes. It marks a time for the Highlanders to finetune things as they ramp up for the North Coast Section postseason, while also making sure they can remain healthy for the final stretch. “One thing we need to do Ayla Blanford also had a goal and assist against San Leandro. Olivia Nealon had a shot on target against Bishop O’Dowd. Miranda Liu had a goal and assist against San Leandro. Staff Photos is make sure everyone is fit. A couple of injuries and the trajectory changes completely. I’m trying to be smart with the load management of what we’re doing in practice and preparing for games. We want possession-based football,” Spencer-Harty said. 3-1 over San Leandro Miranda Liu struck first for Piedmont in the 14th minute. In the buildup, Makenna Small sprung Ayla Blanford out wide down the left side around the midfield line. Blanford took a couple of dribbles before feeding a pass to Liu bursting past the Pirates’ back line. Liu took one touch with her right foot before following through with her left, catching San Leandro’s keeper far off her line for the goal. Piedmont next goal in the 38th was a product of terrific interplay, including six completed passes before Liu found Blanford for the goal. It started with defender Erica Smith sending a pass to Olivia Kan-Miller, who passed to Arden Sorensen-Wald. The midfielder hit a first-touch pass to Chloe Toyama, who sprang Liu in behind. Liu took one dribble into the box before sending a pass from the right side across the face of goal to Blanford, scoring on a first-touch shot. San Leandro got one back in the 59th minute after their forward took a nifty touch between Piedmont’s defenders to put herself in a 1-on-1 situation with PHS goal keeper Rachel Young. Piedmont’s final goal came 10 minutes later in the 69th. PHS initially gained a corner, where Sorensen-Wald whipped in a cross from the right side. SLHS’ keeper botched a high claim, bobbling the ball to the ground. In a scrum, Emily Hu was able to chip the ball in from close range for her first varsity goal. 2-0 to Bishop O’Dowd The Highlanders’ didn’t shy away from the highly ranked O’Dowd side. Sorensen-Wald had the game’s first shot on target in the very first minute after Liu won a free kick on the edge of the Dragons’ box on the right side. Freshman Olivia Nealon had another shot on target in the 11th minute, but the Dragons’ defense adjusted well from then on. Siedel scored for O’Dowd in the 16th on a nice flick and volley to herself. O’Dowd scored again just two minutes later on a welltimed run in the box. Liu had a shot roll wide in the 44th minute of the second half. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-2-4 overall, 1-1-2 league) hosts Encinal tonight, January 28, at 7:00 p.m. They also host Berkeley on Friday, January 30 at the same time.

Blanford took a couple of dribbles before feeding a pass to Liu bursting past the Pirates’ back line. Liu took one touch with her right foot before following through with her left, catching San Leandro’s keeper far off her line for the goal. Piedmont next goal in the 38th was a product of terrific interplay, including six completed passes before Liu found Blanford for the goal. It started with defender Erica Smith sending a pass to Olivia Kan-Miller, who passed to Arden Sorensen-Wald. The midfielder hit a first-touch pass to Chloe Toyama, who sprang Liu in behind. Liu took one dribble into the box before sending a pass from the right side across the face of goal to Blanford, scoring on a first-touch shot. San Leandro got one back in the 59th minute after their forward took a nifty touch between Piedmont’s defenders to put herself in a 1-on-1 situation with PHS goal keeper Rachel Young. Piedmont’s final goal came 10 minutes later in the 69th. PHS initially gained a corner, where Sorensen-Wald whipped in a cross from the right side. SLHS’ keeper botched a high claim, bobbling the ball to the ground. In a scrum, Emily Hu was able to chip the ball in from close range for her first varsity goal. 2-0 to Bishop O’Dowd The Highlanders’ didn’t shy away from the highly ranked O’Dowd side. Sorensen-Wald had the game’s first shot on target in the very first minute after Liu won a free kick on the edge of the Dragons’ box on the right side. Freshman Olivia Nealon had another shot on target in the 11th minute, but the Dragons’ defense adjusted well from then on. Siedel scored for O’Dowd in the 16th on a nice flick and volley to herself. O’Dowd scored again just two minutes later on a welltimed run in the box. Liu had a shot roll wide in the 44th minute of the second half. articles.text: The 2026 Winter Olympics are quickly approaching, They will be held from February 6 through February 22. We’ll be doing a rundown of the most popular events in the weeks leading up to the winter games. In this week’s edition, we’ll take a look at the most-watched Winter Olympics event: figure skating. The United States leads the all-time medal count in figure skating with 54 medals and 17 Gold, but Russia led 2022’s medal count with six. Men’s singles Ilia Malinin of the United States is the overwhelming favorite for this year’s men’s singles event. The 21-year-old from Virginia is nicknamed the “Quad God” and is highly decorated. He is a two-time World champion (2024, 2025), three-time Grand Prix Final champion (2023, 2024, 2025), and a four-time U.S. national champion (2023-2026). Women’s singles Amber Glenn, 26, is the favorite going into her second Olympics after being an alternate in 2022. This will be the first time she will appear for Team USA. She recently won her third consecutive U.S. National title and is the 2024- 2025 Grand Prix champion. Alysa Liu, 20, from Clovis will also compete in the event. She is currently surging and Photos courtesy of Brittanica Team USA’s Ilia Malinin is the favorite for the Olympics’ men’s singles event. Madison Chock and Evan Bates are the favorite duo for Ice Dance and are hoping for a second Olympic gold. Amber Glenn of Team USA is the favorite for the Olympics’ women’s singles event. could challenge for Gold after becoming the 2025 World Champion and winning the 2025–2026 Grand Prix Final. Ice Dance In the ice dance, Madison Chock and Evan Bates make their fourth Olympic Games appearance and look for their second Gold medal. The duo has recently won their seventh National title, which marked their fifth in a row. Fellow Americans Emilea Zingas and Vadym Kolesnik recently finished behind Chock and Bates at the U.S. Championships, while Christina Carreira and Anthony Ponomarenko won Bronze and will also compete for Team USA.

articles.text: Progressive strength and impact training are essential for women’s health at every age CRUfit Montclair For more than a century, women have been reclaiming strength as a marker of health, beauty and vitality. In the early 1900s, Physical Culture magazine celebrated muscular women as symbols of wellness and capability, an idea far ahead of its time. Over the decades, publications such as Strength and Health echoed this message, even as mainstream culture lagged behind. A major turning point came with the passage of Title IX in 1972, which dramatically expanded athletic opportunities for women. As women entered competitive sports in greater numbers, they also adopted training methods long used by men, most notably progressive strength (resistance) training, in which weights are gradually increased to stimulate physical adaptation. The results were unmistakable. Women built muscle, gained strength and improved performance. articles.text: This time of year, many people feel drawn to start fresh with fitness. Routines reset, motivation jumps, and the search for a new gym begins. But while it’s easy to find a gym or sign up for classes, it’s much harder to know what makes one fitness program more effective than others. Movement alone isn’t enough. To get real results, workouts need structure, purpose and progression. That’s where progressive resistance training comes in. Progressive resistance means gradually increasing the challenge placed on the body so it has a reason to adapt. That might look like lifting slightly more weight, performing an extra repetition, slowing a movement for better control, or improving balance and stability. When challenges increase over time, the body responds by building strength, lean muscle and resilience. A common misconception is that resistance training is only for “getting big.” In reality, progressive resistance is one of the most effective tools for a broad range of goals, including weight loss Small groups and hands-on coaching combined with a progressive program encourage consistency. Personalized coaching and the latest technology help people follow – and stick to – the program. and managing important health markers such as ApoB and insulin levels. Building lean muscle helps the body burn more energy throughout the day, improves blood sugar regulation and supports fat loss, without training like a bodybuilder. For most people, the result isn’t bulky muscles, but a stronger, leaner and more efficient body that supports lasting health. Research consistently shows that structured, progressive strength training outperforms unplanned workouts. Studies have found that people following progressive resistance programs gain 20 to 40 percent more strength and significantly more lean muscle than those performing similar exercises without planned progression. Effort matters, but direction matters more, especially when time to train is limited. Without progression, the body adapts and then stops changing. You may feel tired after workouts, but strength plateaus, muscle tone stalls and weight management becomes harder. Progressive resistance gives the body a clear reason to keep improving. articles.text: A very special solo piano musical journey arranged and performed by Cristiana Pegoraro Cristiana Pegoraro will perform at the PCA on Saturday, January 31, at 7:00 p.m. The San Francisco and Philadelphia Consuls General of Italy are expected to join the audience in celebrating this Italian cultural treasure. Ms. Pegoraro will perform a selection of immortal piano masterpieces including works by Chopin, Beethoven, and Mozart, interwoven with favorite Neapolitan songs, tangos, and her own imaginative piano transcriptionas, arrangements, and compositions, and enriched by her inspiring stories that invite reflection and emotion. Back home in Narni, a town very near the exact center of Italy, Ms. Pegoraro is President of Narnia Arts Academy and serves also as Executive Director of the annual Narnia Festival, an international summer training program for singers, instrumentalists, and dancers, with extensive programs in language, culture, and leisure, all presented in English. Ms. Pegoraro has performed on the world’s most prestigious stages, including Lincoln Center, Carnegie Hall, the United Nations (NYC), the Sydney Opera House, Festspielhaus (Salzburg), Musikverein (Vienna), Royal College of Music (London), Auditorium Parco della Musica (Rome), Teatro alla Scala (Milan), and many others, and at music festivals throughout the world. The PCA concert will be followed by a reception to meet Cristiana. Join us at PCA and make this a truly memorable Saturday evening! Advance tickets may be purchased at https://events.com/r/ tickets/1023245. Limited tickets may also be available at the door.

articles.text: Exhibition on view now through March 1 Patrons view Suzanne Jackson retrospective at SFMOMA. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) exhibits the first major retrospective of painter Suzanne Jackson, entitled Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love, on display now through March 1. Organized in collaboration with the artist, the exhibition spans six decades of Jackson’s multifaceted career. Featuring more than 80 works, including paintings, drawings, and a new large-scale commission, the show explores Jackson’s novel approach to color, light, and structure, as well as her deep connection to nature, poetry, and performance. Jackson is known for her ethereal early canvases and her recent three-dimensional “floating” acrylic paintings that challenge traditional notions of painting. The exhibition also examines her interdisciplinary background as a dancer, poet, and theater designer, highlighting how these influences and her ties to radical artist communities shaped her art. “Suzanne Jackson: What Is Love promises to be a groundbreaking exhibition,” said Christopher Bedford, SFMOMA’s Helen and Charles Schwab Director. “Jackson continues to innovate by extending paint into three dimensions and embedding it with found materials to reflect on personal and cultural histories.” “Suzanne Jackson’s life has been driven by an insistent search for creative freedom and a bohemian spirit that is indebted to the San Francisco ethos in which she was raised,” added Jenny Gheith, curator of the exhibition and SFMOMA’s Interim Head of Painting and Sculpture. “What Is Love captures the curiosity, wonder and resilience of Jackson’s life’s work.” Visit sfmoma.org or call 415.357.4000 for more information. > edwardjones.com | Member SIPC Dreaming up the ideal retirement is your job. articles.text: Marin Theatre Company premieres a new production of Anton Chekhov’s classic play The Cherry Orchard tomorrow, Thursday, January 29. Directed by Carey Perloff, artistic director emerita of American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.), Chekhov’s final work centers on an aristocratic family facing the loss of its estate at the turn of the 20th century as debt threatens both their home and its famed cherry orchard. Despite looming foreclosure, the family resists practical solutions, clinging to tradition as social and economic change advances around them. Perloff returns to Marin Theatre after directing last season’s critically-acclaimed play Waste. In a press release, she said The Cherry Orchard remains one of Chekhov’s most radical plays, blending comedy and melancholy while examining why people resist necessary change. “The Cherry Orchard is one of the most radical and remarkable plays ever written about change,” Perloff said. “It’s about why change is crucial and why we always resist it. It’s incredibly funny and incredibly sad, full of narcissistic characters who are sure they’re the star of their own story, but fail to realize the damage they’re causing to the people around them. And it’s about how love is always irrational and surprising. I’m deeply grateful to Marin Theatre for giving all of us the chance to re-explore this big, juicy classic in light of our own times.” The production features a cast of Bay Area theater veterans and visiting New York actors. Lance The Cherry Orchard cast. Gardner, Marin Theatre’s executive artistic director, plays Yermolai Lopakhin, a former peasant turned businessman. Liz Sklar stars as Lyubov Ranevskaya, the indebted estate owner, with Anthony Fusco as her brother, Leonid Gayev. The cast also includes Danny Scheie, Leontyne Mbele-Mbong, Jomar Tagatac, Howard Swain, Joseph O’Malley, Rosie Hallett, Anna Takayo, Molly Ranson and Joel Morel. Photo by Chris Hardy Gardner said Chekhov’s characters are “profound and amusing,” describing them as nostalgic, hopeful and deeply flawed. The production uses Paul Schmidt’s translation. The Cherry Orchard runs January 29 through February 22 at Marin Theatre, 397 Miller Ave. in Mill Valley. Tickets range from $38 to $89, plus handling fees, and are available at MarinTheatre.org or by calling 415-388-5208.
articles.title: Marin Theatre premieres Chekhov’s The Cherry Orchard tomorrow

articles.text: Gregory Porter Jazz vocalist and two-time Grammy Award winner Gregory Porter returns to Davies Symphony Hall for a concert drawing on music from across his career as well as new material from an upcoming album. Porter was raised in Bakersfield, California, where he was influenced by gospel music, church singing and the legacy of Nat King Cole. Before turning fully to music, he studied at San Diego State University and initially pursued athletics. He began performing professionally in San Diego jazz clubs in the early 2000s, building a reputation for his rich baritone voice and thoughtful songwriting. He achieved wider recognition with his debut album “Water” in 2010 and his 2012 album “Be Good.” Both recordings earned Grammy nominations and helped establish Porter as a leading voice in contemporary jazz. He achieved broader recognition with his Blue Note debut, “Liquid Spirit,” which won the Grammy Award for best jazz vocal album in 2014 and became a commercial and critical success. Porter won a second Grammy in the same category for “Take Me to the Alley” in 2017. In addition to his original work, Porter has been widely praised for his interpretations of jazz standards. His 2017 tribute album, “Nat King Cole & Me,” paid homage to one of his earliest influences. Porter has toured internationally and performed at major jazz festivals and concert halls around the world. Porter has since received additional Grammy nominations for “Nat King Cole & Me” and for 2020’s “All Rise.” His work blends jazz with soul and gospel elements, a style shaped by his upbringing and early experiences singing with his family in community and church settings. He has toured internationally and performed at major concert halls and jazz festivals, earning praise for expanding the reach of jazz while remaining grounded in its traditions. The concert, presented by SFJAZZ, begins at 8 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/25-26/gregory-porter/ for more information and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: Gregory Porter performs at Davies Symphony Hall Feb. 22

articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet celebrates the work of choreographer and “Father of American Ballet” George Balanchine, with a specially-curated program presented in February featuring three of his signature ballets performed over a weeklong run. The program highlights Balanchine’s role in shaping ballet in the United States and offers audiences multiple opportunities to attend performances and related events throughout the week. Performances include “Diamonds,” “Serenade” and “Stars and Stripes,” tracing Balanchine’s development as a choreographer and his influence on American ballet, and are scheduled from February 10 through February 15 with evening and matinee options. “Diamonds,” set to music by Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, reflects Balanchine’s grounding in classical ballet and Russian tradition. “Serenade,” his first ballet created in the United States, is also set to Tchaikovsky and is widely regarded as a landmark work that helped establish a distinctly American ballet style. The program concludes with “Stars and Stripes,” a work set to music by John Philip Sousa that incorporates marches and patriotic themes. Photo courtesy of San Francisco Ballet The program highlights Balanchine’s role in shaping ballet in the United States. Performances begin at 7:30 p.m. on February 10, 11 and 12, and at 8 p.m. on February 13. Matinee performances are scheduled for 2 p.m. on February 14 and 15, with an additional evening performance at 8 p.m. on February 14. Post-performance activities will take place in the War Memorial Opera House lobby on select nights. Square dancing accompanied by Evie Ladin and her string band is scheduled following the February 10 and February 13 performances. Line dancing hosted by Sundance Saloon will follow performances on February 11, 12, 14 and 15. In addition to the performances, a panel discussion is scheduled for Tuesday, February 10, prior to opening night. The discussion will feature artistic director Tamara Rojo and author Elizabeth Kendall, whose books focus on Balanchine’s career and influence. The conversation will be moderated by James Steichen, author of “Balanchine and Kirstein’s American Enterprise.” Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/balanchine/ to learn more and to purchase tickets.
articles.title: SF Ballet performs Balanchine program Feb. 10 - 15

articles.text: The de Young Museum in San Francisco is presenting Boom and Bust, a photography exhibition examining cycles of growth, destruction and renewal in Northern California. The exhibition is on view now through June 2026. The exhibition traces how California has been shaped by repeated periods of opportunity and upheaval, from the Gold Rush of the 19th century to the region’s rise as a global center of technological innovation. Through photography, Boom and Bust documents how the landscape has been built, damaged and rebuilt over time. Featured works chronicle major moments in San Francisco’s history, including the city’s reconstruction following the 1906 earthquake and fire, the construction of the Golden Gate Bridge and Bay Bridge, and the development of the South of Market neighborhood. Together, the images show how urban settlement and infrastructure projects have transformed the region’s physical and social environment. The exhibition also addresses the environmental forces that continue to threaten California’s habitability, highlighting how natural disasters and human development are closely intertwined. Since the 19th century, photographers have played a key role in recording these changes, using the camera to bear witness to both progress and vulnerability. According to the museum, Boom and Bust emphasizes that periods of expansion and decline are not exceptions but recurring features of Northern California’s history. The photographs underscore the resilience of the land and its residents, illustrating how communities have adapted to repeated challenges while continuing to reshape the region. The exhibition is on display at the de Young Museum through June 2026. Visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/ boom-bust-photographing-northern-california#exhibition-preview for more information. and making it look like child’s play. Every piece was notable for sophisticated rhythms, colorful harmonies, and multifaceted subtleties. Imagination was encouraged, and it took flight. Unlike classical music, the audience is given the opportunity to applaud after each individual solo. The solos were impressive indeed. I would prefer to hear the composition in its entirety because the applause interferes with the totality. Hendelman encouraged solos from his bass player (Kevin Axt) and his drummer (Lorca Hart). Each of them responded brilliantly. I wish that classical music concerts would be as imaginative. It’s really wonderful to see each musician be encouraged to attain the summits of artistry and imagination. That’s another cool aspect of jazz. The President of Narnia Arts Academy and the Artistic Director of Narnia Festival, hailed by the New York Times as “an artist of the highest caliber,” Italian-born pianist Cristiana Pegoraro has performed on the world’s most prestigious stages, including Lincoln Center, Carnegie Hall, the United Nations (New York), the Sydney Opera House, Festspielhaus (Salzburg), Musikverein (Vienna), Royal College of Music (London), Auditorium Parco della Musica (Rome), Teatro alla Scala (Milan), and many others, and at music festivals throughout the world. articles.text: Sunday, February 8, 4:00 p.m. Carl Blake / Will Underwood Piano & Flute Duo William Underwood III performs across traditional, avant-garde, social, and sacred arenas. He holds a B.S. in Music from Florida A&M and a Master of Music in Flute Performance from Wayne State. William has toured extensively in Japan with Kyodo Tokyo and regularly works as a soloist, collaborator, and recording artist. He started playing the flute at age 11, saying the flute chose him, and has stayed with it because of the beautiful form of communication it offers, the opportunity to share in a cherished art form, and the deep lessons of confidence and growth he encountered at a young age. Dr. Carl Blake, a local piano master who has performed worldwide to constant acclaim, has happily introduced Will to the best of the Bay Area, often playing together as a duo exploring piano and flute repertoire. This concert is free to all, and donations are welcome. Thursday, February 12, 6:30 p.m. Sacha Grippando Jewelry Arts Lecture Throughout history, jewelry and watches have played a vital role in the visual arts, imbuing the wearer with power, wealth, and status. This illuminating and sparkling lecture will explore how the visual arts utilize jewelry and watches to define characters and convey specific traits. We will analyze significant works of art, ranging from paintings by masters like Leonardo Da Vinci and Vermeer to modern and contemporary artists like Salvador Dali and Kehinde Wiley. The discussion will also cover examples from popular culture, including films and TV shows such as Sunset Boulevard, Breakfast at Tiffany’s, Crazy Rich Asians, Ocean’s 8, The White Lotus, and The Gilded Age. Admission is by $20 suggested donation at the door and includes light refreshments afterwards. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, January 28, 2026 de Young Boom and Bust photo exhibit on display now through June By Allyson Aleksey The de Young Museum in San Francisco is presenting Boom and Bust, a photography exhibition examining cycles of growth, destruction and renewal in Northern California. The exhibition is on view now through June 2026. The exhibition traces how California has been shaped by repeated periods of opportunity and upheaval, from the Gold Rush of the 19th century to the region’s rise as a global center of technological innovation. Through photography, Boom and Bust documents how the landscape has been built, damaged and rebuilt over time. Featured works chronicle major moments in San Francisco’s history, including the city’s reconstruction following the 1906 earthquake and fire, the construction of the Golden Gate Bridge and Bay Bridge, and the development of the South of Market neighborhood. Together, the images show how urban settlement and infrastructure projects have transformed the region’s physical and social environment. The exhibition also addresses the environmental forces that continue to threaten California’s habitability, highlighting how natural disasters and human development are closely intertwined. Since the 19th century, photographers have played a key role in recording these changes, using the camera to bear witness to both progress and vulnerability. According to the museum, Boom and Bust emphasizes that periods of expansion and decline are not exceptions but recurring features of Northern California’s history. The photographs underscore the resilience of the land and its residents, illustrating how communities have adapted to repeated challenges while continuing to reshape the region. The exhibition is on display at the de Young Museum through June 2026. Visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/ boom-bust-photographing-northern-california#exhibition-preview for more information. articles.text: The pleasures of an innovative story ballet , P PI IE ED DM MO ON NT T, , C CA A 9 94 46 61 11 1 lies in his path -including the heart of a provincial girl Tatiana Larin; the engagement of her sister Olga; and the life of Olga’s groom Lensky, whom he kills in a duel. He finally gets himself broken when Tatiana, transformed by time and an advantageous marriage, turns away from his belated declaration of love, even as she acknowledges the persistence of her youthful feelings. Unlike many 19th century novels, where lovers are often victims of class or circumstance, the failed romance of Eugene Onegin is a matter of wrong choices and poor timing, particularly on Onegin’s part. Unable to feel deeply, he fails to recognize the real thing—Tatiana’s sincere and passionate love; when the epiphany finally arrives, it comes too late. This realistic core is what keeps the story relevant to modern sensibilities, in a world where formal obstacles to happy love stories are largely gone. The key to unhappiness, the Onegin confirms, is often hidden in ourselves. Adapting a novel in to ballet is hard. Its main currency— words—cannot be used in dance. Adapting poetry (Pushkin’s Onegin is written as a novel in verse) is harder still. Not only do you have to convey that complexity without words, but a choreographer also has to translate the poem’s rhythm, tone, and narrative intelligence into movement. In that regard, Possokhov’s Onegin is a stunning success. With a choice of scenes, the emotional intelligence of the dancers’ interpretation, and the innovative use of multimedia effects, Possokhov renders the novel’s core while steadily raising the emotional stakes for both performers and audience without losing narrative clarity. Among the ballet’s most intense sequences is Tatiana writing her letter, an iconic moment for anyone who has read the novel, in which she boldly confesses her love for Onegin, only to be rejected. Danced in the Saturday, January 24 performance by Max Cauthorn and Nikisha Fogo, the scene unfolds as a masterful crescendo of emotion. Their pas de deux begins with Tatiana leading, buoyed by the exhilaration of first love, and ends with her crushed by Onegin’s cool lecture on emotional restraint. Tatiana’s final gesture—a graceful folding of her hands over her face—is a rending moment that Fogo handles with precision and tenderness. Tatiana’s vivacious sister, Olga Larina (Isabella De Vivo), and the romantic Vladimir Lensky (Victor Prigent) are equally compelling: Lensky in the famous solo preceding the duel, where he reflects on love and fate, and Olga in the aftermath of her groom’s death, when she relinquishes her mourning black scarf after being courted by dashing officers. In her case, at least, youth and life win out and carry her away dancing. In contrast to the complexity of human feeling at the ballet’s center, the spirits of nature—who in Possokhov’s telling mark the changing seasons—provide some of the production’s most delightful interludes, as well as an opportunity to showcase the company’s roster of gifted young dancers. © San Francisco Ballet © San Francisco Ballet, photo by Lindsey Rallo Katherine Barkman and Joseph Walsh in Possokhov’s Eugene Onegin Their costumes, flaming red and orange in summer and icy blue in winter, were designed by Academy Award-winner Tim Yip (of Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon fame) whose imaginative flair and theatrical precision shape the visual world of the ballet. Yip’s work is especially effective in the two ball scenes, which alternate between the simpler styles of the Larin country estate and the taffetas and formal wear of the imperial ball in St. Petersburg. His designs are particularly arresting in Tatiana’s dream sequence, where her premonition of Lensky’s death unfolds as a phantasmagoria of animal figures: dancers wearing full sculptural animal heads, including a bear that resolves into Onegin, reminiscent of The Nutcracker’s Mouse King but far more unsettling, transforming the stage into a waking nightmare. The staging amplifies the ballet’s emotional force. Set design by Tom Pye is paired with Jim French’s lighting and Finn Ross’s projections, creating immersive environments that enhance Possokhov’s choreography. Several of Pushkin’s verses are projected onstage and underscored by a voiceover. In the final act, a vivid red backdrop gives way to a swirling storm, snow falling from above in a visual echo of Onegin’s inner turmoil. Elsewhere, metaphors are used with precision: a raven projected onto the curtain suddenly takes flight, and Onegin’s recurring black coach comes to symbolize his restless, unmoored existence. The resulting effect is brisk and cinematic, while staying true to the classical ballet language. To this drama, Ilya Demutsky’s original score provides an ideal frame, weaving Onegin’s unsettling, foreboding motifs with Tatiana’s youthful hopefulness, growing gravitas, and capacity for love. Given that Eugene Onegin is inseparable, for many audiences, from Tchaikovsky’s beloved opera score, the bar for this commission was considerable. Demutsky rises to the challenge, creating a score that gives the ballet a musical voice of its own without overwhelming it. Eugene Onegin is a bold opening note for the Company’s 93rd season, the third under the artistic leadership of Tamara Rojo. Judging by this performance, the season is her most ambitious ever, setting a tone that favors narrative clarity, emotional intelligence, and theatrical imagination as highly as technical rigor and expressive dancing for which San Francisco Ballet is known. Eugene Onegin will be onstage at the War Memorial Opera House until February 1. articles.text: Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed another clear, sunny morning for its weekly walk last Wednesday, with a strong turnout of 47 walkers and four canine companions gathering at the Exedra to begin the route. The previous week, walkers had briefly discussed Frank C. Havens and F.M. “Borax” Smith’s Realty Syndicate, formed in 1895, and Smith’s role in acquiring streetcar lines beginning in 1890 to establish the Key System transit network. This week’s walk looked further back in time, focusing on an earlier and often overlooked figure whose vision and enterprise helped shape what would later become the City of Piedmont. That figure was Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area. Blair Avenue bears his name, and his story was shared with the walkers using material from Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website and a past Piedmont Post article by Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi. Blair arrived in San Francisco from Vermont in 1852 during the Gold Rush, at the age of 22, and settled in Alameda County the following year. In 1853, he purchased approximately 600 acres in the Piedmont hills, land that had been part of the original Vicente Peralta Spanish land grant. Blair bought the property from the U.S. government for $1.25 an acre, a total of $750. The land extended from what is now the Mountain View Cemetery wall along Moraga Avenue to Scenic, Magnolia, and Grand avenues. The cemetery itself came later, established in 1863 and opened in 1865. Blair initially camped on the land before building a one-room cabin near a freshwater spring at what is today 111 Highland Avenue. He named the street “Vernal Avenue,” inspired by the lush ferns and shrubs that grew nearby. In 1862, Blair married fellow Vermont native Phoebe Harvey. The couple had two daughters, and Blair built a larger ranching visitors seeking health benefits. One notable guest was Mark Twain, who sampled the waters in 1871. The hotel was considered one of the finest resorts in California at the time. It featured 20 bedrooms and five dining rooms. The main dining room, which could seat 35 guests, was adorned with a crystal chandelier, fine china, and velvet drapes. The hotel met a tragic end in 1892, when sparks from its chimney ignited the roof and the building burned to the ground. Transportation was another of Blair’s major contributions to the region. In 1875, he partnered with other investors to build the Broadway & Piedmont Horsecar Line. Construction began in April of that year, and the line officially opened in 1876. It ran from downtown Oakland up Broadway to Piedmont Avenue and Mountain View Cemetery, providing transit for residents and bringing potential property buyers to the Piedmont hills. In 1878, Blair went a step further by building his own horsecar line, the first to transport visitors directly from Oakland into Piedmont. The cars ran hourly along Moraga Avenue, beginning at the terminus of the Piedmont Avenue line at the gates of Mountain View Cemetery. From there, they traveled through Blair’s fields to Vernal Avenue and the Piedmont Springs Hotel. In 1884, Blair developed a 75-acre amusement park in Moraga Canyon known as Blair’s Park. The park was designed to attract riders to his streetcar lines. Visitors could sail small boats, ride ponies, watch acrobats suspended from hot air balloons, picnic near waterfalls, and listen to music. This original Blair Park should not be confused with the open area on Moraga Avenue above Highland Avenue that many people today associate with the name. Many visitors who picnicked at the park or stayed at the hotel later purchased land, built homes, and became some of Piedmont’s earliest residents. Blair moved to downtown Oakland later in life and lived at the Centennial Hotel, which he built Walter Blair’s portrait style home with formal gardens to accommodate his growing family. This homestead stood on what is now Waldo Avenue. The house remained until 1924 and was demolished in 1926 to make way for Waldo Avenue itself. Blair was a farmer and dairyman by trade. His dairy farm occupied the southwest corner of what are now El Cerrito and Blair avenues, with pastures extending to Grand Avenue. The dairy supplied milk and butter to surrounding communities and to San Francisco. Blair also raised cattle and planted wheat and barley on his land. Shortly after arriving in the area, Blair developed a quarry in the early 1850s, located diagonally across from his dairy. He sold rock from the quarry to pave streets in Oakland and Piedmont. The quarry site is now Dracena Park, and some of its stone can still be found in Mountain View Cemetery, where it was used for gravestones. When the quarry filled with water around 1890, operations ceased, and it became a popular swimming hole for local boys. Reports later surfaced of drownings in the 1920s, after which the city partially filled the quarry with construction debris. Blair’s interests extended beyond agriculture. He became involved in real estate development and hospitality, building the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1872 near Bushy Dell Creek, where natural sulfur springs bubbled from the ground.
