articles.title: Following Walter Blair: a walking tour of Piedmont’s origins

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, January 28, 2026 Features Walking on Wednesday By Dick Carter Walking on Wednesdays group enjoyed another clear, sunny morning for its weekly walk last Wednesday, with a strong turnout of 47 walkers and four canine companions gathering at the Exedra to begin the route. The previous week, walkers had briefly discussed Frank C. Havens and F.M. “Borax” Smith’s Realty Syndicate, formed in 1895, and Smith’s role in acquiring streetcar lines beginning in 1890 to establish the Key System transit network. This week’s walk looked further back in time, focusing on an earlier and often overlooked figure whose vision and enterprise helped shape what would later become the City of Piedmont. That figure was Walter Blair, the first European settler in the area. Blair Avenue bears his name, and his story was shared with the walkers using material from Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website and a past Piedmont Post article by Piedmont Historical Society president Gail Lombardi. Blair arrived in San Francisco from Vermont in 1852 during the Gold Rush, at the age of 22, and settled in Alameda County the following year. In 1853, he purchased approximately 600 acres in the Piedmont hills, land that had been part of the original Vicente Peralta Spanish land grant. Blair bought the property from the U.S. government for $1.25 an acre, a total of $750. The land extended from what is now the Mountain View Cemetery wall along Moraga Avenue to Scenic, Magnolia, and Grand avenues. The cemetery itself came later, established in 1863 and opened in 1865. Blair initially camped on the land before building a one-room cabin near a freshwater spring at what is today 111 Highland Avenue. He named the street “Vernal Avenue,” inspired by the lush ferns and shrubs that grew nearby. In 1862, Blair married fellow Vermont native Phoebe Harvey. The couple had two daughters, and Blair built a larger ranchFollowing Walter Blair: a walking tour of Piedmont’s origins ing visitors seeking health benefits. One notable guest was Mark Twain, who sampled the waters in 1871. The hotel was considered one of the finest resorts in California at the time. It featured 20 bedrooms and five dining rooms. The main dining room, which could seat 35 guests, was adorned with a crystal chandelier, fine china, and velvet drapes. The hotel met a tragic end in 1892, when sparks from its chimney ignited the roof and the building burned to the ground. Transportation was another of Blair’s major contributions to the region. In 1875, he partnered with other investors to build the Broadway & Piedmont Horsecar Line. Construction began in April of that year, and the line officially opened in 1876. It ran from downtown Oakland up Broadway to Piedmont Avenue and Mountain View Cemetery, providing transit for residents and bringing potential property buyers to the Piedmont hills. In 1878, Blair went a step further by building his own horsecar line, the first to transport visitors directly from Oakland into Piedmont. The cars ran hourly along Moraga Avenue, beginning at the terminus of the Piedmont Avenue line at the gates of Mountain View Cemetery. From there, they traveled through Blair’s fields to Vernal Avenue and the Piedmont Springs Hotel. In 1884, Blair developed a 75-acre amusement park in Moraga Canyon known as Blair’s Park. The park was designed to attract riders to his streetcar lines. Visitors could sail small boats, ride ponies, watch acrobats suspended from hot air balloons, picnic near waterfalls, and listen to music. This original Blair Park should not be confused with the open area on Moraga Avenue above Highland Avenue that many people today associate with the name. Many visitors who picnicked at the park or stayed at the hotel later purchased land, built homes, and became some of Piedmont’s earliest residents. Blair moved to downtown Oakland later in life and lived at the Centennial Hotel, which he built Walter Blair’s portrait style home with formal gardens to accommodate his growing family. This homestead stood on what is now Waldo Avenue. The house remained until 1924 and was demolished in 1926 to make way for Waldo Avenue itself. Blair was a farmer and dairyman by trade. His dairy farm occupied the southwest corner of what are now El Cerrito and Blair avenues, with pastures extending to Grand Avenue. The dairy supplied milk and butter to surrounding communities and to San Francisco. Blair also raised cattle and planted wheat and barley on his land. Shortly after arriving in the area, Blair developed a quarry in the early 1850s, located diagonally across from his dairy. He sold rock from the quarry to pave streets in Oakland and Piedmont. The quarry site is now Dracena Park, and some of its stone can still be found in Mountain View Cemetery, where it was used for gravestones. When the quarry filled with water around 1890, operations ceased, and it became a popular swimming hole for local boys. Reports later surfaced of drownings in the 1920s, after which the city partially filled the quarry with construction debris. Blair’s interests extended beyond agriculture. He became involved in real estate development and hospitality, building the Piedmont Springs Hotel in 1872 near Bushy Dell Creek, where natural sulfur springs bubbled from the ground. The waters were believed to have curative properties, attractBlair Quarry photo in 1876 at 14th and Clay streets. He died suddenly in 1888 at the age of 57 from complications related to diabetes and was buried in Mountain View Cemetery. After his death, Blair’s widow and business associates formed the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company. The company began cable service in 1890, replacing the horsecar line. Financial difficulties followed, and the system was reorganized, electrified, and ultimately absorbed into the Key System by 1904. Blair’s Park was abandoned in 1901, leaving the land vacant for several years. Development resumed in 1917, when new homes were built on the site. Builder Guy Turner constructed 11 bungalows along the cemetery side of Moraga Avenue, with at least six more added in 1922. Standing at the Exedra, the walkers were at the site of the former Piedmont Springs Hotel. From there, they traced the route of Blair’s horse-drawn line and the edges of his former park. The group walked down Highland Avenue to Moraga Avenue, stopping in front of the home of longtime Fourth of July Parade announcer Patty Edmonds for a group photo. Edmonds noticed the group and came outside to take the picture herself. Across Moraga Avenue, the walkers could see where the arched entrance to Blair’s Park once stood. The group continued down Moraga Avenue, observing the homes built by Turner a century ago. At the end of the long wall bordering Mountain View Cemetery, they crossed Moraga and walked the quiet, one-way Oakland portion of Ramona Avenue. At the street’s end on Piedmont Avenue was the starting point where Blair’s trolley cars once began their climb toward Vernal, now Highland, Avenue. Across the street, walkers paused to admire the Chapel of the Chimes mausoleum, founded in 1909 as the California Electric Crematory and Columbarium. A major expansion in 1928 and 1929, designed by Julia Morgan, added the ornate mausoleum, gardens, and architectural details seen today. The group then walked up Piedmont Avenue toward Pleasant Valley Road and took a hidden path between 4476 and 4464 Piedmont Avenue. The path cuts across the horseshoe-shaped North and South Pleasant Valley Court to Pleasant Valley Avenue. Across the street, a group of preschoolers waved as they set out on their own Wednesday walk. From there, the walkers continued to Arroyo Avenue, down the newly repaved York Drive, and up a path leading to Ricardo Avenue and the base of Dracena Park, the site of Blair’s former quarry. The group climbed the steep 100 block of El Cerrito Avenue to Blair Avenue, once home to Blair’s dairy, then continued along Hillside and Magnolia avenues before returning to the Exedra. The approximately three-anda-half-mile loop offered walkers a living history lesson, tracing the land, enterprises, and vision of Walter Blair and his lasting impact on Piedmont. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or contact (510) 420- 3070 for more information Among those on hand were Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Gwen, Alicia Rivera, Dave DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Cathy Laymon, Gloria DaSilva, Betsy Lim, Debbie Powell, Ken Moy, Alissa Quan, Peggy Shultz, Edith Lee, Caskey Weston, Albert Chen, Chuck Oraftik, Phil Witte, Jeff Kasmar, Julia Chin, Jim Kuo, Helen Dong, Denny McGee, Hulda Nelson, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best Kojak, Audrey Sung, Mike Gallant, Tina Shum, Quincy Dong, Stella Houston, Deborah Curtin, Bill Ahern, Marcia Arthurs, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Judy Sokoloff, Ken Hubbert, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Liz Dalrymple, Phil Chin with K-9 best friend Rocky, Mary Ann Barnes, Irene Thompson, Melba Yee, Bonnie Sherwood with K-9 best friend Zippy, Karen Palmer, Jasmin Cai, Shirley Nakao, Dan Scdoris, Brenda Ferrero, and Dick Carter. articles.text: Historic Buena Vista Winery was built in 1857 Buena Vista Winery in Sonoma, California holds a remarkable place in American wine history. It is one of the oldest premium wineries in the state, founded in 1857 by the intrepid Count Agoston Haraszthy. Often considered the “father of California viticulture,” Haraszthy was an Hungarian immigrant, adventurer, and visionary who brought European winegrowing ambition to the young American West. He established Buena Vista at a time when Napa and Sonoma were hardly known for wine at all. He believed California had the potential to rival the great vineyards of Europe, and he spared no effort in importing hundreds of vinifera grape varieties and innovating early wine production techniques. The winery’s early years were as colorful as its founder: Haraszthy’s life spanned roles as a sheriff in Southern California, a pioneer of modern viticulture, and a tragic figure whose death in Nicaragua, falling into a river and being devoured by an alligator, became part of wine lore. Through boom, bust, phylloxera, and Prohibition, Buena Vista endured — though not without interruptions. In the 20th century, the estate passed through various owners, and much of its historic site fell into disrepair before renewed interest in its legacy emerged. In May 2011, Jean-Charles Boisset and the Boisset Family Estates acquired Buena Vista Winery, marking a new era for the storied property. Boisset’s family winery group — rooted in Burgundy, France and known for crafting wines around the world — brought fresh energy, respect for heritage, and investment to restore Buena Vista’s historic structures, including its mid- 19th-century press house and underground wine caves. Under his stewardship, Buena Vista blends tradition with modern hospitality, positioning the estate as both a tribute to California’s wine pioneers and a vibrant tasting destination. Today, visitors can explore Buena Vista’s historic press house, experience guided tastings, and enjoy exhibits that illuminate its role in American wine history. The winery produces an array of expressions — from cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay sourced in Carneros to Carignane, Syrah, French Colombard, and other varietals — reflecting both its deep roots and contemporary winemakBuena Vista Winery 18000 Old Winery Rd. In the news Remember when we used to smoke in our homes? The state now requires we disclose it. AB 455, signed into law October 3, 2025, places sole responsibility on sellers to disclose any actual knowledge of thirdhand smoke residue or history of tobacco use on the property—in writing. The law applies to all sales, exchanges, and real property sales contracts. In addition to firsthand (you) or secondhand (your guests) smoking, you now must disclose any knowledge of thirdhand smoke as of January 2026. For example, my fond memory of my grandmother Mary Loretta surreptitiously smoking Marlboro Reds, with Stella her schnauzer, outside the kitchen entrance of her house is not only nostalgia but also a trigger for mandatory disclosure. Reader question This week’s reader question is best encapsulated by the National Association of Realtors® Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice: Article 3 REALTORS® shall cooperate with other brokers except when cooperation is not in the client’s best interest... (Amended 1/95) Q: I am interviewing real estate agents, and one is telling me to get work done with their concierge service and pay for staging but doesn’t want to put my house on the MLS. She’s very successful, but how do I know I’m getting the best price? Why stage it or do any work if it isn’t going on the market? A: Sounds like the agent is pushing the concierge service and staging hard, fine. That part usually makes sense. But recommending not marketing your home on the MLS? That’s where you should start asking questions. The MLS isn’t an outdated relic; it’s the main stage where nearly all buyers and agents look first. Data shows homes on the MLS sell for 17 to 19 percent more. Unless the agent’s secret network of unicorn buyers is ready to swoop in and pay market price, you’re about to leave serious money on the table. Ask them how long this “private” phase lasts and if they don’t have an answer that satisfies you, don’t be afraid to shop for someone who understands that “exclusive” shouldn’t mean “exclusive to a tiny, invisible audience.” Bottom line, staging is about making buyers fall in love, but MLS exposure is what Article 3 is talking about. Cooperation is how you get buyers in the door. If you aren’t seeing transparency or a realistic strategy to reach a broad audience, push back or keep interviewing agents. There are quite a few who’ll actually put you in the best position to get top dollar. Did you know Piedmont just had a big birthday, 119 years old, January 26, 2026! articles.text: Eleanor Moore, 94, of Piedmont, California, passed away peacefully on October 23, 2025. A devoted wife, mother, grandmother, and beloved member of her community, Eleanor will be remembered for her kind spirit, her radiant smile, and her unwavering optimism. Born on January 24, 1931, in San Jose, California, Eleanor was the second child of William Bailey and Ethel Hjelm. She grew up in Lompoc, California alongside her older brother Earl. When she was just 5 years old, the unexpected passing of her father, left her and her brother to be raised by their devoted mother, a school teacher. Eleanor attended Lompoc High School and graduated from UCLA with a degree in geography, a field that reflected her fascination with travel, cultures and the wider world. Following a memorable mother-daughter graduation trip to Europe — traveling by train and boat — she returned to Lompoc, where she married James Moore, the brother of her best friend from high school. After their wedding, Jim worked in the Bay Area and Eleanor relocated to Oakland, eventually moving to Piedmont in 1964. Together, they raised two children, Bill and Marilyn. Their partnership was grounded in love, laughter and shared adventures, and they enjoyed a wonderMerritt Peralta Foundation where she was a board member, as well as the East Bay Zoological Society Foundation and the Cancer League. She was a member of the Claremont Country Club, the Bellevue Club, and the Piedmont Community Church. Eleanor also enjoyed engaging her mind as a member — and often treasurer — of various investment clubs, where her keen interest in the stock market met her sharp intellect. Yet, no matter how busy her calendar, she always found time for bridge, travel, and time with family and friends. An avid traveler, Eleanor and Jim visited all seven continents together, collecting memories, friendships and stories along the way. Eleanor is survived by her son Bill Moore (Monica Cardoni), her daughter, Marilyn Moore Weber, and her three grandchildren: Jim and John Weber and Shannon Moore. She is predeceased by her husband Jim, her brother Earl and her son-in-law Bill Weber. Kind, generous, and adventurous, Eleanor brightened every room she entered. Her example of empathy, honesty, and grace will remain a lasting legacy to all who knew her. A private service was held in her honor. In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to the Oakland Museum, the Oakland Zoo or a charity of your choice. Eleanor Moore passed away peacefully on Oct. 23, 2025. ful marriage that lasted over 50 years. Eleanor’s deep commitment to community and service was reflected in her extensive volunteer work. She served as president of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board and was a familiar, welcoming face in the cashier’s booth at the museum’s White Elephant Sale. Among her proudest accomplishments during her tenure at the Oakland Museum were her key role in purchasing and securing a permanent warehouse for their annual fundraiser and her collaboration with Senator Nick Petris to create and pass a state bill that exempted the Museum’s White Elephant sale from sales tax. At the young age of fourteen, Louise began to hone her legendary fashion expertise at the spectacular I. Magnin department store in San Francisco’s Union Square. The encounter was happenstance and began with Bill inquiring if Louise owned the establishment, to which she confidently replied, “No, I just walk around like I own everything!” For those who were fortunate enough to know her, she had quite the presence and navigated her journey in a take charge/ make anything happen type of manner! A rather brief courtship ensued and six months later Bill and Louise were married. Shortly thereafter, the birth of their daughter Lauren completed their family. Bill and Louise remained lovingly dedicated to one another for 51 years! For many years, Louise managed clothing boutiques in San Francisco, and in 1978 with the encouragement of her husband she opened her own boutique, eponymously named ‘Louise’ on Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. Louise held steadfast to the belief that her passion for fashion was not solely reliant upon the garments but how the designs made her clientele feel. She was known to abstain from pursuing a sale if her client(s) did not feel fabulous in the garment. The year 1978 was an impactful time for women as they were entering and moving forward in what were previously male-dominated fields. Numerous clients were ‘firsts’ in their fields: doctors, lawyers, businesswomen, scientists, etc., who sought to break free from the socialized standards and norms of dressing in the expected fashion of the skirt suit and were inspired by the daring pantsuit, to which Louise introduced and encouraged women to wear with pride. In-house tailoring, purchasing from small manufacturers and artisans, catering to her clients’ achievements and upcoming events created a depth of trust and a curated experience for her clients, thus allowing them to feel the utmost care and consideration from Louise’s boutique. She preferred wearing a tailored ‘uniform’ consisting of her favorite color, black on black, in order for her “clientele to shine”! All were welcomed, including children who had access to baskets of toys and books to provide entertainment while their parent shopped. Due to the ‘come one come all’ nature of her store, her clients, and community at large, often referred to Louise as the Cheers of women’s fashion! In addition, Louise volunteered her time as the vice president of the Piedmont Avenue Merchants Association, working tirelessly to ensure the Avenue was predominantly occupied by small businesses. Following the closure of Louise’s boutique in the mid-1990s, she was forever approached by former clients declaring their love of her store, her personalized and dedicated approach, and her keen eye. Louise continued dressing her community by becoming a personal clothing consultant and a volunteer at Dress Best for Less. In addition to her love of fashion, sports, and being an avid reader, Louise was a lifelong advocate. Her advocacy began as a young woman when she joined Civil Rights marches and continued for the rest of her life by contacting, at times daily, our local and national representatives to voice her unwavering opinion(s) and commitments to justice. In her honor, please use your voice! Call the General Capitol Switchboard at: 202.224.3121 and ask to be connected to your local representative. While Louise’s bright and magnetic presence is greatly missed, her fabulous memory will be honored by her husband Bill, daughter Lauren, sister-in-law Rita, sister-in-law Jane, brother in-law Gene, nephew Jake, niecein-law Sarah, her close friends and extended community. Since the late 20th century, many women have embraced strength training for its visible benefits—a leaner, stronger physique. What wasn’t fully understood at the time were the far broader effects of progressive strength training on long-term health. Studies conducted over the past thirty years have shown that regular strength training can also: • Increase metabolic efficiency • Improve glucose control and insulin sensitivity • Support brain health and cognitive function • Enhance focus, mood, and resilience Today, many health and fitness professionals consider strength training a non-negotiable foundation of healthy aging. Yet one crucial question lingered for years: Could post-menopausal women safely gain these benefits, especially when it comes to bone health? The answer is a clear and confident YES. The science confirms that progressive strength training—when combined with impact training (activities such as controlled jumping and firm landings)— places healthy stress on bones, stimulating ossification (bone formation). A couple of important studies brought this into focus: • A 2011 randomized controlled trial found that post-menopausal breast cancer survivors who engaged in moderate-intensity resistance training plus impact training improved both lumbar spine bone density and lean muscle mass, compared to a low-intensity stretching group. • The landmark LIFTMOR study (Australia, 2017) took a bolder approach, testing an eight-month, supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training program in post-menopausal women with low bone mass. Participants experienced significant gains in lumbar spine bone mineral density, femoral neck (hip) bone strength, and functional strength and balance. Importantly, these benefits occurred even without hormone replacement therapy. The takeaway is powerful and encouraging: Women of all ages— including peri- and post-menopausal women—can safely build strength, protect their bones, and enhance long-term health through progressive strength and impact training. As with all training, outcomes are influenced by nutrition, genetics, hormone levels, post-exercise recovery practices, and other factors. Mia Honore and Mark Sutro founded CRUfit Montclair in 2013. CRUfit offers a diverse mix of group classes, small group training and personal training to meet the fitness needs of all ages. This philosophy is central to modern strength-based training approaches, including programs like BodyFit Training, where workouts are designed to build on one another over time rather than repeating the same routine week after week or randomly choosing exercises. As exercise physiologist Dr. Andy Galpin explains, “The goal of training isn’t to get tired — it’s to create a specific adaptation.” Why this matters: Strength training supports metabolic health, preserves bone density and improves sleep and mental well-being. It has also become especially important as more people use GLP-1-based weightloss medications, which can reduce both fat and muscle when strength training is not prioritized. Progressive resistance helps protect lean muscle during weight loss, supporting healthier, more sustainable outcomes. Strength isn’t just about how you look. It’s about managing weight, moving well and staying independent for life. articles.text: Piedmont police received an alert from the Oakland Police Department of a police chase entering Piedmont city limits early in the morning of Tuesday, January 20. A stolen white 2011 Mitsubishi Lancer was being pursued by OPD patrol vehicles following an armed high jacking with a rifle. The vehicle was first reported in the area of Pacific Avenue at 4:00 a.m. and then continued onto Highland and down Wildwood to Palm. OPD authorized the use of road spikes by PPD officers but the suspect did not go onto the street with the tack strips. The stolen vehicle eventually turned onto El Cerrito and attempted to enter Witter Field at the El Cerrito gate, which was locked. The vehicle became wedged under the gate and the driver fled on foot. The suspect, Carleton Ferguson, was apprehended and arrested by OPD at 4:16 a.m. He was charged with carjacking, possession of a firearm, and evading police. The rifle was recovered and a female passenger was detained. The driver was taken to a hospital. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has provided a much-needed update on the Community Pool. Since the project’s last update in November, isolated system testing has been completed, and the project has moved into its final phase of the commissioning process. During the final phase, the contractors will conduct a “functional” system testing process. They run all the core systems together and monitor them to ensure the systems are working properly. This process will be conducted over an extended period of time until the contractors believe the systems are ready for operation. Communications Officer Echa Schneider informed the Post that the commissioning process will not always be linear. “When testing identifies gaps, the steps needed to address the issue can range from simple software calibration to hardware modifications. After these steps are taken, the system must then be retested and validated, and the cycle begins again. Each cycle of calibration, adjustments, and testing involves monitoring across multiday datasets,” said Schneider. The City plans to commit to increased transparency regarding the project’s status. articles.text: The Havens Dads Club hosted its 18th annual Poker Night on Friday, Jan. 9, at Veterans Hall, raising $66,500 for the school. The final hand of the Texas Hold’em tournament was won by Wildwood dad Patrice Fayet, who held a king of hearts and a four of diamonds. Havens mom Julie Moravy finished in second place. All proceeds from the event went directly to the school, surpassing last year’s total by $4,000. About 130 players took part in the tournament, with an additional 20 attendees purchasing social-only tickets. The evening ran from the first card dealt at 6:30 p.m. through the excitement of the final eight-player table. “The team and I try to dial up the fun factor,” said Havens Dads Club President Ted Kinch. “People can give money because charity demands it or because the school needs funding — or they can play some poker.” Poker Night organizing committee members included Andrew Johnson, Andy Meakins, Babak Sanii, Brandon Bercovich, Kyle Killian, Mike Cvet, and Kinch. This year, the team introduced a perpetual trophy engraved with the names of past winners, with space to add future champions in the years ahead. Players and guests enjoyed food from Robert Dorsey Catering, Arthur Mac Pizza, and Top Dog, along with a full bar. New Photo by Babak Sanii Patice Fayet, winner of the 2026 Havens Poker Tournament.

articles.text: International speaker Janet Hegarty, a Christian Science practitioner and member of the Christian Science Board of Lectureship, will host a talk at 2 p.m. on January 25 at the Christian Science Reading Room, 3976 Piedmont Avenue, Oakland. Metered street parking is available. AC transit lines 12 or 57 can be taken to access the event’s location. In her free talk titled “How to Make Change for the Better,” Hegarty will share powerful, spiritual tools to address the variety of challenging issues facing us all. Her ideas are from the Bible and are practiced in a prayerbased method of healing called Christian Science, founded a century ago by spiritual healer Mary Baker Eddy, who herself faced poverty and lack of stable housing over many years. This talk is open to anyone seeking fresh ideas to help themselves or others. It is sponsored by First Church of Christ, Scientist, Oakland, and will be simulcast on Zoom at zoom.us/j/94684138210. articles.text: The California Public Utilities Commission has published the Final Environmental Impact Report for Pacific Gas and Electric Company’s Moraga-Oakland X 115-kilovolt Rebuild Project. The Final Environmental Impact Report evaluates potentially significant environmental impacts associated with the project and identifies mitigation measures and alternatives that would avoid or reduce those impacts. After the release of the Final Environmental Impact Report, a CPUC administrative law judge will prepare a proposed decision and present the project to the commission. Commissioners will then consider whether to certify the Environmental Impact Report as meeting the requirements of the California Environmental Quality Act and whether to grant PG&E a Permit to Construct. No construction timeline has been set, and work cannot begin until the CPUC completes this process. The Moraga-Oakland X project proposes upgrades to approximately five miles of four existing 115-kilovolt transmission lines between the Moraga and Oakland X substations. The route passes through the City of Orinda, unincorporated areas of Contra Costa County, the cities of Oakland and Piedmont, and existing PG&E utility rights-of-way. Within Piedmont, the project would remain within an existing PG&E transmission corridor. Any work in the city would occur along current rights-of-way rather than new routes. The project would rebuild the four overhead transmission lines into four hybrid lines, with approximately four miles remaining overhead and about one mile placed underground. Existing towers, poles, and conductors would be replaced with either overhead or underground components, and minor modifications would be made at existing substations. The rebuild would also include the installation of optical ground wire on aboveground structures, with a communications cable continuing through the underground segments. The Final Environmental Impact Report and related documents are available on the CPUC project website at https://bit. ly/49IGwZB.
articles.title: Final EIR for PG&E’s Moraga-Oakland X 115 kV Rebuild Project

articles.text: City Council will consider adopting a resolution in compliance with California’s Surplus Land Act at its meeting on Tuesday, Jan. 20. Approval would allow the city to take the next step toward implementing the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. Before a city can lease or sell public property, it must follow the requirements of the Surplus Land Act. Recent amendments to the law are intended to promote affordable housing development on surplus public land statewide as a response to California’s housing shortage. The act provides two possible pathways for disposing of land: an “exempt” or a “non-exempt” declaration. Planning and Building Director Kevin Jackson outlined the differences between the two approaches in a press release issued earlier this week. For non-exempt sites, the state sets the process for notifying developers, establishes negotiation parameters and determines which developers receive preference, leaving the city with limited control. For exempt sites, the city has greater flexibility to select a developer based on local criteria, but the pathway comes with deeper Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson on the video discussing the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan affordable housing requirements. In practice, this generally means a higher share of units must be reserved for lower-income households and remain affordable for longer periods than under the standard non-exempt process. Jackson wrote that the exempt option aligns with the goals of the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. “These deeper affordability requirements associated with an ‘exempt’ determination are consistent with the affordable housing targets that already exist in the adopted Specific Plan,” Jackson said. In December, the California Department of Housing and Community Development confirmed that a Moraga Canyon project would qualify for an exempt determination. City Council is now considering a resolution to pursue that path in order to retain greater local control. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan remains controversial among some residents living along Moraga Avenue. Several households have posted signs expressing concern about traffic and safety, particularly for children biking along the roadway. In response, the city has released an informational video addressing these concerns, available on the City of Piedmont’s YouTube channel at https://bit. ly/4r5vHYP The sign showing displeasure with the housing plan, placed in front of a house on Moraga Avenue Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Protesters hold signs and stand in opposition to Trump’s second presidential term. A small group of protesters gathered at the Exedra at 2 p.m. on Tuesday, Jan. 20, to protest President Trump and what they described as “an escalating fascist threat.” Nationwide, more than 1,200 “Free America” walkouts were organized that day by Women’s March. Protesters carried signs opposing the Trump presidency and the changes they say have occurred during his time in office. “On January 20 at 2 p.m. local time, we will walk out of work, school, and commerce. We will withhold our labor, our participation, and our consent. A free America begins the moment we refuse to cooperate,” the Women’s March website states. Piedmont’s protest was small Piedmont’s Free America Walkout protesters stood on the street in front of the Exedra. but grew over the course of the hour, with passersby stopping to join and drivers honking in support. Participants spoke among themselves about what motivated them to attend. “It’s really everything — nothing works now. I can’t believe it’s only one year in,” said physicist Pitra Specht. “I was naturalized in 2011, and one of the questions on the test required us to know that no one is above the law. They don’t follow that in the White House.” Specht said her top concerns include the lack of universal health care, ICE raids, the weakening of environmental protections, and what she described as the killing of people without consequence. Her husband, physicist Christian Kisielowski, said he is worried the current situation in the country may not be easily repairable. Larger “Free America Walkout” protests were held throughout the day at Lake Merritt and San Francisco Civic Center. To learn more visit Action.womensmarch.com
articles.title: Piedmont’s “Free America” Walkout

articles.text: Dream and Padrick are a bonded pair with a gentle connection and a shared love of calm routines. Dream, four, is thoughtful and observant, taking her time to warm up. Once she feels safe, her playful and confident side emerges. Padrick, three, is her steady companion—gentle, curious and just a bit braver—helping Dream feel secure as they explore together. Both cats enjoy daily playtime with wand toys, occasional bursts of zoomies, and long hours of birdwatching and sunbathing. Dream loves a good chase and a well-earned treat, while Padrick is known for his soft purrs and polite way of asking for Churu, sometimes resting a paw on your hand. They nap together, play side by side and happily share sunny spots. They are seeking a calm, indoor-only home with an adopter who respects feline Cats of the Week: Dream & Padrick boundaries and understands that trust takes time. With patience and routine, Dream and Padrick offer quiet companionship and rewarding moments of connection. Dream and Padrick are spayed/neutered, vaccinated, microchipped, and negative for FeLV and FIV. Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@cattownoakland.org.
articles.title: Adoptable Cat of the Week

articles.text: Archie and Edith are available for adoption at Oakland Animal Services Meet Archie and Edith, the sweetest senior duo. They are a bonded pair of gentle, 7-year-old Chihuahua mixes who have survived tough beginnings and are now ready for the soft, loving home they have always deserved. Timid at first, they become incredibly sweet, loyal and oh-so lovable once they learn to trust you. This pair has peacefully coexisted with other small dogs in the shelter and absolutely adores one another. Their foster reports that they have been easy to train and are now housetrained. Archie and Edith are looking for a quiet, adults-only home where they can stay together. If you are searching for an affectionate, low-key duo who will adore you and keep a watchful eye on the neighborhood, this pair could be your perfect match. Follow them in foster with @mooncakesmom on Instagram. Submit your adoption questionnaire online at Oakland Animal Services to meet the pair and you will be contacted by their foster who can arrange a meet-and-greet. articles.text: Record breaking dollar amounts and participation Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has announced that this year’s Giving Campaign has raised more than $4,000,000 in gifts and pledges in support of Piedmont’s public schools. This represents an increase of 9% over last year and is the strongest Giving Campaign in history. Kim Hunter and Catie Osborn have led the Giving Campaign for the past three years, raising increasing amounts each year, totalling over $11,000,000 for Piedmont’s public schools. When asked about their success, Osborn shared, “Our community gets it. We’ve all seen the increasing costs of living and doing business, and the increasing needs of our schools. We know what we want for our kids and our community is here to meet those needs.” Hunter added, “It seems to me that the community made a really loud statement this year about what is important. The Giving Campaign exists to continue the betterment of our public schools, and that’s something we have control over. Our community has been showing up for our schools for 50 years and we’ll keep showing up for 50 more.” So far this year, PEF has received gifts and pledges from 1,161 households, the highest number of donor households since 2022. Parent participation is currently at 61%; the final total will be calculated at the end of June as donors will have until then to make their Giving Campaign contribution for the year. The Giving Campaign would like to congratulate the 1st grade families for winning the class participation challenge with 79% overall participation. 3rd grade families came in second place with 74%. Across schools, Beach has the highest participation at 76% followed by Havens at 73%, Wildwood at 68%, PMS at 58% and PHS/MHS at 50%. Approximately $300,000 of Giving Campaign contributions are donor designated to the endowment fund. At the end of the school year, PEF will add the remaining $3.7 million to the endowment distribution and other fundraisers, subtract expenses, and grant those funds to PUSD for the 2026-27 academic year. A survey will be released this spring to ascertain parent funding priorities for the grant. PEF thanks everyone that made a contribution, reached out to their company as part of the corporate matching program, contributed via DAF, and talked to neighbors and friends about the importance of The Giving Campaign. Every single donation, no matter the amount, supports the students and the schools. Catie Osborn (left) and Kim Hunter, chairs of the 2025-26 Giving Campaign, celebrate surpassing $4 million for Piedmont schools.
articles.title: PEF Giving Campaign surpasses $4 million

PEF Giving Campaign surpasses $4 million Record breaking dollar amounts and participation Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) has announced that this year’s Giving Campaign has raised more than $4,000,000 in gifts and pledges in support of Piedmont’s public schools. This represents an increase of 9% over last year and is the strongest Giving Campaign in history. Kim Hunter and Catie Osborn have led the Giving Campaign for the past three years, raising increasing amounts each year, totalling over $11,000,000 for Piedmont’s public schools. When asked about their success, Osborn shared, “Our community gets it. We’ve all seen the increasing costs of living and doing business, and the increasing needs of our schools. We know what we want for our kids and our community is here to meet those needs.” Hunter added, “It seems to me that the community made a really loud statement this year about what is important. The Giving Campaign exists to continue the betterment of our public schools, and that’s something we have control over. Our community has been showing up for our schools for 50 years and we’ll keep showing up for 50 more.” So far this year, PEF has received gifts and pledges from 1,161 households, the highest number of donor households since 2022. Parent participation is currently at 61%; the final total will be calculated at the end of June as donors will have until then to make their Giving Campaign contribution for the year. The Giving Campaign would like to congratulate the 1st grade families for winning the class participation challenge with 79% overall participation. 3rd grade families came in second place with 74%. Across schools, Beach has the highest participation at 76% followed by Havens at 73%, Wildwood at 68%, PMS at 58% and PHS/MHS at 50%. Approximately $300,000 of Giving Campaign contributions are donor designated to the endowment fund. At the end of the school year, PEF will add the remaining $3.7 million to the endowment distribution and other fundraisers, subtract expenses, and grant those funds to PUSD for the 2026-27 academic year. A survey will be released this spring to ascertain parent funding priorities for the grant. PEF thanks everyone that made a contribution, reached out to their company as part of the corporate matching program, contributed via DAF, and talked to neighbors and friends about the importance of The Giving Campaign. Every single donation, no matter the amount, supports the students and the schools. articles.text: The stars in our sky are among the greatest things humans share. No matter where we are in the world, the same stars stretch above our heads. Every day, stars are born and, like humans, they Stars form inside nebulae, vast molecular clouds made of gas and dust. These star-forming regions, often called stellar nurseries, contain all the building blocks Stellar nursery nebulae are rich in hydrogen and helium, the primary gases involved in star formation. In the cold temperatures of a nebula, gases clump together, creating regions of higher density. Over time, these regions collect more matter, increasing their mass and strengthening their gravitational pull. As gravity causes the material to collapse inward, friction generates heat. Eventually, this process ignites, and a star is born. While some nebulae mark the beginning of a star’s life, others form after a star’s death. What happens at the end of a star’s life depends largely on its mass. When a low-mass star dies, it sheds its outer layers, creating an expanding cloud of gas and dust known as a planetary nebula. When a high-mass star reaches the end of its life, it explodes in a powerful event called a supernova. In the aftermath, the remaining material spreads into space and can eventually become part of new nebulae, supplying the raw ingredients for future stars. A nebula near you Not every nebula is visible from Earth, but some can be seen with the naked eye under the right conditions. In the Northern Hemisphere at this time of year, the Orion Nebula, also known as Messier 42, is one of the most famous examples. Located about 1,500 light-years away, it is the closest stellar nursery to Earth. With a telescope, its structure and activity become even more striking, offering observers a rare glimpse into the process of star formation. The stars are closer than you think The Chabot Space & Science Center offers free public telescope viewings every Friday and Saturday from 7:30 to 10:30 p.m., weather permitting. During these sessions, visitors can learn about the center’s historic telescopes and observe stars, planets and other celestial objects. For those interested in an even closer look at the cosmos, Chabot also hosts small astrophotography workshops. Participants learn how to operate telescope rigs and create polished night-sky photographs of their own. The next astrophotography class is scheduled for Jan. 29, offering an out-of-thisworld opportunity to explore the universe through the lens. You can find more information about these programs and more at chabotspace.org. The magic of the Milky Way is closer than you think

articles.text: (Beach 5th grader) You think math is boring? Think again! More than 120 Piedmont kids and adults came together last Wednesday, January 14 at Ellen Driscoll to celebrate math. No matter what game you were playing, there was fun to be had at the Advancing Learning for Piedmont Students (ALPS) Math Fair. Games like Prime Climb were big hits, and roulette and bingo attracted large crowds. The most surprising part was that chess was the most popular game, with spectators gathering around to watch. “All 11 games were a hit, but chess was the most popular,” said volunteer Ariel Shusteff. There were games for everyone, from first grade all the way to tenth grade. Another great thing about the event was seeing older kids teaching younger kids how to play the math games. The camaraderie created a really nice overall vibe for all. “I loved how many games there were. I had so much fun with my friends,” said Rydia Sun. But the whole point of the math event was “to bring people together and have fun while learning math,” said Ella Grossberg, an ALPS member and the event organizer. And it wasn’t just math. You could earn candy for playing games, and there was even a snack bar just outside. Many Piedmont community members also came out to show support. School board member Susy Struble and Board VP Michael Malione discussed an interesting book brought by Maxim Shusteff about using technology in the classroom. Superintendent Dr. Hawn and Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich checked out the Math Kangaroo competition information table too. One of the best parts was when Kate Waldron, a teacher and head of the math department, brought super challenging practice questions for the AMC 8 competition. It took three kids and 30 minutes to finally solve one really hard problem, but they did it! “So much fun and so many games!” said Luke Shin about the Math Fair. Linda Tao, one of the organizers, wondered if it would make sense to have this event more than once a year. With candy prizes and an insane amount of pizza, this kid’s vote is a big YES. Kid and adults react to a spin on the one to twelve roulette wheel, during the Math Fair in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on January 14. Stiff chess competition ensued from start to finish. A bingo table set up for the Math Fair. Kids and adults play Prime Climb at the Math Fair. Students build a cup stack up beyond their heads and then ponder how many cups are in the stack with a base level of 15.

articles.text: Piedmont’s 29th annual Martin Luther King Jr. Celebration on Monday, January 19 included a display in the Alan Harvey Theater of Piedmont student artwork and literature. More than 130 students submitted artwork or writing pieces, showcasing the next generation’s creative representations on Dr. King’s legacy. The theme guiding the art was: “In his 1967 book, Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. asked, ‘Where Do We Go from Here? Chaos or Community?’ What do you choose? What would you like our future to look like?” This was the fifth year that Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) has hosted the student showcase. Most of the student submissions came from Havens and Wildwood students, and one PHS student, Hunter Fasteau, the school’s fall representative to the school board. Most of the work came from 3rd, 4th and 5th graders whom were instructed to create 2-D art, photos, essays, or poems in response to the theme. Some teachers had their students create the art as a class or talked about the theme and the showcase in class. PADC President Ellen Lee was thankful for the large student response this year. w ww ww w. .w wi il ld dw wo oo od dc cr ra ab bf fe ee ed d. .c co om m

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Loss to Priory in MLK tournament while short-handed Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team won one and lost one over the past week, bringing its record to 10-3 overall. They beat Bishop O’Dowd 51-47 in a critical Western Alameda County Conference opener on Tuesday, January 13 at Binks Rawlings Gym, then lost 48-46 to Priory of Portola Valley at the MLK Classic hosted by O’Dowd on Monday, January 19. Against Priory, Piedmont was without lead point guard Jenelle Solis and forward Saniyah Johnson, both out with injuries. “We had to adjust on the fly a bit. Everyone has to be the point guard now, so we’ll approach things by committee. No one person has to shoulder the responsibility,” coach Bryan Gardere said. Andrea Martin puts up a contested shot against Priory. She had 24 points against Priory and 18 points in the game with Bishop O’Dowd. Savannah Dennig drives in against Priory. She had 15 points against O’Dowd. Staff Photos Piedmont split its last two games while dealing with some key injuries. Even while missing 2 key players, PHS still had a chance to win, tying the game at 46-46 with 15 seconds left. The Panthers converted a shot near the basket with nine seconds remaining. “We had a few less turnovers in the fourth. We were taking care of the ball and made some plays. Andrea stepped up,” Gardere said. The win over O’Dowd puts Piedmont on-track to win its fourth straight WACC Foothill Division title. 48-46 loss to Priory Piedmont led 14-9 through the first quarter, which included six total lead changes. Priory took control in the second quarter, going up 16-14 at the 4:32 mark, limiting Piedmont to just six points to take a 25-20 lead into halftime. In the third quarter, Priory continued its strong defense to hold the Highlanders to just 10 points while putting up 17 of its own to lead 42-30. PHS began to turn the tide in the fourth quarter, 13 of 15 points to put itself within onepoint down 44-43 with 1:28 left in the game. With 15 seconds left in the game, Taylor White found Andrea Martin for a 3-pointer to not it up at 46-46. However, the joy was short-lived with Prior scoring the would-be game-winner with nine seconds left, 48-46. With four seconds left, White heaved a long pass from midcourt to Martin in the low post, but Martin’s shot missed and buzzer sounded shortly after. Final stats: Martin led with 24 points, Alexa Ba scored nine, White had eight points, Savannah Dennig had five. 51-47 victory over Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont led 12-6 in the first quarter and 30-21 by halftime. BOD clipped away at PHS’ lead to make it 44-36 going into the fourth quarter. PHS was limited to eight points in the final going while conceding 11. The Highlanders leaned on Martin, White, and Dennig to score. With Solis hampered by an injury, they combined for 48 of their 51 points. Final stats: Martin led with 18 points, White and Dennig had 15 points, while Solis had three. NEXT UP Piedmont (10-3 overall, 1-0 league) hosts Alameda tomorrow, January 22, at 6:30 p.m. at Binks Rawlings Gym. They will host Antelope on Saturday, January 24 at 5:30 p.m.
articles.title: Girls’ basketball team beats O’Dowd

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team split its last two games against Western Alameda County Conference opponents, falling 2-0 to Castro Valley on Tuesday, January 13 at the Trojans’ field, and winning 4-0 over Alameda at Witter Field on Friday, January 16. The pair of results brings Piedmont’s record to 5-2-3 (W-TL) overall and 1-1-1 in league. “The press today [against Alameda] was fantastic. They just started playing it long because they couldn’t get it out of the press. But, honestly, the possession today was the best I’ve seen us play,” coach Matt Spencer-Harty said. It was a stellar performance by senior Arden Sorensen-Wald against Alameda, scoring two goals and an assist. Both of her goals came from distance, including a free kick from 34 yards out and another shot from 29 yards in open play. “We noticed that their goalie was a little shorter, so we wanted to shoot it over her. The second goal was a whole team effort. We were passing around and I got it to around the top of the box where I could get a nice strike on it,” Sorensen-Wald said. Against the Hornets, the Highlanders posed a lot of problems with an aggressive press and frequently looked to get the ball up the field. Piedmont’s last goal was an example. Sorensen-Wald played a long pass to Miranda Liu who sprinted by Alameda’s back line to land her second goal of the game. “We are super direct and just constantly getting forward. Miranda is key to that; it wouldn’t work without her,” SorensenWald said. 4-0 over Alameda Piedmont’s first goal came in the 18th minute when SorensenWald launched her long free kick from 34 yards, placing it above the keeper. She scored again in Staff Photos Arden Sorensen-Wald celebrates one of her two goals against Alameda. Miranda Liu scores one of her two goals against the Hornets. Olivia Nealon, a freshman, had an assist in the 4-nil win over Alameda.

articles.text: Piedmont sent athletes to the newly created California Winter Championship Qualifiers. Pictured are Claire Aubrecht (left), coach Pouyan Assadi, Eric Venner, and Maddox Ma. The three qualified for the Championship in Arcadia in February. Piedmont High’s track and field team recently made a rare winter season appearance, competing in the 2026 California Winter Championships Qualifiers at Pittsburg HS on Saturday, January 17. With a qualifying mark, athletes are eligible to compete in the California Winter Championships in Arcadia on Saturday, February 7. “Since California does not have an official indoor season like most colder states, some of the premier track programs in the state came together and organized our own set of meets,” Piedmont track coach Pouyan Assadi explained. PHS sent 15 athletes to Pirate Stadium. Boys athletes included Eric Venner, Maddox Ma, Rehan Mumtaz, Jason Shum, Noah Baldwin, Noah Hussain, Joshua Bell, John Bunje, Mateo Long, Marius Arno, Dash WatersWorthen, Adrian Kondakov, and Raiden Holt. Representing for the girls’ team included Claire Aubrecht and Gladwin Horsley. The Highlanders had three athletes qualify for the Winter Championships in Southern California: Venner, Ma, and Aubrecht. Venner qualified in two different events, including the 60 and 150 meter dashes. In the 60, he placed seventh of 52 runners with a time of 7.25 seconds. He was also seventh in the 150 out of 54 Piedmont runners Eric Venner (left), Maddox Ma, Rehan Mumtaz, and Jason Shum. Claire Aubrecht (second from right) qualified for the California Winter Championship in the 60- meter sprint.
articles.title: Piedmont competes in California Winter Championships Qualifiers

articles.text: The boys basketball team had a busy week, winning two of its last four games. Boys’ basketball wrapped up a busy week, taking two of its last four games. They most recently demolished Skyline 75-22 at the Oakland High Showcase on Monday, January 19 and beat International in another one-sided 53-29 win on Saturday, January 17 at the Miramonte MLK Showcase in Orinda. However, they suffered league losses against Western Alameda County Conference foes Berkeley 63-56 at home on Thursday, January 15 and lost to Bishop O’Dowd 74-53 in Oakland on Tuesday, January 13. The league losses against O’Dowd and Berkeley were somewhat similar. Against BOD, Piedmont held an early 11-6 lead through the first quarter, but struggled to keep up offensively. With Berkeley, Piedmont held a 56-51 lead in the fourth quarter, but couldn’t find the basket from then on. “We got outscored 12-0 in the final three or four minutes. We committed three or four turnovers down the stretch, and that’s the ballgame. Toughness is something we struggle with; we opened well against O’Dowd and they started to be more physical and we shied away. We got a lead against Berkeley and they started to play more physical,” coach Ben Spencer said following their loss to Berkeley. Piedmont overpowered Skyline and International, limiting both teams to single-digit points in three of four quarters. 75-22 win over Skyline It was a dominant defensive display against the Titans, limiting Skyline to single-digit points in three of the four quarters, including just two and three points in the second and third quarters respectively. Piedmont led 19-12 through the first quarter, and then piled on 26 points while conceding just two in the second quarter to take a commanding 45-14 lead into halftime. PHS then scored 22 points in the third quarter and gave up just three points, now up 67-17. With a running clock, Piedmont added eight more points in the final going. Final stats: Dillon Casey led with 18 points, P.J. Brayer had 16, Ollie Dougan scored 10, Lucian Fang-Ring had five, and Cash Panico scored four. 53-29 win vs. International Piedmont dominated the first quarter to lead 22-6 and took a 28-10 lead into halftime. PHS outscored HIS 10-8 in the third to lead 38-18, while putting up 15 points in the fourth and conceding 11. PHS filled the stat sheet with 10 different scorers. Final stats: Fang-Ring led the way with 20 points, Casey scored 17, Panico had a season-high of 10, Joseph Baskin scored eight, Brayer had seven, Johnny Lee had six, Akash Bornstein had three, Will Hinman had two, while Dougan and Ruben Cohen had one. 63-56 loss to Berkeley Berkeley led 21-15 through the first quarter, while Piedmont clawed away at the lead to make it a 33-31 deficit at halftime. Piedmont inched closer in the third, trailing by just one-point 48-47 in the third quarter, but the Highlanders was outscored 15-9 in the fourth. Piedmont took its first lead of the game in the third quarter when P.J. Brayer knocked down a 3-pointer with 51 seconds left, up 47-45. However, Berkeley answered quickly with a three with 30 seconds left. Brayer helped Piedmont retake the lead 50 seconds into the fourth quarter, converting two free throws after blocking a layup on the opposite end. PHS established a 54-49 lead thanks to a 3-pointer by Bornstein and a basket by Brayer, while Lorin made gave PHS a 56-51 lead after putting back an offensive rebound. But then things went south for Staff Photos Lucian Fang-Ring had a seasonhigh 23 points in a loss to Bishop O’Dowd. He also scored 20 points against International. the Highlanders, going scoreless for the remainder of the game and allowing Berkeley to go on a 12-point scoring run to end the game. BHS took the lead with 1:58 left on a 3-pointer. Final stats: Casey led with 18 points, Brayer had 17, Lorin scored 12, while Hinman, FangRing, and Bornstein had three. 74-53 loss to O’Dowd Piedmont led 11-6 through the first quarter but fell behind 32-24 in the second quarter. O’Dowd extended its lead to 50-39 in the third quarter, while outscoring PHS 24-14 in the fourth quarter. Final stats: Fang-Ring had a season-high of 23 points. Lorin had eight, Brayer scored seven, Casey had six, Panico and Dougan had three, Baskin had two, and Hinman had one. NEXT UP Piedmont (13-5 overall, 1-2 league) visits Alameda tomorrow, January 22, at 7:00 p.m. Beach Lorin drives through contact against Berkeley.

With a qualifying mark, athletes are eligible to compete in the California Winter Championships in Arcadia on Saturday, February 7. “Since California does not have an official indoor season like most colder states, some of the premier track programs in the state came together and organized our own set of meets,” Piedmont track coach Pouyan Assadi explained. PHS sent 15 athletes to Pirate Stadium. Boys athletes included Eric Venner, Maddox Ma, Rehan Mumtaz, Jason Shum, Noah Baldwin, Noah Hussain, Joshua Bell, John Bunje, Mateo Long, Marius Arno, Dash WatersWorthen, Adrian Kondakov, and Raiden Holt. Representing for the girls’ team included Claire Aubrecht and Gladwin Horsley. The Highlanders had three athletes qualify for the Winter Championships in Southern California: Venner, Ma, and Aubrecht. Venner qualified in two different events, including the 60 and 150 meter dashes. In the 60, he placed seventh of 52 runners with a time of 7.25 seconds. He was also seventh in the 150 out of 54 See Track and Field on page 32 Piedmont runners Eric Venner (left), Maddox Ma, Rehan Mumtaz, and Jason Shum. Claire Aubrecht (second from right) qualified for the California Winter Championship in the 60- meter sprint. PHS boys win two of last four games The boys basketball team had a busy week, winning two of its last four games. By Jonathan Comeaux Boys’ basketball wrapped up a busy week, taking two of its last four games. They most recently demolished Skyline 75-22 at the Oakland High Showcase on Monday, January 19 and beat International in another one-sided 53-29 win on Saturday, January 17 at the Miramonte MLK Showcase in Orinda. However, they suffered league losses against Western Alameda County Conference foes Berkeley 63-56 at home on Thursday, January 15 and lost to Bishop O’Dowd 74-53 in Oakland on Tuesday, January 13. The league losses against O’Dowd and Berkeley were somewhat similar. Against BOD, Piedmont held an early 11-6 lead through the first quarter, but struggled to keep up offensively. With Berkeley, Piedmont held a 56-51 lead in the fourth quarter, but couldn’t find the basket from then on. “We got outscored 12-0 in the final three or four minutes. We committed three or four turnovers down the stretch, and that’s the ballgame. Toughness is something we struggle with; we opened well against O’Dowd and they started to be more physical and we shied away. We got a lead against Berkeley and they started to play more physical,” coach Ben Spencer said following their loss to Berkeley. Piedmont overpowered Skyline and International, limiting both teams to single-digit points in three of four quarters. 75-22 win over Skyline It was a dominant defensive display against the Titans, limiting Skyline to single-digit points in three of the four quarters, including just two and three points in the second and third quarters respectively. Piedmont led 19-12 through the first quarter, and then piled on 26 points while conceding just two in the second quarter to take a commanding 45-14 lead into halftime. PHS then scored 22 points in the third quarter and gave up just three points, now up 67-17. With a running clock, Piedmont added eight more points in the final going. Final stats: Dillon Casey led with 18 points, P.J. Brayer had 16, Ollie Dougan scored 10, Lucian Fang-Ring had five, and Cash Panico scored four. 53-29 win vs. International Piedmont dominated the first quarter to lead 22-6 and took a 28-10 lead into halftime. PHS outscored HIS 10-8 in the third to lead 38-18, while putting up 15 points in the fourth and conceding 11. PHS filled the stat sheet with 10 different scorers. Piedmont inched closer in the third, trailing by just one-point 48-47 in the third quarter, but the Highlanders was outscored 15-9 in the fourth. Piedmont took its first lead of the game in the third quarter when P.J. Brayer knocked down a 3-pointer with 51 seconds left, up 47-45. However, Berkeley answered quickly with a three with 30 seconds left. Brayer helped Piedmont retake the lead 50 seconds into the fourth quarter, converting two free throws after blocking a layup on the opposite end. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team lost a pair of games on the road last week, falling 1-0 to Berkeley on Friday, January 16 and 2-1 at Mt. Eden in Hayward on Wednesday, January 14. The Highlanders are struggling to create offensive opportunities on consistent occasion after losing most of its roster from last year’s team. With a young group, coach Ben Russell knew there would be an adjustment period. “We talk about being a taxi driver as opposed to being a bus driver. A bus driver has the same loop over and over, a taxi driver goes to multiple destinations. We need to solve multiple problems and understand there are multiple ways to play the game. The ability to solve multiple problems is what we are lacking right now,” Russell said. 1-0 loss to Berkeley The Yellowjackets had many shot attempts in the first 40 minutes, but only two were on target and were easily handled by goalkeeper Tobias Tsai. In at goalkeeper in the second half Colt Hitchcock, made a big stop in the 47th minute by rushing off his line to thwart a Berkeley forward before he could take a shot. However, Berkeley broke the deadlock in the 51st minute after their right winger wheeled into the area down by the end line, centering a pass while Hitchcock tried to press him. With an empty net, Berkeley scored what proved to be the game-winner. Travers Kemp logged Piedmont’s first shot attempt in the 57th minute when Elias Reed-Miguel sent a long pass toward him when making a run into the box. Kemp leaped to get his head on the ball, but it looped far wide of the mark. Shortly after, Kemp nearly scored in the 60th minute when splitting two defenders with a nifty touch, taking a low rolling shot from atop the box that forced a diving save out of Berkeley’s keeper. 2-1 loss to Mt. Eden Piedmont scored the game’s first goal in the 15th minute. After a corner sailed through the area to the right side, Maxwell Rodriguez gained possession near the right corner flag, turning to send a cross on his first touch. His pass took one bounce, finding Reed-Miguel standing unmarked. Reed-Miguel caught it out of the air and sent a header into the net. Six minutes later, Tsai made a huge diving save to keep PHS ahead. Mt. Eden found the equalizer Staff Photos Elias Reed-Miguel scored Piedmont’s only goal against Mt. Eden. Travers Kemp had a couple of scoring chances against Berkeley. Jackson Van-Kleeck looks to make a play. on a questionable offside no-call. The ball whipped in from the right side found their striker in close distance in front of the net. The Monarchs’ forward looked a couple of feet past Piedmont’s back line when the ball was played. The Monarchs’ game-winner came in the 71st. This time, a low pass was played down the right wing. Hitchcock rushed off his line to greet the attacker at the top of the area, but the Mt. Eden forward took a nice touch past the keeper and slotted the ball into the empty net. NEXT UP The results bring the Highlanders’ record to 2-0-8 (W-TL) with eight matches left in the season against league foes in the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division. Piedmont (2-0-8 overall, 0-0-1 league) hosts Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, January 23.

articles.text: [Reprinted from January 2021] We return to one of our earlier Hiking With Jon ventures from 2021, where you can find groves of first- and second-generation old growth redwood trees in Portola State Park. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than those found here in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bares its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. The Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within Portola Redwoods. Aside from the awe striking size, the thousand year old tree is among the few old growths to make it through the mass lumbering of the 1800s. Continuing back to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill ascent through the hill sides for near two-miles and gaining 550 feet in elevation until intersecting with the Slate Creek Trail—turning left to start your loop back to your car, intersecting with Peter’s Creek. Turning right starts a 1.5 mile hike to a historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles and jolting 500 feet in elevation until its end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to less than 6-feet wide, so you’ll have to be patient when crossing other hikers. If you turned left, the trail continues another 0.8 mile until intersecting with a T—turning right to make our way to Upper Escape Road, turning right again to get a brief glimpse of Peter’s Creek on the trip back to the car—making it a 4-mile day. We passed 40 people on the day, so just 10 people per mile on average. But it’s worth noting that Downed trees line your path on many of the 18 miles of hiking trails at Portola Redwoods State Park. Take the Summit Trail to start your loop. The path becomes narrow on the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail.
articles.title: HIKING WITH JON Walk along old growths at Portola Redwoods State Park

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery in Walnut Creek is hosting a Valentine’s Day-themed wreath-making workshop on Sunday, February 1. Attendees of all skill-levels may join the workshop and will be guided through the wreath-making process by an instructor who is trained in working with succulents, drought-tolerant, and native plants. Supplies include a heartshaped grapevine wreath, succulents and dyed corn husks. When moistened, corn husks become flexible and can be shaped into soft curls that bring movement and a pop of color to your wreath. Those who prefer a more “traditional” look may choose from a selection of ribbons. The instructor on-site will offer tips on composition and balance while encouraging attendees to interpret the materials in their own way. Succulent varieties may vary. Photo courtesy of Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery Create a unique wreath at Ruth Bancroft Garden. Two workshops are offered on February 1, at 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. Both workshops last approximately 90 minutes. Ticket purchases include supplies. Visit https://www.ruthbancrof tgarden.org /event /evergreen-love-succulent-valentine-wreath/ to reserve your spot. ®
articles.title: Ruth Bancroft Garden hosts Valentine wreath-making workshop on Feb. 1

articles.text: Light festival ends Jan. 25 Oakland Zoo’s popular “Glowfari” evening light festival ends on January 25. Glowfari features hundreds of life-sized glowing animal lanterns and all-new light fixtures this year. The family-friendly lantern festival invites guests to stroll among larger-than-life illuminated animal sculptures during festival hours from 4:30 to 9 p.m. “Glowfari” joins dozens of holiday-themed light festivals across the Bay Area, but this long standing event, previously named “Zoolights,” focuses on wildlife, sustainability and animal conservation. The reinvented event features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more available dates and has been a wildly successful fundraiser for the Zoo since its inception. Each handcrafted lantern creates a colorful journey through Oakland Zoo’s themed zones, including the savanna, the ocean, and a whimsical bug tunnel. Seasonal treats will be available for purchase. While animal displays are closed for late night events, “Glowfari” ticketholders can still take a gondola ride to the California Trail for panoramic views of the illuminated exhibits spread across the zoo’s hillsides. Timed-entry tickets are required and often sell out early. Admission prices vary by date, and parking is included with each reservation. Children under two are free. Proceeds from Glowfari help support the Oakland Zoo’s wildlife conservation programs and animal care initiatives. More information is available at www.oaklandzoo.org. Tickets are available online for Oakland Zoo’s annual light festival.
articles.title: Last chance to see Oakland Zoo’s “Glowfari”

articles.text: Museum offers football-themed programs, workshops first week of February The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is inviting the public to experience this year’s Super Bowl through art by offering a variety of public art displays, workshops and programs leading up to the event. SFMOMA will unveil the official Super Bowl XL roman numerals in its Evelyn and Walter Haas Jr. Atrium on January 29. The addition will be on view through February 8, offering a free public viewing ahead of the Super Bowl in the Bay Area. The installation is part of a broader partnership between SFMOMA and the Bay Area Host Committee surrounding Super Bowl LX. The museum will also host several public programs and events during the first week of February. On Thursday, February 5, SFMOMA and the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) will present “Building Universes,” an evening program running from 5 to 8 p.m. The event will feature poetry and dance performances across both institutions, with artists responding to works on view in the galleries. The program is inspired in part by the 1972 Black Art Expo curated by Suzanne Jackson. Photo courtesy of the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art SFMOMA will unveil the official Super Bowl XL roman numerals in its Evelyn and Walter Haas Jr. Atrium on January 29. SFMOMA will be closed to the public on Friday, February 6, for the Bay Area Host Committee’s Super Bowl LX Innovation Summit. The invitation-only event is expected to draw about 500 participants from the technology, sports, investment, and cultural sectors. The summit will include main stage sessions and breakout panels focused on technology and innovation in sports and large-scale events. A public workshop on Bay Area graffiti and street art is scheduled for Saturday, February 7, from 2 to 4 p.m. Led by artist and educator Dregs One, the program will explore the history and styles of regional graffiti and include a hands-on component. Artist Ruby Neri will join the discussion during the latter portion of the workshop. Family programming will conclude Sunday, February 8, with a free Family Studio activity from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on the museum’s second floor, where participants can create sportsthemed pennants. The museum store will also offer limited-edition hats throughout February while supplies last. For more information on Super Bowl-themed programming at SFMOMA, visit www. SFMOMA.org.
articles.title: Celebrate the Super Bowl at SFMOMA

SFMOMA will unveil the official Super Bowl XL roman numerals in its Evelyn and Walter Haas Jr. Atrium on January 29. articles.text: American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) in San Francisco is showing Tennessee Williams’s landmark play A Streetcar Named Desire at the historic Toni Rembe Theater from January 21 to February 1. Streetcar is a classic 1947 play following Southern belle Blanche DuBois, who moves in with her sister Stella and brutish brotherin-law Stanley Kowalski in New Orleans, leading to a clash of cultures, desires, and illusions that ends in tragedy. A.C.T. ‘s production features intimate staging and seating in the round by utilizing onstage seats. Director Nick Westrate presents Williams’s complete, unabridged text with four performers and no props. The cast includes Screen Actors Guild and Theater World Award-winner Heather Lind, as well as Brad Koed, James Russell, and Lucy Owen, under the direction of Nick Westrate. “After touring A Streetcar Named Desire to found spaces around the country for three years, we can’t believe we are finally bringing it…to a theater,” said co-creators Lucy Owen and Westrate. “We are thrilled to be collaborating with Pam MacKinnon and all of the amazing artists at A.C.T. to explore what it means to use a theater as a found space. We can’t wait to let Tennessee Williams’s beautiful souls haunt San Francisco.” A.C.T. Artistic Director Pam MacKinnon said she “leapt at the chance to make A.C.T. ‘s Toni Rembe Theater a found space for this acting troupe to storm and haunt.” “I saw this production from The Streetcar Project in a Brooklyn warehouse in 2024. The performances were harrowingly lived in. This canonical American play delivered simply, lovingly, anew,” MacKinnon said in a press release. Single tickets (ranging from $25–$130) are on sale now at the A.C.T. Box Office at 415-749-2228 or online at act-sf.org/streetcar. articles.text: Mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato Cal Performances at UC Berkeley will present mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato with the genre-crossing string trio Time for Three in Emily – No Prisoner Be, a new, evening-length song cycle by Pulitzer Prize–winning composer Kevin Puts, on Saturday, February 7 at 8 p.m. in Zellerbach Hall. The new work sets 24 poems by Emily Dickinson to composer Kevin Puts’ score, featuring stage lighting design from Andrew Staples that the creators say “magnifies the emotional terrain of Dickinson’s language.” Mezzo-soprano Joyce DiDonato, making her return to the Bay Area following acclaimed projects including Eden (2023) and In War & Peace: Harmony Through Music (2016), leads the program vocally. Each member of Time for Three, including Nicolas Kendall (viola, violin), Charles Yang (violin) and Ranaan Meyer (bass), will perform alongside DiDonato. Time for Three won a Grammy in 2023 for their recording of Puts’s triple concerto Contact. Emily – No Prisoner Be marks DiDonato’s first appearance with Cal Performances in this collaboration and continues her long creative partnership with Puts.She previously performed a lead role in his opera The Hours. A studio recording of Emily – No Prisoner Be is scheduled Composer Kevin Puts for release on January 30, with four tracks already available on streaming platforms: “Because I could not stop for Death —,” “There is another sky,” “Her Face,” and “They shut me up.” The project reflects DiDonato’s advocacy for making music broadly accessible. A throughline of her career alongside accolades including multiple Grammy Awards and the 2018 Olivier Award for Outstanding Achievement in Opera. Tickets for all performances are available at www.calperformances.org, by phone at (510) 642-9988, or in person at the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, Tuesday through Friday, 12 p.m. to 5:30 p.m. and Saturday through Sunday, 1 p.m. to 5 p.m.
