articles.text: January 17 – February 28 Society of Printmakers’ Art Exhibition The California Society of Printmakers returns to Piedmont with its 111th Annual Members’ Exhibition, showing close to 100 works of printmaking art, demonstrating the incredible variety of style and process that falls within this field. The exhibit will be open on Saturdays and Sundays January 17, 18, 25, and 31, and most February weekends, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.; there will be an opening reception on Saturday, January 24, from 1 to 4 p.m., as well as a closing reception on February 28 from 11 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., providing good chances of meeting and learning from many of the artists, one or two of whom will also be present during the weekend open hours. The exhibition is free to visit, and the works will also be available to enjoy during your attendance at any of PCA’s public events. Saturday, January 31, 7:00 p.m. Cristiana Pegoraro Solo Piano Concert The incomparable Italian pianist Cristiana Pegoraro returns to Piedmont for another recital. As president of Narnia Arts Academy and Artistic Director of the Narnia Festival, she has been hailed by the New York Times as “an artist of the highest caliber.” She has performed on the world’s most prestigious stages, including Lincoln Center, Carnegie Hall, the United Nations (New York), the Sydney Opera House, Festspielhaus (Salzburg), Musikverein (Vienna), Royal College of Music (London), Auditorium Parco della Musica (Rome), Teatro alla Scala (Milan). She brings to Piedmont a program she premiered in November at Carnegie Hall, called Harmonies of Peace. Advance tickets are available at: https://events.com/r/tickets/1023245. Tickets at the door are $40/adult and $20/youth. Sunday, February 8, 4:00 p.m. Carl Blake / Will Underwood Piano & Flute Duo William Underwood III holds a B.S. in Music from Florida A&M and a Master of Music in Flute Performance from Wayne State. He has toured extensively in Japan with Kyodo Tokyo and regularly works as a soloist, collaborator, and recording artist. Dr. Carl Blake, a local piano master who has performed worldwide to acclaim, has introduced Will to the best of the Bay Area, often playing together as a duo exploring piano and flute repertoire. Tickets and more info will be available soon. Thursday, February 12, 6:30 p.m. Sacha Grippando Jewelry Arts Lecture Throughout history, jewelry and watches have played a vital role in the visual arts, imbuing the wearer with power, wealth, and status. From ancient times, the inclusion of jewels, and later watches, in portraits of royalty and significant figures served to highlight their importance. This illuminating and sparkling lecture will explore how the visual arts utilize jewelry and watches to define characters and convey specific traits. Sacha Grippando will analyze significant works of art, ranging from paintings by masters like Leonardo Da Vinci and Vermeer to modern and contemporary artists like Salvador Dali and Kehinde Wiley. Admission is by $20 suggested donation at the door and includes light refreshments afterwards. Saturday, February 14, 7:30 p.m. Richard Dowling Classical/Ragtime Piano Recital Hailed by the New York Times as “an especially impressive fine pianist,” Richard Dowling appears throughout America in solo recitals, at music festivals, and as guest soloist with orchestras. Works of Chopin, Debussy, Joplin, Gershwin, Gottschalk, Ravel, ragtime, and early jazz figures are included. A Steinway artist with degrees from Yale and U of Texas as well as certificates from two French music conservatories, his recordings include a 3-CD album, the Complete Piano Works of Scott Joplin, nominated for a Grammy award. Dowling brings to PCA a unique celebration on Valentine’s Day, consisting of romantic piano favorites, songs by Gershwin and syncopated ragtime tunes Scott Joplin. Tickets $40 at the door or in advance at this link: https://events.com/r/ tickets/1023765.

articles.text: Music and sports share many similarities. Success is measured by a high batting average and errors must be kept to a minimum. The seasons of play are grueling. It is a given that sports heroes must maintain a high level of physical fitness. The same is true with concert musicians. In the past, classical music stars were at the top of the entertainment pay scale. But… things change. Just the other day I noticed that a baseball player signed a contract. The amount was unbelievable… $240 million for four years. Imagine if Babe Ruth or Willie Mays were playing today. If a mediocre, but highly touted, player gets $60 million per year how much would the greatest players of all time get? It’s only January, but I suggest that we begin looking into the future. The concert season used to be from September until the end of May or June. The summers were always reserved for relaxation and study. In Europe, there were absolutely no concerts during the summer. Then the United States initiated music festivals. This idea caught on big time and now the summer season is as busy as the rest of the year. No matter where you go in the world there are music festivals. When I was a kid, the Hollywood Bowl was just about the only summer music festival in Southern California. In Northern California it was the Bach Festival in Carmel. These days when you plan your vacation you should look into Italian concert pianist Cristiana Pegoraro will perform a solo recital at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on January 31.

articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré The mythology of the American west is replete with images of men who are symbols of leathery masculinity and independence, two examples, among many, being John Wayne (The Searchers), and Clint Eastwood (Pale Rider). Now comes The Power of the Dog, released in the latter part of 2021, first in theaters and shortly thereafter on Netflix. It has received 12 Oscar nominations, one for Best Picture, and written and directed by Jane Campion. It is based on Thomas Savage’s 1967 novel of the same name. The film is set on a large cattle ranch in the wide expanses of Montana (the picture was actually shot in New Zealand). The year is 1925. The film stars Benedict Cumberbatch as Phil Burbank, Jesse Plemons as his brother George (they co-own the ranch), Kristen Dunst as the widowed Rose, and Kodi Smit-McPhee portraying Rose’s younger brother, Peter, a medical student. Phil is your classic, deliberately unwashed, and unrepentantly blunt rancher who calls George, always well-groomed, even when riding, “fatso.” He also takes cruel exception to Rose’s younger, somewhat effeminate brother Peter, who waits tables at Rose’s small town café, wears white canvas shoes instead of boots, and poses a startling contrast to the ranch’s cowhands – and to Phil’s departed mentor and role model, the quintessential cowboy known as Bronco Henry. He was a man who was the very definition of masculinity, no matter how toxic. As it turns out, George becomes enamored with Rose, and soon returns to the ranch with her as his new bride. For Phil, Rose’s very presence on the ranch fills him with resentment, seemingly for no other reason than she is a woman, and he takes a cruel pleasure in tormenting her. articles.text: A scene from Disney-Pixar’s Onward Onward, released by Pixar-Disney, once again showcases the studio’s remarkable gift for world-building, creating an imaginative universe that invites children — and the adults watching with them — to step inside. The world of Onward is populated by blue-toned elves living in toadstool houses, alongside dragons, unicorns, spells and the remnants of once-powerful magic. It is a place where enchantment has faded into the background, replaced by modern conveniences, but never entirely disappeared. At the center of the story are two brothers: shy, uncertain Ian Lightfoot (voiced by Tom Holland), who has just turned 16, and his older brother Barley (Chris Pratt), a loud, eccentric and endearingly rebellious presence. Together, they form a study in contrasts, bound by shared loss. The plot is set in motion by a birthday gift left to Ian by his deceased father: a wizard’s staff, a rare phoenix gem, and instructions for a spell that would allow their father to return for just one day. Ian’s first attempt, with Barley’s encouragement, goes awry, producing only the lower half of their dad — pants, socks and shoes included. To complete the spell, the brothers must find a replacement gemstone, which Barley is convinced he knows how to track down. What follows is a quest movie in classic Pixar form. The brothers set off in Barley’s battered van, bickering over directions and debating Ian’s uneven magical abilities. It has received 12 Oscar nominations, one for Best Picture, and written and directed by Jane Campion. It is based on Thomas Savage’s 1967 novel of the same name. The film is set on a large cattle ranch in the wide expanses of Montana (the picture was actually shot in New Zealand). The year is 1925. The film stars Benedict Cumberbatch as Phil Burbank, Jesse Plemons as his brother George (they co-own the ranch), Kristen Dunst as the widowed Rose, and Kodi Smit-McPhee portraying Rose’s younger brother, Peter, a medical student. Phil is your classic, deliberately unwashed, and unrepentantly blunt rancher who calls George, always well-groomed, even when riding, “fatso.” He also takes cruel exception to Rose’s younger, somewhat effeminate brother Peter, who waits tables at Rose’s small town café, wears white canvas shoes instead of boots, and poses a startling contrast to the ranch’s cowhands – and to Phil’s departed mentor and role model, the quintessential cowboy known as Bronco Henry. He was a man who was the very definition of masculinity, no matter how toxic. As it turns out, George becomes enamored with Rose, and soon returns to the ranch with her as his new bride. For Phil, Rose’s very presence on the ranch fills him with resentment, seemingly for no other reason than she is a woman, and he takes a cruel pleasure in tormenting her. Soon the family (Peter has returned to the ranch from school for the summer) slips into dysfunction, and Rose begins to use See Power of the Dog on page 29 Onward – an imaginative universe Kodi Smit-McPhee and Benedict Cumberbatch in The Power of the Dog A scene from Disney-Pixar’s Onward By Chris Honoré Onward, released by Pixar-Disney, once again showcases the studio’s remarkable gift for world-building, creating an imaginative universe that invites children — and the adults watching with them — to step inside. The world of Onward is populated by blue-toned elves living in toadstool houses, alongside dragons, unicorns, spells and the remnants of once-powerful magic. It is a place where enchantment has faded into the background, replaced by modern conveniences, but never entirely disappeared. At the center of the story are two brothers: shy, uncertain Ian Lightfoot (voiced by Tom Holland), who has just turned 16, and his older brother Barley (Chris Pratt), a loud, eccentric and endearingly rebellious presence. Together, they form a study in contrasts, bound by shared loss. The plot is set in motion by a birthday gift left to Ian by his deceased father: a wizard’s staff, a rare phoenix gem, and instructions for a spell that would allow their father to return for just one day. Ian’s first attempt, with Barley’s encouragement, goes awry, producing only the lower half of their dad — pants, socks and shoes included. To complete the spell, the brothers must find a replacement gemstone, which Barley is convinced he knows how to track down. What follows is a quest movie in classic Pixar form. The brothers set off in Barley’s battered van, bickering over directions and debating Ian’s uneven magical abilities. articles.text: As we drove up the driveway approaching DeLoach Winery I felt I was returning home. That’s because the first wine I fell in love with back in the late 70’s was DeLoach White Zinfandel. This is embarrassing for a wine writer to admit. It was 5 bucks a bottle and I thought it was the most delicious thing I had ever tasted. Here I am 45 years later returning for a taste only to find things had totally changed – for the better. They no longer make White Zinfandel but instead craft an amazing variety of cool climate grapes like Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. DeLoach Vineyards stands as one of the foundational wineries of California’s Russian River Valley, shaping the region’s reputation for world-class Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and Zinfandel. Founded in 1975 by Cecil and Christine DeLoach along with partners, the winery grew from a modest estate into a pioneering force in Sonoma County viticulture. Early on, Cecil DeLoach planted some of the valley’s first modern Pinot Noir on the Olivet Bench, recognizing the cooler climate’s affinity with Burgundian varietals, and in 1983 he was among the first producers to use the “Russian River Valley” appellation on a wine label—helping define the region’s identity. Despite rapid growth, financial strains led DeLoach Vineyards into Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2003, opening the door for new stewardship. That same year, the winery was purchased by Boisset Family Estates, a Franco-American wine group led by JeanCharles Boisset with deep roots in Burgundy and a commitment to terroir-driven, sustainable winemaking. Under Boisset’s ownership, DeLoach underwent a transformation focused on organic and biodynamic farming. The estate vineyards were replanted with cover crops to restore soil vitality, and in 2008 the property earned organic certification from the California Certified Organic Farmers (CCOF). By 2009, the vineyards and gardens were certified biodynamic, making DeLoach one of the region’s leading estates in holistic vineyard stewardship. Today, DeLoach remains anchored in the Russian River Valley at its 1791 Olivet Road estate, where its vineyards produce expressive fruit that reflects the region’s cool-climate terroir. The winery’s approach marries traditional Burgundian techniques—such as open-top fermentation, native yeast fermentations, and hand punchdowns—with California innovation, resulting in wines that balance elegance, depth, and a strong sense of place. Current leadership includes Director of Winemaking Brian Maloney, and winemaker Katie Carter. who work to highlight the nuanced personalities of DeLoach’s vineyard sites and the Russian River Valley’s diverse microclimates. DeLoach’s portfolio spans single-vineyard Pinot Noirs, vibrant Chardonnays, and rich Zinfandels, drawing on both estate fruit and trusted grower partners dedicated to eco-friendly practices. The winery also invites visitors DeLoach Vineyards 1791 Olivet Lane Santa Rosa, CA TASTINGS Thursday to Sunday 11:00 to 4:00 (free on Thursdays) Talented winemaker Katie Carter led us through the tasting

articles.text: Last Wednesday dawned sunny and mild, and 49 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group, joined by five canine companions, gathered at the Exedra to enjoy it. The pleasant weather made for an inviting start, though the turnout was a little surprising. Walkers had been warned in advance that this would not be an easy route. The group keeps a soft goal of covering every safe walking street in Piedmont each year, but a few had gone untouched in 2025. Those streets tend to sit on the city’s edges and often come with significant elevation. Crest and Somerset roads, branching off Hampton Road, fit that description perfectly. Long, steep, and far from the center of town, they are seldom visited. In fact, the group had walked them only twice in its eight-year history. With the weather cooperating, it seemed like a good morning to take on the challenge. Adding another dimension to the outing, walker and Piedmont historian Meghan Bennett provided historical context on the early St. James Wood real estate development, making the walk as much about learning as exercise. From the Exedra, the group made its way up Highland, Sheridan, Wildwood and Crocker avenues, reaching Hampton Road in a long line before regrouping at Hampton Park. There, Bennett shared the story of St. James Wood. The land in eastern Piedmont was originally owned by Frank C. Havens and F. M. “Borax” Smith’s Realty Syndicate, formed in 1895. The two men had begun acquiring large tracts of East Bay land even earlier, with Smith buying streetcar lines in 1890 as the backbone of what became the Key System transit empire. Altogether, they assembled roughly 20 square miles of land across Piedmont, Oakland and Berkeley and developed notable landmarks, including the Claremont Hotel. Havens, however, ran into serious financial trouble in the mid-1910s and sold off nearly all of his land and other assets before his death in 1918. In the 1920s, the St. James Wood property was acquired by James Howard L’Hommedieu, born in New York in 1884 and later a resident of Oakland and Piedmont. L’Hommedieu saw the site as an opportunity to create something finer in residential development than had ever been attempted in the East Bay. He believed Piedmont was restricted to homes of “the better type” and that eastern, or “upper,” Piedmont had already established itself as “the site of the finest homes in the bay district.” In his view, this “high-class district” needed room to expand, and St. James Wood was the only place it could. L’Hommedieu laid out a subdivision of winding streets and spacious homesites. All utility wires were placed underground, and he spent thousands of dollars on trees, shrubs and lawns. Six entrances to the development featured “stately gates” formed by pairs of white columns. Parks were included, and each section of sidewalk throughout the neighborhood was marked with four terracotta tiles set into the concrete. It was the Roaring Twenties, and money did not appear to be a limiting factor. He also established strict development restrictions to ensure each home fit its surroundings. Minimum construction costs ranged from $6,000 to $15,000 depending on location, and designs had to be approved by a board of leading architects. These guarantees were to be maintained under a plan overseen by the St. James Wood Homes Association, founded in 1926 to govern the neighborhood. Construction began that year and continued through the mid-1960s. In a testament to the area’s enduring appeal, a home on one of the last remaining, very steep lots on St. James Drive was built as recently as 2018. Many of the neighborhood’s homes were designed by individual builders working alongside prominent architects. L’Hommedieu died in 1950 at age 66 and is buried in Mountain View Cemetery. At its height, the St. James Wood Homes Association represented more than 185 homes. Its covenants, conditions and restrictions required board approval for changes to exterior color schemes and for tree removals. Owners also needed approval for changes to the location or height of structures, including walls and fences. Annual dues were $25. The last annual meeting was held in 2012. Phil Chin, a neighborhood resident, said he received notice a few years ago that the association was being dissolved and that the roughly $1,000 remaining in its bank account was donated to charity. After a group photo at Hampton Park, some walkers opted for a shorter route and returned toward the city center. The rest crossed La Salle Avenue and passed through the large white columns flanking Hampton Road that mark the main entrance to St. James Wood. The group was pleased to have Hulda Nelson and Fleurise Montecillo and with her mother-in-law, Gloria Michael who was visiting from Australia, walking with them for the first time.

articles.text: Piedmont Recreation Department (PRD) offers dozens of youth sports camps for a wide range of ages, abilities, and interests throughout the summer, covering everything from longtime favorites like soccer and basketball to less ubiquitous options like lacrosse, pickleball, fencing, and ultimate frisbee. For summer 2026, PRD is offering several new programs. Coaching certificate This summer, teens can earn a coaching certificate through Make Me a Pro, with two dedicated programs for ages 15 to 17. These camps are designed for teens interested in working with younger athletes while building leadership skills, learning how to run practices, and gaining hands-on coaching experience. Two sessions will be offered: Soccer Teen Coaching Certification from June 8 to 12, and Basketball Teen Coaching Certification from Aug. 3 to 7. Participants who complete the program will be considered for Make Me a Pro volunteer coaching opportunities, providing a pathway to additional on-field experience. Tennis programs Tennis programming will also expand this summer with the addition of longtime Piedmont resident Jeff Machle to the PRD instructor roster. Machle is entering his third season as head tennis coach at The College Preparatory School and brings extensive experience teaching both youth players and competitive athletes. In addition, instructor Jim Landes’s popular beginning and advanced tennis clinics will return throughout the summer. Registration is available at http://piedmont.ca.gov/CommunityPass. New participants will need to create an account to register for programs. articles.text: Start planning your summer with the Piedmont Recreation Department now. PRD’s Summer 2026 Activity Guide will be published online January 26, with camp registration opening soon after – the earliest summer registration date we’ve offered: • Resident registration: Opens Monday, February 3, at 6 p.m. • Non-resident registration: Opens Monday, February 10, at 6 p.m. Piedmont Recreation offers summer programming for all ages – from Mini Campers (ages 3-5) to Funtopia (grades K-2) to Camp Everything (grades 2-6) and NextGen C.I.T. (grades 7–10) – with expanded options and new additions for 2026. Camp Everything Camp Everything returns with an affordable, traditional day-camp experience offered throughout the summer. Families can choose 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. or 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. camp days, with free early drop-off beginning at 8:30 a.m. We’ll be offering field trips weekly this year. The Funtopia age group at last year’s summer camp Piedmont kids playing at Camp Everything’s day camp. Piedmont kids playing a fun game at Camp Everything. An instructor teaching the mini campers at last year’s summer camp. Next Gen C.I.T (formerly VolunTEENS) We’re expanding capacity and leveling up our Councilor in Training program for teens in grades 7 to 10. The new curriculum adds practice job-readiness training, resume building, interview skills, and workplace etiquette. Participants will also earn CPR certification and receive water safety instruction. This summer, C.I.T.s will support Funtopia in addition to Camp Everything. Sidekicks (programs for neurodiverse children ages 3.5–14) Sidekicks are programming every week, and five full-day adaptive camps are planned this summer. New additions include a full-day “Mindful Movement” camp and a full-day academic and sports camp offered the week before school starts, in partnership with NeuroAffirm, to help ease the transition back into the classroom. Families can also combine half-day camps to create a full day of coverage, including the returning combination of LEGO (morning), Lunch Bunch, and Cooking (afternoon). articles.text: Pictured inside the entrance to the Buck Institute for Research on Aging are docent Mike Noel (left), Jim Ayotte, Janice Subotnick, Elene Manolis, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Judy Wang, Edith Hereso, Yorkman Lowe, Sue Getreuer, Sandra Ponce, Carole Jones, Gloria Wilmer, Greg Jurin, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Susan Silva, and George Epstein. The Piedmont Seniors recently traveled to Novato for a guided tour of the Buck Institute, a research center focused exclusively on the biology of aging. Its work aims to help people live not only longer lives, but healthier ones. Research has shown that aging is the No. 1 risk factor for chronic disease, and the Buck’s mission is to end the threat of age-related disease for this and future generations. The institute’s vision is that people should be able to enjoy life at 95 as much as they do at 25, a goal that requires a deeper understanding of how aging itself works. As the world’s first independent biomedical research institute, the Buck had a running start in the field. It is home to the nation’s first PhD program in the biology of aging. What once sounded like science fiction is now established fact: aging is malleable. Discoveries at the Buck are already being translated into drug-based and lifestyle interventions designed to help people live better, longer lives. The institute’s goal is to develop new therapies and interventions that improve what researchers call “healthspan.” The Buck Institute employs 270 people, including 170 scientists, representing 37 different countries. According to Eric Verdin, The buck Institute docent, Mike Noel, is showing the Piedmont Seniors a miniature scale of the Buck campus. MD, the Buck Institute’s president and CEO, “What I want people to know about the Buck is the incredible commitment and excitement that permeates the walls of this institution. We are pushing the frontiers in an area that is going to impact all of humanity. I cannot tell you exactly when this will happen, but I can tell you big discoveries are in the works and will come out of the Buck.” Tours and periodic seminars are open to the public, with seminars and Zoom meetings available for a nominal fee. After the tour, the Piedmont Seniors took a short drive around the area before heading to HopMonk Tavern in Novato for lunch. HopMonk is a casual restaurant known for its inviting beer garden, varied menu and friendly service. Overall, it was a wonderful and enlightening day for everyone. To find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on the fourth Wednesday morning of each month from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. The Piedmont Seniors enjoyed a wonderful lunch at the Hopmonk Beer Garden. Pictured at its entrance are Jim Ayotte (left), Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, Janice Subotnick, Sandra Ponce, Sue Getreuer, Gloria Wilmer, Carole Jones, Yorkman Lowe, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Judy Wang, Elene Manolis, Edith Hereso, and Susan Silva.

articles.text: Winter in Piedmont brings cooler temperatures, seasonal rain, and a natural slowdown in outdoor activity. While February may feel like a quieter time of year, it is actually one of the most important months for homeowners to assess, protect, and maintain their homes. Thoughtful winter care not only preserves a property’s condition but also prevents small issues from becoming costly repairs. Inspect Roofs, Gutters, and Drainage: Piedmont homes, many of them older and architecturally distinctive, are especially vulnerable to winter wear. Rain highlights problem areas that may go unnoticed during dry months. Homeowners should check roofs for loose tiles, worn flashing, or signs of leaks. Gutters and downspouts should be cleared of debris to allow proper water flow and reduce the risk of water pooling near foundations. Ensuring that soil slopes away from the home helps prevent moisture intrusion and long-term structural damage. Heating Systems and Fireplace Safety: have been running for several months. A mid-season check of furnaces or HVAC systems can confirm that everything is operating efficiently and safely. Fireplaces and chimneys should be inspected and cleaned if they’ve been used regularly, as buildup can create fire hazards. Smoke detectors and carbon monoxide alarms should be tested, and batteries replaced if needed—simple steps that significantly improve household safety. Watch for Moisture and Air Quality Issues: Cool weather combined with rain can create ideal conditions for moisture accumulation. Basements, crawl spaces, garages, and window frames are common areas where condensation or dampness may appear. Homeowners should look for musty odors, peeling paint, or visible mold. Addressing moisture early helps protect indoor air quality and prevents damage to walls, flooring, and insulation. Exterior Maintenance Still Matters: While winter is not typically a time for major landscaping, basic exterior maintenance remains important. Overgrown branches should be trimmed back from roofs and gutters to reduce storm damage risk. Loose fencing, gates, or handrails should be secured, and exterior lighting checked for safety and visibility during shorter days. These small efforts contribute to overall home longevity and neighborhood appeal. Use Winter as a Planning Period: February is also an ideal time to review household paperwork and long-term plans. Organizing insurance policies, warranties, and property records can simplify future decisions. For homeowners considering renovations, downsizing, or a future move, winter provides a calm window to explore options and prepare without pressure. Taking a proactive approach during winter helps Piedmont homeowners maintain their properties, protect their investments, and enter the spring season with confidence and clarity. Whether you’re curious about your home’s value, considering a sale, or exploring a lifestyle change, I’m here to offer clarity, strategy, and a personalized approach. 510.414.6777 | Debbi. DiMaggio@corcoranicon.com

articles.text: One of the most common concerns among parents of young puppies is car sickness. Many new owners arrive to collect their eight-week-old bundle of joy, only to receive an unwelcome surprise in their lap on the drive home. While most dogs will eventually grow out of car sickness, there are several steps you can take during puppyhood to make travel easier for both you and your dog. So what causes car sickness in puppies? In most cases, it stems from their still-developing inner ears. The vestibular system, which controls balance, is not yet fully mature, leading to sensory confusion between what the puppy sees and what it feels during movement. This mismatch can cause nausea and may be worsened by stress. Common symptoms include excessive drooling, restlessness, frequent yawning, lethargy, shaking or trembling, and, of course, dry heaving and vomiting. There are several simple ways to improve your puppy’s comfort during car rides. Cracking a window can provide fresh air, and allowing your puppy to see outside may help their inner ear better process movement. Puppies who ride in the trunk are far more likely to experience car sickness. An elevated puppy booster seat can also improve visibility and make the ride more comfortable. Your veterinarian may recommend a medication called Cerenia (maropitant citrate) to prevent nausea and vomiting. When given a few hours before travel, it is often very effective, though it can be expensive. Ask your vet about possible over-the-counter alternatives such as meclizine or Dramamine. It is important to remember that dosages for dogs are very different from those for humans, so never give your puppy human medication without Missy the Australian Shepherd enjoying a drive car sicknessfree! veterinary guidance. Even if your puppy gets carsick on every ride, a little planning can go a long way in reducing stress. For longer trips, typically 30 minutes or more, avoid feeding your puppy within two hours of departure. Bring puppy pads, towels and wipes for easy cleanup. A bib can help keep chest fur clean if your puppy drools excessively. Never reprimand your puppy for car sickness, as this can create a negative association with car rides. Finally, resist the urge to feed your puppy immediately after an episode, even if they appear hungry. Most puppies outgrow car sickness within the first six months of life, but that does not make the experience any less challenging in the moment. With patience and preparation, these tips can help make traveling with your new puppy more manageable for everyone involved. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. articles.text: John K. Uilkema died peacefully at home in Piedmont on January 5, 2026 at the age of 90. John was born in Illinois on March 11, 1935 to Mildred and T. John Uilkema. John grew up in Indiana. He attended the University of Michigan, obtaining a degree in Mechanical Engineering. He then studied law at George Washington University in Washington D.C. at night while he worked by day as a patent examiner. Upon graduation from law school, John married Gayle Burns and they moved to California. John became licensed to practice Patent, Trademark and Copyright Law in multiple jurisdictions, and started his practice at Shell Oil in Emeryville before transitioning to the patent, trademark and copyright firm of Naylor and Neil in San Francisco, where he soon became a named partner. The couple moved to Moraga where their daughter Lynn was born. Shortly after, their daughter Sharon was born and the family moved to Lafayette. In the 1980’s, John moved his law practice to Limbach, Limbach and Sutton in the Ferry Building of San Francisco where he served for years as managing partner. John was very active in the American Bar Association and held positions on the Board of Directors. He was president of the Patent Section and was elected to the House of Delegates for multiple decades well past retirement. He received numerous awards for over 50 years of service. Later in his career, he worked at Thelen, Reid and Preist and then at the boutique Intellectual Property firm of Dergosits & Noah. On a personal level, John married the love of his life, Gail Anderson in 1996. They lived in Piedmont with Gail’s son Yung. John was passionate about cars, showing numerous cars over the years including his original 1957 Chevy Bel Air Convertible. He served as a car show judge, and attended the Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance annually on Gail’s birthday. His home office was filled with car awards and memorabilia. He was an active member of the Candy Store in Burlingame, where he kept his Chevy on display. John shared his love of cars with his best friend George Marin. The two not only raced, but also enjoyed weekly breakfasts at his favorite place, the Orinda Village Cafe. Throughout his life, John spent much time John Uilkema died peacefully at home in Piedmont on January 5, 2026. exploring his Dutch roots and connecting with his relatives in the Netherlands. John is survived by his wife Gail, daughters Lynn (Damien), Sharon (Curtiss), and grandchildren Natalie, Nicholas, Henry and Sophie. He is predeceased by his younger sister Jackie. To do something in memory of John, please go to the Orinda Village Cafe and have a lovely meal and think of him. He would recommend the three-egg omelet with the waffle.

Notably, Crest’s sidewalk lacked the tile inlays seen elsewhere, suggesting it may not have been a primary street in the original development. Homes along Crest span several decades, from the 1920s through the 1950s. Crest begins with a moderate slope, but over roughly a quarter mile the grade increases sharply toward Somerset Road. Walkers paused to admire a home with a dramatic steep slate roof before turning onto Somerset, where the climb remained demanding. Somerset starts very steep and gradually levels out. The hillsides showed signs of past slides, with some homes perched on significant slopes. Farther up stood a large, modern, multi-story white house with a metal gate blocking its steep driveway. Scaffolding surrounded the exterior as it was being painted by a worker clearly untroubled by heights. The house had the feel of a fortress overlooking the valley below. The group crossed the Oakland-Piedmont city line twice and continued for nearly another half mile before emerging on Estates Drive. A lingering haze muted what might otherwise have been expansive views of Oakland, the Bay, and San Francisco. By then the temperature had risen, jackets were shed, and a cool breeze was welcome. The walkers headed down Estates to the top of the steep upper stretch of Hampton Road, descended it, and returned toward town via La Salle Avenue and St. James Drive, noting a set of smaller columns that mark yet another entrance to the St. James Wood neighborhood. At four miles and just under two hours, it was a longer walk than usual. Still, the group took pride in meeting the challenge. It was a satisfying way to begin 2026 for the Walking on Wednesdays group, combining history, scenery and a reminder that some of Piedmont’s most rewarding streets require a bit of extra effort to reach. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to call (510) 420-3070 for more information. Most of the children were five to six years old. While some struggled at the start, their confidence grew as the ride continued. “I think the kids didn’t know they could do it,” Horowitz said. “And once they did it, they felt like rock stars.” The bike bus was created in response to AC Transit’s decision to replace bus line 33 and eliminate extended school-hour service that previously connected the Hampton and Estates Drive area with Piedmont High School, Millennium High School and Havens Elementary School. Co-founder Melissa Partovi said the goal of the bike bus is to build a community culture that supports child independence and autonomy. “We want to give kids the confidence to bike to school on their own and parents the fortitude to let this happen,” Partovi said. “The idea is to move toward riding solo, without these guardrails. pages.text: 2 2 Wednesday, January 14, 2026 Opinion By Jay Russell QUESTION: Aside from picking up trash and donating to the Marine Mammal Center, what can you do to save the planet? Asked on Friday, May 23, 2025, to Ben Spencer’s 4th grade class at Beach School. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on May 28, 2025. FRANCES OATES-STERNGLANZ Use less single-use plastic. LUKE SHIN I would recycle daily and not waste food, water, etc. OPINION Making the case for progressive school tax By Rick Schiller Editor: In 2013 PUSD went from a progressive tiered tax to a regressive flat tax. The flat tax resulted in 76% of Piedmont taxpayers whose parcels are under 10,000 sf paying 6% to 21% more. A small percentage of taxpayers with homes on large parcels and commercial/multi-unit building owners enjoyed tax decreases of 7% to 80%. The school’s pollster Dr. McLarney in 2019 when asked to compare a per square foot of building tax (PSFBT) to a flat rate tax, found 73.5% of voters would support a 125% increased PSFBT. Dr. McLarney found less enthusiasm at 62.1% of voters supporting a 115% increased flat tax. In summary the PSFBT generated 9% more income and 11% more support. Dr. McLarney summarized: “more tax sensitivity for flat tax, less tax sensitivity for square foot version.” The School Board chose to ignore its contracted pollster and put before voters the lower polling regressive flat tax rather than the PSFBT. However, the Board did place a supplemental PSFBT before voters which suggests they recognized two fundamental concepts. First a larger home will cost more initially and will sell for more than a smaller home of equivalent quality. If over a given period of time home prices double, then the $1M home nets $1M profit and the $2M home nets $2M. Secondly a family in a large home will put more children in our schools than a smaller home. In fairness those in larger homes that enjoy greater financially benefit at time of sale and use more school resources should pay a tax based on larger home size. Only a progressive PSFBT brings our tax structure closer to equality for taxpayers of California’s most expensive school support tax, a tax critical to land value in Piedmont. The School Board can now place before voters a progressive tax based on square foot of building. Such a tax makes small incremental increases easy going forward. A PSFBT also attracts young families to the smaller starter homes and encourages increased enrollment. The Alameda School District and others use a PSFBT with a legally allowed lower flat tax on undeveloped parcels and a maximum cap so very large homes are not taxed exorbitantly. The School Board proposes an Evergreen tax which will preclude a tax conversation going forward if passed. This makes a progressive PSFBT critically needed now and for the future of Piedmont. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council voted Jan. 5 to approve an overall budget and authorize the city administrator to negotiate contract amendments with Hood Design Studio for the Sidney & Irene Dearing Memorial Project. The project has a total budget of $417,250. Of that amount, $107,250 is allocated for design and construction-ready drawings. The remaining $250,000 is designated for fabrication of the structure, the foundation, transportation and installation of the artwork. The project is budgeted in the city’s fiscal year 2025–26 budget. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation is partnering with the city on fundraising efforts, with a goal of raising $30,000 for the project. The city is working with renowned artist and landscape architect Walter Hood of Oakland-based Hood Design Studio. The studio presented a preliminary design concept in June, and the next phase will focus on advancing that concept into a and mailbox. Inside, interpretive features will share the Dearings’ story and invite reflection on broader themes of racial exclusion and resilience. The memorial is planned for Triangle Park at the intersection of Magnolia and Wildwood avenues. City parameters for the site include no tree removal and visibility from the street. City staff anticipate completing design work in the spring. Fabrication is expected to take several months, followed by one to two months of on-site construction, with project completion anticipated in summer 2026. In 2020, the City Council adopted a resolution committing to examining Piedmont’s history as part of an effort to become a more inclusive and equitable community. The council formally initiated the memorial project in 2022. Progress was delayed as the city focused on construction of the dispatch center and community pool, but with those projects now completed, attention has returned to the Sidney & Irene Dearing Memorial Project. Sidney Dearing and Irene moved to Piedmont, California, in January 1924 and became the community’s first black residents. final design ready for fabrication. articles.text: Green-eyed Venus is a quiet, thoughtful presence. This four-year-old tabby is cautious around new people and is looking for a bighearted adopter who will give her the time and trust she needs to blossom into an affectionate companion. Her foster describes her as a “wonderful cat” and says watching her personality unfold is deeply rewarding. Over time, Venus reveals herself as a charming little friend who values both her relationships with people and her independence. She lets you know when she is ready for affection with a gentle nose nudge or by settling into your lap, and prefers soft petting in small doses. Giving her personal space is key to her happiness, but she is not aloof. Talking to her sweetly goes a long way, and she enjoys chatting back. Venus is currently on a wet-food-only diet to support Adopt Venus through Cat Town. healthy weight loss and digestion, and has begun to explore playing with toys, an exciting new way for her to bond with a future adopter. She may prefer to be the only cat and will thrive in a calm, indoor-only, cat-savvy home. Venus is spayed, vaccinated, microchipped, and negative for FeLV and FIV. Learn more at www.cattownoakland.org or email adopt@ cattownoakland.org.

articles.text: The Planning Commission is considering whether to recommend that the City Council adopt proposed “Objective Design Standards” that would govern new housing construction in Piedmont. The proposal updates existing standards for accessory dwelling units, mixed-use projects and multifamily development, and introduces new objective standards for single-family homes and residential projects of up to four units. The draft Objective Design Standards are intended to create clear, measurable and enforceable rules for housing design, giving residents, property owners and developers a better understanding of what new housing in Piedmont is expected to look like. While the standards do not prescribe specific architectural styles, they are designed to produce housing that is consistent with existing development in the city. The draft standards reflect community feedback as well as existing design guidelines. They were informed by two open house events, an online survey and two Planning Commission study sesDraft Objective Design Standards cover page sions. Proposed standards related to driveways and window placement address commonly raised concerns about safety and privacy. State law now requires cities to approve certain types of housing, including accessory dwelling units and SB 9 applications, using “objective” standards that do not rely on subjective judgment by public officials. These state-mandated, ministerial permits do not consider public comment and are not reviewed by the Planning Commission at a public meeting, unlike the traditional design review process. If the Planning Commission votes to recommend the draft Objective Design Standards, the proposal is tentatively scheduled to come before the City Council for adoption in February. Learn more about this initiative and see materials and video from previous discussions at piedmont.ca.gov/ObjectiveDesignStandards.
articles.title: Planning Commission to consider recommendation on proposed “Objective Design Standards” for new homes in Piedmont

articles.text: Cardigan is a five-year-old French bulldog mix with quiet charm and amusing, grunty purrs. He is a wonderful walking partner, checking back whenever his walker stops to make sure all is well. He comes when called and sits on command for a treat. At 27 pounds, he is the perfect size. Cardigan greets new people politely with a gentle sniff of the hand, then gives a small wiggle once he feels safe. Well-behaved French bulldogs do not often end up in the shelter system, so those interested should make an appointment to meet him through Oakland Animal Services’ website. Walk-ins are also welcome this week, with earlier visits encouraged: Thursday from noon to 6:30 p.m., and Friday, Saturday, or Sunday from Presenting Cardigan – The Polite, Petite Gentleman noon to 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12, or with a dog weighing 25 pounds more or less than Cardigan, must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council awarded a $147,557 contract for the city’s annual sidewalk repair project at its Monday, December 15, meeting. The work will involve concrete shaving to address sidewalk offsets throughout the city and is expected to begin in January. The contract includes a required 10 percent construction contingency, bringing the total estimated project construction budget to $162,313. Each year, city staff inspect sidewalks to identify damage and offsets directly attributable to city-owned trees. Public Works reviews reported offsets and determines which locations are suitable for the selected repair method. This year, the city identified 1,403 locations where concrete shaving can be used. According to City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore’s report to the council, concrete shaving was selected as the preferred method for the project. “Concrete shaving is a fast, efficient, and green alternative to grinding,” Moore said. “It allows for edge-to-edge repairs that eliminate the entire trip hazard at precisely calculated slopes.” The 2026 Sidewalk Repair Program recommends concentrating most of the work on the following streets: Grand Avenue, Arbor Drive, Nova Drive, Fairview Avenue, Dale Avenue, Magnolia Avenue, Rose Avenue, Kingston Avenue, and Cambridge Way. The project is expected to be completed in winter 2026. Sidewalk offset on Grand Ave.

pages.text: 4 Wednesday, January 14, 2026 Adoptable Dog of the Week By Jessica McDevitt Cardigan is a five-year-old French bulldog mix with quiet charm and amusing, grunty purrs. He is a wonderful walking partner, checking back whenever his walker stops to make sure all is well. He comes when called and sits on command for a treat. At 27 pounds, he is the perfect size. Cardigan greets new people politely with a gentle sniff of the hand, then gives a small wiggle once he feels safe. Well-behaved French bulldogs do not often end up in the shelter system, so those interested should make an appointment to meet him through Oakland Animal Services’ website. Walk-ins are also welcome this week, with earlier visits encouraged: Thursday from noon to 6:30 p.m., and Friday, Saturday, or Sunday from Presenting Cardigan – The Polite, Petite Gentleman noon to 3 p.m. Potential adopters with a child younger than 12, or with a dog weighing 25 pounds more or less than Cardigan, must bring them to the shelter for the meeting. For more information about adoption or about how to temporarily foster a puppy or dog, contact Piedmont resident Jessica McDevitt at jessicamcdev@gmail.com. Lee, PHS alums Planning Commission to consider recommendation on proposed “Objective Design Standards” for new homes in Piedmont The Planning Commission is considering whether to recommend that the City Council adopt proposed “Objective Design Standards” that would govern new housing construction in Piedmont. The proposal updates existing standards for accessory dwelling units, mixed-use projects and multifamily development, and introduces new objective standards for single-family homes and residential projects of up to four units. The draft Objective Design Standards are intended to create clear, measurable and enforceable rules for housing design, giving residents, property owners and developers a better understanding of what new housing in Piedmont is expected to look like. While the standards do not prescribe specific architectural styles, they are designed to produce housing that is consistent with existing development in the city. The draft standards reflect community feedback as well as existing design guidelines. They were informed by two open house events, an online survey and two Planning Commission study sesDraft Objective Design Standards cover page sions. Proposed standards related to driveways and window placement address commonly raised concerns about safety and privacy. State law now requires cities to approve certain types of housing, including accessory dwelling units and SB 9 applications, using “objective” standards that do not rely on subjective judgment by public officials. These state-mandated, ministerial permits do not consider public comment and are not reviewed by the Planning Commission at a public meeting, unlike the traditional design review process. If the Planning Commission votes to recommend the draft Objective Design Standards, the proposal is tentatively scheduled to come before the City Council for adoption in February. Learn more about this initiative and see materials and video from previous discussions at piedmont.ca.gov/ObjectiveDesignStandards. Piedmont to award $147,557 contract for annual sidewalk repair program By Jake Lannon The Piedmont City Council awarded a $147,557 contract for the city’s annual sidewalk repair project at its Monday, December 15, meeting. The work will involve concrete shaving to address sidewalk offsets throughout the city and is expected to begin in January. The contract includes a required 10 percent construction contingency, bringing the total estimated project construction budget to $162,313. Each year, city staff inspect sidewalks to identify damage and offsets directly attributable to city-owned trees. Public Works reviews reported offsets and determines which locations are suitable for the selected repair method. This year, the city identified 1,403 locations where concrete shaving can be used. According to City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore’s report to the council, concrete shaving was selected as the preferred method for the project. “Concrete shaving is a fast, efficient, and green alternative to grinding,” Moore said. “It allows for edge-to-edge repairs that eliminate the entire trip hazard at precisely calculated slopes.” The 2026 Sidewalk Repair Program recommends concentrating most of the work on the following streets: Grand Avenue, Arbor Drive, Nova Drive, Fairview Avenue, Dale Avenue, Magnolia Avenue, Rose Avenue, Kingston Avenue, and Cambridge Way. The project is expected to be completed in winter 2026. Sidewalk offset on Grand Ave. ADVERTISE IN THE POST

articles.text: The Piedmont Garden Club is inviting residents to a discussion on preparedness titled “Living With Wildfire.” The event is on January 21 at 9:30 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall, and is free to the public The Pacific Palisades fire, which burned in January 2025, served as a reminder that wildfire danger is no longer limited to rural areas. Suburban and urban neighborhoods, including those in the East Bay, face growing risk due to changing climate conditions, dense development, and landscaping choices. The Living With Wildfire program, featuring Piedmont Fire Chief Dave Brannigan and photographer Saxon Holt, will present essential practices to help keep your home safe from wildfires and showcase effective fire-wise landscaping techniques you can use. Chief Brannigan will also explain the importance of the recent designation of Piedmont as a Wildland Urban Interface (WUI) and the adoption of the State’s new WUI Fire Code. “Last year’s Palisades Fire was a stark reminder that wildfire isn’t a ‘what if’ — it’s a reality that communities across California need to adapt to, now,” said Brannigan. “The good news is there are practical steps everyone can take today to reduce risk. I’m excited to partner with the Piedmont Garden Club and Saxon Holt to show that outdoor spaces can be both fire-smart and beautiful.” HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: The Grand-Mandana Gas Station is fenced off Several Piedmont-area gas stations have temporarily closed after a long-planned state requirement took effect January 1, mandating the removal or replacement of older single-walled underground fuel tanks that lack modern leak-detection systems. The closures stem from a California law adopted September 25, 2014, which updated the state’s underground storage tank (UST) program governing tank design and construction. The law requires any single-walled storage tank that lacks secondary containment and a continuous leak-detection system to be permanently closed by December 31, 2025. Single-walled storage tanks are considered higher risk because they are more susceptible to leaks caused by rust and corrosion. The intent of the law is to prevent hazardous substances from contaminating soil, groundwater, streams and other sources of drinking water. Owners of single-walled UST systems were notified of the requirement in 2014. As of 2024, Alameda County had 469 gas stations, and five percent, or 23 stations, had not complied with the law ahead of the closure deadline, according to county data. AddiA tank is being delivered to the Grand-Mandana Gas Station tional information is available at https://tinyurl.com/mphd94ad. The State Water Resources Control Board’s UST map identifies Piedmont Gas and Auto Repair, Piedmont Market 76 and the Grand-Mandana gas station as locations required to replace their single-walled tanks. The map can be viewed at https://tinyurl.com/ WaterBoardMapUST. Stations that remain out of compliance face penalties ranging from $500 to $5,000 per day per underground storage tank, according to the State Resources Control Board. Noncompliant stations may also be red-tagged by the Unified Program Agency, which can prevent fuel deliveries and dispensing. To support compliance, California established the Replacing, Removing, or Upgrading Underground Storage Tanks (RUST) program. Since 2015, the State Water Board has provided $183.1 million in loans and grants to assist with the permanent closure of single-walled tanks. Work is already underway at the Grand-Mandana station, where removal and replacement of its single-walled tank began in December. A large excavation is visible at the site where the tank was removed. An employee at Piedmont Gas and Auto Repair told the Post the station expects to remain closed for approximately three months while completing the required work. The dug-out hole for UST replacement at the Grand-Mandana Station

articles.text: Ruchi Medhekar presided over her first full school board meeting as President on January 7. Since the meeting was held in the Alan Harvey Theater’s drama classroom, she still awaits her first chance to sound the gavel in City Hall to open a meeting from the center chair of the council chamber room. This meeting kicked off new leadership tenures and also served as a farewell and thank you to the fall semester student representatives of the board Hunter Fasteau (PHS) and Saniyah Johnson (MHS). The presentation on the evening was delivered by Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich, focusing the council on their current place in time at the midpoint of the board’s three-year Local Control & Accountability Plan (LCAP). “It’s really hard to believe we are in year two of our three-year LCAP, halfway through. I’m such a huge fan of everything we have done this year from Fish Tank to the World Language update,” said Medhekar. Medhekar’s vice president title was filled by second year board member Michael Malione who will also serve an important leadership role on the board this calendar year. As president, Medhekar introduced her first new resolution for the board, a first reading seeking to renewing the Measure G school parcel tax for $3174 per parcel. Medhekar thanked board members Max Roman and Lindsay Thomasson for putting a special tax on the ballot, “It’s not something that any of us take lightly, so thank you for that,” Medhekar said. Piedmont resident Rick Schiller spoke in the public comment portion of the meeting promoting a shift of the financial burden to the square foot tax. He suggested large homes use more school resources and should pay more accordingly. “Only a progressive per square foot of building tax makes equality and fairness possible,” said Schiller. Schiller went over his allotted time, requiring new president Medhekar, for the first time, to inform a speaker that their time was up. Mehhekar handled this delicate responsibility with grace, affecting the appropriate concern and care with her words and tone. A significant part of the role is being the public facing voice for the board, and encounters with public speakers will provide a continual test of empathy. Medhekar’s first meeting as president took place on the first day back from school, beginning a new spring semester for students. The meeting was relatively short, lasting only one hour. The newly reorganized board will next meet on Wednesday, January 21, which will include Superintendent Jennifer Hawn’s State of the District report.

articles.text: At the beginning of a new year, we often ask big questions: What do I want to change? What do I want to make? What do I want to become better at? They are reasonable questions. They can also be completely paralyzing, because they are so big. Creativity often stalls not because people lack ideas, but because the imagined next step feels too large or too loaded with expectation. We leap immediately to outcomes like mastery, consistency or meaning before giving ourselves permission to simply begin. I’ve been wondering what might happen if we made the entry point much smaller, maybe even just one thing. Not “what should I commit my entire being to this year,” but a simple experiment: • A new walking route. • A different genre of book. • Learning to cook a new recipe. • Saying yes to an invitation you would normally decline. • Moving one idea from germ to first step. When the stakes are low, something interesting can happen. Curiosity has room to breathe. Attention sharpens because you are no longer trying to prove anything. You are simply gathering information. This is how creativity often works. Not in sweeping gestures or giant leaps, but in small acts of willingness, a quiet openness to what might happen if you do something slightly different than yesterday. What I like about starting here is that it does not require confidence, talent or clarity about where things are headed. It only requires noticing a flicker of interest and being willing to follow it. You might try this experiment for the next week or month: when something catches your attention, try it, even once. Do not worry about whether it is useful or impressive. In fact, aim for the novel. Not everything you try will lead somewhere, and that is not the point. The point is to remind yourself that creativity does not begin with certainty. It begins with small movements. One small step is often enough to change the energy of an entire year. Nina Meehan is a keynote speaker, workshop facilitator and coach with a specialization in creativity and communication. https://ninameehan.com/
articles.title: Creativity experiment: trying one new thing

articles.text: the return to school. As we enter the spring season, the Piedmont Unified School District is preparing for upcoming negotiations with our employee associations. We are writing to share the Board’s priorities and reaffirm our appreciation for our educators and staff who serve our students each day. Perhaps most important, we want to be clear that we view our staff as the heart of our schools. Their expertise, care, and dedication create the learning environments that allow our students to thrive academically and socially. The Board is committed to supporting their professional success and well-being. As we approach negotiations, the Board has identified several key priorities that reflect our shared values and our long-term responsibility to students, staff, and our community. Ensuring Competitive and Sustainable Compensation Attracting and retaining outstanding educators and staff require a salary structure that is competitive within our region. We continue to review comparable school districts and believe that improving the salaries of our newest teachers must be a priority for our district in order to attract and retain beginning teachers. We are pleased with our progress in raising veteran teacher pay, but our work is not finished. We are now focused on increasing starting salaries to ensure we attract the best new educators. Investing in our beginning teachers is an investment in a stable, high-quality workforce for the future. Providing Affordable and High-Quality Healthcare The Board recognizes that access to affordable healthcare is a critical component of employee wellbeing. Two years ago, rising healthcare costs posed significant challenges for the District. Through thoughtful research, improved $0 cost and multiple low-cost options were identified this year, offering better access to healthcare for employees and their families. Maintaining fiscally responsible, high-quality healthcare options for our staff remains a priority for our District. Protecting the District’s LongTerm Fiscal Health The Board prioritizes longterm fiscal stability to protect our staff and students from economic uncertainty. By maintaining a healthy reserve, the District can manage rising costs and enrollment shifts without compromising class sizes or staffing levels. This responsible management ensures we can provide competitive compensation while maintaining a stable environment for the entire school community. Maintaining Low Class Sizes Small class sizes, particularly in our elementary schools, are foundational to high quality teaching and learning. Low class size allows educators to know students well, personalize instruction, and provide the academic and social emotional support young learners need. We are also analyzing middle and high school class sizes to ensure they remain balanced and low. Earlier this fall, the District held a Board workshop and provided direction for staff to continue to prioritize small class sizes in our core classes in the master schedule in an effort to balance classes. Preserving low class sizes remains a central priority for the Board alongside maintaining flexibility to ensure financial viability for all the priorities articulated above. Sincerely, Ruchi Medhekar, Board President Michael Malione, Vice President Max Roman, Member Susy Struble, Member Lindsay Thomasson, Member Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D., Superintendent

pages.text: Wednesday, January 14, 2026 7 Piedmont Pulse Continued from page 1 the return to school. As we enter the spring season, the Piedmont Unified School District is preparing for upcoming negotiations with our employee associations. We are writing to share the Board’s priorities and reaffirm our appreciation for our educators and staff who serve our students each day. Perhaps most important, we want to be clear that we view our staff as the heart of our schools. Their expertise, care, and dedication create the learning environments that allow our students to thrive academically and socially. The Board is committed to supporting their professional success and well-being. As we approach negotiations, the Board has identified several key priorities that reflect our shared values and our long-term responsibility to students, staff, and our community. Ensuring Competitive and Sustainable Compensation Attracting and retaining outstanding educators and staff require a salary structure that is competitive within our region. We continue to review comparable school districts and believe that improving the salaries of our newest teachers must be a priority for our district in order to attract and retain beginning teachers. We are pleased with our progress in raising veteran teacher pay, but our work is not finished. We are now focused on increasing starting salaries to ensure we attract the best new educators. Investing in our beginning teachers is an investment in a stable, high-quality workforce for the future. Providing Affordable and High-Quality Healthcare The Board recognizes that access to affordable healthcare is a critical component of employee wellbeing. Two years ago, rising healthcare costs posed significant challenges for the District. Through thoughtful research, improved $0 cost and multiple low-cost options were identified this year, offering better access to healthcare for employees and their families. Maintaining fiscally responsible, high-quality healthcare options for our staff remains a priority for our District. Protecting the District’s LongTerm Fiscal Health The Board prioritizes longterm fiscal stability to protect our staff and students from economic uncertainty. By maintaining a healthy reserve, the District can manage rising costs and enrollment shifts without compromising class sizes or staffing levels. This responsible management ensures we can provide competitive compensation while maintaining a stable environment for the entire school community. Maintaining Low Class Sizes Small class sizes, particularly in our elementary schools, are foundational to high quality teaching and learning. Low class size allows educators to know students well, personalize instruction, and provide the academic and social emotional support young learners need. We are also analyzing middle and high school class sizes to ensure they remain balanced and low. Earlier this fall, the District held a Board workshop and provided direction for staff to continue to prioritize small class sizes in our core classes in the master schedule in an effort to balance classes. Preserving low class sizes remains a central priority for the Board alongside maintaining flexibility to ensure financial viability for all the priorities articulated above. articles.text: Student representatives on the Piedmont Unified School District Board of Education occupy a distinct role – balancing life as students while representing thousands of peers in district decision-making. The second semester at Piedmont High marks a transition from outgoing student board members Hunter Fasteau and Saniyah Johnson to incoming representatives Charli Panico and Ben Ramakrishnan, highlighting both the promise and limits of student voice in district governance. As Panico begins her term, she is motivated by a desire to move student concerns beyond informal conversations and into action. “I saw an opportunity to speak for my peers,” she said. “This role allows me to turn concerns into actions and make sure student experiences are truly represented.” Ahead of her first board meeting, Panico has focused on gathering perspectives from students across campus on two major issues: the district’s cell phone policy and the introduction of new courses. Rather than assuming a single viewpoint, she has sought out a range of perspectives. “I’ve been going around and talking to people at school and writing down what people need,” she said. Panico has been encouraged by the board’s use of smaller, topic-based meetings and is interested in expanding them at PHS as a way to lower barriers to student participation and connect students directly with board members. While the current pilot limiting phone use during brunch and passing periods has had little impact so far, she expressed concerns about a full ban next year, citing enforcement challenges, safety issues, and accessibility for students with medical needs. She also views new course offerings as an opportunity, but noted that the expansion of weighted classes may increase academic stress. That belief is echoed, albeit more cautiously, by Fasteau, who completed his term last semester. Like Panico, Fasteau ran to represent student perspectives and influence policy, but quickly realized how demanding the role could be. “I wasn’t able to separate this role at all from my life as a student,” he said. One moment that stood out was staying late to cast a vote on the second reading of PHS course additions. “It was about fulfilling the promise I made to the students that informed my decision,” he said. While Fasteau believes board members care about student input, he identified structural challenges that limit consistent representation. He noted that student voice often depends on a single individual and suggested more permanent systems for student feedback. After learning about the Brown Act, which restricts discussion of non-agendized items, he said he sometimes felt “more like an extension of a system as opposed to the voice of the student body.” Despite these limitations, Fasteau emphasized the power of participation. “Students and other adults should know that their voice matters,” he said. “They can influence policy just by showing up.” At the January 7 board meeting, the final meeting for Fasteau and Johnson as student board representatives, Superintendent Hawn publicly thanked both students for their dedication and advocacy. Board President Ruchi Medhekar also addressed the representatives directly, emphasizing the lasting impact of their work. “Every student board member has an opportunity to leave their mark,” Medhekar said. Reflecting on their terms, she expressed gratitude for the ways both students shaped board discussions. She recalled first meeting Fasteau early in his time at PHS and recognizing his deep care for the district, noting that it made him a strong candidate for the role. She also highlighted Johnson’s influence on board decision-making, adding that there are “only a handful of times” when a student is able to meaningfully shift the direction of a resolution, and credited Johnson with changing the board’s perspective on NCAA-related issues. Together, Panico’s forward-looking approach and Fasteau’s reflections illustrate the realities of student representation in Piedmont, defined by opportunity, responsibility, and institutional constraints. As Panico begins her term alongside Ramakrishnan, representing both Piedmont High School and Millennium High School, her leadership builds on lessons from those who came before her. Ultimately, the strength of student voice depends not only on who holds the seat, but on how consistently students are invited and supported to participate. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern reporter for the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: Piedmont Cub Scouts in Packs 3, 4, 5 and 6 joined together to help unhoused neighbors by assembling hygiene kits and donating them to the East Oakland Collective. On December 10 more than 80 people, including Cub Scouts (Kinder-5th grade) with their families, adult Cub Scout leaders, Den Chiefs and Scouts helped assemble over 600 hygiene kits at Havens Elementary School. Pack 3 started this annual holiday tradition of assembling hygiene kits in 2023 by donating 300 hygiene kits to East Oakland Collective. Now in its third year, the event has expanded to include all four Piedmont Cub Scout Packs and has more than doubled its giving. This community service project is supported by the four Packs as well as individual Scout families. The hygiene kits included toiletries such as soap, toothbrushes, toothpaste, toilet paper, washcloths, and winter hats. The Programs Manager at the East Oakland Collective said, “We are beyond thankful for the continuous support and generosity of … [Piedmont Cub Scouts]. Their commitment to service and care for our community makes a meaningful impact, and the hygiene kits assembled by the Cub Scouts are a powerful example of how young leaders can truly make a difference.” If you are interested in joining Cub Scouts or Scouts, contact the Piedmont Scout Council at contact@piedmontbsa.org. The East Bay Collective is a non-profit organization that helps East Oakland residents live comfortably in their neighborhoods. One of their biggest events, hosted quarterly, is Feed the Hood, where they distribute food and hygiene kits to the unhoused. If you want to support the East Oakland Collective, please visit eastoaklandcollective.com Cub Scouts, their families, and Scout Leaders

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: It’s been a strong start to the New Year for Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team, tying Western Alameda County Conference rivals Berkeley 2-2 on Thursday, January 8 at the Yellowjackets’ home field, and thrashing Gateway 11-0 at Witter two days later. The results push Piedmont’s unbeaten run to five games with four wins and one draw. “We’re starting to play the kind of football we want to see. The press was really good against Berkeley, they are a very good team. We played well against Berkeley, we moved the ball well, but there’s still things we want to work on as a team,” coach Matt Spencer-Harty said. The result against Berkeley was Piedmont’s first league match of the season, giving them an important point against a school with 19 upperclassmen. “Our press was outstanding. They struggled to get out of their own half,” Spencer-Harty said. “Berkeley was definitely a hard game. We didn’t know what to expect, but a tie is good for what we got. We’re still figuring out how to work together, plus a new coach is a change. It’s just nice to be back and play,” senior Miranda Liu added. Piedmont’s record is now 4-2-2 (W-T-L) under first-year head coach Spencer-Harty, who came to the Highlanders as another product of the coaching tree produced by the 24-7 UK Soccer Academy. Former girls’ soccer coach Dan Chubbock and former boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan also came from 24-7, as does current boys soccer head coach Ben Russell. “It’s great. I feel like all the 24-7 coaches have a similar vibe, so it doesn’t feel much different. The teams doing great working together, and having four freshmen [Olivia Nealon, Makenna Piedmont is 4-2-2 and on a five-game unbeaten run. Staff Photos Small, Olivia Kan-Miller, Olivia Luccacini] is a big change, but they are great,” Liu said. The Highlanders look ahead to its league schedule ramping up with critical matches against Castro Valley, Alameda, and Bishop O’Dowd ahead. Spencer-Harty likes what he sees out of the group, but still has things he wants to work on. “There’s a little work to be done in our combination play and getting our wingbacks a little higher a little earlier. A lot of time we isolate our two nines, so we want to get support 4-v-3 instead of a 3-v-2 against us,” Spencer-Harty said. 11-0 over Gateway The shellacking started in the third minute following a corner, where Erica Smith turned in a loose ball in front of the net. Seven minutes later, Liu scored on a rebounded initial shot by Ayla Blanford in the box. Liu scored again two minutes later, making a run in behind to put herself 1-on-1 with the goalkeeper. Blanford scored in the 17th after Elia Kwong’s shot on target rebounded into play. Elspeth Grippando made it 5-nil in the 25th in another 1-on- 1. Kwong scored in the 35th, holding off a defender in a long run in possession—bringing it to 6-0 by halftime. Olivia Luccacini scored in the 49th on a nice run down the right side. Grippando scored again in the 51st on a dribble down the left. Lila Rosen scored on a composed shot in the box in the 55th, while freshman Olivia Nealon scored five minutes later. Piedmont’s last goal came by Makenna Small in the 69th minute. 2-2 with Berkeley Berkeley took an initial lead in the 10th minute on a looping header from a corner. Piedmont equalized in the early minutes of the second half when Kwong slotted in a penalty kick off the underside of the crossbar. It came after Liu drew a penalty, weaving her way around three defenders before being pulled down in the box. Berkeley went ahead again a few minutes later when a well struck free-kick rocketed into the top side of the net, giving the Jackets a 2-1 lead. Piedmont started to connect passes, leading to Liu scoring the equalizer in the 60th minute. Liu found a little space on the right side of the box, lofting an inch-perfect shot over the keeper.
