Elspeth Grippando fits one of her two goals past Gateway.

articles.text: Staff Photos P.J. Brayer scored a career high 27 points in Piedmont’s win over St. Joseph. He also logged 19 points in victory over San Leandro. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team is on a hot streak, with a winning streak now at six games with a pair of victories over the last week on the road. The Highlanders recently beat St. Joseph 69-58 on Saturday, January 10, while they bashed San Leandro 73-49 two days earlier for their first Western Alameda County Conference game of the season. “It feels great, it’s the most wins we’ve had in a row since 2024. Top to bottom, we’re playing really well defensively. I’m proud of the way the guys are competing,” coach Ben Spencer said. Piedmont’s lineup continues to be bolstered by its “Big Three” of upperclassmen, seniors Dillon Casey and P.J. Brayer, and junior Beach Lorin. The trio combined for 116 points over the two games. “They are tough to guard. Dillon is probably going to get the best defender on the other team, Beach will get their second defender, and P.J. is a really tough matchup because he can stretch the floor. A lot of bigs have a hard time guarding P.J. and it just opens things up,” Spencer said. “It’s not just us three, we have guys coming off the bench that I can trust just as much as I can trust the starters. We’re deep this year. Dillon and Beach are helluva players. I just try my best to do my job. I don’t try to do too much, just do my role, and play the best defense I can, get every rebound, and knock down open shots,” Brayer mentioned. Brayer scored a career-high 27 points in their win over St. Joseph. He’s a three-year varsity player, emerging as a marquee scorer and a major presence on the boards. “I think my game is at its peak right now. I’ve put in a lot of work and it’s starting to pay off. The competition in practice has only made me better,” Brayer said. 69-58 victory over St. Joseph Piedmont led 18-15 through the first quarter and extended the score to 26-19 in a low-scoring second quarter. PHS then more than doubled their points total in the third quarter, exploding for 31 points while allowing 17 to build a 57-36 lead. St. Joe finished with 22 points in the fourth, while PHS put up 12 toward the 69-58 final score. Brayer scored 16 of his 27 points in the third quarter, when he knocked down three 3-pointers. Final stats: Brayer led with 27 points, Casey had 20, Lorin had 11, Lucian Fang-Ring scored seven, while Akash Bornstein and Nick Riordan had two. 73-49 over San Leandro San Leandro opened with a 7-4 advantage in the early minutes, but Piedmont took an 8-7 lead with 3:52 left in the opening quarter when Lorin landed a layup. The Highlanders never trailed, puting up another 14 points while allowing four to lead 22-11 by the end of the first quarter. PHS made things comfortable in the second quarter, adding 17 points to the tally to establish a 17-point lead by halftime, up 39-22. The Highlanders added 16 more points in the third while only conceding eight points to Dillon Casey had 22 points against San Leandro and 20 points in a game with St. Joseph.

Piedmont’s record is now 4-2-2 (W-T-L) under first-year head coach Spencer-Harty, who came to the Highlanders as another product of the coaching tree produced by the 24-7 UK Soccer Academy. Former girls’ soccer coach Dan Chubbock and former boys’ soccer coach Todd Sullivan also came from 24-7, as does current boys soccer head coach Ben Russell. “It’s great. I feel like all the 24-7 coaches have a similar vibe, so it doesn’t feel much different. The teams doing great working together, and having four freshmen [Olivia Nealon, Makenna Piedmont is 4-2-2 and on a five-game unbeaten run. Staff Photos Small, Olivia Kan-Miller, Olivia Luccacini] is a big change, but they are great,” Liu said. The Highlanders look ahead to its league schedule ramping up with critical matches against Castro Valley, Alameda, and Bishop O’Dowd ahead. Spencer-Harty likes what he sees out of the group, but still has things he wants to work on. “There’s a little work to be done in our combination play and getting our wingbacks a little higher a little earlier. A lot of time we isolate our two nines, so we want to get support 4-v-3 instead of a 3-v-2 against us,” Spencer-Harty said. 11-0 over Gateway The shellacking started in the third minute following a corner, where Erica Smith turned in a loose ball in front of the net. Seven minutes later, Liu scored on a rebounded initial shot by Ayla Blanford in the box. Liu scored again two minutes later, making a run in behind to put herself 1-on-1 with the goalkeeper. Blanford scored in the 17th after Elia Kwong’s shot on target rebounded into play. Elspeth Grippando made it 5-nil in the 25th in another 1-on- 1. Kwong scored in the 35th, holding off a defender in a long run in possession—bringing it to 6-0 by halftime. Olivia Luccacini scored in the 49th on a nice run down the right side. Grippando scored again in the 51st on a dribble down the left. Lila Rosen scored on a composed shot in the box in the 55th, while freshman Olivia Nealon scored five minutes later. Piedmont’s last goal came by Makenna Small in the 69th minute. 2-2 with Berkeley Berkeley took an initial lead in the 10th minute on a looping header from a corner. Piedmont equalized in the early minutes of the second half when Kwong slotted in a penalty kick off the underside of the crossbar. It came after Liu drew a penalty, weaving her way around three defenders before being pulled down in the box. Berkeley went ahead again a few minutes later when a well struck free-kick rocketed into the top side of the net, giving the Jackets a 2-1 lead. Piedmont started to connect passes, leading to Liu scoring the equalizer in the 60th minute. Liu found a little space on the right side of the box, lofting an inch-perfect shot over the keeper. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team split its last two matches, beating Encinal 2-1 on Friday, January 9 in Alameda and losing 3-0 to non-conference Chico two days earlier at Witter Field. The results bring Piedmont’s record to 2-0-6 (W-T-L) to start the new year, which is shaping up to be a season of transition for the defending Division 5 CIF NorCal champions. “We’ve had a lack of ability to execute in overload situations; just poor execution and decision-making. Defensively, we need awareness to manage space and runners,” said coach Ben Russell. Piedmont has shown flashes of its potential and creating chances, but has lacked the finishing touch. Russell said growing pains were expected with a young roster that includes three freshmen, 10 sophomores, five juniors and five seniors, though there are signs of progress. “Individual brilliance is great, but there are basics you have to execute every single day. That’s the habit piece we are preaching. You have to do the basics really well, like connecting the right pass, making sure your touch is good and not allowing attacks to die,” Russell said. Now approaching the midway point of the season, Russell is hopeful Piedmont can mirror last year’s second-half turnaround. The 2024 team finished the early portion of its schedule 2-2-4 before improving during its NCS and CIF runs. “We have to pick up the habit. That’s my big philosophy: intention, behavior, habit. Having good habits, and then good confidence throughout the team. They know what I want and can tell me what I want. Now it’s transferring that and giving each other the confidence,” Russell said. 3-0 loss to Chico Piedmont conceded the opening goal within the first five minutes. Ben Gerber had a looping header on target in the 12th minute, and Robert Piniella had a shot blocked in the box a minute later. Chico scored again in the 15th minute on a shot inside the box to go up 2-0. Travers Kemp sent a shot just high in the 19th minute, while Henry Devan had an effort on target pushed wide for a corner in the 29th. On the ensuing corner, Elias Reed-Miguel headed a ball past the keeper, but a defender cleared it Staff Photos Ben Russell and the boys’ soccer team opened 2026 with a loss to Chico and a win over Encinal. Elias Reed-Miguel sends in a pass from a free kick against Chico. Freshman Travers Kemp looks for a way around Chico’s defenders.

articles.text: In August last fall, PHS Class of 2020 and St. Mary’s College 2025 graduate Luke Barrett signed a contract to play for AMW Arka Gdynia of Poland — joining the professional ranks in European basketball. So far this season, Arka Gdynia is in second-place of the Polish Basketball League with an 11-4 record midway through its 30-game season. Barrett has appeared in all 15 games as a rookie. He is averaging 19.7 minutes per game, converting 67.3 percent of his field goals, 45 percent of 3-pointers, and 81.8 percent of his free throws for 111 points. He’s averaging 5.4 rebounds per game, which is third on the team. “The type of basketball I want to play and type of places that I fit, I knew that from the start. This is a lot closer (in style) to college than the NBA. It is a lot more tactical. It is faster out here than college because of the 24-second shot clock. Here you have guys who have different skillsets. We run the same exact defense we ran in college,” Barrett said, via the Mercury News. Gdynia is a city on the Baltic coast of northern Poland, resting along the Gulf of Gdansk with a population of 257,000. Arka is a nine-time championship winning team and have had several former players appear in the NBA. Barrett joined the team on a one-month trial before landing his first full-time professional contract after finishing his collegiate career at St. Mary’s as a leader. Barrett called the time before landing a deal an excruciating “waiting game.” “Obviously I knew the goal was to get somewhere and play overseas, to play pro and keep playing basketball somewhere. As soon as the season was over, I tried to get an agent. I ended up with an agent that represented three or four of my former college teammates. Those three months (this summer) were tough; it was a waiting game. For me, it took a while to hear anything concrete. articles.text: The rains from recent weeks have tapered off but the results can still be seen in flowing gulches, streams, and creeks. Winter hiking is the best time to visit the local waterfalls, and the Post has ventured to several around the Bay Area. Here’s a collection of local waterfalls to try. Uvas Canyon’s Waterfalls Loop Trail, Morgan Hill In Morgan Hill’s Uvas Canyon County Park are a collection of five accessible waterfalls in 5.2 miles of total hiking. You’ll still require 1,273 feet in elevation gain to see all five in the entire loop—but four of those waterfalls within the first 1.6 miles—making the last long trip to Triple Falls, and optional excursion if you’re worried about tired legs. Cataract Creek, Mt. Tamalpais Watershed The Cataract Falls Trail in the Mt. Tamalpais Watershed is a 4.8 out-and-back with around 1,000 feet in elevation gain. There are two trailheads, parking on Bolinas Fairfax Road will provide just a 0.5 walk to the first waterfall and another 0.2 to its most famous Helen Markt Falls. Should you walk the entire Cataract Falls Trail, you will encounter cascades along cataract creek. Murietta Falls, Del Valle Regional Wilderness Murietta Falls in Livermore’s Del Valle Regional Park is considered the highest waterfall in the entire Bay Area at an elevation of near 3,000 feet in the Ohlone Wilderness, where a small stream cascades over 100 foot cliff-face—meaning this location should only be taken by experienced hikers looking for a challenge. The entire day required 12.1 miles of hiking and near 5,000 feet in elevation gain; it is considered a good training spot for those interested in Half Dome. Alamere Falls, Bolinas The trek to Alamere Falls is a total of 13.6 miles and an elevation gain of 1,811 feet taking Uvas Canyon County Park has five accessible waterfalls to enjoy, including four in the first 1.5 miles

articles.text: Left Coast Chamber Ensemble Left Coast Chamber Ensemble will present Metamorphosen, a chamber music program centered on themes of transformation and reflection, with performances January 31 in Berkeley and February 1 in San Francisco. The concert’s centerpiece is Richard Strauss’ Metamorphosen, or “Transformations,” one of the composer’s most intimate works which provides a resonating response to the devastation of World War II. The piece was composed in 1945 originally written for 23 solo strings. Metamorphosen will be performed in an intimate arrangement by Rudolf Leopold of the Vienna Philharmonic. “Composed in 1945, Strauss’s Metamorphosen is at once a memorial and a transformation,” said LCCE Artistic Director Matilda Hofman in a press release. She described the work as “a hauntingly nostalgic eulogy for a world which was falling apart before his very eyes, while at the same time inspired by the idea that all life, even as it changes and varies, is fundamentally connected.” The program also includes works by Luciano Berio, Robert Hughes and local composer Hendel Almétus, each selected for its ability to draw expressive power from small instrumental forces. Almét us’ Tounen (“To Return”) for solo flute reflects a personal transformation rooted in a deliberate return to his Haitian heritage and cultural values, and invites listeners to dwell within its inner world,” Almétus said, “where unity, balance, and wholeness emerge from diversity — a musical reflection of the perfect place I seek to paint through sound.” The concert will be performed at 7:30 p.m. Saturday, Jan. 31, at the First Church of Christ, Scientist, 2619 Dwight Way, Berkeley, and at 4 p.m. Sunday, Feb. 1, at Noe Valley Ministry, 1021 Sanchez St., San Francisco. Tickets purchased at the door are $43 for general admission and $18 for students. Advance tickets are available for $40 general admission and $15 for students. Visit https://www.leftcoastensemble.org/ for more information. articles.text: Concert held at First Congregational Church of Berkeley Jan. 25 Berkeley Symphony closes its 2025–26 Symphonic Series with Fables & Folklore, a program centered on storytelling and cultural tradition, on Sunday, January 25 at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The concert begins at 4 p.m., marking the fourth and final performance of the Symphony’s 54th season series. Internationally acclaimed conductor Carolyn Kuan, music director of the Hartford Symphony Orchestra, will lead the program. “This program celebrates imagination and heritage, honoring cultural roots while inviting audiences to experience the power of storytelling through music,” said Executive Director Marion Atherton in a statement. The evening opens with Folk Songs for Orchestra by composer Huang Ruo. The work draws on traditional Chinese folk melodies, blending them with contemporary orchestral textures to evoke both personal memory and shared cultural history. Guitarist Marc Teicholz will then join the Symphony for O Saci-Pererê, a guitar concerto by composer Clarice Assad inspired by Brazilian folklore. The piece centers on Saci, a mischievous trickster figure from Indigenous and Afro-Brazilian mythology, and features rhythmic energy and playful character alongside deeper reflections on Brazilian identity and oral tradition. Following intermission, the program concludes with Antonín Dvořák’s Symphony No. 8, a work rooted in the folk music of the Czech countryside. Known for its melodic richness and pastoral warmth, the symphony’s triumphant finale provides a celebratory close to the series. Single tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the box office at 510-841- 2800. All Symphonic Series concerts take place at the First Congregational Church of Berkeley. The Berkeley Symphony ends its 54th symphonic season next week.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony ends 54th season with Fables & Folklore

articles.text: Monty Python’s Tony Award– win ning musical comedy SPAMALOT will play a limited engagement at San Francisco’s Golden Gate Theatre from March 3 through March 22. The production is part of the show’s North American tour following a critically acclaimed Broadway revival in 2023. First premiering on Broadway in 2005, SPAMALOT features a book and lyrics by Eric Idle, with music by John Du Prez and Idle. The original production received 14 Tony Award nominations and won three, including Best Musical. The current touring production is directed and choreographed by Josh Rhodes and has been praised for its inventive staging, design, and performances. The cast includes Major Attaway as King Arthur, Sean Bell as Sir Robin, Chris Collins-Pisano as Sir Lancelot, Ellis C. Dawson III as Sir Bedevere, Leo Roberts as Sir Galahad, and Amanda Robles as the Lady of the Lake. Steven Telsey appears as the Historian and Prince Herbert. Adapted from the film Monty Python and the Holy Grail, the musical features well-known songs such as “Always Look on the Bright Side of Life,” “The Song That Goes Like This,” and “Find Your Grail.” Single tickets are on sale now through BroadwaySF. Group sales are also available. Visit www.broadwaysf.com to purchase tickets. Monty Python’s SPAMALOT performed in Washington, D.C.
articles.title: Monty Python’s SPAMALOT premieres at Golden Gate Theatre March 3

articles.text: Festival runs Jan. 21 - 25 The FOG Design+Art fair returns to San Francisco’s Fort Mason Center for Arts and Culture next week, featuring artwork from more than 60 leading galleries from the Bay Area and around the world. Now in its 14th year, the showcase highlights contemporary art and design through gallery presentations and special installations. The 2026 fair will include both new and returning exhibitors, along with the largest presentation to date of FOG FOCUS, a platform highlighting artists in the earlier stages of their careers. The fair opens on January 21 with a preview gala benefiting the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s (SFMOMA) education initiatives. “This year’s exhibitors embody the spirit of curiosity and collaboration that makes FOG such a vital part of the Bay Area’s cultural community,” said Sydney Blumenkranz, director of FOG Design+Art, in a press statement. Sixteen galleries will participate in the fair for the first time, including David Nolan Gallery, Goodman, Josh Lilley and Vielmetter in Pier 3, as well as Anat Ebgi, Charlie James Gallery and re.riddle in FOG FOCUS. More than 20 international galleries are expected, representing cities such as London, Paris, Mexico City, São Paulo and Kyoto. Fifteen Bay Area galleries will also take part. FOG FOCUS will feature 16 galleries and offer works at more accessible price points. The fair will also mark the return of FOG MRKT, an entryway installation highlighting artists, designers and makers through editioned and singular works. The showcase also includes FOG Talks, a series of conversations exploring art, design, technology and culture, curated by Susan Swig and included with admission. FOG is open Thursday, January 22 through Saturday, January 24 from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., and Sunday, January 25 from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. A preview gala is held Wednesday, January 21. Purchase a preview, single-day ticket or a four-day fair pass at the door or online at https:// www.fogfair.com/. articles.text: January 17 – February 28 Society of Printmakers’ Art Exhibition The California Society of Printmakers returns to Piedmont with its 111th Annual Members’ Exhibition, showing close to 100 works of printmaking art, demonstrating the incredible variety of style and process that falls within this field. The exhibit will be open on Saturdays and Sundays January 17, 18, 25, and 31, and most February weekends, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.; there will be an opening reception on Saturday, January 24, from 1 to 4 p.m., as well as a closing reception on February 28 from 11 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., providing good chances of meeting and learning from many of the artists, one or two of whom will also be present during the weekend open hours. The exhibition is free to visit, and the works will also be available to enjoy during your attendance at any of PCA’s public events. Saturday, January 17, 5:00 p.m. Michael Stehr Art History Lecture The Impressionist movement is regarded by many as the most important revolution in Western art since the Renaissance. When the Impressionist renegades gathered in 1874 to hold their very first group exhibition outside the state-regulated parameters, many thought they were building the next revolution to upend Paris. In light of the challenges these artists were facing, they relied heavily on their relationships with each other. The most compelling of these relationships was between Berthe Morisot and Édouard Manet. Join local art historian Michael Stehr as he presents a 50-minute illustrated lecture at PCA that celebrates the fascinating relationship between these two titans of the Impressionist movement. The lecture is designed to prepare attendees for the exhibit currently running at the Legion of Honor until March 1, entitled Manet et Morisot. Admission to the lecture is $20 per person, Cash only, at the door. For more info, email Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com. Saturday, January 31, 7:00 p.m. Cristiana Pegoraro Solo Piano Concert The incomparable Italian pianist Cristiana Pegoraro returns to Piedmont for another recital. As president of Narnia Arts Academy and Artistic Director of the Narnia Festival, she has been hailed by the New York Times as “an artist of the highest caliber.” She has performed on the world’s most prestigious stages, including Lincoln Center, Carnegie Hall, the United Nations (New York), the Sydney Opera House, Festspielhaus (Salzburg), Musikverein (Vienna), Royal College of Music (London), Auditorium Parco della Musica (Rome), Teatro alla Scala (Milan). She brings to Piedmont a program she premiered in November at Carnegie Hall, called Harmonies of Peace. Advance tickets are available at: https://events. com/r/tickets/1023245. Tickets at the door are $40/adult and $20/youth. Sunday, February 8, 4:00 p.m. Carl Blake / Will Underwood Piano & Flute Duo William Underwood III holds a B.S. in Music from Florida A&M and a Master of Music in Flute Performance from Wayne State. He has toured extensively in Japan with Kyodo Tokyo and regularly works as a soloist, collaborator, and recording artist. Dr. Carl Blake, a local piano master who has performed worldwide to acclaim, has introduced Will to the best of the Bay Area, often playing together as a duo exploring piano and flute repertoire. Tickets and more info will be available soon. Thursday, February 12, 6:30 p.m. Sacha Grippando Jewelry Arts Lecture Throughout history, jewelry and watches have played a vital role in the visual arts, imbuing the wearer with power, wealth, and status. From ancient times, the inclusion of jewels, and later watches, in portraits of royalty and significant figures served to highlight their importance. This illuminating and sparkling lecture will explore how the visual arts utilize jewelry and watches to define characters and convey specific traits. Sacha Grippando will analyze significant works of art, ranging from paintings by masters like Leonardo Da Vinci and Vermeer to modern and contemporary artists like Salvador Dali and Kehinde Wiley. Admission is by $20 suggested donation at the door and includes light refreshments afterwards.

By Jake Lannon One Battle After Another is about dispirited people searching for the will to survive under an all-powerful government. The film is hilarious, action-packed, and filled with moments that land with real emotional weight. The story opens with the plans of a far-left revolutionary group known as the French 75. Lovers and central figures “Ghetto” Pat Calhoun (Leonardo DiCaprio) and Perfidia Beverly Hills (Teyana Taylor) are active members, taking part in a mission to break detained immigrants out of custody. During the operation, Perfidia humiliates the commanding officer at the detention center, Steven J. Lockjaw (Sean Penn), who later becomes obsessively fixated on her. On a later mission, Perfidia is caught planting a bomb by Lockjaw. He releases her after coercing her into sex, a violation that results in Perfidia becoming pregnant and giving birth to a daughter, Charlene. articles.text: Brown Gables, the Alexander home at Sea View and Hampton, was named for its prominent gables, painted brown. Their grand three-story mansion was completed in 1909, which they named “Brown Gables” for its massive gabled dormers with bargeboards, painted brown. The first floor was faced in brick and half timbering covered the upper stories. Two large porte cocheres were also trimmed in brown gables. Diamond-paned, leaded glass windows graced the entry and large bay windows offered expansive views from every room in this most elegant early home in Piedmont. City records indicate that the Alexander house had three living rooms, five bedrooms and five bathrooms. Koa wood and other exotic woods enhanced the interior. It was an exceptional house in 1909 with 3240 square feet and was the site of many festive balls. The gardens of the Alexander home also hosted many garden parties that benefited local charities. Mary Alexander was a strong supporter of the Ladies Relief Society, the Matilda Brown Home and the Women’s Guild of the Piedmont Church. She also organized the Bay Area chapter of the Red Cross at the onset of World War I and led it for over 30 years. Their beautiful gardens extended over nine of today’s lots on Sea View and King Avenues. A low brick wall with a subtle detail surrounded the property. The wall is visible in the photo of the house and portions still stand today on Hampton. The Alexander carriage house, which still exists at 84 King, had servants’ quarters and an indoor swimming pool. Helen Wills Moody, the Wimbledon tennis star in the 1920s and 1930s, practiced on the tennis court there. The Alexander family formed a small community near Sea View and Hampton. In 1911, Wallace’s mother built her own home across the street at 92 Sea View — designed by Charles W. Dickey — and Mary’s mother built her home down the street at 236 Sea View. Wallace Alexander was president of the Alexander and Baldwin sugar firm, Vice President of the Matson Navigation Company, director of several other Hawaiian companies and a trustee of Stanford University. Although he was active in many businesses, he found time for many civic and charitable organizations in Piedmont. In addition to constructing the stores and saving Piedmont Park, Alexander was also the driving force behind the construction of the Piedmont Interdenominational Church (now Piedmont Community Church), arranging for the purchase of the land and again hiring Albert Farr to design the church. Wallace Alexander also established the Piedmont Boy Scout Council. He arranged for the scouts to meet in the basement of the church, as they still do today. In 1929, he leased land from the Forest Service near Keddie in Plumas County and established Camp Wallace Alexander, a Piedmont scouting tradition fondly remembered by generations of Piedmont Boy Scouts. The land lease expired in 1982 and Camp Wallace Alexander was dismantled. In 1939, Wallace Alexander suffered a fatal stroke at his second home in Honolulu. He was eulogized as “Piedmont’s leading private citizen.” Wallace left a large bequest to the Piedmont Community Church and to the Piedmont Boy Scouts. His philosophy was that he “was but a trustee of the money that came to him.” Upon his death, Mary Alexander followed her husband’s wishes that the property be subdivided into 13 lots. The entire estate would not be sold to a single builder. She stated that the lots would be purchased by individuals who intended to build their own homes. The Alexanders wanted more families to live in Piedmont. Footnote on the Stores My previous column on Piedmont’s “stores” brought out a few comments by readers. One fondly remembers the steps leading up to the stores. They were a favorite place for students to hang out. “Kids with cars would ‘cruise by’ checking out the scene. articles.text: Wallace Alexander was Piedmont’s premier philanthropic citizen and a leader in establishing many of Piedmont’s institutions. In previous columns I have mentioned Wallace Alexander. He was instrumental in the 1913 construction of the Piedmont Commercial Center, Piedmont’s first stores, and in the 1921 purchase of the upper Piedmont Park land, saving it from development. Wallace Alexander, a profile Wallace McKinney Alexander was born on the island of Maui in 1869. His father, Samuel Alexander, was related to the Baldwin and Cooke families and was a pioneer in sugar planting and refining. When it was time for Wallace and his sisters, Juliette and Annie, to attend high school, the family moved to Oakland where Wallace attended Oakland High School. He later attended Andover and graduated from Yale University. He married his Oakland classmate Mary Barker in 1904. In her memoir, Queen of the Hills, Evelyn Craig Pattiani tells the story of the Alexanders choosing their homesite at the prominent corner of Sea View and Hampton (then called Union Street). articles.text: Members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group welcomed a return to dry weather last Wednesday, stepping out after recent rains for a sunny, cool morning walk. A strong turnout of 54 walkers and four K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra at the group’s regular weekly meeting time. The group had walked the Piedmont High School campus the previous week during the holiday break, focusing on its history. This time, the walk followed the story of one of Piedmont High’s most prominent alumni, Robert S. McNamara, and led participants to his childhood home on Annerley Road, just over the Oakland-Piedmont city line. In those days, Oakland students could attend Piedmont High, and Piedmont students also enrolled in Oakland schools. The route also allowed walkers to explore streets along the city’s southern border that were missed last year, including a hidden path and a back alley unfamiliar to many in the group. Before setting off, walkers shared background on McNamara’s early life. He graduated from Piedmont High in 1933 and was among the school’s brightest students. His graduation photo in the school’s Clan O Log yearbook lists him as editor and a member of student government, the Rigma boys club, the Alpha Clan honor society, Glee Club, Opera, and French Club. T h e D e p r e s s i o n l e f t McNamara’s family with limited resources for college, but tuition at the University of California, Berkeley, was just $52 a year. He graduated in 1937 with a bachelor’s degree in economics, with minors in mathematics and philosophy, later earning a master’s degree from Harvard Business School. He became an accountant with Price Waterhouse and later joined Harvard’s faculty. The walk led the group down Highland and Wildwood avenues in a long column to the lower section of Wildwood Avenue, where they found a hidden path between homes at 216 and 220 Wildwood. The steps descend to an alley bordered by Winsor Avenue, Ranleigh Way, and Harvard Road. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, January 14, 2026 Features Walking on Wednesday Tracing Robert McNamara’s path, from Piedmont to power By Dick Carter Members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group welcomed a return to dry weather last Wednesday, stepping out after recent rains for a sunny, cool morning walk. A strong turnout of 54 walkers and four K-9 companions gathered at the Exedra at the group’s regular weekly meeting time. The group had walked the Piedmont High School campus the previous week during the holiday break, focusing on its history. This time, the walk followed the story of one of Piedmont High’s most prominent alumni, Robert S. McNamara, and led participants to his childhood home on Annerley Road, just over the Oakland-Piedmont city line. In those days, Oakland students could attend Piedmont High, and Piedmont students also enrolled in Oakland schools. The route also allowed walkers to explore streets along the city’s southern border that were missed last year, including a hidden path and a back alley unfamiliar to many in the group. Before setting off, walkers shared background on McNamara’s early life. He graduated from Piedmont High in 1933 and was among the school’s brightest students. His graduation photo in the school’s Clan O Log yearbook lists him as editor and a member of student government, the Rigma boys club, the Alpha Clan honor society, Glee Club, Opera, and French Club. T h e D e p r e s s i o n l e f t McNamara’s family with limited resources for college, but tuition at the University of California, Berkeley, was just $52 a year. He graduated in 1937 with a bachelor’s degree in economics, with minors in mathematics and philosophy, later earning a master’s degree from Harvard Business School. He became an accountant with Price Waterhouse and later joined Harvard’s faculty. The walk led the group down Highland and Wildwood avenues in a long column to the lower section of Wildwood Avenue, where they found a hidden path between homes at 216 and 220 Wildwood. The steps descend to an alley bordered by Winsor Avenue, Ranleigh Way, and Harvard Road. Along the way, Leigh Sorensen, who lives in an accessory dwelling unit behind her Winsor Avenue home, invited the group inside her ADU, which she has named “Winsor Castle.” The walkers agreed it lived up to the name. Continuing down the alley, the group passed bamboo, palms, and sequoias tucked into backyards, crossing the invisible city line into Oakland. After a short walk Robert McNamara’s with President Kennedy Robert McNamara’s graduation photo in the school’s “Clan O Log” yearbook along Harvard Road, they climbed Annerley Road to McNamara’s childhood home, where remodeling work was underway, and shared more of his story. Poor eyesight initially kept McNamara from military service during World War II, but he volunteered to train Air Force staff and served in the United States Army Air Forces from 1943 to 1946. He played a key role in the Office of Statistical Control, applying statistical analysis to improve bombing mission planning and logistics. After the war, McNamara joined a team of former military colleagues offering management expertise to companies. Hired by Henry Ford II, the group helped reorganize Ford Motor Company. McNamara rose steadily and became the first non-family member to serve as the company’s president. When John F. Kennedy was elected president, he offered McNamara his choice of serving as secretary of the treasury or secretary of defense. McNamara chose defense. During his tenure, he became deeply involved in the Vietnam War, which grew increasingly controversial. By 1967, McNamara privately urged President Lyndon Johnson to deescalate, arguing the war was unwinnable. Johnson rejected the recommendations, and weeks later announced McNamara’s departure to become president of the World Bank. McNamara later expressed regret over his role in the war, most notably in his 1995 memoir, In Retrospect. While he acknowledged the United States had been “terribly wrong,” critics, including his son, questioned why he did not speak out sooner. After a group photo in front of McNamara’s childhood home, the walkers headed back along Annerley Road to Harvard Road and Prospect Avenue, passing through Piedmont Park and along Bushy Dell Creek, flowing steadily after the recent rains, before returning to the Exedra and the group’s familiar weekly rhythm. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration is required. Those interested should go to https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu to register or call (510) 420-3070 for more information. pages.text: Wednesday, January 14, 2026 23 BUSINESS SPOTLIGHT Harmony brings innovative dentistry to downtown Oakland By Allyson Aleksey A new dental practice is taking an unconventional approach to oral health, blending dentistry with medical screening and preventative care while offering a full range of services under one roof in the heart of downtown Oakland. Harmony Whole Person Oral Dental Care, led by longtime dentist and educator Dr. Greg Kaplan, integrates routine dental care with screenings for blood pressure, sleep disorders and chronic conditions, aiming to catch health issues early while Dr. Greg Kaplan M y little p a t i e n t n making care more accessible to East Bay residents. Kaplan said the concept grew out of decades in dentistry and a belief that dental offices can play a larger role in preventive health, particularly for patients who may not regularly see a primary care provider. “About 29 million Americans every year see a dentist and don’t see another health care provider,” Kaplan said. “That creates both a responsibility and an opportunity.” At Harmony, every patient over age 12 receives a blood pressure screening as part of a standard visit. Adults and children are also evaluated for sleep-related issues, including sleep apnea, which research has linked to cardiovascular disease, learning difficulties and behavioral challenges. New patients are offered optional A1C testing, which can help identify diabetes or prediabetes. The screenings are noninvasive and included as part of care. Dr. Kaplan said they have been widely accepted by patients since the practice’s opening in late 2025, and added that they are just as essential to dental health as physical health. In one early case, a patient was referred immediately to urgent care after an elevated blood pressure reading during a dental visit. “[The patient] later called and said her doctor told her she could have had a stroke or heart attack that day,” Kaplan said. The practice’s pediatric focus extends beyond cavities and braces. By evaluating jaw development and facial growth in young children, Kaplan said dentists can help reduce the risk of future sleep disorders and related health problems. e “It’s not just about straight e teeth,” he said. “It’s about how a d child breathes, sleeps and functions.” p a ti e n s Harmony also emphasizes coordination with physicians, particularly when treating sleep apnea through oral appliances or combined therapies. Kaplan said collaboration between dental and medical providers is imperative “if health care systems are to become more preventive and data-driven.” That data-driven approach is central to the practice’s design. Harmony uses an electronic health record system adapted for dentistry, allowing clinicians to track trends such as links between periodontal disease and diabetes while protecting patient privacy. Kaplan said the goal is to better understand how dental and medical care intersect and how c e . that information could improve outcomes over time. “Small steps can lead to big changes,” he said. “If dentists and physicians work together, we can catch problems earlier, improve outcomes and maybe even lower health care costs over time.” Kaplan has been practicing dentistry for decades and taught at the University of Southern California’s dental school for 12 years. Harmony, he said, represents a culmination of those experiences, like a “concept car” for what dentistry could become. “I’m not a young guy just starting out,” he said. “At this point in my career, I wanted to see if we could raise the profession to a new level. Not just great clinical care, but care that’s integrated, transparent and focused on wellness.” The office’s opening comes at a time when many dental practices are moving away from traditional insurance models. Harmony, by contrast, accepts major PPO dental plans and is currently seeking approval to accept Medi-Cal patients, a process Kaplan described as lengthy but necessary. “We want to be available to the community,” he said. “There are a lot of families in the East Bay who need care that’s affordable and accessible.” The downtown Oakland location was chosen intentionally, Kaplan said, despite concerns about post-pandemic foot traffic in downtown centres. He said he believes health care providers play a stabilizing role in city cores and can help support surrounding businesses and community life. “Communities are stronger when people invest in them,” he said. The practice itself was designed to reduce “dental office” anxiety, housed in a bright, fullfloor office space with open spaces, digital check-in options and an emphasis on same-day exams and cleanings when possible. The building is LEED Gold certified, reflecting a commitment to environmental sustainability alongside patient care. Patient response has been largely positive, Kaplan said, with strong online reviews and high participation in optional screenings. As Harmony Whole Person Oral Dental Care settles into its role downtown, Kaplan hopes the practice will not only serve patients, but help reshape how dentistry fits into the broader health care system. “If we can help people live longer, healthier lives by taking a few extra steps,” he said, “that’s a change worth making.” Harmony Whole Person Oral Dental Care is located at 1333 Broadway in Downtown Oakland, third floor. articles.text: Marilyn Farran Clowdsley, born May 6, 1930, passed away peacefully on January 8, 2026. She was the daughter of Dorothy Seawell Farran and Reginald Mansfield Farran and grew up in Piedmont, California, where she spent most of her life. In her later years, Marilyn resided in Rossmoor. Marilyn attended Piedmont schools and graduated from Piedmont high in 1948. She then attended UC Berkeley, graduating in 1952 with a teaching degree, where she was a member of the Alpha Phi sorority and met her husband of 59 years, John Upton Clowdsley Jr. They raised their family in Piedmont where Marilyn was a substitute teacher and a long-time member in the Hoe and Hope garden Club. She had a passion for gardening which lasted until her last days. Marilyn is survived by her sons Reginald Clowdsley (Cydney) and Stephen Clowdsley Marilyn Farran Clowdsley passed on January 8, 2026. (Cammie), and her daughter Jane Johnson (Kurt). She was a devoted mother and grandmother and is also survived by seven grandchildren and three great-grandchildren. Marilyn was deeply loved and will be greatly missed by her family and all who knew her. Services will be privately held for family only.

articles.text: On a cool, rainy Januar 5 afternoon, 22 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group gathered inside Piedmont Community Hall for their monthly book discussion. The group met to discuss its December selection, Cry, the Beloved Country by Alan Paton, suggested by Bob Hall. Published in 1948, the same year apartheid was formally instituted in South Africa, the novel follows a Zulu pastor searching for his son in Johannesburg. The son becomes involved in the murder of a white man who was an advocate for racial justice. Set against the backdrop of South Africa just before apartheid became law, the novel is a social protest written by a white South African author. Readers noted that Paton explores themes of love, hope and separation, as well as the devastating effects of racial segregation. The story also examines the breakdown of tribal life, family disintegration, urban poverty, crime and environmental destruction, while still offering the possibility of reconciliation and hope. Sometimes the most challenging discussions arise when everyone likes the book, and that proved to be the case this month. Several readers found the novel easy to read, with one saying she “didn’t want to put it down.” The group praised Paton’s fluid, rhythmic writing style and agreed the book was powerful when it was published and remains so today. Many found the story deeply moving, particularly the parallel grief experienced by the fathers of the murdered man and the young killer. While the losses were heartbreaking, readers also pointed to acts of kindness in the story that felt uplifting. Some members had read the book earlier in life and initially wondered whether it would still resonate. They agreed it remains both wonderful and relevant, though a few felt that little has changed since it was written. Issues such as racial discrimination, crime, environmental damage, immigration struggles and family breakdown still feel painfully familiar. Readers discussed how the young murderer’s actions were shaped by his circumstances. Many felt he was not inherently evil, but a product of his environment, where theft could seem like survival and violence a tragic consequence. Several noted parallels with how some people caught in similar conditions may act today. The group observed that South African politics were largely absent from the novel, which readers felt allowed them to focus more closely on the characters themselves. Even so, many believed the reality of the time was likely harsher than what was depicted. The word “cry” in the book’s title resonated in multiple ways for readers, reflecting sorrow over the deaths of young people, damage to the land, and the African population’s resignation to unbearable conditions. Discussion turned briefly to the present day, with differing views on whether current times are worse than those of the past. While acknowledging real challenges, some readers expressed optimism, noting that progress is rarely linear and that many lives have improved over the past eight decades. Others questioned the novel’s hopeful conclusion, describing it as overly idealistic, but agreed it left much to reflect on. After the discussion, the group December book, Cry, the Beloved County by Alan Paton revisited its use of a handheld microphone to help amplify comments in Community Hall’s large, high-ceilinged space. While passing the microphone around the circle can feel awkward, members agreed it improves accessibility and helps ensure everyone can fully participate in the discussion. The readers had previously selected The Wide Wide Sea: Imperial Ambition, First Contact and the Fateful Final Voyage of Captain James Cook by Hampton Sides for their February read and Harlem Shuffle by Colson Whitehead for their March book. After Phyllis Van Kranenburgh’s presentation of three non-fiction candidates the group selected Secondhand Time: The Last of the Soviets, a 2013 book by Belarusian Nobel laureate Svetlana Alexievich for April The group will meet at the Community Hall for their next discussion that on February 2 at 1:30 p.m. New readers are welcome. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required. Go to https://bit.ly/3R86PP4, or call 510 420-3070, to register. Among those participating in the discussion were Mary Carter, Peggy Shultz, Heidi Schmidt, Laura Goldman, Hilary Honore, Lois Price, Phyllis Van Kranenburgh, Rich Siegel, Orrel Lanter, Bella Almanzan, Phil Witte, Madie Hall, Ken Young, Adrienne Hamlin, Mike Henn, Melba Yee, Bob Hall, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. The group was pleased Robert White and Odette Pollar were with them for the first time.

articles.text: Each week the Piedmont Post prints excerpts from the Piedmont Police Department’s daily log, highlighting the crimes and reports of the greatest intrigue to residents. Some reports to the police that may sound odd, or even comedic end up as the Post’s PPD Pick of the Week. The list below is a collection of our favorite PPD Picks of the Week from 2025.

articles.text: Staff Photos A stolen truck leveled a tree before coming to rest on the sidewalk and the yard of a home. Piedmont Police and Fire Departments respond to a truck and trailer that crashed into a residence’s side yard after being stolen. A brand-new 2026 GMC Sierra 3500 HD truck was stolen on Wednesday, January 7, from near the Blair and Hillside Avenue intersection. After being stolen the vehicle and attached trailer, filled with concrete and dirt from the City’s paving project, crashed into a tree on Ricardo Avenue, coming to rest just feet from a residence’s living room. A male suspect in a ski mask entered the vehicle whose keys were inside and fled with the vehicle and trailer westbound on Blair toward Ricardo where the driver lost control of the vehicle. The truck then collided with a tree in the side yard of a residence. No injuries were reported to the residents or any bystanders. Piedmont Police Department units were dispatched to the area of Blair Avenue and Hillside Avenue following an initial report of a theft of tools at 4:45 p.m. Upon arrival, officers determined that the suspect had just stolen a 2026 GMC Sierra 3500 with an attached trailer hauling a large quantity of dirt and concrete. Captain Chris Monahan of the Piedmont Police explained that the truck struck a tree in the yard of the residence and then the tree hit a wall and window of the home, causing only minor damage to the home. The truck, weighing more than three tons empty, and trailer came to a halt jackknifed just feet from the side of the residence. The truck and trailer jumped the curb, collided with and unearthed a tree in the yard, then came to The side yard as it appeared on Thursday, January 8, the day after the crash The trailer is towed away later that evening. Photo by PPD rest firmly planted in the side yard of the residence. The t wo suspects are described as males wearing ski masks. Following the crash the auto theft suspect entered a dark gray Honda and fled the scene with a getaway driver toward Grand Avenue. After contacting the truck owners, D’s Engineering, Piedmont Police determined that the keys were left in the truck as the driver was making contact with other street paving workers nearby. Piedmont Police promptly closed the roadways and called in the fire department to confirm that no gas leaks were caused. This investigation remains ongoing at this time. Anyone with information or relevant video footage in the area is encouraged to contact the Piedmont Police Department at (510) 420-3000.

She has also served as city attorney for several other California cities, including Rohnert Park, Calistoga, Pacifica and Moraga. Former mayor Teddy Gray King, who attended the meeting, spoke about Kenyon’s professionalism and passion for public service. “Michelle Kenyon was the voice of reason, the one who brought professionalism to this body with her deep experience and love of government,” King said. Kenyon’s legal expertise was instrumental in several local initiatives, including the climate action plan, the implementation of automatic license plate readers, the Linda Beach pickleball courts and the Sidney and Irene Dearing Memorial project. Kenyon thanked the Piedmont community and city staff in a statement to the council. “It has truly been my pleasure to serve the City of Piedmont, not just the council, but your community,” she said. “I’m looking forward to seeing what you all do in the future. Thank you all from the bottom of my heart.” The council also approved the appointment of Deepa Sharma as the new city attorney. Sharma was mentored by Kenyon and has served as Piedmont’s assistant city attorney since 2020. Heading in the right direction – with a long way to go By Pastor Jim Hopkins Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep. (Romans 12:15) I am grateful to Fr. Aidan McAleenan and the congregation of St. Columba Catholic Church in North Oakland for hosting the annual Ceremony of the Crosses on New Year’s Eve. It allowed us to remember those who were murdered in Oakland in the year gone by, to pray for the grieving, to pray for the perpetrators of violence and to recommit to the works of violence interruption, violence prevention and community transformation. They are the lifelines to healing at the heart of the significant decline in homicides and shootings in Oakland in 2025. It is true. 2025 saw an approximately 20% reduction in homicides and shootings in Oakland. This is significant. We are headed in the right direction. While not a reason for rejoicing, it is a reason to applaud those people and programs, like Oakland Ceasefire, who are part of the needed efforts to reduce gun violence, reduce recidivism and help build healthy communities. It is also true that the over 60 homicides are over 60 too many. It is true that these deaths represent shattered families, grieving communities, searing trauma. They are reason for us to weep. The Oakland Ceasefire Partnership is committed to keep heading in the right direction in the year ahead. We would love to see a year in which no one dies from gun violence. Realistically, our goal for 2026 is a 10% reduction in shootings and homicides. While not a cause for rejoicing, it would mean a significant reduction in weeping. Let’s head in that direction. Rev. articles.text: As the Post celebrates its 28th year of publication, it may bring a smile to the faces of our readers as they see a list of the top newspapers in the country. 1. The Wall Street Journal is read by the people who run the country. 2. The Washington Post is read by people who think they run the country. 3. The New York Times is read by people who think they should run the country and who are very good at crossword puzzles. 4. USA Today is read by people who think they ought to run the country, but don’t really understand The New York Times. They do, however, like their statistics shown in pie charts. 5. The Los Angeles Times is read by people who wouldn’t mind running the country if they could find the time, and if they didn’t have to leave Southern California to do it. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. The Boston Globe is read by people whose parents used to run the country and did a poor job of it, thank you very much. The New York Daily News is read by people who aren’t too sure who’s running the country and don’t really care as long as they can get a seat on the subway. The New York Post is read by people who don’t care who is running the country as long as they do something really scandalous, preferably while intoxicated. The Miami Herald is read by people who are running another country but need the baseball scores. The San Francisco Chronicle is read by people who aren’t sure if there is a country, or that anyone is running it; but If so, they oppose all that they stand for. There are occasional exceptions, such as if the leaders are handicapped minority feminist atheist dwarfs who also happen to be illegal aliens from any other country, or galaxy, provided, of course, that they are not Republicans. The National Enquirer is read by people trapped in line at the grocery store. The Piedmont Post is read by people who quietly run everything but the country, and who prefer a smaller newspaper for Where In the World Are We photo ops when they travel. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: Hampton Field is being worked on . Hampton Field and Coaches’ Field will be closed from mid-December through mid-February as the City undertakes seasonal maintenance to restore heavily used natural turf and prepare the fields for spring use. Both fields have seen extensive wear from year-round activity, leaving bald spots and uneven surfaces. The maintenance work is designed to repair damaged areas and level worn sections to improve safety and playability. Crews will use slit-seeding and aeration to rehabilitate the turf. This process embeds seed directly into the soil, improving seed-to-soil contact and increasing the likelihood of successful germination. Hampton’s turf field will be fenced off during this period to prevent activity that could interfere with the work. Another key component of the project is fertigation, a method that delivers organic amendments and soil-building additives through the irrigation system. Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent explained the approach during a Nov. 5 presentation to the Parks Commission. “Precise micro-dosing through an irrigation system is a far more efficient method of amendment application than manual application,” Kent said. “Traditional topical fertilizing results in a lower product absorption, with Coaches’ Field (Photos courtesy of the city) a large amount of run-off. Constant micro application of organic-based nutrients increases soil and plant health.” The project also includes importing materials to address surface and soil conditions. Crews will add 25 cubic yards of Pac Bell cinders to the infield, a specialized mix once used at the San Francisco Giants’ field at Candlestick Park. An additional 75 cubic yards of sand will be applied to the outfields to fill low spots, improve aeration, and support reseeding. Kent noted that weather conditions play a critical role in the success of the work, particularly during the reseeding phase. Fields must be dry enough for tractors to operate safely, even as consistent moisture is needed for seed growth. “To perform re-seeding and germination, the field has to be dry enough for a tractor to navigate,” she said. “The upshot of this is that if rain slows down and we get a stretch where it’s dry enough to perform the work, then re-seeding will go on as planned. If it were to rain continuously throughout January, then we would simply not do re-seeding this year.” Although the fields will be closed during the maintenance period, the batting cages will remain open. City officials said recent rains have not set the project back, and both fields remain on track to reopen in February.
articles.title: Hampton and Coaches’ Fields closed for maintenance

articles.text: Piedmont Unplugged will launch a new “bike bus” this Friday, Jan. 9, offering families a supervised group ride to Havens Elementary School in response to recent changes in local bus service. Participants will meet at Bear Park, at the corner of King and Hampton avenues, at 8 a.m. and ride together to Havens. For the first day, organizers will also coordinate a return ride back to Bear Park after drop-off. The bike bus will be led by experienced parent volunteers and accompanied by a Piedmont Police Department officer on its inaugural ride. The goal is to help students ride safely while learning basic street awareness and rules of the road. Helmets and bikes are required, and students may park their bikes on the Havens campus without a lock. Ryan Moore of Oakland Trek will be on hand to check bikes and equipment before departure. The effort follows AC Transit’s decision to replace Line 33 and eliminate extended schoolhour bus service serving the Hampton and Estates Drive area, which previously connected students to Piedmont High School, Millennium High School, and Havens Elementary School. Piedmont Unplugged founder and resident Danielle Horowitz said the loss of the route created an immediate gap for families and prompted the community-led solution. Horowitz, who is originally from Boston, previously helped launch a neighborhood bike bus there. “It emboldens free play,” Horowitz said. “Lots of communities around the country are doing this for fun, community building, and to implement independence.” Organizers hope to continue the bike bus on a regular schedule, either every other Friday or on the first Friday of each month.
articles.title: Piedmont Unplugged’s bike bus to roll out this Friday, Jan. 9

articles.text: Meet Cinnamoroll, a Velcro sweetheart. This three-yearold American Pit Bull Terrier mix weighs about 60 pounds, though she could use a little fattening up. Highly affectionate, she bonds quickly and thrives on close human connection. Oakland Animal Services staff and volunteers say Cinnamoroll loves people and will sometimes even try to crawl into laps, despite her size. She takes treats gently and responds well to “sit.” While she shows interest in other dogs on walks, she is easily redirected with treats and guidance. Cinnamoroll could happily join a home with existing canine companions or be your cherished solo dog. articles.text: The Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee invites K-12 students to contribute to the 2026 Art and Writing Showcase celebrating Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. All student work will be featured at the annual Dr. King Celebration, taking place Monday, January 19, at 11 a.m. at the Alan Harvey Theater. All contributors will also be entered into a raffle to win one of ten $25 gift cards. The theme of this year’s event is inspired by King’s 1967 book, “Where Do We Go from Here? Chaos or Community?” The book expanded on a lecture Dr. King gave in 1964 after receiving the Nobel Peace Prize. “This is a great new problem of mankind,” he said. “We have inherited a big house, a great world house in which we have to live together.” “Black men and white men, Easterners and Westerners, Gentiles and Jews, Catholics and Protestants, Muslims and Hindus, a family unduly separated in ideas, culture, and interests, who, because we can never again live without each other, must learn somehow in this one big world house to live with each other,” Dr. King wrote. The deadline is Wednesday, January 14. More information is available at: https://www.padc. info/showcase.

articles.text: A school board meeting will be held tonight, Wednesday, January 7, at an alternate location. The 7:00 p.m. meeting will be held at 800 Magnolia Avenue in the Alan Harvey Theater’s Drama classroom on the second floor. This will mark the first meeting of the school board after they reorganized with Ruchi Medhekar being elected President and Michael Malione earning the Vice President position. The board will hold a first reading to put a renewal of the “Measure G” parcel tax on the June 2 election ballot with a 2/3 vote requirement. The qualified special tax, which annually provides $12,000,000, was set to otherwise expire on June 30, 2028, unless renewed, replaced, or continued by voter approval. The district is seeking to evergreen the continuation of the tax, with an up to 3% increase annually, as determined by the board. articles.text: Chief Teaching & Learning Officer, Exploratorium It’s 5 p.m., and it’s already growing dark outside. The holiday break is over, routines are settling back in, and everyone is feeling a bit cooped up. But here’s what I’ve learned over decades as an educator and a parent: winter’s early darkness isn’t something to simply endure. It’s an invitation. When the sun sets before dinner, we notice light differently. Suddenly, the glow of a streetlamp becomes fascinating. Shadows stretch across the living room floor. These aren’t distractions from learning. They are learning, happening in real time in the curious moments of daily life. This is the season when questions about light come naturally. Why does it get dark so early? Why do car headlights look different in the rain? Where do the colors in a rainbow come from? These wonderings are examples of thinking like a scientist, approaching the world with curiosity about the how and why. They invite us to pause, notice and explore. During these still-dark evenings, simple experiments with light become even more magical. Try creating a “Pixel Tube” with your kids. Roll strips of shiny Mylar or aluminum foil into small tubes, bundle them inside a larger tube made from construction paper, and add a wax paper screen on one end. When you look through it at different light sources, a lamp, a TV screen or holiday lights still up around the neighborhood, you’ll see pixelated, kaleidoscope-like patterns. It’s beautiful, and it’s also science in action, with light reflecting, bouncing and mixing in surprising ways. The genius of winter’s darkness is that it makes light more noticeable. In summer, we take brightness for granted. On a January evening, when a child aims a flashlight at the wall and discovers shadow puppets, or sees how light bends through a glass of water, they’re exploring how light works. They are watching it travel, reflect and refract, and interact with other materials in delightful ways. © The Exploratorium Visitors play at the Exploratorium’s iconic Colored Shadows exhibit, one of the museum’s most photographed experiences.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. Compostable bags are also available from Republic Services (1-800-320-8077) for a fee. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont ranked No. 3 in NCS, No. 30 in State It was a busy end of December for the girls’ basketball team which heads into 2026 with a 9-2 overall record. The Highlanders recently reached the championship game of the 2025 SoCal Holiday Classic In San Diego from December 26-30, a tournament which brings together some of the top teams in California. Piedmont won opened with a 53-39 win over La Jolla Country Day, 75-36 against Santa Margarita in the quarterfinals, and edged out Iolani of Hawaii 48-46 in the semifinals. They advanced to the finals where they lost 55-48 to Brentwood School of Los Angeles. Jenelle Solis was named to the SoCal Holiday Classic’s All-Tournament team. She scored 51 points in the four games, to go along with 16 assists. Despite the title loss, Piedmont fought hard against a ranked team. Brentwood School enters the New Year ranked No. 34 in the State, while Piedmont is ranked 30th by MaxPreps, which dictates playoff seeding. Santa Margarita is No. 41, while La Jolla Country Day is No. 61. Piedmont looks ahead to the start of its Western Alameda County Conference schedule with a heated rivalry game against Bishop O’Dowd on January 13 at home in the Binks Rawlings Gym. It’s a game with league title and North Coast Section seeding implications, as O’Dowd comes in ranked No. 9 in NCS while Staff Photos Taylor White had 18 rebounds against Brentwood School and 16 rebounds against La Jolla Country Day. Savannah Dennig led scoring in the SoCal Holiday Classic finals with 17 points. Jenelle Solis earned All-Tournament honors at the SoCal Holiday Classic, which features top teams in California. Piedmont ranks No. 3. 55-48 loss in finals to Brentwood Piedmont trailed 22-15 to end the first quarter while both sides were even on scoring in each of the remaining three quarters. Piedmont and Brentwood each scored 13 points in the second quarter, 10 points in the third, and another 10 points in the fourth. Final stats: Savannah Dennig led with 17 points, seven rebounds, and three assists. Taylor White had 12 points, 18 rebounds, six assists, three steals, and a block. Solis had seven points, two assists, four rebounds, and a steal. Alexa Ba had six points and two rebounds. Andrea Martin had five points, five rebounds, two steals, an assist and block. 48-46 victory over Iolani Piedmont trailed 15-10 to end the first quarter but knotted things up by halftime, 25-25. The Highlanders took a narrow 40-39 lead in the third quarter, while they outscored ‘Iolani 8-7 in a low-scoring fourth quarter. Final stats: Martin led with 19 points, three rebounds, two assists, two steals, and three blocks. Solis had 15 points, six assists, two rebounds, and three steals. Ba had seven points and four rebounds. Dennig had four points, seven rebounds, three assists, and one steal. White had two points, seven rebounds, one assist, and one steal. Johnson had one point, three rebounds, and a block. 75-36 blowout of Santa Margarita Piedmont dominated the first quarter to make it 32-8 through the opening eight minutes. They extended the lead to 56-15 by halftime, while scoring 10 points in the third quarter and nine in the fourth. Final stats: Marin had 29 points, nine rebounds, two assists, five steals, and two blocks. Solis had 20 points, five assists, two rebounds, and two steals. Ba had 12 points, two rebounds, and a steal. Dennig had seven points, four rebounds, four assists, and two steals. White had four points, nine rebounds, nine assists, and two steals. Jaden Jones had three points and two rebounds. 53-39 win vs. La Jolla Country Day Piedmont got out to a 15-8 lead through the first quarter and extended the lead by one point in the second quarter to lead 29-21 by halftime. It was similar in the third with Piedmont outscoring La Jolla 12-11, leading 41-33 to start the final going. PHS added 12 points in the fourth, allowing seven. Final stats: Martin had 13 points, eight rebounds and two steals. White had 12 points, 16 rebounds, three assists, and four steals. Dennig had 10 points, seven rebounds, six assists, and three steals. Solis had nine points, one rebound, and three assists. Ba had nine points and six rebounds. NEXT UP Piedmont (9-2 overall) hosts Bishop O’Dowd at home on Tuesday, January 13 at 6:30 p.m.
articles.title: Girls reach finals of SoCal Holiday Classic

articles.text: Dillon Casey scores career-high against Redwood Christian Staff Photos Dillon Casey scored a career-high of 35 points in Piedmont’s win over Redwood Christian. Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team started 2026 in a strong way with two wins at Binks Rawlings Gym to stretch its winning streak to four games. They most recently beat Redwood Christian 57-51 with a comeback on Monday, January 5 and beat McKinleyville 65-50 on Saturday, January 3. The pair of wins brings Piedmont’s record to 9-3 as they get their Western Alameda County Conference schedule started. Senior guard Dillon Casey had a career game against Redwood Christian, scoring 35 points to help lift the Highlanders over the Eagles. “We kind of struggled,” Casey said. Usually we’re a very good 3-point shooting team, but we missed a lot in the first quarter. When your team is missing threes, you’ve got to go to the rim. Some of my shots kept on falling.” Piedmont didn’t gain a lead against Redwood Christian until the early seconds of the fourth quarter with 7:50 left. The Highlanders were cold from beyond the arch, shooting 1/11 for 3-pointers in the first quarter and 1/15 by halftime. “We were down seven in the third quarter and Dillon hit a couple big shots. Once we got the lead, I felt like we settled in a little bit better. We started the game 1/15 from three, but we were getting good looks. The defense and rebounding kept us in the game,” coach Ben Spencer said. The Eagles had multiple blocks around the basket in the first half, which led to some tentative shots around the post. However, Piedmont stayed aggressive in the second half, including Casey weaving his way around Redwood’s defenders with smooth finishing. “You have to have the mindset of staying the course. It may not work once, but you’ve got to go back and try again. If it fails, go back quicker, faster, stronger, and more explosive,” Casey mentioned. 57-51 win vs. Redwood Christian Redwood Christian led 5-0 before Piedmont got on the board after nearly three minutes after Ollie Dougan put back an offensive rebound for a basket. The Eagles led 11-8 to end the quarter. In the second, Piedmont cut the deficit to one point four different times. PHS went into halftime trailing 22-21. It was more back and forth scoring to start the third quarter until the Eagles established a 38-32 lead. But from there, PHS scored five straight to trail 38-37 to start the fourth. In the final going, Casey converted a layup to give PHS its first lead of the game, 39-38, after 10 seconds. Soon after that, Casey knocked down a 3-pointer to make it 42-38. The Highlanders scored five of the next seven points to go up 47-40. Beach Lorin scored 13 points on Redwood Christian and seven on McKinleyville.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team closed 2025 on a high note with back-to-back 4-nil wins. They beat Oakland Tech on Wednesday, December 17 and Head-Royce on Friday, December 19. The results put Piedmont on a three-game winning streak with all three being shutouts after beating Marin Academy 1-nil on December 13. Their record improved to 3-1-2 (W-T-L) as they get their Western Alameda County Conference schedule started against rivals Berkeley on Thursday, January 8. Miranda Liu had a three-goal hat trick against Oakland Tech, and Piedmont had four different players scoring against HeadRoyce: Makenna Small, Miranda Liu, Ayla Blanford and Elia Kwong.. 4-0 shutout of Head-Royce Piedmont got the show started quickly with freshman Makenna Small scoring her first varsity goal in the first minute. It happened after Miranda Liu dribbled into the box, leading to HeadRoyce’s goal keeper rushing to make a slide tackle. The ball fell opportunely to Small, sending in a left-footed shot in the box. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team closed 2025 with a 4-2 loss to Tennyson at Witter Field on Friday, December 19. The Highlanders open the New Year looking to build on its 1-0-5 (W-T-L) record tonight, January 7, hosting Chico. The opening of the season has been a time of transition for Piedmont after winning last year’s Div. 5 CIF NorCal title. Coach Ben Russell has a young team that includes 10 sophomores and three freshmen. “We want to play with organization defensively and a little more quality when we have the ball. articles.text: In this week’s Athletes in College, we take a look at former basketball stars still active in college: JoJo Murphy at Seattle University, Samantha Smith at Emory University, and Hannah Govert at Bryn Mawr College. CCAA Men’s Basketball Player of the Week winner and earned CCAA All-Tournament honors. The Wildcats went 24-6 last season with Murphy leading the team with 279 total minutes and 155 points. He’s converting 44 percent from the field and 34 percent from 3-pointers. He was named the CCAA’s Freshman of the Year in 2023 and was first-team All-CCAA. He was an honorable mention for All-CCAA in 2024. Samantha Smith Macalester College Samantha Smith, PHS Class of 2024, is a sophomore at Macalester College. She was a twoyear varsity member at Piedmont High. Macalester College is currently 1-9 this season. Smith has appeared in all 10 games and started four times, playing 17.8 minutes per game for 32 points, 18 rebounds, one assists, two steals, and three blocks. At Piedmont High, Smith helped the Highlanders win the 2023 D4 NCS title as a senior and claim back-to-back Western Alameda County Conference firstplace banners. articles.text: Honorable Mention: Miranda Liu, Taylor White We’re awarding Jenelle Solis of the girls’ basketball team and Dillon Casey of boys’ basketball our Athletes of the Week. Honorable mentions go to Miranda Liu of girls’ soccer and Taylor White of girls’ basketball. JENELLE SOLIS Jenelle Solis was the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2025, and is already off to a hot start with the 9-2 girls’ basketball team, one of the top ranked in California. She earns Athlete of the Week honors after being named to the SoCal Holiday Classic’s All-Tournament team. In the four-game tournament, Solis finished with 51 points and 16 assists. Staff Photos We name Jenelle Solis our girls’ Athlete of the Week after earning AllTournament honors at the SoCal Holiday Classic. After opening the game with five points in the first quarter, Casey changed the game with 10 points in the second quarter, nine points in the third, and another 10 in the fourth. Dillon Casey is our boys’ Athlete of the Week after scoring a career-high of 35 points against Redwood Christian. Miranda Liu gets an honorable mention for Athlete of the Week after scoring 3 goals against Oakland Tech, along with a goal and an assist in a win over Head-Royce. Holiday Classic, including a huge 18 rebounds and 12 points in their 55-48 championship loss to Brentwood School on December 30. She also had 12 points and 16 rebounds in their opening round 53-39 win over La Jolla Country Day on December 26.

As KCOM-TV Station Manager, Shaw oversees all video production for the City, broadcast systems, and Council Chambers AV equipment. The Piedmont City Council voted to award a contract to Rapid Grading Services to repave the length of Grand Avenue in Piedmont. The project added bulb-outs, ADA-compliant curb ramps, bicycle markings, and a bioretention basin that provides soil-filtering of storm water. The contract was approved for an amount of $1,414,102 with a construction budget of $1,555,513. On February 28, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers was honored with the Hometown Hero Award from the San Francisco District Attorney’s Office in celebration of Black History Month. District Attorney Brooke Jenkins honored Bowers and his fellow awardees for their longstanding commitment to the African American community in the Bay Area. March Piedmont’s City Council provided a highly anticipated update on the progress of the construction of the Community Pool. Construction was delayed in February and January due to heavy rains, forcing workers to wait for the site to dry enough to excavate the smaller non-competitive pool. The report stated June 2, 2025, as the completion date for construction, roughly one year later than originally planned. This date was later pushed back again as construction was completed in August, 2 months after the promised date. The $34.9 million project still lacks clarity regarding its full completion and opening. J. Miller Flowers celebrates its 55th anniversary. The family-owned florist and gift shop hosted a Spring Open House and Pop-up Art Show with 12 local artists. The community came together to celebrate a special milestone in the florist’s history. Piedmont Scout and PHS baseball player Sammy Ragones worked with the City of Piedmont to dismantle and replace the batting cages at Coaches Field. The previous batting cages at Coaches Field were installed 20 years ago and showed signs of heavy damage. Ragones worked with scout volunteers to prepare the site by dismantling the original cage in December 2024. After clearing away the old nets, poles, mats, and fencing, a contractor came in to install the replacement cage. After that, Ragones returned to install new nets and turf, completing the project with a plaque recognizing the partners who worked hard to bring the new cages to life. The project replaced a bridge that had required repairs over the past five years due to rotting wood and holes in the wood decking. The project cost the city $200,000, with $119,000 coming from California Proposition 68. The new bridge was built off-site and installed by crane. The City of Piedmont released a public review draft of the Moraga Canyon housing plan.
