articles.text: In a short video, the people behind Piedmont’s everyday services share highlights from the past year and what they mean for the community: https://tinyurl.com/4p6bmv7f Featured highlights of the video include: Access & community support • New online services: Community members can now file, search, and monitor Public Records Requests online. Members can register or renew a business license anytime, day or night, from the convenience of their homes. • Expanded after-care options: When school returned this fall, PRD launched “The Hangout,” a new after-school option designed to meet the needs of older elementary students. • Linda Beach Tot Lot: In November, this popular playground re-opened as Piedmont’s first inclusive-play tot lot, with improved ADA access and new equipment designed for children of all abilities. Safety & resilience • New 9-1-1 Dispatch Center: Piedmont’s most significant public safety investment in decades, the new Dispatch Center strengthens emergency response capabilities and positions the City for the next generation of 9-1-1 technology while delivering a major infrastructure upgrade to the Police Department, including secure, independent power with dedicated backup. • Community wildfire evacuation exercise: Residents in the Blair/Scenic neighborhood practiced evacuation alongside first responders, while dozens of Piedmonters joined in at home, conducting evacuation decision-making with their families using our video guide. Infrastructure, sustainability & planning for the future • Moraga Canyon Specific Plan: In October, after more than two years of public discussion, the City Council adopted a vision and implementation plan for a new neighborhood in Moraga Canyon – grounded in what community members value most. The Specific Plan provides a framework for future development that prioritizes wildfire resilience and improvements to pedestrian, bicycle, and traffic safety, while creating opportunities for more people to call Piedmont home. • Piedmont’s first green infrastructure: At Grand and Fairview, a new landscaped bioswale now captures and filters stormwater through native plantings, cleaning runoff before it drains to the Bay. • Greening the City fleet: This year, the City added two e-bikes, a low-speed electric utility vehicle, and a fully electric closed-circuit TV van used for sewer inspections, which helped reduce emissions in day-to-day operations. Looking ahead to 2026 In 2026 the city will open the new community pool, install new swings in Piedmont Park, install a memorial to Sidney & Irene Dearing at Triangle Park, and take the next steps to begin implementing the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan – all alongside the ongoing work that keeps essential services running smoothly every day.

articles.text: Dark Star Orchestra, a seven-piece band best known for recreating historic live performances by the Grateful Dead, performs live at the Fox Theater in Oakland on February 6 and 7. Formed in 1997, the cover band has perfor med more than 3,000 concerts across the United States and internationally, earning acclaim from Grateful Dead fans and featuring occasional guest appearances with original Grateful Dead members. Dark Star Orchestra aims to immerse audiences in the live “Dead experience,” using era-appropriate instrumentation, vocal harmonies and improvisational interplay that reflect the evolving sound of the original band. Over nearly three decades, the cover band has grown from club dates to headline larger venues and festivals, developing a dedicated following that includes multiple generations of fans. Their work preserves and extends the legacy of the Grateful Dead’s music, making it accessible to longtime “Deadheads” and new listeners alike. The band performs at Fox Theater on Friday, February 6 and Saturday, February 7. Both concerts begin at 7:30 p.m. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https://thefoxoakland.com/. articles.text: Four-day festival held Jan. 15 - 18 Bay Area theatre artist Dan Hoyle moderates festival discussions. Berkeley Repertory Theatre will host a four-day festival of solo performance work by formerly incarcerated artists next week, marking the culmination of a three-year residency by the Formerly Incarcerated People’s Performance Project (FIPPP). The festival will take place Thursday, January 15, through Sunday, January 18 at Berkeley Repertory’s Roda Theatre. It celebrates the completion of FIPPP’s tenure as the theatre’s first-ever company-in-residence, a partnership that began in 2023. Founded six years ago, FIPPP develops and presents solo performance stories by formerly incarcerated people with the aim of fostering understanding and social change through personal storytelling. The organization produced festivals in Oakland in 2021 and 2023 before joining Berkeley Repertory Theatre. It has since grown into a full-scale theatre company with eight professional directors and 15 formerly incarcerated artists. The festival will feature five distinct programs presented over four days. Each show includes multiple solo performances, as well as short documentary films by filmmaker Jim Granato that complement the live work onstage. Three of the performances will conclude with panel discussions featuring the performers, offering audiences an opportunity to engage more deeply with the material. The conversations will be moderated by Bay Area theatre artists Dan Hoyle, Wayne Harris and Mark McGoldrick, all of whom also serve as coaches with FIPPP. Twelve formerly incarcerated performers will appear in the festival, bringing diverse backgrounds that include stand-up comedy, TEDx talks, The Moth storytelling competitions, Shakespearean theatre and appearances at the San Francisco Fringe Festival. Their stories explore paths to incarceration, life inside prison and the challenges of reentry, shaped and directed by FIPPP’s professional creative team. For more information, visit https://fippp.org/.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep hosts exhibition in partnership with Formerly Incarcerated People’s Performance Project

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum’s newest exhibition, Rave into the Future: Art in Motion, is on view now through January 26, 2026. The exhibition spotlights women and queer artists from the West Asia diaspora currently based in the United States and Europe and is inspired by West Asian rave and underground music culture. Oakland-based Arab Persian American artist Sahar Khoury contributes a multimedia sculpture equipped with a functioning DJ deck that will be activated by local Asian and Asian diaspora DJs. Los Angeles–based Yemeni American artist Yasmine Nasser Diaz’s installation For Your Eyes Only recreates an intimate bedroom where projections of dancers, archival clips, and protest materials form a layered portrait of generational expression and activism. Disguise as Dancefloor, a nearly 100-square-foot copper dancefloor by London-based Lebanese American artist Joe Namy, is designed to record the footsteps of visitors while symbolizing the healing properties associated with the material across cultures. Other featured pieces bring humor, futurism, and fantastical narrative into the mix, including Meriem Bennani’s Party on the CAPS, Sophia al Maria and Fatima al Qadiri’s bass-driven Spiral, and Farah Al Qasimi’s horror-comedy Um Al Naar. The exhibition culminates in a glitter-filled “after-party” animated by robotic vacuum cleaners in Puff Out by the Brussels-based duo :mentalKLINIK. Curated by Naz Cuguoğlu, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art, the exhibition has already earned significant recognition. Cuguoğlu received a curatorial research fellowship from The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts last year, and the museum was recently awarded an additional foundation grant to bring the project to fruition. “I wanted to create a space for narratives that build solidarity through joy, pleasure, and laughter,” Cuguoğlu said, noting the need to counter dominant Western portrayals of West Asia rooted in Orientalism and suffering. “This exhibition asks what we can learn from the autonomy, healing, and bliss that unfold on the dancefloor,” Cuguoğlu said. Museum Director and CEO Soyoung Lee added that the show offers a timely opportunity to broaden public understanding of West Asia while celebrating the universal joy of collective dance. Rave into the Future: Art in Motion is on view at the Asian Art Museum now through January 26, 2026.

Formed in 1997, the cover band has perfor med more than 3,000 concerts across the United States and internationally, earning acclaim from Grateful Dead fans and featuring occasional guest appearances with original Grateful Dead members. Dark Star Orchestra aims to immerse audiences in the live “Dead experience,” using era-appropriate instrumentation, vocal harmonies and improvisational interplay that reflect the evolving sound of the original band. Over nearly three decades, the cover band has grown from club dates to headline larger venues and festivals, developing a dedicated following that includes multiple generations of fans. Their work preserves and extends the legacy of the Grateful Dead’s music, making it accessible to longtime “Deadheads” and new listeners alike. The band performs at Fox Theater on Friday, February 6 and Saturday, February 7. Both concerts begin at 7:30 p.m. For more information, and to purchase tickets, visit https://thefoxoakland.com/. Berkeley Rep hosts exhibition in partnership with Formerly Incarcerated People’s Performance Project Four-day festival held Jan. 15 - 18 Dark Star Orchestra By Allyson Aleksey The Asian Art Museum’s newest exhibition, Rave into the Future: Art in Motion, is on view now through January 26, 2026. The exhibition spotlights women and queer artists from the West Asia diaspora currently based in the United States and Europe and is inspired by West Asian rave and underground music culture. Oakland-based Arab Persian American artist Sahar Khoury contributes a multimedia sculpture equipped with a functioning DJ deck that will be activated by local Asian and Asian diaspora DJs. Los Angeles–based Yemeni American artist Yasmine Nasser Diaz’s installation For Your Eyes Only recreates an intimate bedroom where projections of dancers, archival clips, and protest materials form a layered portrait Rave into the Future leaves Asian Art Museum Jan. 26 of generational expression and activism. Disguise as Dancefloor, a nearly 100-square-foot copper dancefloor by London-based Lebanese American artist Joe Namy, is designed to record the footsteps of visitors while symbolizing the healing properties associated with the material across cultures. Other featured pieces bring humor, futurism, and fantastical narrative into the mix, including Meriem Bennani’s Party on the CAPS, Sophia al Maria and Fatima al Qadiri’s bass-driven Spiral, and Farah Al Qasimi’s horror-comedy Um Al Naar. The exhibition culminates in a glitter-filled “after-party” animated by robotic vacuum cleaners in Puff Out by the Brussels-based duo :mentalKLINIK. Curated by Naz Cuguoğlu, Assistant Curator of Contemporary Art, the exhibition has already earned significant recognition. Cuguoğlu received a curatorial research fellowship from The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts last year, and the museum was recently awarded an additional foundation grant to bring the project to fruition. “I wanted to create a space for narratives that build solidarity through joy, pleasure, and laughter,” Cuguoğlu said, noting the need to counter dominant Western portrayals of West Asia rooted in Orientalism and suffering. “This exhibition asks what we can learn from the autonomy, healing, and bliss that unfold on the dancefloor,” Cuguoğlu said. Museum Director and CEO Soyoung Lee added that the show offers a timely opportunity to broaden public understanding of West Asia while celebrating the universal joy of collective dance. By Allyson Aleksey Berkeley Repertory Theatre will host a four-day festival of solo performance work by formerly incarcerated artists next week, marking the culmination of a three-year residency by the Formerly Incarcerated People’s Performance Project (FIPPP). The festival will take place Thursday, January 15, through Sunday, January 18 at Berkeley Repertory’s Roda Theatre. It celebrates the completion of FIPPP’s tenure as the theatre’s first-ever company-in-residence, a partnership that began in 2023. Founded six years ago, FIPPP develops and presents solo performance stories by formerly incarcerated people with the aim of fostering understanding and social change through personal storytelling. The organization produced festivals in Oakland in 2021 and 2023 before joining Berkeley Repertory Theatre. It has since grown into a full-scale theatre company with eight professional directors and 15 formerly incarcerated artists. The festival will feature five distinct programs presented over four days. Each show includes multiple solo performances, as well as short documentary films by filmmaker Jim Granato that complement the live work onstage. Three of the performances will conclude with panel discussions featuring the performers, offering audiences an opportunity to engage more deeply with the material. The conversations will be moderated by Bay Area theatre artists Dan Hoyle, Wayne Harris and Mark McGoldrick, all of whom also serve as coaches with FIPPP. Twelve formerly incarcerated performers will appear in the festival, bringing diverse backgrounds that include stand-up comedy, TEDx talks, The Moth storytelling competitions, Shakespearean theatre and appearances at the San Francisco Fringe Festival. Their stories explore paths to incarceration, life inside prison and the challenges of reentry, shaped and directed by FIPPP’s professional creative team. For more information, visit https://fippp.org/. Rave into the Future: Art in Motion is on view at the Asian Art Museum now through January 26, 2026.

articles.text: The San Francisco Botanical Garden in Golden Gate Park hosts a free birdwatching tour the first Sunday of every month, guided by members of the Golden Gate Bird Alliance. Golden Gate Bird Alliance is a nonprofit organization dedicated to the conservation of birds, wildlife and their habitats in the San Francisco Bay Area. Founded in 1917 and formerly known as the Golden Gate Audubon Society, the group works to engage the public through education, advocacy and hands-on activities such as free bird walks, habitat restoration and community science projects. Its mission is to inspire people to protect Bay Area birds and the shared natural environment, and its programs span birding outings, speaker events and youth education. Based in Berkeley, the organization serves San Francisco, Oakland and surrounding communities, aiming to foster a broad conservation community and support long-term habitat stewardship across the region. Every month, members visit the San Francisco Botanical Garden to offer a free, community bird-watching tour. The event, entitled “Birding at the Garden,” invites birdwatchers of all ages and skill levels to attend. Attendees are encouraged to bring their own binoculars and a water thermos. The next event is held on Sunday, February 1, between 8 a.m. and 11 a.m. Attendees meet at the Botanical Garden front gate. Registration will open one week before the scheduled walk, on Sunday at 8 a.m. Heavy rains cancel the event. To register, visit https://gggp. org/event/birding-at-the-garden-with-golden-gate-bird-alliance-16/. Photo courtesy of Gardens of Golden Gate Park Birdwatchers of all ages and skill levels are invited to attend.

articles.text: Exhibition on view through March 1 Continuum is on view through March. The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) is marking its 20th anniversary with Continuum: MoAD Over Time, an exhibition examining the museum’s history, on view now through March 1. Continuum presents a chronological and thematic overview of MoAD’s development from its founding to the present, while also addressing its future direction. The exhibition features archival materials, fine art, interviews and community narratives that document the museum’s impact on arts education, cultural programming and public engagement, as well as its artistic influence in the Bay Area and beyond. Exhibition highlights include materials related to long-running initiatives such as the museum’s Emerging Artist Program and “MoAD in the Classroom,” as well as community events including the Afropolitan Ball and Diaspora Dinner. These elements illustrate how the institution has supported artists of the African Diaspora and expanded access to cultural resources over two decades. Continuum includes works by Cheryl Patrice Derricotte, Chester Higgins Jr., JoeSam., Richard Mayhew, Ramekon O’Arwisters, Gordon Parks, Lava Thomas and Sam Vernon. These artists’ contributions reflect a range of media and perspectives connected to the Photo courtesy of Museum of the African Diaspora museum’s mission. According to MoAD, Continuum is intended to document the organization’s institutional history while providing context for its next phase of growth. The exhibition is supported by the KHR McNeely Family Foundation, with major funding from the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, CommonSpirit Health and San Francisco Grants for the Arts. Additional support is provided by several foundations, corporations and individual donors, including the Richard Mayhew Exhibition Fund. Continuum: MoAD Over Time is now on view at the Museum of the African Diaspora. For more information, visit https://www. moadsf.org.

articles.text: Exhibition leaves Jan. 25 Art of Manga is on view now at de Young, featuring over 600 drawings by more than a dozen iconic Japanese artists, comics and novelists who specialize in the genre. Manga, a type of imagedriven narrative storytelling in Japan, has become widely popular in Western culture over the last two decades. The de Young is the first North American museum to highlight Manga and its prominent, modern-day artists in a major exhibition. Featured artists include Chiba Tetsuya, Akatsuka Fujio, Takahashi Rumiko, Taniguchi Jiro, Yamazaki Mari, Araki Hirohiko, Yamashita Kazumi, Tagame Gengoroh, Yoshinaga Fumi, Oda Eiichiro, and Tanaami Keiichi. “Captivating millions around the world with dynamic graphic narratives, manga is one of the most significant visual mediums of our time,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “San Francisco has long been a gateway for Japanese cultural exchange in the United States, and we are delighted to honor this legacy by showcasing the artistry and power of contemporary Japanese narrative art in Art of Manga.” Art of Manga organizing curator Nicole Coolidge Rousmaniere said the genre cultivates “an ease of visceral understanding that enables readership from around the world.” “We are living in a time when the narrative shift from text to images is increasingly becoming a reality,” she added. “Readers become invested in characters and their stories, and manga publishers and artists take their letters and social media comments into account and adapt the ongoing story or create new manga, which often then becomes a forerunner to greater cultural shifts.” Art of Manga is on view at de Young museum now through January 25, 2026. For more information, visit https://www.famsf.org/. Photo courtesy of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco Museum patrons view the Art of Manga exhibition at de Young.

articles.text: Recently, a Post reader asked whether the paper would again review or critique newly released feature films: those that still open in familiar walk-in movie theaters. The question was born of observation and curiosity. Yet something has clearly changed, not only at the Post but also in this century-old form of entertainment and the venues that have long defined it. This raises two related questions: What is happening, and what does it mean? In thinking about this, I searched for an analogue; something equally transformative, even revolutionary. I settled on Johannes Gutenberg, who around 1450 invented movable metal type, a compatible oil-based ink and a screw-down press. His first major work was reportedly the Bible. Before Gutenberg, copies of the Bible were painstakingly produced by hand. What his invention unleashed was an explosion of accessible knowledge and the broad sharing of information, leading to scientific inquiry, global exploration, and advances in architecture and philosophy. It marked a Renaissance of creativity, made manifest in the arts, including theater and literature, as well as in innovation. One could argue we now find ourselves in a similar period, a breathtaking technological renaissance that began in the early 1900s and continues today. Consider the telegraph; photography, including cameras and movie projectors; the automobile; the telephone; radio; flight; space travel; television; the computer; Wikipedia; the internet; email; smartphones; and more; a kaleidoscope of change. And now, artificial intelligence. Filmmaking, moving from celluloid to digital technology, has not been exempt. Hollywood content now streams on platforms such as Prime, Netflix and Disney+, among many others. As with books in the 1450s, this shift has produced an explosion of change: series, episodes and a new richness of character development for writers. For audiences, the change has meant access. A vast historical archive of films is now readily available. Will movies watched on high-tech, large screens at home prove transformative? Will walk-in theaters become relics of the past? Likely. composer Louise Farrenc. This composer has recently become a “cause célèbre”…musically speaking. Judging from the single movement it seems that Farrenc was inf luenced by both Beethoven and Mendelssohn. I hope that the orchestra will present Farrenc’s entire Symphony in the near future. Youthful virtuosity can be awe inspiring. While some important musicians of the past rejected youthful virtuosity, I am amazed by it. The soloist of the evening was the very young violinist Lisa Saito. Her performance was, in a word, amazing. Judging from her all-encompassing technique and rich tone, she has a promising future. Her vehicle of the evening was the monumental First Violin Concerto of Niccolo Paganini. While a few chronic mal-contents continue to downgrade Paganini, he was held in the highest esteem by superlative musicians like Rossini, Liszt, Chopin and Schumann. Rossini once said: “It is a very good thing that Paganini did not write operas because he would have eclipsed all of us.” Paganini was probably the most astonishing musician of all time. The world would be a poorer place if Paganini had not asserted his genius in all aspects of music and all aspects of publicity. As a musician, the Italians adopted the phrase “Paganini never repeats” to describe his unlimited imagination in music. If the young violinist Lisa Saito adds this aspect to her playing… Watch out. After intermission, the concert concluded with the entire Beethoven Symphony No. 7. As the concert proceeded, I observed the conductor carefully. Fankuchen is a real maestro. In many ways he resembles the renowned conductor Raphael Kubelik both on appearance and conducting style. He inspires his orchestra at all times and especially in the climactic phrases. After the concert, I spoke with a number of the musicians. They all agreed that Fankuchen is an inspiring musician, and they are happy to have him as their director. In this respect, he is the true inheritor of the conducting mantle of Edgar Braun. Edgar was the most generous and openminded musician I have ever met. Thanks to him, I had opportunities to present my first important concerts in San Francisco. The good memories remain. It was a perfect way to end the year.

articles.text: Edgar Braun, founder of San Francisco Chamber Orchestra On New Year’s Eve in Berkeley the streets were deserted. It seemed that all of the people were inside at the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra concert in First Church. Wednesday’s concert was billed as a memorial to Edgar Braun, founder of the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra, and Ida Braun. The house was filled to overflowing. Warm applause greeted concertmaster Robin Sharp and conductor Jory Fankuchen. The conductor took his position and presented the first piece, the last movement of Symphony No. 1 by newly discovered French Jory Fankuchen, conductor of SF Chamber Orchestra

articles.text: Shorthand for romantic comedies is rom-com, a go-to genre long favored by Hollywood. These films generally open with what filmmakers refer to as a “meet-cute” moment. There’s a wonderful scene in The Holiday wherein Eli Wallach (so good) portrays Arthur Abbot, a wellknown screenwriter, long ago retired. He defines meet-cute as two people who get into a NYC cab at the same time and look at each other, immediately, ready to declare ownership, but suddenly sense a spark of attraction. articles.text: Kiki’s Delivery Service, created by master storyteller and animator Hayao Miyazaki, who is regarded as the Walt Disney of Japan, was adapted from a popular Japanese coming-of-age novel by Author Eiko Kadono. It’s an extraordinary example of Studio Ghibli’s prodigious talents, incorporating fantasy and a benign crisis into a remarkable tale about a spunky young witch (never sinister) on the cusp of womanhood. Kiki, an adolescent witch, now 13, as tradition dictates, must leave home to complete her magic training in another town. She takes with her talking cat JiJi, a red radio, and hopes to practice her still rocky broom flying skills. She ends up lodging with a baker for whom she begins an airborne delivery service. Beautifully crafted, saturated with rich colors, the story touches on newbie teen issues such as independence, femininity, insecurity, friendship and even (unexpectedly for a children’s movie) sexuality, all in a warm, lighthearted manner. In essence, Kiki’s Delivery Service is a wonderful adventure; however, it is also a personal crossroads for Kiki, who, after an illness, loses her powers and must find a new purpose for her young life. The tale is consistently funny, optimistic, and exciting, finding and holding that coveted sweet spot that makes Miyazaki’s films simply exceptional. Kiki’s Delivery Service. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. Ghibli Studio. With voices of Kirsten Dunst, Debbie Reynolds and Matthew Lawrence. 1 hr., 43 min. Rated G. Released in 1989. articles.text: Reprinted from the San Francisco Chronicle, January 4, 2026. Jeannie Anderson A: The housing market predictions seem to be fairly upbeat and positive, looking to be defined by a combination of items that can create a healthier and balanced market. Mortgage rates seem to have made an improvement and the buyers have come to accept the mid-6% range as tolerable. The softened condo market opens up first time home-buyer opportunities and mid-market prices overall this year will probably stay within a modest gain. Due to the tech-heavy Bay Area boom, cash buyers keep driving the higher end luxury market. The lack of inventory may start shifting as life circumstances will propel longtime homeowners to accept the financially painful aspect of moving and giving up the 3% loan. Another item to note as having an effect on inventory, if it passes in Congress, would be lower capital gains taxes for a personal residence sale — a big factor for 15-year-plus homeowners. This past year saw the real estate industry undergo some volatile changes, lawsuits, MLS rulings and this year’s possible Compass/Anytime merger. The outcomes are meant to improve the transactions for consumers, and add more transparency. Starting the next half of the decade with a stable market should help buyers and sellers in their endeavors. Jeannie Anderson Coldwell Banker Realty 415-271-4887 jeannie.anderson@cbrealty.com Jeremy Davidson A: In 2026, I expect the Bay Area market to be driven largely by necessity. Buyers and sellers who transact will do so because life compels them — a job change, partnering up, family growth, downsizing, or needing to be closer to aging parents. Those circumstances move people to action regardless of what rates are doing. And speaking of rates: yes, they’ll keep some buyers sidelined, but our market has never been typical. The prevalence of cash — fueled by tech equity, AI startup windfalls, and generational wealth — will keep transactions flowing, particularly at the upper end. Conversely, sellers sitting pretty with sub-4% mortgages won’t budge unless they’re decamping for a less expensive market or have enough to buy their next home outright. The AI boom and big tech expansions should persist, meaning jobs and capital will continue pouring into our region, propping up both rents and home prices, especially in the luxury tier. As for what buyers want? That hasn’t changed: turnkey properties close to great schools and neighborhood amenities. Sellers who invest not just in fresh paint and staging but in the bones — roof, foundation, water heater, electrical — will be best positioned. Today’s buyers don’t want a punch list waiting for them at the finish line. Jeremy Davidson Compass 415-717-4103 jeremy.davidson@compass.com DJ Grubb A: Market predictions need to be analyzed in our very different market segments. • First-time buyer market: Due to the cost of ownership, this market segment will continue to be very sluggish and will have very little — if any — appreciation over the next 12 months. The average age of the first-time buyer is now in their mid-30s and many young adults are literally opting not to be burdened by home ownership and would rather travel the world. • Mid market: A very awkward market segment due to the fact that the move-up buyer does not want to leave a sub-3% mortgage and the basic cost of living has accelerated so dramatically in the Bay Area. This segment of the market should continue to appreciate at a very conservative 5%, with maybe a bump if mortgage interest rates decline in the second quarter of the year. • High-end luxury market: This marketplace had a tremendous amount of momentum in 2025. This is very evident in sales volume, all-cash sales and the abundance of remodeling of significant larger homes. The rejuvenation of San Francisco and the new tech market push will maintain a very healthy luxury market in the Bay Area. articles.text: Hello, 2026! We were surprisingly busy this past Holiday Season as both Buyers and Sellers began to seriously contemplate a move in 2026. WHAT WILL OUR RESIDENTIAL REAL ESTATE MARKET be doing as we move forward? Many have asked what the market “temperature” will be. Some economists are whispering “possible recession” as unemployment has risen, as have the cost of everyday goods and services (we know from a simple trip to the grocery store what shockingly little $100 will buy these days) The good news is that the residential real estate market in S.F., particularly in the “luxury home” sector, is booming (due, in primary part, to the proliferation of AI start-ups) History reminds us that the market trends in The City always precede ours, in the East Bay, by about 6 months or so; reason for optimism, for sure. WHAT WILL INTEREST RATES be doing? Our “go to” Mortgage Broker, Brady Thomas, LaSalle Mortgage, reports the following: Rates remained relatively stable at the end of 2025, with the average 30-year fixed rate hovering around 6.25% (as anticipated, the short-term rate cut in December did not have a major impact on mortgages.) 2026 is already seeing “uncertainty” as its dominant theme. The Federal Reserve has shifted its focus from inflation toward the labor market as job growth has slowed and unemployment has edged higher. If this trend continues, it increases the likelihood of lower mortgage rates over the next year. Another factor to watch is leadership at the Fed. With Jerome Powell stepping down in the first half of this year, markets anticipate a new chair who may be more aggressive in using rate cuts to stimulate growth. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group says it never rains on Wednesday mornings in Piedmont, but there was a “very heavy mist” last Wednesday morning. It and this being New Year’s Eve reduced the group’s size. Eighteen water-resistant walkers and two of their K-9 best friends were on hand at the Exedra at their regular weekly gathering time. The Piedmont schools were still on their Holiday break and their campuses were open. Piedmont High, Piedmont Middle School, Millennium High School, and Havens Elementary were all in close proximity and a safe, short walk on a wet morning. Before they got started walking, some background school information was provided. The City of Piedmont was incorporated in September 1907. Since its population was growing dramatically after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, city leaders decided to build two schools to serve the community. The first school was built in 1910 and opened its doors in 1911. It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land donor. It turned out that Havens would be part of the high school’s history too. The walkers started off going behind the Exedra to a path along the top of the park that is a back, side entrance to the high school. They entered the campus and walked down a breezeway to covered area and some more PHS history was shared. In 1916 Havens was in big financial trouble. The Oakland Tribune reported lawsuits totaling $90,000 were filed against him. He had only a little land left from his fortune and it was in his wife’s name. The Anglo-California Trust Company held the mortgage on the Piedmont Park for $172,000, and neither the interest nor the principal had been paid. Havens had auctioned off his art collection and wanted to sell the park to raise funds. The Piedmont School Board voted to purchase some of the park for a new high school and athletic field. They wanted 13 acres, but Havens would not sell less than the park’s entire 27 acres. The City wanted to save the park from residential development but did not have money to purchase the remaining parkland, and in 1916 Piedmont voters defeated a measure to raise funds to buy the land. Havens died suddenly in 1918 from food poisoning. The parkland was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to purchase fourteen acres of the park in 1921 if the City would reimburse them, which it did in 1922 after a bond issue was approved by voters. This plan allowed the school district to buy the 13 acres it wanted and the City to have its park. Construction began immediately in 1921 on the high school. It was a reinforced concrete building with terra cotta trim for five hundred students. An auditorium spanned the front of the school with two stories of classrooms behind and two wings held more classrooms. Piedmont Junior High School and the athletic field were added in 1924, and other additions were built in 1937 and 1939. In 1974, the original school building was declared unsafe under state earthquake laws and was demolished. However, the demolition took longer than anticipated because the buildings were so well built that it was difficult to tear them down. Three new classroom buildings and a gymnasium were built, and the original library, quad, and administration buildings were rehabilitated. The new construction was done in the “back-to-nature” style that was then popular with a wood exterior. However, by the mid-2010s this construction was also deemed earthquake unsafe and these buildings had to be demolished too. The school was reconstructed and opened in the fall of 2021 with a new STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art, and Mathematics) building and a new theater after voters approved $56 million in bonds. Some more interesting facts were also shared. PHS girls were required to wear middy blouses and pleated skirts until the early 1960s. It was the last public school in California to resist pressure from the State to stop enforcing a dress code which required students, and specifically girls, to wear a uniform. The walkers admired the quad area in front of the Student Center and took a group photo. Then they walked over to Millenium High School (MHS) and talked about its history. The school was officially started in 2000 and named for the new millennium. It evolved from the school district’s previous alternative program, the Piedmont Independent Learning High School, that had opened in 1980. MHS has a small enrollment, usually around 60 students in grades 9 to 12. Classes are small, with about 10 to 20 students per class. A fun fact is that George Lucas, the creator of the Star Wars films, granted the school the right to use the image of the Millennium Falcon on school sweatshirts, as well as to represent it as its mascot, effectively creating the Millennium (High School) Falcon. Participating in last week’s Walking on Wednesdays were Jasmine Cai, Jim Kuo, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Mike Gallant, Denny McGee, Brian Hamlin, Mary Carter, Karen Palmer, Karin Fetherston, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Sherry Jacobs, Mark Davis, Dave DeRoche, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Jill and Ron Day were in from England visiting family and that Jing Jing Liu was walking with them for the first time.

The first school was built in 1910 and opened its doors in 1911. It was originally named “The Bonita Avenue School,” but was later renamed “Frank C. Havens Elementary School” after the land donor. It turned out that Havens would be part of the high school’s history too. The walkers started off going behind the Exedra to a path along the top of the park that is a back, side entrance to the high school. They entered the campus and walked down a breezeway to covered area and some more PHS history was shared. In 1916 Havens was in big financial trouble. The Oakland Tribune reported lawsuits totaling $90,000 were filed against him. He had only a little land left from his fortune and it was in his wife’s name. The Anglo-California Trust Company held the mortgage on the Piedmont Park for $172,000, and neither the interest nor the principal had been paid. Havens had auctioned off his art collection and wanted to sell the park to raise funds. The Piedmont School Board voted to purchase some of the park for a new high school and athletic field. They wanted 13 acres, but Havens would not sell less than the park’s entire 27 acres. The City wanted to save the park from residential development but did not have money to purchase the remaining parkland, and in 1916 Piedmont voters defeated a measure to raise funds to buy the land. Havens died suddenly in 1918 from food poisoning. The parkland was still available in 1921 when Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander and others offered to purchase fourteen acres of the park in 1921 if the City would reimburse them, which it did in 1922 after a bond issue was approved by voters. This plan allowed the school district to buy the 13 acres it wanted and the City to have its park. Construction began immediately in 1921 on the high school. It was a reinforced concrete building with terra cotta trim for five hundred students. An auditorium spanned the front of the school with two stories of classrooms behind and two wings held more classrooms. Piedmont Junior High School and the athletic field were added in 1924, and other additions were built in 1937 and 1939. In 1974, the original school building was declared unsafe under state earthquake laws and was demolished. However, the demolition took longer than anticipated because the buildings were so well built that it was difficult to tear them down. Three new classroom buildings and a gymnasium were built, and the original library, quad, and administration buildings were rehabilitated. The new construction was done in the “back-to-nature” style that was then popular with a wood exterior. However, by the mid-2010s this construction was also deemed earthquake unsafe and these buildings had to be demolished too. The school was reconstructed and opened in the fall of 2021 with a new STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, Art, and Mathematics) building and a new theater after voters approved $56 million in bonds. Some more interesting facts were also shared. PHS girls were required to wear middy blouses and pleated skirts until the early 1960s. It was the last public school in California to resist pressure from the State to stop enforcing a dress code which required students, and specifically girls, to wear a uniform. The walkers admired the quad area in front of the Student Center and took a group photo. Then they walked over to Millenium High School (MHS) and talked about its history. The school was officially started in 2000 and named for the new millennium. It evolved from the school district’s previous alternative program, the Piedmont Independent Learning High School, that had opened in 1980. MHS has a small enrollment, usually around 60 students in grades 9 to 12. Classes are small, with about 10 to 20 students per class. A fun fact is that George Lucas, the creator of the Star Wars films, granted the school the right to use the image of the Millennium Falcon on school sweatshirts, as well as to represent it as its mascot, effectively creating the Millennium (High School) Falcon. From Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website A1918 photo of the high school From Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website An early photo of the Bonita Avenue School. Participating in last week’s Walking on Wednesdays were Jasmine Cai, Jim Kuo, Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Mike Gallant, Denny McGee, Brian Hamlin, Mary Carter, Karen Palmer, Karin Fetherston, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Sherry Jacobs, Mark Davis, Dave DeRoche, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased that Jill and Ron Day were in from England visiting family and that Jing Jing Liu was walking with them for the first time. From Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society website A photo of the 1955 Havens School Next to Millennium is the middle school. In the late 1960s the then “Piedmont Junior High School” became a separate entity from the high school. However, like the high school, its building was considered unsafe in an earthquake and was also torn down in 1974. A new Piedmont Junior High School was built and opened in 1975. It was built down Magnolia Avenue largely on what was once the site of the Jasaitis family’s home. An iron fence that is still below the middle school was part of their property and its tea house was moved to up Piedmont Park where it is today. The school initially served grades 7 through 9. In 1978 the school officially took on its current Piedmont Middle School name and transitioned to a middle school format serving grades 6 through 8. The group exited the campus and went up Hillside and Vista Avenues to Bonita Avenue and Havens School. The 1910 school was expanded under the New Deal in the 1930s. There had been three previous efforts to replace temporary school buildings in Piedmont in the 1920s because about one-third of Piedmont students were being taught in buildings that were derisively called “shacks” by the locals. However, all the school bond votes lost. After the school board gained a promise of funding from the Depression Era Public Works Administration (PWA) in 1933, a new bond issue passed that year. A new five-classroom wing and an auditorium were built in 1937-38 on the eastern edge of the school grounds and an auditorium, named in honor of Ellen Driscoll, the school’s first principal who taught at the school for 20 years, was added in 1940-42. A new Havens School building was built at the same school site in 1955. The 1910 school, which faced Bonita Avenue, was torn down. The new school held a kindergarten, eleven new classrooms, library, cafeteria, and administration wing. The New Deal classrooms and auditorium in the back remained, but in 2010, the 1938 classrooms were demolished and the school was rebuilt. The walkers found a gate to the school’s turf playground. They walked through it, went past classrooms, and exited through a gate on Oakland Avenue. The group made their way back to the Exedra going down Highland, Vista, Bonita Avenues to Magnolia for one more look of the historic Piedmont High School. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu.

articles.text: As the New Year begins, many people resolve to prioritize their health and well-being. For individuals living with disabilities, however, achieving wellness goals and carving out time for self-care can be far more challenging. Many disabilities are not visible, and people who live with them often assume they are less deserving of support than someone with an obvious impairment. That misconception can stand in the way of meaningful help. This is where service dogs can be life-changing. Trained to support individuals with both visible and invisible disabilities, service dogs increase independence, build confidence and improve overall quality of life. Their impact reaches far beyond companionship, offering daily, practical support that can make routine activities safer and more manageable. Service dogs offer benefits that extend beyond companionship, providing practical support for daily life. At a basic level, dogs provide unconditional love, which improves quality of life, reduces loneliness and supports better physical health. People who have dogs are more likely to get regular exercise, which research shows can be as effective as medication for those experiencing mild to moderate depression. Studies also indicate that petting a dog can lower heart and breathing rates, helping to reduce anxiety. Beyond the benefits of dog ownership in general, service dogs are trained to perform specific tasks that increase handler safety and comfort. Many people are familiar with mobility assistance, hearing alerts and guide dog work. Less visible, but equally important, are the tasks that support individuals with invisible disabilities such as post-traumatic stress disorder. These tasks can include deep pressure therapy for grounding and stress relief, panic attack mitigation, interruption of harmful behaviors, medication reminders and item retrieval. In addition, allergen and migraine alert tasks can dramatically improve a handler’s safety and sense of control. So how does someone take the first step toward prioritizing their well-being and beginning the serMissy, a psychiatric service dog, rides the train to support her handler’s invisible disability. vice dog training process? Some organizations breed and train dogs for specific handlers, while a growing number of service dog trainers work with existing pets to prepare them for service work. Although training typically takes six months or more and represents a significant financial investment, the long-term benefits often far outweigh the time and cost involved. Experts recommend reaching out to a local service dog trainer to learn more about the process. Because this is specialized work, it is important not to settle for just any dog trainer. Look for someone with experience training the specific tasks you need and who can provide references. Starting the process may feel daunting, but the New Year offers a natural moment to take a meaningful step toward better health. A service dog’s care, attentiveness and training have the potential to create a life-changing improvement. Putting your own needs first can be the beginning of a safer, more independent and more fulfilling year. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507–2017, email Sierra109@gmail.com, or visit her website at www.oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com.

articles.text: The late Herb Stansbury was a meaningful contributor to Piedmont in many ways, not the least of which were his weekly cartoons, Dude, which appeared in the Piedmont Post from July 1999 until his passing on July 31, 2010. In his honor – and for the enjoyment of our readers – the Post continues to print Dude cartoons. The ones shown below are our favorites from the past year. “My partners and I have a perfectly normal relationship . . . we all hate each other.” “Try to look ashamed... you ordered all the wrong wines.” “The stars are tired of telling you how to run the corporation.” “That’s the month we did everything correctly, but no one can remember what we did.” “I Like to do everything your way, Dude, but when I do I get a migraine.” “I retained Dude’s grandson to get our computer back online.”
articles.title: BEST OF DUDE IN 2025

articles.text: We Are Growing Together in Faith and in Love For more than a century, Piedmont Church has been a church of open doors - welcoming and affirming all who wish to gather, worship and serve. This history of acceptance provides a powerful atmosphere where our faith in God, combined with the love for our neighbor, creates the perfect ‘church home’ for many. Some say they attend Piedmont Church to rest, to find shelter from many of life’s challenges. Others find spiritual strength by participating in worship, preparing them for the week ahead. Those who enjoy serving their community explore ways to give back through our local and international Mission Partners. And, fellowship brings vivid life to it all. For the many reasons we give thanks during this season, we are most grateful for our church and for you - the friends we’ve known, and those we’ve yet to meet. Come and see Piedmont Church, where everyone is welcome. WORSHIP IN PERSON OR ONLINE SUNDAYS, 10AM
